title: War review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive fun | Television | The Guardian
description: This brilliant piece of balderdash – packed with money, class warfare, sex and dastardly lawyers – is the perfect antidote to life right now. We need this!
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: This brilliant piece of balderdash – packed with money, class warfare, sex and dastardly lawyers – is the perfect antidote to life right now. We need this!
Content: Let the legal shenanigans begin! … James McArdle as Nick, Sienna Miller as Carla and Phoebe Fox as Serena in War.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreenLet the legal shenanigans begin! … James McArdle as Nick, Sienna Miller as Carla and Phoebe Fox as Serena in War.Photograph: Miya Mizuno/Sky/HBO/New PicturesTV reviewTelevisionReviewWar review – Sienna Miller and Dominic West’s hellish divorce drama is massive, massive funThis brilliant piece of balderdash – packed with money, class warfare, sex and dastardly lawyers – is the perfect antidote to life right now. We need this!Lucy ManganFri 2 Oct 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 20.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWar … what is it good for? At last, we have an answer: delivering eight hours of high-quality balderdash direct to your TV screens for your glorious delectation. Hurrah!For War, you see, is the name of George Kay’s latest venture. As the creator of, among many other things, two series of the impeccably preposterousHijack, you know you are in for a rollicking treat. And so it proves with this story of two horrible rich, famous people, divorcing in the public eye and battling it out in court via two teams of even more horrible, rich lawyers with everyone bent on doing as much harm to the other side as possible.It’s a high-stakes drama you don’t need to invest in. A wonderful palate-cleanser. Who has any emotions left after a day of news headlines, scrolling and life any more? We need this.‘I’d strip for £100!’ Dominic West and Sienna Miller on nudity, narcissism and their juicy new show WarRead moreDominic West plays social media mogul and philanderer Morgan Henderson. I’m not sure West is so much cast in these parts any more as simply manifests in the role as soon as someone writes “wealthy cad” into a script, but his agent must be delighted either way.Sienna Millerplays his film star wife Carla Duval, who, after 10 years, has had enough and – against the advice of her lawyers – has found a legally and morally grey way of gaining leverage over him, involving a hot friend willing to do her a favour and her husband.War is a “yes – but!” drama. Yes, there is a prenup! It says they both walk away with whatever assets they brought to the marriage. Is this is a problem? Yes, for Carla, whose earnings have lately nosedived. But! Prenups can be set aside if there has been a big enough change of circumstances. Yes, but what constitutes a big enough change in circumstances? Morgan becoming a squidillionaire and the beloved stepdad of Carla’s son Gabriel (Aran Murphy)? That oughta do it! But what would be a reasonable settlement in this situation – some millions? Yes, but what about the Manhattan apartment? But what about a monthly stipend?Morgan retains the services of Cathcarts & Sons, an old-school outfit – offices oak-panelled throughout and Pip Torrens prowling through them as the scheming St John Smallwood, looking for weaknesses in opponents and occasionally snacking on rats and interns. Carla goes with younger, shinier firm Taylor & Byrne, recently created by married couple Serena (Phoebe Fox) and Nick (James McArdle). They are chrome and glass offices and eager new recruit Johnny (Archie Renaux), originally from the mean streets of Peckham and more recently from a prestigious US firm he left under mysterious circumstances, scampers through them.So, we have money, class warfare, sex and more money. Let the legal and non-legal shenanigans begin! We have the lawyers strategising in seven dimensions. If they do this, will the other side guess that? If they really must abide by this requirement, despite having the most expensive tailoring in the business, how can they make it work for their client? Or against the other? Can they reconstruct a paper trail that will protect them, if not their client, from future liability? What matters more – having the better case or the better lawyers or the better press? Should they stop St John coming into court with a twitching rodent in his bloodied jaws? Or would that play well?It’s massive, massive fun, with a ripped-from-the-headlines feel to it that only adds to the entertainment. Oh, the back-stabbing! Oh, the double-crossings! Oh, the last-minute aversions of disaster! Until the next one!Kay keeps a firm hand on the tiller, and although War weaves through its intricate plot at speed you never get the sense that things are going to spiral out of control. It’s helped by great performances throughout, from the anchors West and Miller – venal but just likable enough, at least before a certain stripping scene involving Morgan, to keep our interest even if they don’t need our sympathy – through Torrens’ brilliant turn and on to Celia Imrie and Archie Panjabi as the barristers who are eventually instructed to represent the couple, and from everyone else in between. Soap opera with money, talent and plot to burn. What more could you ask at the end of a long, long day?War aired on Sky Atlantic and is on Now in the UK and on HBO Max in Australia.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewSienna MillerDominic WestDivorcereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: These graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of Representatives
Content: Alvaro Dominguez and Angelica Alzona/Guardian Design/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mappedThese graphics explain what the Democrats would need to do to flip the Senate and House of RepresentativesChris Stein,Alex Clark,Andrew WitherspoonandAshley KirkFri 2 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTShareA turning point in Donald Trump’s second term will soon arrive. On 3 November, voters across the US will decide whether to keep the president’s Republican allies in control of Congress, or return Democrats to the majority.Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of theHouse of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.These charts and maps reveal where the battle for Congress will be fought.The 2026 midterms offer Democrats the chance to win the Senate, and in turn the ability to put a serious check on Trump's agenda – including blocking any new appointments to the supreme court or his cabinet.Republicans currently hold a majority with 53 seats out of 100, while the Democrats and their allies hold the remaining 47.Thirty-five seats are on the ballot this November. Senators serve six-year terms, with a third facing voters at each two-year election cycle.Current SenateRep. majority475335 seats upBut in practice, the battle for the Senate is being fought across a very small map.The Cook Political Report, a prominent US election forecaster, currently lists seven seats as tossups: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.A further two – North Carolina and Kansas – are leaning Democrat and Republican respectively.Democrats must win at least four seats that are held by Republicans to gain a majority.Latest Senate ratings0 competitive seatsLean DemocratTossupLean RepublicanCook Political Report ratings, as of 1 October 2026At the start of 2026, Republicans appeared well positioned in the battle for the Senate, with many seats rated by Cook as solid for the party and a host of others currently held by Democrats as tossups.But as Trump's approval ratings fell over the course of the year amid discontent withthe Iran war and rising gas prices, Cook shifted several races in Democrats' direction, as did other major forecasters.A key example of this is Georgia, which is now rated as a likely win for the Democrats.How the Senate map shifted towards DemocratsStart of 2026 ratingCurrent ratingLikelyDem.LeanDem.TossupLeanRep.LikelyRep.Cook ratings. A Democratic gerrymander in Virginia was struck down by the state supreme court, and the US supreme court rejected a Republican attempt in Missouri.Yet the redistricting has not dashed Democratic hopes of taking the House.The Cook Report rates more than 40 races as competitive.Winning around half would hand Democrats a majority.Latest House ratings0 competitive seatsLean DemocratTossupLean RepublicanCook Political Report ratings, as of 1 October 2026In New York City’s exurbs, Republican Mike Lawler hopes to win a third term representing his swing district by turning voters against democratic socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani.“Socialism, communism and Marxism have no place in New York City and no place in America,” said Lawler, a top target of Democrats.New York 17th2026 House electionMike LawlerIncumbentCait ConleyFormer army officerPolling averages unavailable for districtsOne of nearly two dozen Democrats in districts Trump won in 2024, Marcy Kaptur has represented northwestern Ohio since 1983, the longest-ever tenure for a woman in Congress.Newly redrawn boundaries have increased her district’s Republican lean, making her re-election bid an important test of whether voters are still willing to split their tickets between parties.Ohio 9th2026 House electionMarcy KapturIncumbentDerek MerrinFormer Ohio state representativePolling averages unavailable for districtsThe One Big Beautiful Bill is a major issue in this California district.The Republican incumbent David Valadao voted for the Trump-backed measure, which extends tax cuts for wealthy people and corporations while slashing the Medicaid program for poor and disabled people. His constituents have some of the highest Medicaid enrollment rates in the country.California 22nd2026 House electionDavid ValadaoIncumbentRandy VillegasFormer teacherPolling averages unavailable for districtsIt’s possible whichever party wins the House achieves only a single-digit majority of seats, as Republicans have had for the past four years. But there’s also a chance that this year will see a “blue wave” of wins by Democratic candidates even in districts that Trump won by wide margins in 2024.Either way, history favors the party out of power in the midterms, particularly in the battle for the House. All recent presidents have lost control of a chamber in midterm elections, including Trump, in the 2018 election.Presidential party and congressional controlYearPresidentHouseSenateTrifecta2008ObamaDemDem✓2010Lost House →RepDem✕2012RepDem✕2014Lost Senate →RepRep✕2016TrumpRepRep✓2018Lost House →DemRep✕2020BidenDemDem✓2022Lost House →RepDem✕2024TrumpRepRep✓Polling shows there has been a nationwide shift towards the Democrats in the run-up to the midterms, even in statesRepublicanshave dominated for decades.Many recent surveys of the generic ballot, a key indicator of voters’ intent in congressional elections, give theDemocratsan edge ranging from the high single digits to the low double digits.Democrats have a healthy lead in national pollingAverage of polls for the 2026 generic congressional ballot, which asks voters at a national level who they intend to vote for in the House midtermsOct40%45%50%Guardian graphic. Source: Silver Bulletin polling average, which weights individual polls based on sample size, recency and pollster ratingThe events of this year – notably the Iran war and its impact on inflation – have undoubtedly changed the race, and much of the advantage seems to have swung towards the Democrats.Across all key races, Democratic candidates have been campaigning on affordability, at a time when the Trump administration’s actions in the Middle East have pushed up prices, particularly for gasoline and diesel.It is a reflection of just how concerned US voters are about the economy, rating it as the most important issue in surveys, far ahead of immigration, healthcare or civil rights.Meanwhile, Trump’s personal ratings have also fallen, with Reuters/Ipsos finding only 32% of US adults now approve of his job performance.That is worse than his previous low of 34%, recorded by Gallup at the end of his first term in 2021 after the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.The 2026 midterms may be another brutal reckoning for the US president – the question is whether punishment from voters will lead him to change course.

title: At Brighton, Polanski raised his arms in triumph. It felt more like a wave goodbye | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The Greens’ leader seems long on agitprop but short on ideas – and one byelection away from losing his job
Author: John Crace
Headline: The Greens’ leader seems long on agitprop but short on ideas – and one byelection away from losing his job
Content: Like Blue Peter presenters on amphetamines: Hannah Spencer (left), and Siân Berry join Zack Polanski on stage at the party conference in Brighton.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLike Blue Peter presenters on amphetamines: Hannah Spencer (left), and Siân Berry join Zack Polanski on stage at the party conference in Brighton.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianThe politics sketchZack PolanskiAt Brighton, Polanski raised his arms in triumph. It felt more like a wave goodbyeJohn CraceThe Greens’ leader seems long on agitprop but short on ideas – and one byelection away from losing his jobFri 2 Oct 2026 13.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareThe Chronicle of a Death Foretold. It must be weird to realise that you have in effect made yourself obsolete inside a year. Worse, that you have actively accelerated your demise. Even AI doesn’t work at that speed. But that’s precisely what it looks as ifZack Polanskihas done. Maybe he should just look on the bright side. He’s managed eight Liz Trusses. Not to be sneezed at.Polanski is partly a victim of his own success. A cautionary tale of being careful what you wish for. Like Nigel Farage, the leader of the Green party was one of Keir Starmer’s fiercest critics. Andy Burnham and Wes Streeting excepted. Keir wasn’t radical enough. Did not care enough about Gaza. Was too dull. And under Zack’s leadership, voters swarmed from Labour to the Greens. The party climbed to a record high of 18% in the polls andwon the Gorton and Denton byelectionagainst the staggeringly dim Matt Goodwin.But then Keir was airbrushed out of history and Labour chose a prime minister that a lot of people in the country actually liked. Someone who could communicate. Even if they weren’t in love with Andy, voters were willing to give him a chance. Ever since, the Greens have tanked. Now they are down to 11%. Zack’s net approval rating’s almost as bad as Nige’s. Not content with this, Zack has almost certainly fatally holed his credibility by standing in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which he is very likely to lose. Shares in brand Polanski have never been lower.The Green party conference in Brighton could not have come at a worse time. Zackdidn’t want it to go aheadbecause he wanted to concentrate on his byelection campaign. Senior members of the leadership were briefing that the whole conference was pointless.But the conference did go ahead, and on Friday lunchtime it began with the local MP, Siân Berry, and Gorton and Denton MP, Hannah Spencer, doing their best impressions of a Duracell bunny. High energy, hyperactive enthusiasm. Like Blue Peter presenters on amphetamines. Everything was great. Never better. “Come on, everybody,” said Siân. “We think the best of everyone.” We’ll reserve judgment on that till Sunday when some of the more toxic issues are aired. Hannah was also rushing on her run. “We have forced the government to change course,” she said. Mmm. And that’s sort of the problem.Siân and Hannah were just the warm-up acts for the main event. And with the arrival of Polanski to give his leader’s speech, almost all the excitement was sucked out of the room. The packed hall became like a dead zone. The slogan on the back of the stage said “real hope” but all you could feel was desperation. The sense that the Greens had had a fleeting moment in the sun and the long nights were drawing in.It is customary for a leader’s speech to be punctuated with standing ovations. That’s the whole point of them. Even if the leader is talking pure bollocks. Zack got two. One for saying Palestine and the other for “green revolution”. In Brighton, everyone gets a standing ovation for saying Palestine and green revolution. It’s written in the city’s DNA.Zack looked down from the start. Normally he’s an animated speaker, but today he just looked defeated. As if he was trying and failing to will himself to care. It was just too big an ask. And maybe you couldn’t blame him. His team had chosen this day to brief the media that if they could persuade 30% of Labour voters in Holborn and St Pancras to vote for Zack, he would lose by only four points. That’s a bit like walking into A&E and being told by the doctors they can give you a heart and lung transplant but you are going to die regardless.“What a year,” he began. Indeed. Though maybe he didn’t need to spell it out so clearly. From fringe party to something more mainstream and back again. All over in a heartbeat. Zack couldn’t disguise the look of regret in his eyes. From time to time his head bobbed up and down, as if trying to get his brain to agree with him, but his body language spoke of an inner despair. Rather than the leader of a national political party, he came across as a rather shouty undergraduate student. Long on agitprop and soundbites. Short on genuine argument.Sure, there were nods to taxing the rich more, imposing rent controls, Free Palestine and environmentalism. But these were just words to try to please the crowds. There was no sense of how much this would cost, how it would be done or where the money would come from. “I say to government, ‘Slogans aren’t enough’,” he said without a hint of self-awareness. You could only put it down as a man who knows his political career could be as good as over by this time next week.There was something rather sad about it all. The Greens had wanted so much more than this. They had believed they had elected a man of substance – someone less polite and deferential than previous leaders such as Caroline Lucas and Carla Denyer – who would go toe to toe with the other mainstream parties. But he had turned out to be a chimera. Just another hollow man. Long on slogans, short on ideas. A leader who had briefly burned brightly but had fizzled out. A victim of his own success. A one-year wonder destined to become a man of absence. Losing the byelection would only hasten the end.Most leader’s speeches last about an hour. Zack was done and dusted in just over half that. Even then, it felt far too fluffy, far too long. Come the end, Hannah and Sian came on stage to raise his arms aloft in triumph. It felt more like a long wave goodbye.Explore more on these topicsZack PolanskiThe politics sketchGreen partycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘You could have an amazing time for £30,000’: UK castles cash in on Traitors-style events | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: From stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit show
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: From stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit show
Content: Duns Castle estate in Berwickshire, Scotland, plays host to murder mystery events.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyView image in fullscreenDuns Castle estate in Berwickshire, Scotland, plays host to murder mystery events.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyThe Traitors‘You could have an amazing time for £30,000’: UK castles cash in on Traitors-style eventsFrom stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit showPatrick GreenfieldFri 2 Oct 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Thursday night, the singer-songwriter James Blunt, Love Island host Maya Jama and mathematician Hannah Fry were among the 21 Celebrity Traitors returning to UK screens for another round of deceit and detective work. Famously, contestants do not stay at Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands during filming, and the venue is not a hotel, so fans cannot book their own overnight stays without hiring the entire Ross-shire estate. But that has not stopped people from trying to recreate their own versions.Theshow’s surging popularityhas been accompanied by a bonanza in Traitors-style events across the UK. From stag and hen dos to castle conspiracy weekends, event companies now host year-round imitations for fans looking to recreate the drama of the candle-lit roundtable. The show is also proving to be a boom for the owners of Britain’s crumbling castles – with wealthy fans even hiring them out for their own private events.The Celebrity Traitors: episode one – as it happenedRead more“We see a huge spike in people searching for Traitors-style experiences on our pages every time it comes back on TV,” said Roger Masterson, founder of Celtic Castles, which specialises in castle stays and rentals. “We’ve got castle hotels that put together Traitors packages. A 15-bedroom castle might sleep 30, so they’ll bring in couples and organise the faithfuls and traitors over the weekend. They build a story around it and play the game. There are huge varieties with how it’s done.”View image in fullscreenThe dining room at Duns Castle.Photograph: groupaccomodation.com/PACompanies organising team bonding exercises are by far the most common customers. GOTO Events, which runs tailored Traitors-style experiences, offers packages from five people to 1,000, complete with their own version of the missions that contestants play to build up the prize pot and a Claudia Winkleman-style host. A GOTO spokesperson said these had become the most popular experience they offer.“Ever since the show launched, it’s just not died down. We keep thinking things will slow down and they haven’t,” the spokesperson said.“Everyone pretty much takes it as a bit of fun because you know that someone is lying. In one of my first events, the big boss was one of the betrayers and got called out in the first round. It was funny. Everyone loves calling out their boss.”But a Traitors-style experience often does not come cheap. Daylong events are a few hundred pounds, while those looking for the full castle experience pay much more. Rothes Glen castle in the Scottish Highlands is offering a three-night package from £4,388 a room for two guests for a castle conspiracy weekend in August next year. A private event will set you back even more: hiring a luxury castle for the weekend can set you back tens of thousands of pounds – and that’s before the cost of organising the game, says Masterson.View image in fullscreenGuests stay in luxury at Dalhousie Castle, near Edinburgh.Photograph: Dalhousie Castle/PA“If you were looking at an exclusive-use property, let’s say for 30 people, they might charge £10,000 a night on a bed and breakfast basis. So, a two night stay would be 20 – then add another 10 for the event. You could have an amazing time for £30,000 for the whole weekend,” he says.The boom is also helping fund repairs to Britain’s crumbling castles, he says. “I’ve been with owners and I ask them why they’re moving into the hospitality market. And they say: ‘Well, we need £100,000 to replace the roof’.”Since the first episode on Thursday, Traitors mania is set to take over the country once again, running until Friday 30 October. Celebrities will compete for up to £100,000 for their chosen charities.“We are expecting another surge [with the new series]. We are ready to go,” said GOTO.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Feeling wired? The truth about ‘nervous system resets’  | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The internet is full of warnings about our ‘dysregulated’ nervous systems. But, experts say, you don’t need to reset yours – you might just need to make it more flexible. Here’s how (and no, you don’t need an acupressure mat)
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The internet is full of warnings about our ‘dysregulated’ nervous systems. But, experts say, you don’t need to reset yours – you might just need to make it more flexible. Here’s how (and no, you don’t need an acupressure mat)
Content: Illustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianLife and styleFeeling wired? The truth about ‘nervous system resets’The internet is full of warnings about our ‘dysregulated’ nervous systems. But, experts say, you don’t need to reset yours – you might just need to make it more flexible. Here’s how (and no, you don’t need an acupressure mat)Hannah CoatesFri 2 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTShareWhether it’s tapping the side of your hand or standing on a vibrating plate, suggestions on how to “reset” your nervous system are saturating the internet. Cold water plunges, humming, gargling, yawning and spiky acupressure mats are all being touted as ways to help us “regulate” and return to calm. If you’re still talking about feeling “stressed”, you’re behind the times; now, says the internet, you are “dysregulated”.The nervous system is an integral part of being human. “It’s essentially the body’s communication and control network,” says Dr Serena Lai, consultant psychiatrist and associate medical director at London Psychiatry Clinic. “Made up of the brain and spinal cord, it communicates with the entire body through nerves, helping us to sense what is happening around and inside us. When we have that information, we can process it and coordinate a response.”The autonomic nervous system is one part of this network, regulating things the body does automatically, including heart rate, blood pressure and digestion. It has two main branches. “The sympathetic system creates our fight or flight response, helping us mobilise resources when we need to respond to a challenge,” says Lai. “The parasympathetic nervous system – or rest and digest mode – conserves energy, slows the heart and supports recovery.”Sympathetic activity increases during stress, whether that’s an urgent email or a family bereavement. The heart beats faster, muscles tense, digestion can change and we become more alert. These evolutionary responses help us respond to threats – but while once that might have been a predator, now it’s as everyday as seeing a celebrity death on Instagram. Perhaps it’s no surprise, then, that the idea of a nervous system reset is so appealing to so many of us – we’re overstimulated and in desperate need of ways to feel more level.Except, as every expert I spoke to agreed, there is no such thing as “resetting” the nervous system – nor should we want to. We need sympathetic activation to exercise, concentrate, meet deadlines and respond to demanding situations. The problem is when we struggle to recover once that demand has passed, leaving us feeling wired and tired, and potentially contributing to increased inflammation and cardiovascular and metabolic problems. A healthy autonomic nervous system is not permanently calm; it’s able to adapt to changing circumstances.Much of the conversation about nervous system regulation revolves around the vagus nerve – which is actually a pair of nerves, made up of about 80,000 fibres apiece – that starts in the brain and travels down through the neck into the chest and abdomen. Because it helps slow heart rate and plays a role in the body’s rest-and-recovery processes, it is associated with stress relief and relaxation – you might see people referring to increased “vagal tone” as a sign of enhanced vagus nerve activity.One of the most common ways vagal and parasympathetic activity is assessed is through heart rate variability (HRV), says neurosurgeon Dr Kevin Tracey, author ofThe Great Nerve.“This is the time in between individual heartbeats – generally, greater variability is associated with greater vagal influence,” he explains. The higher the vagal influence, the more likely our parasympathetic system is to be dominant – cue feeling of calm. “Sympathetic activity tends to shorten the time between heartbeats.”Learning how to work with your nervous system could make it more flexible, meaning you rise to challenges when you need to, then recover when they have passed. These simple, science-backed habits can help.Slow breathingBreathing slowly has been shown to increase HRV and promote parasympathetic dominance. “One study showedthat slow-paced breathing of around six diaphragmatic breaths [breathing deeply into the belly rather than just into the chest] a minute is one of the most effective ways of producing an acute change in heart rate variability,” says Lai. She recommends inhaling for about five seconds, exhaling for five, and repeating for five to 10 minutes.Cyclic sighing is another option. It involves taking one deep inhale, followed by a second, shorter “sip” of air to fully inflate the lungs, before a long, slow, lung-emptying exhale through the mouth.In one study, practising for five minutes a day improved mood and reduced respiratory rate – an effect that became more pronounced over the course of the month-long trial.Mindfulness, meditation and contemplation“Meditation – where you practise bringing your attention to the present moment – is a great way to help slow down the heart rate,” says Tracey. “It’s especially good when done in tandem with paced breathing, as you can really measure your heart rate decreasing.” Apps includingHeadspace,Insight TimerandCalm, he adds, can make it easier to build the practice into everyday life.Other contemplative practices, from body scanning (where you relax, close your eyes and contemplate physical sensations) to yoga, may also support parasympathetic activity. One2018 paper proposedthat many of these practices naturally slow the breath, which in turn influences vagal activity.“Sensory quiet” in general may be important for autonomic recovery, explains Dr Vishnuraj Prakash, head of Ayurveda and functional medicine at Tulåh Clinical Wellness in Kerala, India, so practise doing nothing – no podcasts, phones or other stimuli.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Carl Godfrey/The GuardianMove“Movement is incredibly useful because it changes your state,” says somatic practitioner Nahid de Belgeonne. “For example, if you sit at a desk for a long time, your muscles are contracted and fixed and your breathing shallow. As soon as you get up and move, you interrupt that fixed state.” She advises embracing being “fidgety” throughout the day and taking regular walks.There isplenty of evidencethatregular aerobic exercise– whether walking, cycling or swimming – can improve autonomic regulation and HRV over time. Tai chi is particularly interesting because it combines movement, breathwork and meditation and itproduces more parasympathetic activationthan conventional exercise of the same intensity.Crucially, more exercise isn’t necessarily better.Research has foundreduced HRV in athletes who overtrain, so recovery matters too. “Simple exercises are really all that’s needed,” says Dr Karen Chung, consultant neurologist at Welbeck. “I often tell patients who are overwhelmed to get off the bus a stop early and walk a little further. ”Book in for a massageModerate-pressure massagehas been associated with reduced heart rate, anxiety and cortisol, as well as increased parasympathetic activity – and as little as 20 to 30 minutes seems to be enough. Pressure does matter: a very light, feathery touch could actually be more stressful than calming. Even 10 minutes of head massage can increase HRV – by as much as 66%, according toone small study.Stimulating acupressure points, whether through touch or acupuncture needles, may also help, although, as Lai points out, the evidence is less consistent. Auricular acupuncture is one obvious route in – a branch of the vagus nerve supplies parts of the outer ear. Other commonly used acupuncture points to promote parasympathetic activity are found around the wrists, outer shins, top of the head and sternum – although which are used, and why, is best left to a qualified practitioner.Some research suggests acupuncture can influence autonomic activity, including increasing parasympathetic action. The evidence is thinner when it comes to acupressure mats. Anecdotally, they may help some people relax, but there are cheaper and better evidenced ways to achieve the same end.Slow downOur nervous systems respond well to regularity – consistent sleep and wake times, eating at similar times each day and resting. “For many of my patients, life is incredibly fast-paced, so mostly it’s as simple as going to bed a little earlier or taking an hour away from our phones,” says Chung. “Repeating the same behaviours daily helps the body’s ability to move from activation back into recovery,” adds Lai.Building breaks into the working day can help too. For those spending hours on screens, de Belgeonne recommends working in focused 90-minute blocks, followed by a 20-minute break. Evenings should signal a change of pace where possible. “Reduce evening stimulation during stressful periods,” advises Prakash.Do a face dunkDoes cold exposure work as well as social media influencers would have us believe? As Tracey explains, the body’s initial response to cold water immersion is actually a sympathetic one, triggering the release of stress hormones and increasing the heart rate. It is only afterwards,research suggests, that there is a parasympathetic rebound, which could help explain why some people report feeling calmer after a cold plunge.You don’t necessarily need to submerge yourself. Dunking your face in cold water can trigger the diving reflex, which slows the heart rate through increased parasympathetic activity – even a couple of splashes may be enough to elicit a response. However, Tracey points out that there still isn’t enough credible evidence to conclude that cold water immersion has meaningful benefits for nervous system regulation. But if you enjoy it and find you feel calmer afterwards, great – that’s really all the evidence you need.What about devices?Surgically implanted vagus nerve stimulation is an established medical treatment for conditions including epilepsy and treatment-resistant depression. But that doesn’t mean the consumer device showcased on your Instagram feed is backed by the same evidence.What does stress really do to our bodies – and when does it become a big problem?Read moreNoninvasive devices typically use electrical stimulation through the skin – often at the ear or neck – in an attempt to stimulate branches of the vagus nerve. While the US Food and Drug Administration has cleared some for specific medical conditions, such as migraines, that is very different from being approved to reduce stress, says Tracey. For the majority of wellness devices, independent clinical evidence is limited. That’s not to say they definitely don’t work, but the less exciting basics – sleep, movement, slow breathing and rest – might be a better first port of call.Immerse yourself in natureOne study foundthat just 15 minutes of walking in a forest reduced sympathetic and increased parasympathetic activity,while othershave linked time in nature with lower cortisol levels. So get outside – ideally without your phone.“Eat a balanced diet, get regular exercise, spend time in nature and with people you love, and get some hobbies,” says Tracey. “And have a plan for dealing with stress. Beyond all the elaborate reset practices, these are the things that are actually worth doing.”

title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Content: A woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacksMayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridgePjotr Sauerin KyivFri 2 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleValeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”View image in fullscreenSmoke rises after a Russian drone hit the Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackling a blaze in the city centre.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAcross the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, asintensifying Russian attacksreshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plungeUkraineinto darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.View image in fullscreenRescue workers running to a shelter during an air threat.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor,Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in aninterviewwith the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.View image in fullscreenA volunteer medic crew on patrol in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUntil recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.‘We just have to adapt’: Kyiv residents prepare for a hard winter aheadRead moreKyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.View image in fullscreenA man with a tattoo reading ‘immortal’ standing near the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVitali KlitschkonewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community | UK news | The Guardian
description: Man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police say
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police say
Content: At the time of the arrests, police said they were doing everything they could to keep Manchester’s Jewish community and the wider public safe.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAt the time of the arrests, police said they were doing everything they could to keep Manchester’s Jewish community and the wider public safe.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUK newsTwo Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish communityMan, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police sayVikram DoddandHannah Al-OthmanFri 2 Oct 2026 18.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community.​Police say another man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with them as part of a plot to get a bomb to attack Jewish targets.They were arrested two Sundays ago in broad daylight in a Manchester street during the Jewish holiday period.Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.Police said the two men face charges that they gained materials and instructions to make a homemade bomb, identified possible targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack.Police said: “It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot.”The development, terrorism charges and detail given so far by British authorities marks an extraordinary chapter in British and Iranian relations.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran had a link to a weekend scare at RAF Fairford when five men were arrested close to the military base, along with three vans, one of which contained petrol in a barrel. Those men have now been bailed, having been arrested in the early hours of Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing a terrorist act.Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner and the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism, said: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran.“While this [Manchester] incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”The alleged plot in Manchester, where the two arrests followed a joint counter-terrorism police and MI5 investigation, has significant potential ramifications on several fronts.A government statement, minutes after the police announced the charges, revealed one of those accused over the Manchester plot had been granted asylum status in the UK and the other had an asylum application pending.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said that both of the accused had come to Britain via small boats, one in 2020 and another in 2023, when the Conservatives were in power.Mahmood said Iran had shown hostile intent to the UK in a series of incidents.“The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country,” she said. “While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.“We will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security.“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime. They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement.“The prime minister has been clear there are strong indications of Iran’s involvement in the events near RAF Fairford. We are responding to these threats with new powers and record funding to disrupt hostile activity.This week marked the anniversary of an attack on the Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester, where two worshippers died, as well as the attacker who said he supported Islamic State and was shot dead by police.Jews in Britain have faced a dramatic increase in attacks since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, which has ties to Iran. It led to an internationally condemned military response by Israel in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people.The Community Safety Trust, which offers security and advice to British Jews, said: “The charging of two men in connection with an alleged plot targeting the Manchester Jewish community will be deeply concerning to Jews across the UK.“These charges come exactly a year after the appalling terrorist attack at Heaton Park synagogue, and are a reminder of the ongoing terrorist threats facing British Jews.“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and report any suspicious activity to police and CST.”In a statement, counter-terrorism police said the charges will allege the two men were “communicating with others using encrypted applications to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device”.Furthermore, the charges allege they obtained a document called “Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb”, obtained video instructions on how to make an improvised explosive device (IED), and got the “liquids, components and equipment” to make an IED.The charges also allege the men carried out internet research on targets, acquired “images, plans and maps of potential targets for attack” and carried out reconnaissance.Iran has faced attack by the US, with Britain allowing the RAF Fairford base to be used, which it said is for defensive operations by its Washington ally. Tehran’s embassy in London this week denied any involvement in the events at RAF Fairford.Evans said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”The men were arrested on 20 September in ​Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester’s city centre, just before 3pm, hours before Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.Salehi and Ahmadyan are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October.Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.”As part of the investigation officers raided and searched properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints | Schools | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Education secretary sends Ofsted back to ‘drawing board’ as teachers raise serious concerns about new system
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Education secretary sends Ofsted back to ‘drawing board’ as teachers raise serious concerns about new system
Content: Sources say Powell wants ‘Ofsted to go back to the drawing board when it comes to measuring inclusion in particular’.Photograph: Abstract Aerial Art/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSources say Powell wants ‘Ofsted to go back to the drawing board when it comes to measuring inclusion in particular’.Photograph: Abstract Aerial Art/Getty ImagesSchoolsEngland school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaintsExclusive: Education secretary sends Ofsted back to ‘drawing board’ as teachers raise serious concerns about new systemKiran StaceyandRichard AdamsFri 2 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchool inspections inEnglandwill be overhauled for the second time in a year, after a barrage of complaints that the new system was dangerously stressful and damaging teachers’ mental health.Lucy Powell, the education secretary, will tell the schools regulator Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after becoming concerned that inspection changes overseen by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, were creating problems for headteachers.Sources say Powell does not want to scrap the new system of ratings, which score schools from “exceptional” to needing “urgent improvement” in six key areas, but she does want inspectors to take greater account of the social and economic background of each school and its pupils.New Ofsted inspection regime is damaging our health, headteachers sayRead morePowell’s changes, which will be communicated to Ofsted in the coming weeks, will be the second set of major alterations to the school inspection regime in just over a year, after Labour’s election manifesto pledge to replace the previous inspection framework in the wake of the death ofthe headteacher Ruth Perry.One source said: “She wantsOfstedto go back to the drawing board when it comes to measuring inclusion in particular. That’s where most of the problems seem to lie.”Powell’s changes will mean a significant shift from those carried out by Phillipson, who is now equalities minister and party chair.The two MPs fought an occasionally bitter contest to become Labour’s deputy leader last year, during which allies of each traded insults and accusations. Andy Burnham promoted Powell, a long-term ally, to Phillipson’s job as education secretary when he entered Downing Street earlier this year.Powell told an event at last week’s Labour party conference: “I want to see a much stronger emphasis in the current inspection regime on context, much stronger than it is at the moment.“I think this is one of those areas that it’s not straightforward to sort of move the oil tanker around massively quickly, but we absolutely do need to see reforms there.”View image in fullscreenLucy Powell on stage with Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockOfsted declined to comment. The inspectorate has commissioned its own independent evaluation of the new framework, with an interim report due out later this year.Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said he was encouraged that ministers were listening to the criticism of inspections being raised by parents and experts as well as teachers.Whiteman said: “We have serious concerns about fairness and comparability.Schoolsserve very different communities and face very different levels of challenge. Leaders working in areas of greater disadvantage, or with higher numbers of pupils with special educational needs (Send) and disabilities, must not be placed at a systemic disadvantage by an inspection framework that fails to properly reflect those contexts.“Inspection should take account of the circumstances in which schools are operating, while recognising the tremendous work many are doing to support children facing the greatest barriers.“There is a need for an inspection system that is rigorous and proportionate and which genuinely supports school improvement.”The new “report card” systemcame into force last year, replacing Ofsted’s headline inspection grades of “outstanding” to “inadequate”, with a more detailed system intended to put less pressure on schools.The new system was initially welcomed by teachers, though criticised by others who warned it would make it harder for parents to judge a school.Since its implementation however, the regime has been met with a flurry of complaints from school leaders, who say it is harming their mental health and creating greater stress than the system it replaced.Perry’s sister, Prof Julia Waters, said last month thatshe had been contactedby at least a dozen teachers left “feeling suicidal” by Ofsted inspections, and raised her concerns in a letter to the prime minister.Amanda Hulme, the headteacher of Claypool primary school in Bolton,told the Guardianlast month that her most recent Ofsted inspection was the most stressful experience of her career.Unions have called for teachers to be given “urgent relief” from the new system, while some want Ofsted to stop grading their schools altogether.Asurvey of school staffinspected under the new regime found that two-thirds said it was as bad or worse than the framework it had replaced. The survey of National Education Union members also found that three out of four said the inspections had negatively affected their mental health, with one primary school teacher describing it as “a circle of stress and fear”.Ofsted drops ‘clumsy’ and ‘offensive’ guidance linking autism and extremismRead morePowell is understood to be concerned that schools in more “challenging” contexts are doing worse under the new system.A recent study by the former Ofsted inspector Steve Wren found schools with higher levels of children receiving free school meals (a key test of poverty) or Send support were receiving lower ratings than average.Wren also found that ratings for secondary schools were closely correlated with how well pupils had performed before they joined the school, suggesting inspectors were not taking sufficient account of previous attainment levels.Wren said in his analysis: “Do these grades represent the reality that secondary schools with lower prior attainment are doing a markedly worse job of educating their pupils, or is the framework biased against them, or are inspectors not skilled at spotting strengths in such contexts?”Explore more on these topicsSchoolsOfstedLucy PowellEducation policyTeachers' workloadEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage | UK news | The Guardian
description: Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police
Content: Court artist sketch of Joshua Kerry at Westminster magistrates court in July.Photograph: Julia Quenzler/ReutersView image in fullscreenCourt artist sketch of Joshua Kerry at Westminster magistrates court in July.Photograph: Julia Quenzler/ReutersUK newsAnn Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel FarageJoshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say policeNadeem BadshahFri 2 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage.Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said.Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards.Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea.Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”In August, CTP reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.After its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Guarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Guarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says
Content: Andy Burnham delivers his conference speech, in which he set out plans for a national care service in England.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham delivers his conference speech, in which he set out plans for a national care service in England.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAndy BurnhamBurnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next electionGuarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government saysRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 2 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said.The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth.In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to avoid much larger pension increases in years when wages spike.Will pensioners be poorer as a result of Burnham scrapping the triple lock?Read moreIn his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee.However, guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, requiring MPs to vote on the changes.It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether to retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power.The guidance also shows that the government estimates that the adjustment to the triple lock would reduce state pension spending by £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s and by £50bn a year by 2050.However, the Resolution Foundation said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model.Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s.“Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings.“If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.”Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly.Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care changeswould be “electoral suicide”.However, YouGov has publishedpollingsuggesting voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.In his conference speech, Burnham confirmed he wouldend the pension triple lockand use the savings tofund a national care servicein England that would be free at the point of use.He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation.Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourPensionsState pensionsSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Suicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attack | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation
Content: Yaniv Hayoun, who was aboard the flydubai aircraft that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, is welcomed at the arrivals gate at Ben Gurion international airport in Israel on Wednesday.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APView image in fullscreenYaniv Hayoun, who was aboard the flydubai aircraft that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, is welcomed at the arrivals gate at Ben Gurion international airport in Israel on Wednesday.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APFlydubai plane incidentSuicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attackExperts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisationJason BurkeInternational security correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”3:28How the stabbing incident unfolded on Israel-bound flydubai plane | DeconstructedMany of thedetails of what happenedon flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small grouprushed to the cockpitand overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”,Manes saidon eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.Flight mapIn a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been“fighting for my life”.The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by theUnited Arab Emirates(UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.1:18Flydubai pilot tells Indian prime minister Modi that he couldn’t ‘let anyone die’ – videoIn Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airportBenjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister,has claimedthe co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.Experts said there have been only a handful ofinstancesof suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.Flight altitude graphIn 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employersdeliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that thecrash of an AirIndia 787in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have beenfiercely disputed.Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”View image in fullscreenPeople disembark from a flydubai plane carrying Israeli passengers from the disrupted flight at Ben Gurion international airport near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APSecurity services have been warning of awave of radicalisationacross the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”There are now manyquestions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.View image in fullscreenA passenger with blood on his T-shirt onboard the flydubai plane.Photograph: Amit SegalThere are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plungeRead moreDubai international airport, theworld’s busiest airportfor international passenger traffic, has built some ofits appealon a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIsraelUnited Arab EmiratesAir transportMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestine Action activists used whips and hammers to threaten guards at arms factory, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Five defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near Bristol
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Five defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near Bristol
Content: Prayers took place at lunchtime outside Woolwich crown court on 25 September.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPrayers took place at lunchtime outside Woolwich crown court on 25 September.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockUK newsPalestine Action activists used whips and hammers to threaten guards at arms factory, court hearsFive defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near BristolHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePalestine Action activists brandished whips, hammers and kebab skewers to intimidate security guards and keep them at bay during a break-in at an Israel-linked arms factory, a court has heard.Five defendants are accused by prosecutors of being part of a “black team”, wearing black jumpsuits, whose role was to overwhelm security guards, so that a “red team”, wearing red jumpsuits, could break into the Elbit systems factory in Filton, near Bristol, and smash up equipment including drones.Qesser Zuhrah, 21, Zahra Farooque, 26, Kamran Ahmed, 29, Heba Muraisi, 31, and Liam Mullany, 34, went on trial at Woolwich crown court on Friday charged with criminal damage and violent disorder over the raid during the early hours of 6 August 2024. They deny the charges.The prosecutor Deanna Heer KC told the jury that an alleged plan of the raid, discovered by police, said: “Shut Elbit Down. This is our primary objective as Palestine Action. We can do that by sticking together and ensuring its destruction with our brains and muscle.”Jurors were told that a security guard, Nigel Shaw, who had struck a member of the black team across the back of his legs with an umbrella, suffered a 4cm laceration to his head after being attacked.Heer said: “The role of the black team was to overwhelm the security guards so that the red team could break into the factory. They did so by threatening, intimidating and, if necessary, assaulting the guards, by throwing fireworks at them and brandishing weapons, such as whips and hammers and large kebab skewers.“When one of the black team was detained by a security guard, other members of the group attacked him, hitting him until he released their colleague, leaving the security guard with a laceration to his head.”She told the court the break-in was carefully planned and a prison van, driven by a member of the red team, crashed through the first perimeter fence surrounding Elbit’s factory at about 3.30am.The black team followed on foot shouting slogans including “Free Palestine” as the van was driven through a second perimeter fence at the site of the firm, whose parent company is based in Israel.Heer said: “The footage shows that the black team used or threatened violence against the security guards that night.
