It is clear, the prosecution submit, that Nigel Shaw was physically attacked and [was] caused injury but violence was also used or threatened by the black team before then when they threw fireworks or smoke grenades or cracked whips and brandished skewers in order to intimidate the security guards and keep them away.”She said the idea was for the red team to destroy “as much property as possible” before the police arrived and they used fire extinguishers filled with red paint to spray the walls and floor, crowbars and sledgehammers to smash apart computer equipment and drones and also damaged a disabled toilet.The court was told that the plan for the break-in described the black team, who had their faces covered, as “coverts” because the intention was “to get away without being caught”, unlike the red team who were labelled “overts”.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son  | Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva | The Guardian
description: President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades
Content: The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a huge rally in the streets of Rio de Janeiro two days before the election.Photograph: António Lacerda/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a huge rally in the streets of Rio de Janeiro two days before the election.Photograph: António Lacerda/EPALuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s sonPresident leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decadesTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 2 Oct 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brazilian president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election.Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lulatold a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”View image in fullscreenLula led a campaign march through central Rio de Janeiro, travelling from Candelária toward Cinelândia.Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockHours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.View image in fullscreenLula, who is seeking re-election, used the the march to mobilise supporters two days before voters head to the polls on 4 October 2026.Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock“No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-presidentJair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election.View image in fullscreenTwo Lula supporters.Photograph: António Lacerda/EPAMany Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, at Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years.Photograph: Pilar Olivares/ReutersValmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”.“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they ​do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote.In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.Explore more on these topicsLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazilAmericasThe far rightActivismJair BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: Olivia Dean accused of plagiarism on her I’ve Seen It track | Olivia Dean | The Guardian
description: Mattie Music Group, owners of Bill Withers’ back catalogue, contend the Grammy winner infringed on Just the Two of Us
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Mattie Music Group, owners of Bill Withers’ back catalogue, contend the Grammy winner infringed on Just the Two of Us
Content: Olivia Dean performs on stage during The BRIT Awards 2026 at Co-op Live on 28 February 2026 in Manchester, England.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOlivia Dean performs on stage during The BRIT Awards 2026 at Co-op Live on 28 February 2026 in Manchester, England.Photograph: JMEnternational/Getty ImagesOlivia DeanOlivia Dean accused of plagiarism on her I’ve Seen It trackMattie Music Group, owners of Bill Withers’ back catalogue, contend the Grammy winner infringed on Just the Two of UsRamon Antonio VargasFri 2 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlivia Deanhas been accused of plagiarizing theBill Withersclassic Just the Two of Us.The owners of Withers’ back catalogue aimed that allegation at his fellow Grammy winner in a copyright infringement lawsuit filed on Thursday in US federal court in Los Angeles.Mattie Music Group contended that Dean’s trackI’ve Seen Itstole “substantial” aspects of Withers’ 1981 collaboration with Grover Washington Jr,whichascended to No 2 on Billboard’s Hot 100 before enjoying a comeback much more recently on the TikTok social media platform.“In early August 2026, upon listening several times to I’ve Seen It, representatives of plaintiff came to what they considered to be the obvious and inescapable conclusion that I’ve Seen It copied in large and significant part [Just the Two of Us], including without limitation repeated copying of the distinctively protectable melody, and clearly infringed plaintiff’s copyrights in and to the original work,” Mattie’s lawsuit said.Mattie’s lawsuit recounted how the group hired musicologist Alexander Stewart to analyze I’ve Seen It and compare it to Just the Two of Us. Stewart “concluded that the works contain substantial similarities in protectable musical expression”, according to the plaintiff.“The number, character, and arrangement of the shared musical features are so striking that they support an inference that the similarities did not result from coincidence, independent creation or reliance on common musical elements,” Mattie’s lawsuit continued.The lawsuit does not list as defendants Dean or her I’ve Seen It collaborators, Bastian Langbaek and Max Wolfgang. But the lawsuit alleges the three “had a reasonable opportunity to encounter the original work before creating I’ve Seen It”, the last track on Dean’s 2025 album The Art of Loving.Sony Music Publishing and Universal Music Group’s Capitol Records – Dean’s publisher and record label, respectively – were named as defendants by Mattie. So was Kobalt Music Publishing America, Wolfgang’s publisher.Mattie’s lawsuit added the plaintiff provided “written notice to each defendant identifying the registration, the accused composition and the material musical similarities” on 17 August. But, the lawsuit said, “defendants continued reproducing, distributing, licensing, publicly performing and commercially exploiting” I’ve Seen It.Beside damages, the lawsuit said it seeks an injunction that permanently would “restrain further ongoing acts of copyright infringement by [the] defendants”.Representatives for Dean, Capitol Records and Kobalt did not immediately respond to requests for comment from the Guardian on Friday. Billboardreportedthat a Kobalt representative declined to comment on the lawsuit.Dean, 27, won the Grammy award for best new artist in February. The London native had also won four Brit awards at the time of Thursday’s lawsuit – including for album of the year with The Art of Loving.Furthermore, on 31 July, Dean and Sam Fender’s Rein Me Inbecamethe longest-running No 1 single in UK history.Withers, meanwhile, was a three-time Grammy winner originally from Slab Fork, West Virginia. His and Washington’s Just the Two of Us won the 1981 Grammy for best R&B song.Mattie Music Group administers the estate of Withers, who died in Los Angeles at age 81 in March 2020. The entity is named after the crooner’s late mother, Mattie, and run by his widow, Marcia Johnson.Explore more on these topicsOlivia DeanBill WithersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fires, fury and hundreds of arrests as France gripped by student protests | France | The Guardian
description: Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations
Content: Firefighters tackling a blaze near the Lycée Berthelot high school in Aubervilliers near Paris on Friday. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersGovernment struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrationsByAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 2 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 08.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class.“We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”1:21Fires burn as French students protest against lack of investment in education – video“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers acrossFrance: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during theheatwaves in May and June.View image in fullscreenStudents protesting in Lyon on Friday.Photograph: Laurent Cipriani/AP“The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support.The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by thethousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schoolsacross the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week.Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.View image in fullscreenStudents kick back teargas canisters in Strasbourg.Photograph: Romeo Boetzle/AFP/Getty ImagesThe government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”.View image in fullscreenStudents gather outside the Lycée Voltaire in Paris.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersOutside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year.“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”View image in fullscreenHigh-school students face off with riot police in Montpellier.Photograph: Horcajuelo Guillaume/EPAOn Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.”Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”View image in fullscreenBins burning, with graffiti on one reading ‘fuck RN’, in Paris.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesFarther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special€1 mealsfor struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technology | Special educational needs | The Guardian
description: Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system
Content: Patrick McCabe used eye-tracking technology to take his GCSEs and has just started his A-levels.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPatrick McCabe used eye-tracking technology to take his GCSEs and has just started his A-levels.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSpecial educational needs‘Just like my big brothers’: boy with cerebral palsy passes GCSEs with eye-tracking technologyPatrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities systemSally WealeEducation correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield,Cheshireas they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around.His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead.In person, Patrick is impish, thoughtful, articulate, witty, intelligent and honest. Using his augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, he tells the Guardian school has been a good experience overall. Born in Switzerland, his family moved back toEnglandwhen he was six. Since then, he has gone to local mainstream schools, where he wanted to learn like everyone else.“The best thing has been that, just like my big brothers, I’ve been able to learn and develop skills and gain knowledge of the world around me,” he said. “Even if some days I didn’t always want to go [to school], I think the opportunity to learn has helped me to grow and develop an independent mind.”It has not been easy. “The most difficult things have been building meaningful relationships, and communication barriers do exist,” said Patrick. “People are not always familiar with Eyegaze technology and are not always willing or able to give it a chance in terms of friendships.”View image in fullscreenPatrick with his mother Jo.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn many ways, Patrick epitomises the Labour government’s ambitions for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Forthcoming reforms arebuilt on an inclusive approach, keeping children and young people in local – rather than special – schools with all the necessary expertise and support on hand.But Patrick’s story also illustrates the scale of change required if education and assessment in England are to be truly inclusive. His experience shows that exams are far from accessible to all, his family and school say vital expertise is not always available and – crucially – funding is never enough.“All we wanted was for Patrick to have the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge and be given something resembling a level playing field compared to other students,” said the headteacher, Ross Martland. The school and Patrick’s mother, Jo, battled with the exam boards to try to ensure he was given a fair chance.In the end, it doesn’t sound very fair at all. While his peers spent the first part of the year revising, Patrick’s exams got under way on 2 February and went on every morning until 5 June. It required a herculean effort from him, which left him exhausted, frustrated and sometimes ill.View image in fullscreen‘I felt I had to work harder to express what I know,’ said Patrick about using the eye-tracking technology.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianA 30-mark question that might form just one element of an exam could take up to six hours. Patrick was supported throughout by CandLE, an organisation that helps students using AAC technology to access education across the UK. That he passed all seven GCSEs and achieved the grades he needed to continue into sixth form is testament to his determination.“Revising for my GCSEs was very exhausting because it took extra time and effort to revise in the first place,” said Patrick. “I felt I had to work harder to express what I know, even when I understand the subject. This was tiring, both physically and mentally. I needed extra breaks to rest, but I still wanted to do my best to show what I had learned.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMartland is fully supportive of the government’s Send ambitions. “I think the plans are right. Morally and values-wise, it’s absolutely right.” The issue is funding, he said, adding: “I’m concerned it will add significant pressures to schools if it’s not resourced properly.”Pupils with Send plans in England likely to double to one in 10 in rush for supportRead moreThroughout his time at Fallibroome, Patrick has worked with a devoted team of teaching assistants who support him not only with his learning in class but also his personal care. “We are incredibly proud of Patrick and all of our Send students,” said Rachel Crew, one of the teaching assistants working with him.Patrick says the transition to sixth form is going well. He’s shed the bottle green uniform in favour of a smart blue suit and he says the school is doing everything it can to support him.He says his mum has been “amazing” and he thinks students with physical disabilities who use eye-tracking technology should be assessed in a more appropriate way, so they don’t face additional barriers. But it is not only exams that worry him. “My concerns remain around friendships, if I’m honest,” he says.So what’s Patrick planning next? After A-levels, he wants to study media at university. “I find it interesting and I’d like to go into the industry.” His mum tentatively suggests nearby Salford. Patrick’s looking at Bournemouth, 200 miles away. Is he daunted? No chance. “I feel excited about the experience.”Explore more on these topicsSpecial educational needsDisabilityEnglandCheshireSchoolsLabourfeaturesShareReuse this content
