title: The simple secrets behind great ramen | Japanese food and drink | The Guardian
description: It’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hit
Content: Top secret: at its simplest, a great ramen is a balance of only five elements.Photograph: Charlie Lee/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha HawkinsView image in fullscreenTop secret: at its simplest, a great ramen is a balance of only five elements.Photograph: Charlie Lee/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha HawkinsJapanese food and drinkThe simple secrets behind great ramenYou need five things: broth, flavour-giving tare, noodles, fat and toppings. And it’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hitWatch our guide to the UK’s best ramen renegades inFeed with Jimi FamurewaJames ChantFri 2 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt its simplest, ramen is the balance of five elements: broth, tare (secret seasoning sauce), noodles, fat and toppings. If you understand that, this seemingly cryptic and complex corner of Japanese food culture opens right up. The first four take time, but if you pick up a shop-bought stock and some decent noodles, I won’t tell anyone. But the toppings are where the real payoff is: the fastest way to turn a midweek nothing into something worth showing off.A universal noteSpring onions should be used to top every bowl (finely diced white onion will work as a backup). Where there’s a broth, aim for 300ml, and where dashi is mentioned, instant is fine – unless you’re vegan, in which case steep 20g each of kombu and dried shiitake in one litre of cold water overnight, and keep the mushrooms for the soboro. Noodle portions are 130g unless stated otherwise, and any specialist items should be available online or at your local Asian supermarket.None of these toppings belong to one bowl, so swap them about – and they’re all good beyond ramen: chashu in a cheese toastie, say, soboro on rice, or ajitama in a caesar salad. The tares are multiuse, too: the tantanmen tare is great in scrambled eggs; the miso tare on corn on the cob, and the shio tare will improve pretty much anything.Tokyo shoyuView image in fullscreenRamen’s platonic ideal, and one piece of pork gives you the topping, tare and fat.Broth50:50 chicken stock and dashiTare3-4 tbsp chashu braising liquidFat1 tbsp, skimmed from chilled braising liquidNoodlesmedium classicToppingspork belly chashu, shop-bought menma (seasoned bamboo), ajitamaFor thechashu(serves 6-8)Roll and tie 500g pork belly and brown it all over in a pan. Deglaze the pan with 150ml sake, add 300ml each of shoyu, mirin and water, 30g demerara sugar, six sliced garlic cloves and a sliced 4cm piece of ginger, and simmer gently, turning, for two hours,. Cool in the liquid to room temperature, then chill overnight. Cut into 1cm-thick slices and torch or pan-fry to serve.TantanmenView image in fullscreenSichuan dan dan noodles, but make it ramen. Sesame, spice, and a soboro that works like a ragu.Broth50:50 kombu-shiitake dashi and unsweetened soy milkTare2 tbsp tahini, 1½ tbsp shoyu, 2 tsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, a pinch each of MSG and ground Sichuan pepperFat1 tbsp rayu chilli oilNoodlesmedium classicToppingsspicy mince soboro, pak choiSpicy mince soboro(serves 6-7)Soften a small diced onion and 2cm piece grated ginger in oil for five minutes. Add five grated garlic cloves followed by 500g fatty pork mince – although any mince works, but vegan mince will need more water - and fry until it’s in grains, not lumps. Add three tablespoons of doubanjiang (chilli bean sauce), one and a half tablespoons each of shoyu and mirin, plus a splash of water. Cook for 15 minutes until glossy.Hakata tonkotsuView image in fullscreenJapan’s most famous ramen export. Thin, straight noodles in a creamy pork bone broth, eaten fast by design.BrothtonkotsuTare30ml shio (30g salt, 10g sugar and 10g MSG dissolved in 70ml sake, 20ml mirin and 110ml water – makes 230ml/about 7 bowls)Fat1 tsp sesame oilNoodlesthin, straightToppingsajitama, pork belly chashu, shop-bought kikurage (wood-ear fungus), beni-shogaAjitama(serves 6)Warm 100ml water, dissolve 10g brown sugar in it, then add 100ml each shoyu and mirin and chill. Pierce six fridge-cold large eggs at the wide end and boil for seven minutes, stirring for the first 30 seconds to centre the yolks. Plunge into iced water, peel, and submerge in the cold marinade for 12-72 hours.Chippy Lane mazesobaView image in fullscreenA late-night Cardiff cult classic – chicken, curry sauce and chips – our version of nagoya mazesoba. Sauce in the bowl, hot noodles on top, toss hard.Brothnone – rules are meant for breakingTare100ml shop-bought Japanese curry roux, made thick and saltyFat1 tbsp each butter and chicken fat (from the thighs)Noodlesthick (200g)Toppingsshio koji chicken, crispy onions, beni-shoga, and grated cheese, if you’re feeling cheekyShiokoji chickenthighs(serves 4-5)Coat 500g skinless and boneless chicken thighs in 50g shio koji, 20g mirin, half a tablespoon of shoyu and one teaspoon each of grated ginger and garlic. Leave up to three hours. Add 100ml water, cover and cook over a low heat for 45 minutes. Uncover and reduce until it crisps. Shred the meat and toss through the glaze.Sapporo yasai misoView image in fullscreenUsually built on pork broth and lard for Hokkaido winters, this version is plant-based, but stands up.Brothkombu-shiitake dashiTare60g a bowl – 100g each white and red miso with 2 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp each mirin and shoyu, 1 tsp each grated raw garlic and gingerFat2 tbsp vegetable oil, fried with grated garlic and gingerNoodlesthick, wavy, yellowToppingsstir-fried cabbage and beansprouts, sweetcorn, toasted sesame seeds, and butter, if you’re not veganStir-fried cabbage and beansprouts(serves 4)Get a wok very hot with a little neutral oil. Add 200g shredded cabbage and 150g beansprouts, and toss hard for two minutes – you want char, not steam. Season with a tablespoon of shoyu, a teaspoon of sesame oil and a pinch each of salt, sugar and shichimi togarashi.James Chant is the owner of Matsudai Ramen in Cardiff.Watch him make ramenin Feed with Jimi FamurewaExplore more on these topicsJapanese food and drinkNoodlesFoodMain courserecipesShareReuse this content

title: Time to ditch the iron? I spent six months testing the best clothes steamers – here are my favourites | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Steam through the laundry pile with our expert’s top picks for smoothing creases on cotton, linen, silk and more
Author: Zoë Phillimore
Headline: Steam through the laundry pile with our expert’s top picks for smoothing creases on cotton, linen, silk and more
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleReviewTime to ditch the iron? I spent six months testing the best clothes steamers – here are my favouritesSteam through the laundry pile with our expert’s top picks for smoothing creases on cotton, linen, silk and moreHow to look after your knitwearZoë PhillimoreFri 2 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIgrew up in a household where everything was ironed. And I meaneverything: tea towels, pyjamas, bath mats. Perhaps as a result of watching my mother (and yes, it was always my mother) spend hours every week standing at an ironing board, I revolted. My heart sinks every time I have to go into battle with an iron. But how do we banish irons while still getting linen trousers to look crisp? I present the clothes steamer.Clothes steamers use heat and moisture rather than pressure to smooth fabric. A small onboard tank heats water into a steady flow of steam, which you run over garments while they hang. Instead of pressing fibres flat like aniron, the steam causes them to swell and relax, releasing creases without the need for an ironing board.Because the fabric isn’t pressed directly against the hot surface of an iron, steamers can be gentler on delicate materials such as silk, chiffon and wool. They’re also useful for refreshing garments between washes: a blast of steam can help reduce odours and restore the shape of fabrics that have been crushed in wardrobes or suitcases.I was already a fan of them on a personal level, and now I’ve taken that enthusiasm professionally by spending the past six months testing to find the best clothes steamers for the Filter. Here’s what I found.At a glanceBest clothes steamer overallRussell HobbsGenie VacuSteam£64.93 at Robert DyasBest budget clothes steamerPhilips1000 Series handheld steamer£24.99 at AmazonBest clothes steamer for travelLakelandFoldable steamer£34.99 at LakelandFastest clothes steamerSteameryCirrus 3 iron steamer£150 at SelfridgesBest steamer for precisionPhilips5000 Series handheld steamer STH5020/40£49.99 at AmazonWhy you should trust meI’ve been a journalist for more than 20 years and have spent the past five specialising in hands-on product testing. In that time, I’ve reviewed everything from mattresses and trampolines to coffee machines and dining tables, testing each in real homes rather than controlled showrooms.That experience has made me sceptical of marketing jargon and overblown claims. I test products as consumers actually use them and I measure what matters. For this feature, that meant timing heat-up speeds, tracking energy consumption, measuring soleplate temperatures and assessing durability alongside day-to-day usability.I also use clothes steamers fairly regularly at home, so I’m interested not just in performance, but also in whether they genuinely save time and effort.How I testedView image in fullscreenHeat check: measuring the surface temperature of a clothes steamer during testing.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianI tested 24 clothes steamers in my home, on my own clothes and bed linen. My three children have a steady stream of school shirts and trousers that need to be pressed every week, so this took care of testing how the clothes steamers performed on cotton – and whatever they’re making school-uniform trousers out of these days.I also tested the clothes steamers on more delicate fabrics. Crumpled linen trousers, silk dresses and formal suits were all unearthed from the depths of my wardrobe to be de-creased. During testing, I looked at how easily creases were released while using the steamer according to the instructions. I was also keen to compare each unit’s ease of use: no dripping or overheated handles escaped my notice. I also noted the onboard tank capacity and how long it lasted before needing to be refilled.Here at the Filter, we are geekily obsessed with the stats during product testing, so I got my trusted infrared thermometer and stopwatch out to measure how long each steamer took to heat up and the temperature the soleplate reached. I also measured each steamer’s run time: how long it could operate on a full tank of water before needing a refill.On a practical level, I also wanted to see how durable the clothes steamers were – after all, many of us will be chucking them into suitcases. So I dropped each steamer from waist height on to a carpeted floor to see if they survived the impact.I returned several of the clothes steamers to the brands that supplied them for testing. Any steamers that weren’t sent back were donated to theSalvation Army.The best clothes steamers in 2026View image in fullscreenSteaming ahead: some of the models that made the final cut.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianBest clothes steamer overall:Russell Hobbs Genie VacuSteamRussell HobbsGenie VacuSteamfrom£64.93£64.93 at Robert Dyas£94 at ArgosWhat we loveOutstripped all competitors on performanceWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit heavy, so it might make your arm acheView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£64.93 at Robert Dyas£94 at ArgosThe VacuSteam stands out from the pack because it sucks fabric to the ceramic plate. While this might sound alarming, it’s actually brilliant. One of the few faffy things about steamers is that you sometimes find yourself chasing fabric around. The suction on this Russell Hobbs model eliminates this frustration. It also offers a decent tank size and run time, and has three settings (you can operate it without the vacuum function).Why we love itThe suction function means anything you hang to steam – dresses, shirts, trousers, or curtains in my case – gets done much quicker. The amount of time faffing to get the steam on to the bit of fabric you want can be considerable, and I’m all about efficiency.This steamer did a fantastic job of getting wrinkles out of pure cotton, releasing even stubborn dried-in creases in one easy swipe. It also coasted through linen trousers in minutes and is gentle enough to use on silk. It heats up quickly, with the soleplate reaching 107C in testing, and it’s simple to use. Russell Hobbs offers a two-year warranty on this product.It’s a shame that …it’s quite heavy, and it’s loud when the suction function is on.Tank capacity:200mlWeight when full:1.28kgCord length:3mRun time on test:7mins 39secsRussell HobbsGenie VacuSteamfrom£64.93£64.93 at Robert Dyas£94 at ArgosWhat we loveOutstripped all competitors on performanceWhat we don’t loveIt’s a bit heavy, so it might make your arm acheBest budget clothes steamer:Philips 1000 Series handheld steamerPhilips1000 Series handheld steamerfrom£24.99£30 at Argos£24.99 at AmazonWhat we loveCheap and low energy useWhat we don’t loveIt can be a bit spitty; short cableView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£30 at Argos£24.99 at AmazonThis simple clothes steamer is small but impressive. Despite having a limited onboard tank, it lasts long enough to steam a whole garment. This is a great model if you’re just dipping your toes into the iron-free life and aren’t ready to commit to a more expensive model.Why we love itWhile I’d stop short of using the phrase “pocket rocket” about this steamer (there are a few drawbacks), it’s lightweight and reasonably powerful. There’s a small tank onboard, which with most steamers means the run time between refills is frustratingly short. However, the 1000 Series lasted a decent length of time, and even outlasted some other steamers with bigger tanks. I could get through a pair of blousy linen trousers in one go.The Philips handheld worked well on cotton, gently releasing creases with only a few passes, and it was even quicker on linen. I did find this steamer a bit spitty, so I was worried about using it on silk – water marks are not a good look, after all. For the price, I was impressed that this model comes with a useful heatproof mitt – many more expensive models don’t.It’s a shame that …there’s no auto-off function, so you need to remember to unplug it after use.Tank capacity:85mlWeight when full:544gCord length:1.6mRun time on test:5mins 40secsPhilips1000 Series handheld steamerfrom£24.99£30 at Argos£24.99 at AmazonWhat we loveCheap and low energy useWhat we don’t loveIt can be a bit spitty; short cableBest clothes steamer for travel:Lakeland foldable steamerLakelandFoldable steamerfrom£34.99£34.99 at Lakeland£34.99 at AmazonWhat we loveReally impressive performance on all fabricsWhat we don’t loveDespite being foldable, it’s still a tad bulkyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£34.99 at Lakeland£34.99 at AmazonThis budget-friendly steamer has a folding head, which is great if you’re short on storage space or want to chuck it in a suitcase for travel. The non-stick soleplate is great for getting out stubborn wrinkles, and the decent run time means you’ll be able to get through a few items from your suitcase without needing to refill.Why we love itOut of all the foldable steamers I tried, the Lakeland was the best. The tank is large enough to get through a few garments at once, and it’s fairly lightweight.The best thing about this steamer is its simplicity. There is just one mode, a light that shows you when it’s on and ready to go, and a lock button so you don’t have to pull the trigger constantly – and that’s it. Performance-wise, the Lakeland steamer excelled – it removed wrinkles from tough cotton and linen with one pass. You can clearly see how much water is left, and the soleplate got to 106C, which is low enough that I’d feel comfortable using it for silk too. Lakeland also includes a fitted brush to create some distance between the soleplate and delicate fabrics.It’s a shame that …it makes a disconcerting fizzing noise when you stand it up before the auto-shut-off kicks in. It is bulkier than other folding models, too.Tank capacity:160mlWeight when full:794gCord length:1.9mRun time on test:8minsLakelandFoldable steamerfrom£34.99£34.99 at Lakeland£34.99 at AmazonWhat we loveReally impressive performance on all fabricsWhat we don’t loveDespite being foldable, it’s still a tad bulkyFastest clothes steamer:Steamery Cirrus 3 iron steamerSteameryCirrus 3 iron steamerfrom£150£150 at Selfridges£150 at AmazonWhat we loveA premium, durable steamerWhat we don’t loveHas a premium price tagView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£150 at Selfridges£150 at AmazonSteamery claims the Cirrus 3 is a superior steaming experience, so I was keen to be the judge of that. It’s designed to combine functionality with aesthetics and has a wide elliptical soleplate for maximum surface area. There are just two buttons on the device: on/off and steam – so it shouldn’t prove hard to master. Another impressive claim Steamery makes about the Cirrus 3 is that it produces “dry steam” – steam with no liquid water droplets, meaning it doesn’t make the fabric wet.Why we love itThere’s much to love about the Cirrus 3. It’s a simple design (and therefore simple to operate), but it has lots of features built into it. I loved that it’s freestanding, so you can put it down while you rearrange garments without burning a hole in your table. It’s also clearly well made, and durable, too. While some steamers feel flimsy, I suspect this is a steamer you’ll have for years or even decades. Plus, it comes with a year-long warranty if bought directly from Steamery.It’s a shame that …there’s no lock button, so you have to press the button down the whole time.Tank capacity:90mlWeight when full:722gCord length:2.3mRun time on test:4mins 22secsSteameryCirrus 3 iron steamerfrom£150£150 at Selfridges£150 at AmazonWhat we loveA premium, durable steamerWhat we don’t loveHas a premium price tagBest steamer for precision:Philips 5000 Series handheld steamer STH5020/40Philips5000 Series handheld steamer STH5020/40from£49.99£59.99 at John Lewis£49.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressive performance even on thick cottonWhat we don’t loveCan’t stand up on its ownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£59.99 at John Lewis£49.99 at AmazonAlthough it comes in a range of finishes, the colour clash of pink and red on the Philips 5000 I tested puts the fun in functional. But colour aside, there’s plenty of design here to like. The active heat in the soleplate allows you to press fabric directly on to it, giving a crisper finish. This is complemented by the precision tip, a generous onboard tank and correspondingly healthy run time.Why we love itThis is one of the few steamers I tested with a precision tip– a feature that made steaming billowy pleated linen trousers a bit easier. The Philips 5000 Series was also incredibly fast at getting rid of wrinkles from cotton. I even tried it on a pair of crumpled jeans, and it blitzed them in seconds. It’s great that you can directly apply the soleplate to the fabric, meaning it almost doubles as an iron.The soleplate got up to 122C during testing – I was a bit nervy about pressing silk with it, but on steam alone, it did a nice job on my silk pillowcases. Other big ticks for me here are an easy-to-fill tank, a head that you can angle, an excellent run time (more than eight minutes on one tank), and the option of turbo or eco modes.It’s a shame that …this has no flat base, so you can’t stand it up while you move garments around.Tank capacity:120mlWeight when full:774gCord length:2mRun time on test:8mins 56secsPhilips5000 Series handheld steamer STH5020/40from£49.99£59.99 at John Lewis£49.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressive performance even on thick cottonWhat we don’t loveCan’t stand up on its ownThe best of the restSteamery Cumulus home steamerSteameryCumulus home steamer£250£250 at SteameryWhat we loveGreat for blitzing big batches in one goWhat we don’t loveIt’s not easy to store awayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£250 at SteameryBest for:an upright clothes steamerIf you’re steaming a lot, you may want to invest in an upright clothes steamer. The Steamery Cumulus is designed so you can hang clothes from the hanger on top and then use the steam head to get garments from all angles. It comes with a brush attachment to protect delicates.The water tank in the base is a voluminous 1.8l. It’s easy to fill and slot back in and, unlike on Steamery’s Cirrus model above, you can see how much water is in the tank while you work. It was really easy to use, with a simple dial to jump between two settings (though I found that all fabrics needed the second setting).This steamer is big and bulky – you can disassemble it when not in use, but it’s a faff. I also found that while it was great on shirts, jackets and dresses, it wasn’t really possible to do trousers or curtains, as they won’t sit on the hanger. If you buy direct from Steamery you get a year-long warranty – definitely worth having on a purchase this expensive.It didn’t make the cut because …it’s expensive considering its limitations.Tank capacity:1,800ml;weight when full:6.8kg;cord length:2.5m;run time on test:44minsSteameryCumulus home steamer£250£250 at SteameryWhat we loveGreat for blitzing big batches in one goWhat we don’t loveIt’s not easy to store awayTefal AeroSteamTefalAeroSteamfrom£139.99£139.99 at Tefal£139.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThe vacuum function takes the faff out of steamingWhat we don’t loveIt’s so heavy you feel like you’re doing weightsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£139.99 at Tefal£139.99 at AmazonBest for:single-stroke resultsThis Tefal steamer has the same brilliant suction function as the Russell Hobbs Genie VacuSteam – our overall king of steamers. This sucks fabric to the soleplate, holding it in place for a more even and thorough dewrinkle than without doing so. During testing, I was thoroughly impressed by the Tefal AeroSteam’s performance. It powered through all the cotton and linen I threw at it. The wrinkles were all gone with only one stroke down the fabric. I was delighted to find it got a crease out of a cotton dressing gown that had been there since I bought it.The soleplate got up to 160C, which meant I was too worried about using it on silk. However, despite a small tank, it ran for more than six minutes. In terms of sustainability, Tefal says it providestechnical spare partsat a fair price for up to 15 years after purchase.There are a few issues to be aware of with the AeroSteam, though. There’s no lock button to keep it on during use, and it’s loud to use when you have the suction enabled (you can steam without it if you want, but why would you?). This meant it was too loud to watch TV at the same time – a major downside for me.It didn’t make the cut because …it’s more expensive than the Russell Hobbs, which effectively does the same thing. And it’s very noisy.Tank capacity:100ml;weight when full:1.4kg;cord length:2.6m;run time on test:6mins 30secsTefalAeroSteamfrom£139.99£139.99 at Tefal£139.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThe vacuum function takes the faff out of steamingWhat we don’t loveIt’s so heavy you feel like you’re doing weightsFridja f10 handheld steamerFridjaf10 handheld steamerfrom£59.84£79.99 at Fridja£59.84 at AmazonWhat we loveEverything you need to start steamingWhat we don’t lovePerformed less well on dried-in wrinklesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£79.99 at Fridja£59.84 at AmazonBest for:a full steamer starter kitThe Fridja comes with plenty of – to use a technical term here – gubbins. Inside the box is a bag, folding hanger, delicates guard, a collar press and a clever bottle adapter for using a water bottle as your tank. During testing, the f10 performed pretty well in full-power mode, but the eco mode just didn’t cut it on cotton creases. It also performed well on silks and linen, gently releasing wrinkles in moments, but if you’re looking for some serious crease-zapping power, the Russell Hobbs Genie VacuSteam is a smarter choice.I found the f10 easy to use during testing – there’s a light indicator on the back, and full-steam mode was ready in 53 seconds, although this was slower than many other steamers on test. You can see how full the tank is while you’re using it, and it has a strong, wide base that feels secure when you want to put it down. There’s also an auto-off function, which provides some peace of mind.It didn’t make the cut because …it lacks the steaming gusto of the other models I tested. It’s a tad heavy and clunky, too.Tank capacity:260ml;weight when full:949g;cord length:1.95m;run time on test:11mins 45secsFridjaf10 handheld steamerfrom£59.84£79.99 at Fridja£59.84 at AmazonWhat we loveEverything you need to start steamingWhat we don’t lovePerformed less well on dried-in wrinklesPhilips 3000 Series handheld steamer STH3000/26Philips3000 Series handheld steamer STH3000/26from£29.99£38 at Argos£29.99 at PhilipsWhat we loveWorks quickly to release creases on all fabricsWhat we don’t loveLeft a bit of water residue on clothesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£38 at Argos£29.99 at PhilipsThe 3000 Series is one of Philips’ cheapest steamers. During testing I was impressed by the whole Philips range, so I was keen to see what this mid-tier steamer was like.First up, it’s lightweight and compact – a solid choice if you’re looking for a budget-friendly folding garment steamer. It heated up quickly (34secs) and quickly removed wrinkles from linen and silk. However, I found that it left a bit of water residue on garments, which can often leave marks after drying. Because of this, I’d be slightly nervous using this on silk or light-coloured linen.I found it easy to use, with the tank on the back easy to fill and load in and a light on the top that shows it’s come up to temperature. It also comes with a two-year warranty.It didn’t make the cut because …it spat and dribbled a bit – not ideal. And it wasn’t the best on any metric I tested.Tank capacity:100ml;weight when full:662g;cord length:2m;run time on test:4mins 48secsPhilips3000 Series handheld steamer STH3000/26from£29.99£38 at Argos£29.99 at PhilipsWhat we loveWorks quickly to release creases on all fabricsWhat we don’t loveLeft a bit of water residue on clothesWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenCrease control: hang garments freely and work from the top down.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianHow to use a clothes steamerAlthough all models vary, there is one thing all steamers have in common: first, you’ll need to fill the tank. Every model I tested has a detachable tank with a fill line, which you can take to a tap to top up. After clicking the tank back in place, you plug in your steamer (I couldn’t find a decent cordless steamer for love nor extensive research during testing). Most steamers will then require you to switch it on manually, although a few will start heating straight away. For safety, I’d prefer a manual on/off button, which gives you more control over when to start steaming.Depending on what you’re steaming, you then hang the garment from a hook or rail and swipe the steamer across the fabric. Make sure it’s hanging freely to give you better access to the garment and to ensure the fabric is hanging naturally as the creases release. This will help prevent you from steaming in new creases. For delicate fabrics or those with printed designs, you may want to steam it inside out. Steaming the reverse side can help protect the outer sheen on silk and preserve the colour of the dyes on printed designs, although always check the garment’s care label and the steamer instructions before you begin.How close you should hold the steamer to the garment depends on the fabric and the power you’re working with. I’d start at 4cm out and then gradually move closer if the wrinkles aren’t relaxing. Use your free hand to hold the fabric taut as you glide the steamer head across it – this helps to relax the fibres.You want to be continually moving rather than hovering in one place, and I recommend starting at the top of the garment and then moving down. The steam rises, so using downward strokes works best.Steaming vs ironingIrons and clothes steamers work in different ways and give different results. You apply irons directly to garments to press and reshape fabric, giving a crisp finish, which is great for pleats and pressing seams. But steamers use heat and moisture to swell the fibres in the fabric, which relaxes them and releases wrinkles. Some steamers do have a heated soleplate, which can be directly applied to the fabric to press it, but others rely on hot jets of steam.Steaming might not make a shirt look as “polished” – for a particularly crisp finish or creases pressed into fabric, you’ll want to deploy an iron. But garment steamers can be useful for delicate fabrics that you might be hesitant to use direct heat on, such as silk and knitwear.Another factor to consider is that irons require an ironing board and the space to store both items. Many steamers are a lot more compact and need no other equipment, except perhaps a regular clothes hanger.How should I steam delicates?While cotton generally tolerates higher heat and steam to release creases, other fabrics require different treatments – but always check the care label.Linenseems to crease if you even look at it. It’s best to steam it when it’s still slightly damp. Linen fibres are strong, so the fabric generally handles higher heat and plenty of steam. You might find you have to steam both sides and pull the fabric taut for stubborn wrinkles.Woolis super sensitive to moisture and heat, and it is liable to shrink. Use a low heat and plenty of patience, and the moisture should release the fibres nicely. Avoid placing the soleplate directly on the fabric.Cashmereneeds a low heat, and you only want to use a little bit of steam as the moisture will quickly distort the fabric. A light touch is the order of the day with this fine, delicate and expensive fibre.Silkis super delicate, so heat can mark it. Keep the temperature low, turn your garment inside out, and keep the steamer head moving across the fabric rather than holding it still for too long.Velvetshould be steamed from the reverse wherever possible, so that the pile isn’t crushed or flattened.Printed or embellished fabricsshould be turned inside out, as heat can damage dyes, sequins and other embellishments.For more:The best steam irons to make light work of the laundry pileThe best heated clothes airers to save time and money when drying your laundryZoë Phillimore is a journalist and product-testing geek. She’s been a journalist for more than 20 years.Mattresses, makeup, trampolines and toys – she’s tested the lot. With three children andplenty of school uniforms to keep presentable,she’s always looking for ways tosave time on ironing. When she’s not manning the washing machine, Zoë spends a lot of time trying to keep her kids entertained – and she shares her endeavours onInstagramExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterHomesGadgetsHygieneInteriorsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ahead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made now
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Ahead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made now
Content: ‘It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden’ … Pete Postlethwhaite in Brassed Off.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden’ … Pete Postlethwhaite in Brassed Off.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMovies‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversaryAhead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made nowRobyn VinterFri 2 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is one of the prime minister’s all-time favourite films and has endured in the hearts of the British public since it was released in 1996. Ostensibly a story about a small town colliery band’s journey to the finals of Britain’s biggest brass band competition at theRoyal Albert Hall, Brassed Off is unashamedly political.“I think the people who went expecting a political film got the bonus of a bit of a comedy,” says its writer, Mark Herman, three decades on. “And the people who went expecting comedy got the bonus of the political message. I think anybody who went got a sort of bonus they might not have expected.“On the face of it, a brass band film is not an easy pitch but word of mouth really rolled and suddenly it went on and on in places for months,” he recalls. “I thought it might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley for about two weeks,” laughs Herman. “So yeah, it’s amazing.”Set in the fictional industrial South Yorkshire town of Grimley a decade after mineworkers brought themselves to destitution trying to save their livelihoods, it captures the hopelessness felt by former miners who struggled to keep themselves out of the dole queue during the slow and painful destruction of the mining industry by the Tory government.StarringPete Postlethwaite, Tara Fitzgerald and Ewan McGregor, it follows the Grimley Colliery Band as they await a judgment from British Coal as to whether their pit will be closed. A resounding success, Brassed Off went on to be number 85 in the BFI’s list of Top 100 British Films and spawned a popular stage play. To add to the plaudits, Andy Burnham recently named it as one of his four favourite films.“How do I feel about that? It’s good!” says Herman. “It’s very flattering, but I’d have been more surprised if he’d have chosen Notting Hill.”On its 30th anniversary, fiction and real life are set to collide when Grimethorpe Colliery Band – the group that inspired the film – heads to the real-life Royal Albert Hall to perform the music alongside a special screening.The film’s success at the time was “surprising and very rewarding” but the enduring appeal, Herman believes, is because, “It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden.“It’s really interesting hearing teens and 20-year-olds talking about the film, because it’s such an old film for them, but it really hits them. They get the message everybody got 30 years ago, because it’s still relevant and still plays.” But these films are a dying breed and Herman admits he is “fairly pessimistic” about the current state of the British film industry. “I feel like films like Brassed Off wouldn’t be made [now].”View image in fullscreen‘It’s still relevant and still plays’ … Ewan McGregor, Tara Fitzgerald and Pete Postlethwaite.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/Alamy“I’ve spent the last 10 years trying to get films similar to Brassed Off off the ground but can’t,” he says. “It seems to be blockbusters or micro-budget at the moment and there’s no space for mid-budget British films like those, films like I want to make.“The studios are not as brave as they were,” he adds. “They’d stick their neck out, in what I call the old days. It was quite a risky film to make, Brassed Off, but now they seem to only want to put money behind dead certs.”His favourite films of the last year wereI Swear, the biography of a man with severe Tourette syndrome, andThe Ballad of Wallis Island, an offbeat comedy drama written by and starring the comedians Tim Key and Tom Basden.His path – from childhood in the East Yorkshire seaside town of Bridlington, to studying graphic design at Leeds Polytechnic (now Leeds Beckett University) and the National Film and Television School – would still open doors for youngsters in the industry, he thinks. But it is not an easy industry to break into, and now, in his early 70s, he thinks the advice he got when he was young – advice he took for a short while – to move to London, probably still stands.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve spent the last 10 years trying to get films similar to Brassed Off off the ground’ … Mark Herman.Photograph: Gary Calton/the Guardian“If I’d have [stayed in] London and networked I’d have probably done more films, but maybe not ones I care about as much,” he says.Instead he wrote a powerful script, unashamed to spell out in no uncertain terms how the Conservative government destroyed communities and ruined lives, the effects of which continue. Higher mortality rates from suicide, alcohol and drugs developed – and persist to this day – in former pit towns and the shadow of Margaret Thatcher still lingers like an oil stain in these communities.In a climactic scene in the Royal Albert Hall, Postlethwaite’s character, Danny, the band’s conductor, gives a memorable speech – later immortalised in the protest song Tubthumping by Chumbawamba – shouting: “I thought that music mattered. But does it bollocks. Not compared to how people matter.”During filming, Birmingham town hall was substituted for the London venue, which was too expensive and “didn’t look anything like the Albert Hall”, Herman jokes.Brassed Off Live will be a “strange experience … when our fake Albert Hall is on screen and you’re sitting in the Albert Hall. It’s a thrill. Thirty years ago would we ever imagine being in the Albert Hall still watching it? It’s amazing.”Brassed Off Live is at theRoyal Albert Hall, London, on Friday 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmAndy BurnhamRoyal Albert HallComedy filmsPete PostlethwaiteDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy  | Television | The Guardian
description: He won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David Brent
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: He won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David Brent
Content: ‘I feel so lucky, it’s insane’ … Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesView image in fullscreen‘I feel so lucky, it’s insane’ … Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesTelevisionInterviewFangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedyZoe WilliamsHe won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David BrentFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly when absolutely badgered willLenny Rushadmit that the title role of The Reluctant Vampire, Val, was written for him: “Shane Allen, the executive producer, loved the books when he was young, and he was the exec onAm I Being Unreasonable?. So yes, the scripts were written with me in mind. I’m so happy they were so good. I’d have felt awful if they said ‘We’ve written this for you’ and …” he trails off, pulling a face of exquisite pained courtesy.Rush likens the show to The Naked Gun and Airplane!, and it has the writing team behind Alan Partridge, so can conjure awkwardness out of thin air. But it also taps into a comic tradition that goes even further back: a delight in the ridiculous, people talking to bats and gargoyles, invisible women interjecting by surprise, a surrealism whose comedy comes from the audacity of acting it with such commitment. “In my opinion,” says Rush, “sometimes things are labelled as a family show but they’re aimed at kids. I really do get the feeling that The Reluctant Vampire is for everyone.”The Reluctant Vampire was written in the 80s by Eric Morecambe, in a surprising digression into children’s fiction from the comedy giant. It’s about the young scion of a bloodsucking household who doesn’t have any skills: his teeth aren’t pointy, he hates the taste of blood, and it transpires that he’s not a vampire at all but a rogue human. In the hands ofNeil and Rob Gibbons, it’s like watching the essence of British comic sensibility – slapstick shot through with genuine pathos.View image in fullscreenRush with Sian Clifford as Valeeta, Gabriel Nagy as Vernon and Tom Davis as Victor in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: James Pardon/BBC/Buffola Pictures“You’ve gotTom Davisplaying a vampire, this big character, with these big movements and this big voice, that can’t not attract a younger audience,” says Rush, “but the lines are genuinely funny.”The show opens with Davis in full vampire regalia, ready to strike an elderly victim in her bed, only for Rush to derail it all by rushing in saying he needs a wee.Still only 17, Rush has been a fixture on TV for many years, starting aged seven in CBeebies documentary series Our Family. Then, aged eight inApple Tree Houseon CBeebies he played Eli, a young rascal on an estate of well-intentioned young rascals. If you have children this age, you’ll feel like you’ve known him for ever, and if you are watching thelatest season of Slow Horses, you’ll know him as the foul-mouthed, ancient-beyond-his-years kid whose steel trap of a mind effortlessly vanquishes the spies.But his breakthrough role was in Am I Being Unreasonable?, for which he won a Bafta at 14 for best male performance in a comedy – and he was nominated again for the same award this year. That role, Ollie, along with his magisterial Bafta acceptance speech, sealed his reputation as a guy who has hacked your mainframe, and could effortlessly make you laugh at any time.View image in fullscreenRush with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/AppleYou can see in Rush’s performance as Val how much he’s gorged on Mr Bean, Alan Partridge, Monty Python. “I probably watched some things I shouldn’t have when I was younger,” he says. Never mind the age-appropriateness, how he found the time is anyone’s guess, since he has spent so long watching the British version of The Office that he knows it episode by episode, and has been working – as well as going to school – since he was seven. David Brent has always been his inspiration, and he delivers the kindest reading of that character I’ve ever heard. “You think: ‘What an idiot.’ Then you think: ‘What a not very nice man.’ Then you get to the end of series two, and there’s a really big element of pity. He’s just a man! Trying to find his way! He just wants to be part of the gang. It’s actually a tragedy.”The opening episode of The Reluctant Vampire makes a lot of his stature, his parents measuring him and wondering if he’ll ever be tall enough to be a vampire. Rush, who has a form of dwarfism known as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, never went into acting for his condition to be a “talking point. I never thought I could be an inspiration for disabled people or young people.” The impact of his visibility on the world around him came as a complete surprise. “When Am I Being Unreasonable? came out, I started to get messages from mums, saying: ‘My little boy’s got a disability or a form of dwarfism, he’s struggling a bit at the moment at school. But he’s seeing you on telly and it’s giving him confidence.’ It’s so mad that I can be doing what I love and making people feel like that. I’m so pleased that that’s how people have seen it.”Actually, though, the unvampiric vampire is a metaphor for belonging that is universal to teenagehood. “Going to school, trying to fit in, trying to impress, failing miserably. I think that’s why it’s so relatable. Even though it’s about vampires. Or you could see it as someone trying to find their place in society: ‘Am I doing this right? Am I good enough?’ It shouldn’t be so awkward, but it is.”View image in fullscreen‘I say I’m working with Gary Oldman and my mates don’t even look up’, say Rush.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesHe’s not bringing a lot of his own experience of school to the travails of Val, incidentally – he never stopped attending, but was always off filming something and must have been artlessly cool. Which also made his parents very focused on his attendance. “My mum took school really seriously – not even necessarily, to be honest, the education side; she just found it very important for me to be seeing my mates. So I’d be on the PlayStation, and go: ‘I’m working with Gary Oldman,’ and they wouldn’t even look up from the game. You can get swept away really easily, on set. You have assistant directors coming into your dressing room, asking what you want for lunch, it’s quite insane. You have to have the right people around you.”After Am I Being Unreasonable?, Rush got two episodes of Doctor Who, even if he wasn’t exactly a devotee. “I’ve not told Russell T Davies this, but I never watched Doctor Who. I knew what it was! I knew it was an honour to get asked. I knew it was a real moment in your career, especially to get cast young – I think Andrew Garfield was in it at a young age.” He played Morris Gibbons, a 13-year-old genius and adviser in the science unit, a really smart move after the role of Ollie, in which he’s also a genius but of a more cunning, domestic kind.Am I Being Unreasonable? sometimes seemed to hang off his every expression – the plot of that show was absolutely wild, full of the worst parenting in the world, elaborately revealed secrets, dead pets. Rush’s command of the mood was what tethered it to earth. “Ollie was the breakthrough part, and after that I saw myself as an actor. But when I’d look online, before and after, people would say ‘He’s a great comic actor’ or ‘He’s a great young comic’. And I’m really thankful for that, but I never saw myself as a comedian or a comic actor. And as much as I love comedy, I don’t want that to stick as my thing.” His mum asked him recently whether he’d ever try standup. “It’s a bit of an annoying thing about British culture, and quite sad in my opinion, that it’s easy to get pigeonholed, and if I ever did try standup, it would take me further away from the Slow Horses kind of work.”His next role is Dobby in the Harry Potter series that’s been beset by controversy – not just about whether actors can be in it without tacitly endorsing JK Rowling’s views, but also bizarre racist death threats to cast members. Rush hasn’t started yet, definitely hasn’t had any death threats, and is tight-lipped, saying only: “It’s pretty incredible – I feel so lucky, it’s insane.” It’s casting against type, this house elf, because Dobby’s not the effortless manipulator of all he surveys: his emotional top note is craven gratitude and anxious helpfulness. Maybe Val is a useful bridging role, because as a not-really-vampire, Rush ventures into new territories of panic and pitfall.The Reluctant Vampire has palpable ensemble chemistry, between Rush, Sian Clifford as his mother, Davis as his dad,Asim Chaudhryas a Lurch-like character. Newcomer Gabriel Nagy is a great foil as his brother, a functioning, evil vampire. “I never felt like anyone was learning from me,” he says. “I felt like I was learning from them. I never felt like number one on the call sheet, having to keep everyone in high spirits. I remember Tom telling me, it sounds obvious but it was so true and so clever – if you’re doing a comedy, you want to make people laugh at home, so your goal in that scene is to make your co-star laugh. Try and get them to break.” They’re all pros, of course, so no sign of anyone corpsing; but like every classic comedy since TV began, you can feel that they’re smiling on the inside.The Reluctant Vampire is on BBC One on Sunday4 Octoberat 6.40pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedyDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More celebrities are embracing grey hair. For other women, it can come at a cost | Women's hair | The Guardian
description: Olivia Colman and Lisa Bonet are among the stars going silver – but workplace ageism means many women still fear ditching the dye
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Olivia Colman and Lisa Bonet are among the stars going silver – but workplace ageism means many women still fear ditching the dye
Content: Olivia Colman unveils her new silver look on the red carpet at the Zurich film festival.Photograph: Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for ZFFView image in fullscreenOlivia Colman unveils her new silver look on the red carpet at the Zurich film festival.Photograph: Andreas Rentz/Getty Images for ZFFWomen's hairMore celebrities are embracing grey hair. For other women, it can come at a costOlivia Colman and Lisa Bonet are among the stars going silver – but workplace ageism means many women still fear ditching the dyeChloe Mac DonnellDeputy fashion and lifestyle editorFri 2 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo dye, or not to dye. That is the decision many people, particularly women, face when their hair starts to grey.This week Olivia Colman joined the growing ranks of women embracing grey hair and ditching the dye. Appearing at Zurich film festival, Colman had swapped her dark signature pixie cut for a grey, curly mane swept to one side.Online, Colman was swiftly lauded for her new look, with Vogue describing her as a “silver hair muse”.The 52-year-old joins fellow actors including Andie MacDowell and Lisa Bonet who have embraced the salt-and-pepper or all-out silver look.View image in fullscreenLisa Bonet has long embraced her natural grey locks.Photograph: Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for the Annenberg FoundationHowever, for women outside Hollywood, escaping the tyranny of the hair dye bottle is not always so easy.“Being able to embrace your grey hair proudly is a privilege,” says Stacey Duguid. In June, Duguid, a former fashion editor, began documenting her struggles to find a job aged 52 despite her decades of experience. She told her followers that she had downsized her house and was now on universal credit. She received thousands of messages from fellow middle-aged women also struggling to find employment.“There is a reluctance for women who are trying to get back into the workplace to go grey,” Duguid says. “To do it, you are most likely already in a senior position in the workplace. As an unemployed, broke, single parent it wasn’t an option for me.”View image in fullscreenAndie MacDowell’s silver hair has become part of her signature look.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesGrey hairs start to emerge, on average, in the mid-30s for white and Asian people and around the mid-40s for Black people.Louise Chunn, a former editor turned founder of the therapist-finding platform Welldoing, first stopped dying her hair when she became the editor of InStyle magazine in the UK.She says: “I didn’t fear how bosses would view my grey hair, because the editor’s job offer came from New York. It was more important that you were well groomed, somewhat sophisticated.”View image in fullscreenBlack people typically begin to go grey in their mid-40s – later than other racial and ethnic groups.Photograph: Cultura Creative/Getty Images/Tetra images RFChunn began dying her hair again in her 50s because she worried it made her look older, but stopped in her 60s.Colman’s new look was created with extensions by the London based hair specialist Inanch Emir. Using four shades of grey, Emir mirrored Colman’s natural colour while adding volume and length.Duguid describes Colman’s hair as “spectacular” but has all the trademarks of a much younger woman. “It’s a sort of fetishised version of grey hair,” she adds.View image in fullscreenFor many women, the decision to stop dyeing their hair is tied to concerns about ageing.Photograph: Andreas Kuehn/Getty ImagesSarah Bower, a grey-blending and colour specialist at Larry King salon in London, says clients considering embracing their grey hair are most concerned about looking older.Bower says going grey isn’t as simple as calling it a day on hair dye. Much of her work involves blending the demarcation line – the visible difference between someone’s natural colour and dyed hair – to “try and make it look like they’ve already got their natural hair colour”. She says it can take up to three years to fully grow out grey hair.According to the Office for National Statistics about 3% of people between the ages of 50 and 64 are unemployed in the UK. Despite the state pension age rising to 67, a recent study by theCentre for Ageing Betterfound that a job applicant is perceived tobecome undesirableto recruiters on average at the age of 55.View image in fullscreenAge discrimination in the UK affects women earlier than men, official data shows.Photograph: Trevor Williams/Getty ImagesResearch by Ian Burn, an economics professor at the University of Liverpool, found that age discrimination in recruitment against women in the UK starts at least10 years earlier than it does against men. Once a woman hits 40, her chances of being called for interview begin to decline. For men, the decline does not start until their 50s.Recent catwalks have been more age inclusive. In January, Stephanie Cavalli, a 50-year-old model, whose hair is peppered with greys, opened the Chanel couture show. Fifty-nine-year-old Evelyn Effrim-Botchey, who stopped modelling in her late 20s after work began to dry up,has spokenabout how her grey-streaked hair has helped her comeback.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStephanie Cavalli wearing her natural grey curls on the Chanel couture runway in January.Photograph: Jumeau Alexis/Abaca/ShutterstockBut most older models continue to have dyed hair. Not one of Gucci’s glamoroussciuracast at itsrecent Milan showwas grey, while 70-year-old Jerry Hall, still blond, fronts this month’s Grazia. Pamela Anderson, 59, has embraced going makeup-free since 2023 but remains blond.Duguid has heard from older women who use filters during video interviews and calls to help mask their age. “It’s completely exhausting” she says. “Grey hair is different, though, because you can’t really hide it. If you are trying to find a job, you will go out and get a box dye.”Alyson Walsh, a former magazine editor who now runs the style platform That’s Not My Age, says: “Despite the fact that older women have lots of experience and knowledge, there’s still the stereotype that you’re not allowed to look old,” she says. Walsh stopped dying her hair in 2015. “I feel empowered,” she says. “It saves me money. There is less maintenance and it’s in better condition. I don’t look older. I just look my age.”‘No one I work with seems to care’: How I let myself go greyView image in fullscreen‘My natural grey hair is only a small part of how others see me.’ Picture posed by a model.Photograph: mjorobles/ShutterstockBack in the distant days of Covid lockdowns,I obsessed over the 3in-wide streak of visible grey in my hair. I’d long stopped using box colours and hair salons were shut. Was it time to let nature take over from chemicals?Working from home and in social isolation, going grey was liberating. My at-home defiance of societal expectations for a middle-aged woman even felt rebellious.The prospect of a new job and new colleagues dented that defiance. Should I abandon my mini revolution and surrender to the salon – fork out for a beautiful toffee brown with caramel lowlights?If I’d known Olivia Colman and other high-profile women were going to publicly raise a metaphorical finger to the expected norms of ageing, I might have held back on the hair therapy.But I battled the toffee cravings and took up a new professional role.My team members are younger than me, and years of messaging that grey equals old, and indicates an end of self-care, is difficult to escape.But I stayed the course. I learned that my all-natural hair, while an integral part of who I am, is only a small part of how others see me. In short, no one I work with seems to care.There is no doubt, a sexist-laden ageism exists. Stereotypical assumptions persist about how older women should age. Why else would we be talking about Olivia Colman’s “daring” grey hair?But my grey hair – along with the lines on my face – tells my story. Both are, I have decided, life affirming.Donna CartonExplore more on these topicsWomen's hairBeautyWomenAgeingDiscrimination at workWork & careersHair carefeaturesShareReuse this content
