title: How best to punish City? Restitution over retribution, then hand club to the fans | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: There are no real precedents and emotions are still raw, but good can come from this mess if ownership models change
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: There are no real precedents and emotions are still raw, but good can come from this mess if ownership models change
Content: Often it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players?Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOften it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players?Composite: Getty ImagesManchester CityHow best to punish City? Restitution over retribution, then hand club to the fansJonathan LiewThere are no real precedents and emotions are still raw, but good can come from this mess if ownership models changeFri 2 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareA17-year transfer embargo. Replay the entire era with all the original players. Restore the 2009 squad and force them to mount a title challenge with Stephen Ireland, Martin Petrov and Richard Dunne. Force Ferran Soriano to drive a parade bus backwards through Manchester, once for every major trophy won. Ban the Poznan, or at least make City fans do it facing forwards.Yes, in the week since it emerged that Manchester City have beenfound guilty of all the financial chargeslaid against them by the Premier League, a great and cathartic silliness has begun to stalk the land. The Sainsbury’s account on Instagram posting a picture that reads “114 unexpected items in the bagging area”. The relentless trolling from Domino’s Pizza, which claims to have “irrefutable evidence that pineapple is the best pizza topping”.Manchester City verdict has big integrity implications, warns FA as club lodge appealRead moreThe City fan on BBC 5 Live arguing that the club’s defiance of unfair rules is part of a rich tradition of civil disobedience going back to the suffragettes and the Peterloo massacre, and therefore justified because “they’re trying to massacre Manchester City”. Liam Gallagher’s late-night diatribes on X, the most unhinged of which compares City to “Jesus prepared to die on the cross”. (The most popular reply, naturally, simply reads: “Sham Pain Supernova”.)And on some level it’s possible to see the ritualistic ridicule of City as the first downpayment on any punishment: a kind of collective healing, banter as therapy. Before the stripping of points and titles, the stripping of dignity. This is always how the British have dealt with anything, from an early general election to the death of a treasured celebrity. I heard my first Princess Diana joke within about 15 seconds of walking through the school gates the following Monday morning.Back in the real world of real consequences, the Abu Dhabi counteroffensive was beginning in earnest. While City launched their appeal,Etihad Airways was threatening to sue the Premier Leaguefor the “damaging implications” of the verdict and government officials from the United Arab Emirates were surreptitiously warning that the case could threaten diplomatic relations and billions of pounds of investment into the UK.Which sounds like a pretty hefty multi-pronged problem until you realise that these are all basically the same entity. Like one of those one-man stage shows you see at the Edinburgh fringe, where all the characters are played by a single guy scurrying around the stage frenetically putting on different costumes. UAE dignitaries? The leadership of Etihad Airways? The board of Manchester City? Goodness, your versatility astonishes us. That’s acting range for you.View image in fullscreenOne suggestion to start reversing the damage: force Manchester City fans to do the Poznan facing forwards.Photograph: Mike EgertonStill, all of this is a long-overdue reminder that when you allow state actors to control your football clubs, even the most minor footballing decisions become matters of diplomacy, geopolitics, peace and war. Witness the desperate contortions this week of Andy Burnham, who offered astiff-armed defence of City’s ownershipbeforebelatedly realisingthat appearing to side with English football’s most notorious cheats may just be the sort of thing that polls badly in certain swing postcodes.None of which, of course, gets us any closer to a workable solution. And of course you will have your own strong views over what should happen to City, assuming their trail of appeals and grievances is finally exhausted at some point. There are no real precedents here, and so there are no wrong answers. The emotions are still raw. Often it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players, broadcasters who as it turned out were pointing their cameras at a sham competition?These are almost philosophical questions, questions of justice and ethics and morality. Do you decide that the strict imperative is to punish or “cancel” the harm done, as Kant or Hegel might have argued? Do you agree with Durkheim that the point of punishment is not exemplary deterrence but the reinforcement of shared moral values, or with Bentham that the infliction of pain for its own sake simply prolongs the original sin, and that the emphasis should always be on averting future evil? And do any of these scenarios end with Victor Lindelöf lifting a Premier League trophy?View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham faced pressure this week after defending Manchester City’s owners.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA WireWhat follows here is little more than a personal prospectus, guided above all by two principles. Firstly that the relitigation of history – the messy and unsatisfactory business of reassigning trophies and medals – is an unserious solution for unserious people. Rewriting the past on the basis of a counterfactual is no more feasible than asking the shark to regurgitate, reassemble and reanimate the body of the surfer he has just crunched to pieces. It is one thing to tell the world that what we saw was not real. It is quite another to perpetrate the compound fiction that something entirely different happened instead.As Jamie Carragher put it so well on Sky Sports this week, winning is less about the silverware and the trinkets than the moments and the memories, the aura of victory and the hangovers the following morning, and those are gone for ever. Carved up, parcelled away. And of course City knew this at the time. The Touré goal, the 6-1 at Old Trafford, the Agüero goal, the Kompany goal: those moments are safe, banked, untouchable. “We know what we felt,” a lot of City fans have been saying in the last few days, and they’re right.The second principle is that any punishment should seek to inflict maximum punishment on City’s owners and as little as possible on City’s fans. The fans may have shared in the proceeds of cheating, may often have defended the owners in obnoxious and myopic ways, and perhaps it feels purgative and satisfying to throw them under the bus too. But ultimately they too are victims of a grand deception. They too were gaslit, lied to, told the dream was real life. In many ways the subterfuge is all the crueller because of how desperate they were to believe it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd so any redress that deprives one of the country’s biggest fanbases of their club, that forces them out of existence, that cuts the body off at the knees and forces it to beg for mercy at the very bottom of the food chain, is also doomed to failure. And let’s be real: this isn’t going to happen in practice. The commercial appeal of Manchester City uplifts the entire league. Broadcast and commercial contracts would need to be redrawn. Ultimately throwing them out of football altogether, kicking them down the stairs, would cost everyone at the top of English football a lot of money. And we know how much they hate that.But there is a recourse, albeit improbable and outlandish, that fulfils all the criteria of restitution, if not retribution. The new football regulator has the power to strip rogue owners of their position and force them to sell up. This sounds like a good punishment. But market intelligence suggests City are worth about £4bn now, compared with about £200m when the Abu Dhabi United Group took over in 2008. What kind of punishment enables the perpetrators to walk away with a 20-fold profit on their investment, much of which can be attributed to their cheating?No, City should not be sold; they should be taken back. Requisition. Nationalise. Give them some patriotic name such as the Great British Manchester Football Club. Return Phil Foden to the exchequer. Enzo Maresca, you are now an employee of the UK government. And while this sounds outlandish because itisoutlandish, there is a recent precedent here. Chelsea’s operations were briefly controlled by the government after sanctions were imposed on their owner Roman Abramovich and he agreed to offload the club. It was surreal, exceptional and only ever intended as a temporary measure.View image in fullscreenManchester city council owns the freehold to the Etihad Stadium.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAThere are plenty of levers that can be pulled here, if there is the political will to do so. Manchester city council owns the Etihad Stadium. A report by Tax Policy Associates has suggested that City may owe HMRC as much as £12m in unpaid tax over the Roberto Mancini contract. The cross-party Treasury committee has urged HMRC to scrutinise the findings of the Premier League case. Meanwhile, every week that City stay in their current ownership is a week in which money flows from fans and broadcasters and sponsors into the pockets of Abu Dhabi. No wonder City’s ruling regime has a vested interest in elongating this process as long as possible.Nobody bats an eyelid at the idea of the state owning a park or a motorway or a museum, or taking over a failing train company or steelworks or bank. In each case there is a recognition that the asset has a broader social value that requires a certain protection against market forces. And of course the longer-term ambition here is not to run Manchester City as an arm of the state, but eventually to give the club back to its people. To gradually assemble the governance structures that would allow fans a genuine voice in the running of their club and facilitate an eventual sale. And in the meantime to maintain one of the country’s most successful football clubs as a going concern, generating revenue that will allow it to pay back its debt to English football.None of this is going to happen. Abu Dhabi would rather hire the world’s 50 best lawyers to sue Burnham for the next 30 yearsbefore it allowed one of its prized assets to be given away for free. But also: is this not what we should want to happen? If any tangible good is to come from the sordid City case beyond memes and banter, perhaps it is a realisation that the ownership model of English football needs to be reimagined on a radical level. That a system built on the wholesale transfer of wealth from fans to owners is exploitation by any other name. That City are not the disease, but the symptom. And that the first rule of politics remains its most crucial: never waste a good crisis.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City’s England players are worried about their futures, admits Tuchel | England | The Guardian
description: England head coach Thomas Tuchel said the Manchester City players in his squad were concerned for their futures
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: England head coach Thomas Tuchel said the Manchester City players in his squad were concerned for their futures
Content: Thomas Tuchel said the Manchester City scandal was a big talking point in the England camp.Photograph: Antonio Bronić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said the Manchester City scandal was a big talking point in the England camp.Photograph: Antonio Bronić/ReutersEnglandManchester City’s England players are worried about their futures, admits Tuchel‘It is of course a topic and we speak about it at dinner’Head coach has right-back dilemma for game in CroatiaJacob Steinbergin RijekaFri 2 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel has suggested Manchester City’s England contingent are worried about the clubbeing found guiltyof breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.Tuchel, who said he would be prepared to keep picking City players if they were relegated, revealed the case had been a major topic of conversation in theEnglandcamp before the Nations League game against Croatia. The head coach said there had been discussions during meals and delivered an honest response after being asked whether the situation had become a distraction.Pickford in spotlight against Croatia with England position under threat from TraffordRead more“If I say now it’s not then I can just speak for myself, which would be totally narrow-minded,” Tuchel said. “I think it is a distraction. It is. Let’s say it is a subject. If it’s a distraction, I don’t know.“It is of course a topic and we speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. We speak about it at breakfast. I know the Man City players get a lot of messages and phone calls and feedback about it.“Are they worried or concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don’t know what’s going on for the club that you signed. They’re still young. They’re ambitious. They’re told they are totally innocent and don’t know what’s going on. It is a subject.“I am again not sure if it’s a distraction. I don’t see it when I see them in my meetings. I don’t see it how they behave with other teammates, and I don’t see it in training being a distraction. But it’s a topic. How can’t it be?”The Football Association blocked a subsequent question to Tuchel on whether the City case represented a danger to English football. City maintain their innocence and on Friday announced an appeal against the verdict.For Tuchel, the focus is on his squad. He selected three City players for this camp: Elliot Anderson, Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly, who has withdrawn injured. Guéhi made a costly error during last weekend’sdefeat by Spainand Anderson was off colour duringthe win over Czechialast Tuesday but Tuchel believes both are ready to start against Croatia on Saturday night.England are second in Group A3 with three points from two games. Jordan Pickford, who remains the No 1, will replace James Trafford in goal and Tuchel must decide whether to restore Jarell Quansah at right-back after Trent Alexander-Arnold shone against Czechia in Prague.Alexander-Arnold was an unused substitute when England drew in Rijeka in 2018. His place remains uncertain and Tuchel considered whether it was now or never for the Real Madrid defender, who turns 28 next week.“Maybe, maybe a little bit,” he said. “Once you are in camp it’s a big opportunity if other players are not here. Trent is a unique player. He is not a runner, he is not someone who runs through the last line, who does overlaps, underlaps.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel has said it ‘may be’ now or never for Trent Alexander-Arnold to win his place in the England team.Photograph: Antonio Bronić/ReutersTuchel explained that Alexander-Arnold is building a connection with Bukayo Saka. “Bukayo is normally used to a lot of movements around him,” he said. “That brings normally the best out of Bukayo. They need also to find a way to not be too static, to not be too ball-position focused and that we play with dynamic movement. That’s maybe the challenge for Trent: to buy a little bit into a new idea and a bit out of his comfort zone. He’s trying and it’s never too late to prove a point.”Tuchel is happy with Saka’s level. The Arsenal winger struggled with fitness during the World Cup but has been a regular for his club this season.“He had a strong start,” Tuchel said. “I could see he was pain-free. He had a bit of a strange ending to last season. He was playing through the pain, he was deciding matches but struggling to have big influence – and yet then having the biggest influence, by scoring decisive goals.“He scored decisive goals without being fit and without having the capability to accelerate and decelerate. Now I felt him more involved, and felt he was more dangerous at the start of the season – and still I think there is some level still to come when he plays for England.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League: Italy earn draw against 10-man France, Northern Ireland stun Ukraine | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Italy denied Zinedine Zidane victory in his first France home game while Northern Ireland boosted their promotion bid with victory in Trnava
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Italy denied Zinedine Zidane victory in his first France home game while Northern Ireland boosted their promotion bid with victory in Trnava
Content: Italy celebrate Alessandro Bastoni’s equaliser as Roberto Mancini’s side spoiled the party at Stade de France.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenItaly celebrate Alessandro Bastoni’s equaliser as Roberto Mancini’s side spoiled the party at Stade de France.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/DPPI/ShutterstockNations LeagueNations League: Italy earn draw against 10-man France, Northern Ireland stun UkraineLeague A: France 1-1 Italy, Belgium 3-0 TurkeyNorthern Ireland boost promotion bid with 3-0 winAgencies andGuardian sportFri 2 Oct 2026 17.11 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZinedine Zidane’s first home game in charge ofFranceended with a 1-1 draw againstItalyin theNations Leagueon Friday. Visiting keeper Gianluigi Donnarumma produced a string of saves to frustrate fans at Stade de France, while the hosts ended the game with 10 men after Dayot Upamecano’s late dismissal.France 1-1 Italy: Nations League football – live reactionRead moreMichael Olise putFranceahead in the 55th minute with a curling shot that went in off the crossbar, following a short free-kick taken by Rayan Cherki. But poor defending midway through the second half allowed Italy defender Alessandro Bastoni to run through and clip a low shot inside the right post.Moise Kean missed a close-range chance early on forItaly, shooting straight at goalkeeper Mike Maignan. Donnarumma made a double save from Ousmane Dembélé and Désiré Doué early in the second half, then produced a brilliant low save to deny Adrien Rabiot moments after Italy’s equaliser.Upamecano was sent off late in the game for picking up a second yellow card, but the hosts kept pushing for a winner, and Donnarumma had to claw away Eduardo Camavinga’s shot in stoppage time to preserve a point.“We would have liked to win for our fans tonight but I was obviously really touched and delighted to be back at the Stade de France,” Zidane said afterwards. “I am happy with the performance albeit not with the result. We had chances to score a second goal and we didn’t do it. But I am really proud of my players.”The Italy manager, Roberto Mancini, was pleased with his side’s efforts. “I think this was a great performance tonight against one of the best teams in the world, with very positive aspects to it,” he said. “We are on the right road, and we need to keep playing this way.”Francestay top of Group A1, a point clear ofBelgiumwho eased to a 3-0 home win over bottom sideTurkeyin Liège. The two neighbours meet again on Monday at the Stade de France, while Italy host Turkey in Bologna.View image in fullscreenKevin De Bruyne celebrates after scoring one of his two goals for Belgium in Liège.Photograph: Virginie Lefour/Belga/ShutterstockKevin De Bruyne, in his 127th match for the Red Devils, scored the opening goal with a cool finish from the edge of the box, after a nice one-two with Dodi Lukebakio. Turkey posed the greater attacking danger after the Napoli midfielder’s opener but could not find a leveller and were punished just before the hour mark.De Bruyne claimed his second goal in the 59th minute, curling a ball from the edge of the box past Turkey goalkeeper Ugurcan Cakir into the top corner. Romelu Lukaku, Belgium’s all-time record goalscorer, added a third in the 76th minute, skewing the ball home from Charles De Ketelaere’s low cross.In League B,Northern IrelandstunnedUkraine3-0 in Slovakia to go clear at the top of their group and boost their hopes of promotion to the top tier.Ciaron Brown, the only player in Michael O’Neill’s starting lineup over the age of 24, scored twice either side of Isaac Price’s goal in Trnava. The away win puts Northern Ireland on seven points from three games, and they are still yet to concede going into Monday’s clash with Georgia in Belfast.Northern Ireland’s positive start was quickly rewarded as Kieran Morrison floated a corner to the back post where Ruairi McConville headed it back for Brown, earning his 33rd cap, to prod home despite the desperate efforts of Illia Zabarnyi on the line.View image in fullscreenCiaron Brown (left, No 22) celebrates his second goal of the night in Trnava.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APGeorgiy Sudakov was the first Ukraine player to get a sight of goal but his 19th-minute effort was straight at keeper Pierce Charles, and moments later the hosts were 2-0 down. Morrison’s first-time ball into the box was met powerfully by Price at the back post – earning Morrison an assist in his first competitive international.Brown’s second came in bizarre fashion just after the hour – the 28-year-old Oxford defender went up to flick on Pierce Charles’ free-kick from inside the Northern Ireland half, and Ukraine goalkeeper Dmytro Riznyk let the bouncing ball slip through his legs to wrap up a remarkable result.“It’s a great result for us, a great performance,” O’Neill said. “The early goal helps settle us into the game. The second goal was a brilliant goal. We worked it the length of the pitch. We were patient. We could have crossed it early but that allowed us to get more men in the box and it’s a brilliant header from Isaac.“The third goal is fortuitous but it’s a mistake by the opposition, so we have to capitalise on that, but I thought throughout our performance was brilliant,” the Northern Ireland manager added. “We limited the opposition to crosses and shots from outside the box and I thought we defended brilliantly.”The Liverpool full-back Milos Kerkez scored the only goal in the other Group B2 tie to earnHungarya 1-0 win overGeorgia, moving the Magyars level with Ukraine in second place with four points from three games.Edin Dzeko brought the curtain down on his international career duringBosnia and Herzegovina’s 1-1 draw withSweden. The 40-year-old was withdrawn after 63 minutes of his 152nd appearance, with the hosts trailing after Viktor Gyökeres had scored two minutes earlier. Kerim Alajbegovic ensured the spoils would be shared with an 80th-minute effort.In the group’s other game,PolandthumpedRomania6-0 with Robert Lewandowski hitting a hat-trick. Radu Dragusin was sent off in the 22nd minute for bringing Lewandowski down in the area, and the veteran striker got up to convert the penalty. Lewandowski struck again in the 47th and 86th minutes, with Piotr Zielinski, Jan Bednarek and a Virgil Ghita own goal completing the scoring in Warsaw.View image in fullscreenRobert Lewandowski scores from the penalty spot to kick off Poland’s 6-0 rout of Romania.Photograph: Marek Antoni Iwańczuk/NurPhoto/ShutterstockTheFaroe Islandsearned an impressive 1-1 home draw with Group C3 leadersSlovakia, Adrian Justinussen’s second-half goal cancelling out a Gunnar Vatnhamar own goal before the break.Moldovamoved up to second in the group with a 2-1 away victory overKazakhstan.Elsewhere in the third tier, Vasilije Adzic scored twice as Group C2 leadersMontenegrowon 2-1 inLatvia, whileCyprusbeatArmenia2-0 despite a second-half red card for Kostas Pileas.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueFranceItalyBelgiumNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bath go top with Finn Russell to the fore in thrilling derby victory against Exeter | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Bath went to the top of the Gallagher Prem after beating Exeter Chiefs 40-34 in a pulsating West Country derby at the Rec
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Bath went to the top of the Gallagher Prem after beating Exeter Chiefs 40-34 in a pulsating West Country derby at the Rec
Content: Bernard van der Linde goes over to score one of Bath’s six tries in a thrilling match of 11 tries.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenBernard van der Linde goes over to score one of Bath’s six tries in a thrilling match of 11 tries.Photograph: David Davies/PAPrem RugbyBath go top with Finn Russell to the fore in thrilling derby victory against ExeterPrem Rugby: Bath 40-34 ExeterHosts made to fight all the way in 11-try thrillerPress AssociationFri 2 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBath went to the top of the Prem after beatingExeterChiefs in a pulsating West Country derby at the Rec but they were made to fight all the way in an 11-try thriller.Exeter trailed 26-10 at the interval but rallied to lead 33-31 midway through the second half before a yellow card for scrum-half Stephen Varney eventually proved decisive.‘They said I ran away from rucks’: Emmanuel Iyogun on going from reluctant prop to England debutRead moreCam Redpath, Dan du Preez, Bernard van der Linde, Ted Hill and Finn Russell scored Bath’s tries. There was also a penalty try award with Russell converting four. The hugely impressive Immanuel Feyi-Waboso scored two tries for Exeter, with Jack Yeandle, Josh Iosefa-Scott and Varney also going over. Henry Slade converted three and Harvey Skinner added a late penalty.Bath’s director of rugby, Johann Van Graan, was delighted with another five points. “We wanted to start well and achieved this to build up a healthy first-half lead but they went on to dominate the third quarter,” he said.“We then brought on our bench and obviously they made a big impact, so we finished strongly to get a valuable five points. It was particularly pleasing to see Jaco Coetzee back in action. He’s been out for nearly two years and he and Will Stuart, who also returned, made a big impact.“One scrum in the first half was huge as we shunted them backwards. It was a big momentum shift as we went to the corner and scored from there.”Rob Baxter, Exeter’s director of rugby, said: “I’m massively pleased with our intent and physicality as we turned up for the fight from the start. Even though we were 16 points down at the interval, I thought we were unlucky to be in that position.“It wasn’t against the run of play, but two of their tries came from when we were attacking with favourable bounces going their way. It was a massive step forward from last week’s disappointing effort and gives us a foundation to move on.”Bath took control as first Redpath intercepted a Skinner pass to run 50m and score before Van der Linde slipped through a gap in the visitors’ defence for an individual try. Russell converted both to give his side a 14-0 lead at the end of the first quarter.Exeter responded thanks to the strong running of Feyi-Waboso. First he evaded a tackle from Ollie Lawrence to put the defence on the back foot and when the ball was recycled he powered past another two coverers with Varney on hand to touch down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenHenry Slade is tackled by Finn Russell, who was in the thick of the action for Bath.Photograph: Rachel Le Poidevin/PPAUK/ShutterstockThe hosts scored their third try when they capitalised on a favourable bounce on halfway. Van der Linde and Ewan Richards took advantage to give Du Preez the chance to force his way over from close range, but Bath bungled the kick-off so Yeandle was able to keep his side in contention with a try from a driving lineout.However, with half-time approaching, Bath exerted a period of pressure that culminated in Russell dummying his way over for the bonus-point try before converting for a 26-10 interval lead.Exeter began the second half strongly and were rewarded with two tries in quick succession. First Iosefa-Scott crashed over from close range before Feyi-Waboso took his opportunity in style by brushing aside two would-be tacklers. Slade converted both and his side were right back in it with just two points between the teams.Exeter took the lead for the first time when former Bath player Will Butt carved the hosts apart to provide Feyi-Waboso with an easy run-in for his second try. The home side were soon awarded a penalty try with Varney given a yellow card for a deliberate knock-on and in the scrum-half’s absence, Hill battered his way over.Slade missed badly with a penalty attempt so Skinner took over the goal-kicking and his success gave Chiefs two deserved bonus points from the match.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyBathExeterRugby unionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daley Thompson: ‘I was happy to sleep on floors to do what I was doing. You know you have to earn it’ | Athletics | The Guardian
description: The double Olympic champion insists a knighthood wouldn’t change his life, still trains on Christmas day and explains why he got a video game and Seb Coe didn’t
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The double Olympic champion insists a knighthood wouldn’t change his life, still trains on Christmas day and explains why he got a video game and Seb Coe didn’t
Content: Last month Daley Thompson became the first British athlete to hold a national record for 50 years.Photograph: Simon HofmannView image in fullscreenLast month Daley Thompson became the first British athlete to hold a national record for 50 years.Photograph: Simon HofmannAthleticsInterviewDaley Thompson: ‘I was happy to sleep on floors to do what I was doing. You know you have to earn it’Sean IngleThe double Olympic champion insists a knighthood wouldn’t change his life, still trains on Christmas Day and explains why he got a video game and Seb Coe didn’tFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘When you’re a kid, you think you can be Superman,” says Daley Thompson, as he gazes back to the era when he was track and field’s ultimate man of steel. “As you grow up, life kind of knocks those edges off you. But that never happened to me. I’ve always gone where I was aiming. I’ve been the luckiest bloke in the world.”Luckiest? Hardly. During the 1980s, Thompson powered to two Olympic decathlon gold medals, broke the world record four times and remained unbeaten for nine extraordinary years. Along the way, self-doubt, like his opponents, was conquered and vanquished. That wasn’t luck, it was talent and unyielding willpower.Underpinning it all was a work ethic that made Stakhanov look like a slacker. Thompson trained 20 times a week. And, famously, when he heard that his great German rival Jürgen Hingsen trained on Christmas Day, he made sure he did two sessions.Ten lessons from Jakob Ingebrigtsen, one of the world’s most beguiling athletes | Sean IngleRead moreBack then, millions of Britons regarded Thompson as the closest thing to a real-life superhero, voting him the BBC’s Sports Personality of the Year in 1982 and revelling in his triumphs. So it remains an enduring mystery that – unlike Britain’s only other three multi-event Olympic track and field champions, Dame Mary Peters, Dame Denise Lewis and Dame Jessica Ennis-Hill – Thompson’s achievements were not rewarded with a knighthood.Does he ever wish he was Sir Daley? “Not really,” Thompson says. “I mean, it would be lovely, and great for all the people that have helped me. But it’s not going to change my life, honestly.”Why do you think you haven’t got one? “Absolutely no idea,” he replies. “Those things for me are really nice to have but if they’re not within your control, then why bother about them?”That is an admirably phlegmatic reaction. But the long-standing suspicion is that the controversy that followed Thompson’s brilliant second Olympic gold medal, in 1984, is to blame. Having whistled to the national anthem, he then wore a T-shirt to the press conference afterwards that asked “Is the world’s second greatest athlete gay?” – an apparent reference to Carl Lewis – before joking that he would like to have Princess Anne’s babies.Writing for the Guardian from Los Angeles, Charlie Burgess began his report with seven words that proved prescient. “Bang goes Daley Thompson’s chance of a knighthood.” The backlash was such that the Royal Family even released an official statement saying that it was “absurd” to think Princess Anne, then the president of the British Olympic Association, had been upset.View image in fullscreenDaley Thompson, Britain’s greatest ever male athlete?Composite: Getty ImagesThese were different times, we suggest to Thompson, as he mulls over his decision to wear that T-shirt. He nods. “Would I do it now? That is the question,” he replies, before answering it himself. “No, of course I wouldn’t. But you’re right, absolutely different times.”Thompson also reiterates that Princess Anne didn’t mind his joke either. “The thing was she wasn’t offended. She was fine with it. It’s a faux outrage.”Yet there is still time for the honours’ committee to think again, given Thompson’s remarkable accomplishments and love of his country. And, as a powerful documentary of his life made clear two years ago, it came despite a tough upbringing.double quotation markWould I do it now? No, of course I wouldn’t. But you’re absolutely right, different times.Daley ThompsonHis Scottish mum raised him while she held down two and sometimes three jobs, with help from food banks. His dad, from Nigeria, was shot and killed when he was only 13. Yet Thompson was never one to let adversity, however extreme, knock him off his stride.Even now, at 68, he is still notching up fresh milestones. Because last month Thompson became the first British athlete to have held a national record for 50 years.That record was set in September 1976 in Talence, France, when he eclipsed Peter Gabbett’s old record by four points. So was that the moment Thompson knew he was going to be great?“Truthfully, no,” he replies. “It was before that, when I did my first decathlon in Cwmbran in 1975. I was 17 years old. I did my first five events and I literally remember waking up on the second day thinking: ‘Oh man, you’re going to be really good at this.’ And that was it.”View image in fullscreenDaley Thompson sports his controversial T-shirt after winning gold at the 1984 Olympics.Photograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesNot that there was much financial help for talented youngsters then. “There was a guy called Tom McNab, who asked Adidas to send me some shoes because I couldn’t afford all of them,” he says. “That was one of the things that made me think I’m going to be really good. Because nobody I knew ever got shoes. I just thought to myself: ‘Oh, they believe in me.’”A year later, after achieving two Bs and a C in A-Level biology, geography and general science, Thompson was making believers out of everyone. First he went to the Montreal Olympics, where he finished 18th, then two months later came the British record.But for years Thompson made very little money, with decathletes seen as far down the pecking order. Indeed, the cash really only started to come in after Daley Thompson’s Decathlon, the computer game that sold more than a million copies, and wrecked nearly as many joysticks and keyboards, was released.“You’re the first to mention today,” he says, laughing, when the damage and destruction he inadvertently wrought is pointed out to him. “Literally there hasn’t been a day since 1984 when somebody hasn’t come up and said: ‘You owe me a keyboard’. Honestly, I can be on a train and somebody will walk all the way through the carriage and say: ‘I had your game, you owe me.’ All the time.”He also smiles when reminded that there was never a video game about his great friend Sebastian Coe, who he believes has done a superb job reviving his sport since being elected president of WorldAthleticsin 2015. “Absolutely, very true,” he laughs. “That’s because they knew how boring he was. And there’s something else I’d like you to put in there, that he never had a statue in Madame Tussauds – I did!”View image in fullscreenDaley Thompson in 1976, the year he first set a British national record for the decathlon aged 18.Photograph: Evening Standard/Getty ImagesThompson reckons he made about £20,000 from the game, which spawned two sequels and gave him a much-needed payday during a time where he never earned megabucks.“Don’t forget, the first six or seven years I was doing it, you weren’t allowed anything,” he says, alluding to how athletes were officially permitted to get money from sponsors and meeting organisers only in 1982. “We were earning literally nothing.”“But I was happy to sleep on floors to do what I was doing. Even at the beginning of the 1980s, when I was already Olympic champion, I would go on warm weather training to California and I would sleep on people’s floors or sofas. But honestly, it forges you, it makes you. Because you don’t expect anything, you know you have to earn it.”Even now, he doesn’t enjoy a life of luxury. “No, I live in a little flat,” he says. “It would be great to earn 100 grand a week, or 500, or whatever it is, but you are a person of your times.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf there is one image that encapsulates Thompson’s dominance, it is Steve Powell’s Last Man Standing photograph from the 1982 European Championships when he stands triumphant as his vanquished competitors lie slumped on the track.It is one of the most iconic sports photographs in history, but Thompson says he would never hang it on his wall. “I’m not like that,” he says. “Once I’ve done it, it’s over. I’m looking for the next thing.”That thinking, it turns out, applies to his gold medals and trophies too. “They’ve all gone to friends and training partners,” he says. “I’ve got two families, and my younger kids, who are 24 and 19, they’ve never seen any of my stuff.”double quotation markHaving long-term friends brings a different kind of joy. And it’s deeper.Daley ThompsonWhat explains Thompson’s approach? “So many people who I used to know really well, they live so much in the past,” he says. “And they miss all the great stuff that’s either going on now or might go on tomorrow. Because they always think: ‘Oh, it was so good then.’ And it was great, it was fantastic. But for me, I’m just trying to move forward.”Inevitably, though, he finds himself drawn back to those great battles down the years – especially as he still sees Hingsen, his great rival from the 80s, a couple of times a year.When they meet Thompson likes to wind his German friend up, but there is clearly a deep mutual respect. As he points out, when you tally up their personal best scores over the 10 decathlon events they come to exactly the same. Yet Hingsen, who broke the world record twice himself, was never able to beat Thompson when it mattered.View image in fullscreenSteve Powell’s iconic Last Man Standing photograph from 1982.Photograph: Steve Powell/Allsport/Getty Images“Physically, we are kind of the same, but I think I competed better,” he says. “I enjoyed the test more.”Thompson also used mind games to persuade Hingsen into thinking he was unbeatable. “If I knew he was going to the track at 11am, at 10.45am I would put the high jump bar really high and I would just sit on the bed and wait for him to come,” he says. “And so then he thinks I’ve been jumping. Or you throw the shot put into the ground 10 feet further than you’ve ever thrown before.“I used to do that kind of stuff. It’s just one of those stupid things you do when you’ve got nothing better to do.”Sometimes Coe would do his bit too. During the 1984 Olympics, when Thompson had gained the upper hand in another epic decathlon battle, the 1500m champion approached Hingsen, who was sitting on a wooden bench with a towel around his neck. “He’s an animal, isn’t he?” Coe told him. Hingsen responded by pulling the towel up, nodding and pulling the towel back down.“I do feel a bit bad for him,” admits Thompson. “Because, if it wasn’t for me, he would be one of Germany’s best ever athletes. Instead, they give him a hard time, which they shouldn’t.”They were great days, weren’t they. “Yeah, of course. But there’s been a couple of fun days since.”And Thompson, who is engaging and fun company, admits that his enduring friendships with Coe and Hingsen mean at least as much to him as the medals ever did.“This is going to sound really simple, but I think as you get older, you get a much better perspective. And while that, at the time, was the greatest thing that ever happened to me, having long-term friends brings a different kind of joy. And it’s deeper.”Some believe that Thompson’s decathlon personal best score of 8,847 points could have been even higher given that he often used the 1500m, the decathlon’s final event, as a victory procession. But his time of four mins and 20 seconds is far from shabby, as Wimbledon’s Crazy Gang found out when he was their fitness coach during the mid-1990s.“This was the era of Robbie Earle and Mick Harford,” he says. “And they were all giving me a hard time. And I said: ‘Let’s go down the track one day and try it’. No one got within 20 seconds of my 1500m time.”Even now, Thompson’s competitive instincts remain undimmed. He still works out four or five times a week and could easily pass for 15 years younger, while on Saturday mornings he can be found training a group of 40-, 50- and 60-somethings in Battersea Park.“We go out in all weather,” he says. “We do sit-ups and press-ups and run up little hills. But basically it’s just all us mates getting together every Saturday. We do a little session, we go to the greasiest spoon in the world.”And does he still train on Christmas Day? You bet he does. Only now he has company. “They’re all there on Christmas Day – they climb over the fence,” he says. “But I don’t do that, before anybody says anything. I just shout through the bars,” he adds, with a mischievous smile.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal shelve plans for major expansion of Emirates Stadium | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium, opting for a programme of smaller improvements in hospitality, retail and matchday experience
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium, opting for a programme of smaller improvements in hospitality, retail and matchday experience
Content: Arsenal had considered expanding the size of the Emirates Stadium, but have instead opted for a range of smaller improvements.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenArsenal had considered expanding the size of the Emirates Stadium, but have instead opted for a range of smaller improvements.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAArsenalArsenal shelve plans for major expansion of Emirates StadiumClub opt for improvements in hospitality and retailAn increase to 60,704 capacity had been consideredEd AaronsFri 2 Oct 2026 16.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal have shelved plans for a major expansion of the Emirates Stadium, opting for a programme of smaller improvements as the club’s owners review the Premier League champions’ wider operation.Arsenal set up a working group led by the chief executive, Richard Garlick, in 2024 to examine the feasibility of increasing the 60,704 capacity, with some reports they could temporarily hold home matches at Wembley. But the club has decided against major redevelopment and will concentrate on what it described as the “continued evolution” of their home since 2006.Have Arsenal been figured out? Three big questions after Brighton’s upsetRead moreArsenal confirmed at a supporters’ meeting that improvements would focus on hospitality, retail, visitor facilities and the matchday experience – an area the co-chair Josh Kroenke previously highlighted.“We shared a commitment to the continued evolution of Emirates Stadium, rather than a huge-scale masterplan, building on improvement we have made to date in partnership with our catering partner, Legends, the introduction of safe standing (this season in the Clock End, and next season in the North Bank), improving hospitality and retail experiences, and upgrading visitor experiences,” Arsenal said.Mikel Arteta, who last season guided Arsenal to their first Premier League title since 2022, is believed to have expressed concern over the disruption that would have been caused by any temporary move. It is understood Arsenal did not apply to host matches at Euro 2028, with a potential redevelopment in mind.The club’s owner, Kroenke Sports & Entertainment, which agreed a record $4bn deal to buy Major League Baseball’s Los Angeles Angels last month, is understood to have brought in Boston Consulting Group (BCG) to examine parts of the operations. The review is understood to be overseen internally by Garlick and to be ongoing.There is no indication the review will necessarily result in job losses among Arsenal’s approximately 800 employees. Sources have suggested the work is principally focused on non-football operations and identifying ways to improve efficiency.The decision over the Emirates comes amid competition from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, which opened in 2019 with a capacity of 62,850 and was designed to host a wide range of sporting and entertainment events, including NFL games and concerts. Arsenal, despite a smaller capacity, have significantly increased their matchday revenue. Income has reportedly doubled over five seasons to more than £150m a season, helped by the club’s return to the Champions League and an expansion of corporate hospitality.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Arsenal Supporters’ Trust said it had been given guarantees the club had “no current plans” to reduce ordinary seating or move fans to increase corporate numbers.Christos Tzolis is to return to Arsenal for assessment after sustaining a suspected muscle injury with Greece. Germany’s Kai Havertz pulled out of international duty after picking up an injury against the Netherlands but Arsenal are believed to be hopeful he could feature against Leeds next Saturday.Explore more on these topicsArsenalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brydon Carse charged by Cricket Regulator over arrest on night out | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Brydon Carse has been charged with improper conduct by the Cricket Regulator after his arrest on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly during a night out in August
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Brydon Carse has been charged with improper conduct by the Cricket Regulator after his arrest on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly during a night out in August
Content: Brydon Carse was dropped from the England squad in August, and Stephen Fleming must decide whether to include him in the South Africa tour party.Photograph: George Franks/ProSports/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBrydon Carse was dropped from the England squad in August, and Stephen Fleming must decide whether to include him in the South Africa tour party.Photograph: George Franks/ProSports/ShutterstockEngland cricket teamBrydon Carse charged by Cricket Regulator over arrest on night outPolice investigated allegations of assault in DerbyCarse faces disciplinary hearing in next few weeksMatt HughesFri 2 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrydon Carse has been charged with improper conduct by theCricketRegulator after his arrest on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly during a night out with his Durham ­teammates in Derby in August.The fast bowler was subsequently interviewed by Derbyshire police, which investigated allegations of assault before closing the case without pressing charges a fortnight ago,as revealed by the Guardian.Carse has been charged by the Regulator, however, and will face a disciplinary hearing in front of the independent Cricket Discipline Committee in the next few weeks.England call up spinner Mason Crane eight years after his solitary Test capRead moreThe 31-year-old was dropped from England’s Test squad for the second and third Test matches against ­Pakistan in August in the immediate aftermath of his arrest, not picked for the white-ball team that played Sri Lanka last month and overlooked for a tri‑series in Pakistan this month, but is currently available for ­international selection.The disciplinary proceedings are unlikely to be concluded before Stephen Fleming names his squad for England’s three-Test tour of South Africa in December, leaving a potentially difficult decision for the new coach. The white-ball captain, Harry Brook, said last month that Carse needed “time away” from international cricket after Joe Root, the Test captain, had expressed “frustration” at his decision-making.Carse has 12 months left on his England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) central contract, but is not facing action from his employers for breaching the terms. The sanctions open to the CDC include a warning, suspension and financial penalties.Brook and Jacob Bethell were both given warnings over their future conduct after bringing the game into disrepute when they were photographed drinking in a Wellington bar the night before a one-day ­international against New Zealand last November.Josh Tongue, who was out with them, was also investigated but escaped without sanction as he was not named in the side, while Brook had already been fined £30,000 by the ECB after it emerged he had an altercation with a nightclub bouncer on the same evening.The Cricket Regulator also conducted an investigation this summer into Ben Stokes’ and Gus Atkinson’s behaviour after they were alleged to have broken an ECB curfew bydrinking in a Chelsea nightclub following victoryin the first Test against New Zealand in June.Neither were charged despite being stood down by the ECB for the next Test, with the resultant ill-feeling from the incident believed to have contributed to Stokes’ subsequentretirement from international cricket.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA statement from the Cricket Regulator said: “Following a Cricket Regulator investigation, Brydon Carse has been charged with breaching regulation 3.2 of the ECB professional conduct regulations, in relation to events in Derby in the early hours of the morning on 23rd August 2026. The matter will now be referred to the independent Cricket Discipline Panel for adjudication. As the process is ongoing, no further comment will be made.”Regulation 3.2 states that “no participant may conduct themself in a manner, do any act or make any omission at any time which is improper or which may be prejudicial to the interests of cricket or which may bring the ECB, the game of cricket or any cricketer or group of cricketers into disrepute”.The ECB added: “We are aware of the Cricket Regulator’s decision to charge Brydon Carse. Brydon now has the opportunity to respond through the established process. As we do not wish to prejudge the outcome, it would not be appropriate for us to comment further.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamECBDurhamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mercedes put team first as Russell and Antonelli face off on F1’s return to Sepang | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Championship leaders bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuit
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Championship leaders bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuit
Content: George Russell receives a fervent welcome from fans in Sepang.Photograph: Annice Lyn/ReutersView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell receives a fervent welcome from fans in Sepang.Photograph: Annice Lyn/ReutersFormula One 2026Mercedes put team first as Russell and Antonelli face off on F1’s return to SepangTitle rivals bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuitGiles RichardsFri 2 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile the byzantine nomenclature of this weekend’s “Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia” will have Formula One’s statisticians muttering darkly under their breath for years to come, the import of the sport’s return to the Sepang circuit remains all too straightforward at the sharp end. Complicated only perhaps by a Red Bull resurgence and an enthused Max Verstappen, determined to make his mark on the championship run-in.The return to Malaysia for its first race since 2017 has been welcomed in F1. It is a much-liked circuit among drivers, albeit the high temperatures and humidity make for an enormous physical challenge.Lewis Hamilton backs Vasseur but believes Ferrari leadership structure could changeRead moreHowever, this is no long-term return to Sepang. It is back, as its torturously titled branding suggests, as a one-off replacement for the Bahrain GP, which wascancelled earlier this yearbecause of the war in the Middle East. The Bahrain GP it is then, right down to the Bahraini backing, a Bahrain GP trophy and Bahraini-themed activities at the circuit but the pole and the victory will most assuredly be earned in Sepang, leading to said statisticians deploying the asterisk on their keyboard.For the title protagonists, however, the name is moot. What matters is the race and both the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, and his rival and Mercedes teammate George Russell want to make a mark in Malaysia. Antonelli leads Russell by 66 points with eight rounds remaining. A handsome lead but he dropped 15 points to the British driver at the last round in Bakuwhere Russell showed the best form of his season, dominant across the weekend.Antonelli, who made a costly error in qualifying and finished fifth, declared it his “worst” weekend and vowed to re-establish the order in Malaysia, while Russell felt a confidence and ease with the car that he has not enjoyed all season. A platform, he felt, from which to build a late title tilt at Antonelli.The prospect of a comeback from Russell, applying pressure to his 20-year-old teammate who is in only his second season in F1, might put Mercedes too under pressure in managing them. A process of which they are all too aware, as the last time F1 was in Malaysia it was the first year after the Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg relationship at Mercedes had come apart with rancour. Nonetheless the team insist they will continue to allow their current drivers to race one another.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli arrives in Sepang having seen his title procession jolted at the last race.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters“Does it [Russell finding form] change the dynamic? I think from the overarching philosopher’s standpoint, no,” said the team principal, Toto Wolff, this week. “Because we want to give both drivers equal opportunity and to go for a championship. But the team comes first. That has always been the Mercedes philosophy.”To that end they have brought a swathe of upgrades to Sepang, only their second major developments of the season, including adaptations to the floor, rear suspension and rear bodywork. They have been long-awaited but as ever with the first year of new regulations there is no guarantee they will simply bolt on and find lap time.Malaysia is the first test and fine-tuning will be required given it is something of a baptism of fire, with the circuit’s heat and its abrasive, high-degradation surface making for a far from normal run-out. Indeed, how the teams handle tyre degradation will probably define the race, a finely balanced test for the strategists of two or even potentially three pit stops.For Mercedes, in Friday’s practice sessions finding the right set-up and operating window to make the most of potential downforce gains was proving tricky, with Russell and Antonelli seventh and eighth in the second session.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey will probably find more pace come Saturday at which point they may have to deal with Verstappen and Red Bull, whose car has come on in leaps and bounds after their upgrade in Baku. Verstappen has yet to win this year and, while the title is gone, he is fiercely competitive and still determined to take the flag. The Red Bull was well balanced out of the blocks in Sepang, and Verstappen declared it “positive” and a “decent start”. Such guarded judgment is praise indeed, given how often this season Verstappen has had to wrestle with a recalcitrant car from the off.View image in fullscreenArvid Lindblad in action during the free practice session in Sepang.Photograph: Fazry Ismail/EPAHe was not quickest in second practice when Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, also showing strong form, took the top spot from Verstappen’s Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar by a tenth. But the Dutchman, in fourth, did not set a time doing a qualifying simulation on soft tyres. Verstappen surely has more to come and will be hungrily eyeing a shot at a win that would make it two in a row separated by almost a decade since hetook the flag when it was last held in Malaysia in 2017.A point to prove then for the four-time champion but for Antonelli and Russell it is relative points that matter and perhaps most importantly in defining the championship, who asserts themself to the greatest effect in this one-off showdown in Malaysia.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Slegers feels support from Arsenal hierarchy despite dismal run but biggest test looms | Arsenal Women | The Guardian
description: Renée Slegers said the board has been ‘really good and positive’ at a ‘difficult time’ as the team prepare to visit WSL leaders Manchester City on Sunday
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Renée Slegers said the board has been ‘really good and positive’ at a ‘difficult time’ as the team prepare to visit WSL leaders Manchester City on Sunday
Content: Renée Slegers (left) has overseen only one win in five matches and Arsenal have slipped seven points behind WSL leaders Manchester City.Photograph: Martin Rickett/Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenRenée Slegers (left) has overseen only one win in five matches and Arsenal have slipped seven points behind WSL leaders Manchester City.Photograph: Martin Rickett/Ben Whitley/PAArsenal WomenSlegers feels support from Arsenal hierarchy despite dismal run but biggest test loomsBoard ‘really good and positive’ at ‘difficult time’Gunners visit WSL leaders Manchester City on SundayTom GarryFri 2 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRenée Slegers says she has felt the full support of Arsenal’s board and praised her senior players for showing “monumental leadership” this week as she vows to find solutions to recent poor form before Sunday’s pivotal trip to Manchester City.One win in five matches has put Slegers under mounting pressure. Arsenal let slip a two-goal leadto draw at Paris FCin the Women’s ­Champions League on Wednesday and in the WSL they have slipped seven points behind City, the ­leaders and defending champions, having scored only twice in their four league games.Shaw secures WCL draw against Real Madrid as Manchester City show spirit after week of turmoilRead moreSlegers was in a determined mood on Friday, speaking of a “strong togetherness” at the club. Asked whether she felt the full support of the board, she replied: “Yes, that’s what I felt. That’s been positive and that’s helped me. The club’s leadership has been really good and positive for me in this moment because everyone thinks this is a difficult time and this is not something that we want for the team and for the club.“But the leadership from Clare [Wheatley, the director of football], Rich [Garlick, CEO], James [King, director of football operations], Jodie [Taylor, technical director] has been superb. So I want to give everything back to the club.“There’s been a lot of contact, of course. There’s a strong­togetherness and I’ve really felt their support and they’re here with us, which I’m very grateful for, of course, because I care so much for the team, for the club. I believe in the potential that we ­possess. I believe we can come out of this.”The 37-year-old Dutchwoman began with an apology to the media for her no-show after Wednesday’s game, whenArsenal conceded a bizarre penaltyafter Leah Williamson was penalised for handling the ball in the area when she thought she was taking a goal-kick. Slegers’s assistant Aaron D’Antino stepped in.PosTeamPGDPts1Man City Women48122Tottenham Hotspur Women413103Chelsea Women48104London City Lionesses4595Liverpool FC Women4476Everton Women4-167Arsenal Women4058Crystal Palace Women4-659Man Utd Women4-5410West Ham Women4-3311Brighton & Hove Albion Women4-3212Birmingham City Women4-4213Aston Villa Women4-7214Charlton Women4-90“After the game there was emotion from my end,” Slegers said. “[I] make the decision to be with the team instead.” She said that had felt important but added: “I will be there next time. I said to the team: ‘I’m angry, I’m really angry, and let’s try to use the emotions that we’re feeling and let it fuel us moving forward, so that’s definitely part of what I hope [to see] and what I believe is going to help us in the right direction.”Sunday presents a huge challenge against a side who have a 100% record in the WSL this season and have won all their home league matches since Andrée Jeglertz took over as head coach in the summer of 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSlegers praised her squad for their response since Wednesday, saying her “players have been brilliant – I’ve seen the best sides of them”.“What the group has shown, it’s something I haven’t seen before,” she said. “The captains in the team they’ve been monumental; it’s the strongest leadership I’ve seen so far working within football, they’ve been amazing. They’re very calm, composed, solution-orientated and laser-focused. It was a great moment and I think vital for us moving forward.“It’s strange because I have to be finding a solution, so I have to be calm, I have to give direction, I have to lead now. But at the same time, what I also feel is gratitude for how everyone is responding and how together we are and how the session on the pitch was today. It was really, really good.”Explore more on these topicsArsenal WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s true: this is my final column. You have exactly 24 hours to complain before my inbox self-destructs | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Yes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Yes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyOpinionThe GuardianIt’s true: this is my final column. You have exactly 24 hours to complain before my inbox self-destructsMarina HydeYes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareJournalism 101 – a course I have yet to complete – dictates that if you have something salient to say you should get there fast. So right now, I should mention that this is my last ever column for the Guardian. I’ll level with you: I spent a long time wondering how to write it. At first, I thought it should be about all the things I’ve learned, purely because that would be a hell of a lot shorter than a column about all the things I keep failing to learn, no matter how many times I make the mistakes. For example: if you’ve got a good joke, you’d best put it in the intro. (Why is there literally no joke in this intro?)Or: remember that people love the piss-taking until it strays into the arena of something they like, when it suddenly becomes wholly unacceptable. Take the time I wrote: “Arguing on the internet is like playing real tennis:even if you win, you’re still a twat”. This prompted an immediate missive from a member of the Cambridge University real tennis club, which appeared on the letters page under the headline “Real tennis has been served badly by this unfair slur” and began: “Like many Guardian readers, I have thoroughly enjoyed and always look forward to reading Marina Hyde’s witty and caustic commentaries on the world about us. However …” Incidentally, I told this story at one book tour event, and then at the signing afterwards, a lovely young lady came up to get a book dedicated to her father, Jeremy. And of course, she said: “I should probably mention, he’s the guy who wrote in from the Cambridge University real tennis club.” Truly, the circle of life. To Jeremy, and the many other Jeremies who have written in over the years, let me just say: we all know the real twats are rackets players.In the end, though, this could only be largely a column of thanks. I’ve ended up covering so many things over my time at the Guardian – from World Cups to Olympic Games to just the 47 general elections – but for the past few years, my permanent berth has been here in the Opinion section. And I want to pay tribute to all the people on this hallowed desk. I have tried to be the easiest columnist to deal with … like that means anything. Columnists are very possibly the worst demographic in journalism. And as you know, that really DOES mean something. As I say, I’ve tried to keep my interventions in the editorial process very limited, but I do have to accept I have basically said three things to the Opinion desk, on repeat. 1. “So what if it’s in bad taste?” (I stand by that one.) 2. “It’s not offensive – what you’ve done is confuse the subject of the joke with the object of the joke.” (I mean … that genuinely is so obnoxious. I can only apologise.) And 3. the extremely timeworn: “why have you put a headline on this that makes me look like a – ”. And then I have to use a word that even in the Guardian you’re only allowed to use if it’s in reported speech.The amazing editors and subeditors have borne all of that with good humour and equanimity. I don’t know what they’ve said after we’ve put down the phone to each other, but God knows they’d have been entitled to it.I think we can all live without my retrospective, but I will say my time at the Guardian began in lively fashion, working on the Diary column. Quite soon after starting, we were given a one-offOsama bin Laden puppetby the Spitting Image creators, which I was dispatched to get photographed on the steps of the French embassy in London. (But why?) The only problem was that the latex Osama was carrying a toy AK-47, and just as I’d propped him against the door of the embassy to get the picture, it swung open and I was pulled inside by French security. Things escalated fast. In the end, the incident was attended by 10 police squad cars and five police motorcycles, and Knightsbridge was brought to a total standstill.Again: why? Why did we do this? Genuinely the reasons for it are lost in the mists of time for me. Like so many stunts pulled by what we used to call newspapers, it made absolute sense in the context of the news cycle in which it happened, and makes absolutely no sense once ripped from those temporal moorings. But over two decades on, I would obviously like to thank the various police forces on the scene – French, Met, and diplomatic – for deciding not to press charges, which would, I sense, have made the rest of my so-called career rather tricky.Over time, that old Fleet Street wild west gave way to the digital wild west in which we live now – a place of no less remarkable incident. One of the bizarre things that came with the advent of social media was seeing which famous people reposted your columns. Probably my favourite was when I wrote one about a new ITV show whereRob Lowe played a police chief in Brexit Britain. (I know – how did it not get a second season?) In the course of this column, I happened to digress all the way back to that time in 1988 when Rob was campaigning for Michael Dukakis at the Democratic national convention, on the eve of which he ended up making a sex tape in his convention hotel in Georgia with two girls, one of whom was 16. And then I mentioned that at my school, we were all totally thrilled and excited when that story came out, because it meant that Rob Lowe was definitely open to sex with 16-year-old girls. (cf “so what if it’s in bad taste?”)Imagine the lift on my eyebrow when Rob Lowe only went andreposted this column, particularly bearing in mind that for the past few years his timeline had consisted of incredibly wholesome content about dropping his children off at university and so on. Did it indicate that he still had a bit of the animal left in him (my preferred reading, as I don’t think you ever truly kill it off) or had he simply not read through to the relevant bit? We will, I think, never really know – and I always enjoyed such mysteries.While we let that one settle, it feels like a great moment to begin my lengthy thanks to the Guardian’s legal department, with whom it may not surprise you to learn I have shared many, many intense moments over the years. There was a point not so long ago when someone on the Opinion desk relayed to me that someone in the legal department had said: “really the best person at legalling Marina’s column is Marina”. First: no. But second: this honestly might be the greatest compliment I ever got. It’s like the old proverb goes: legal a woman’s column and you feed her for a day. Teach a woman to legal her own column and you feed her for a lifetime. I want to thank legal for all the incredibly nutritious masterclasses.And, speaking directly to the department, I am very much hoping we don’t get a complaint on this last column, although that would in some ways be amusingly on-brand. Looking back over what I’ve typed so far … I feel likeRob Loweis the most obvious vulnerability? Alas, my Guardian email address will no longer work, so – hate to say it – you guys will be on your own with this one should it materialise. What we had was simply too special to be exported over to my new inbox. (This regretful bounce-back also applies to any rackets players who may now be seeking to get in touch.)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFinally, then: that email address, and what it has meant to me. Many people don’t believe this, but in all the 25 years I have worked for the Guardian, I never had a private email address. Thus I have been in a constant – constant! – dialogue with Guardian readers who write in about my columns. Long before all the amazing digital metrics that we now have on where and how deeply our work is read, I had multiple daily emails from Guardian readers with subject headlines like “thank you”, “screw you” and – occasionally – “shame on you”. They ran the full gauntlet from adoring to bracing to skin-flaying. I would honestly not have had it any other way.If you write opinion on the news, ultimately you are in the audience business, and to have an ongoing back-and-forth with the one you’re serving has been as much of a privilege as it has been endlessly enlightening and stimulating. So how could I not save the most important people in this column to last? Thank you so much, dear readers – and I hope to see you down the trail. In the meantime, my very best wishes to you and yours. It has, I promise you, been an absolute honour.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistShe’s been making sense of the madness for the last 25 years: celebrate the end of an era with Marina Hyde’s final column collection, What a Time to Be Alive!
