title: The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism works, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism works, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Zack Polanski with Hannah Spencer and Siân Berry at the Green party conference, Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenZack Polanski with Hannah Spencer and Siân Berry at the Green party conference, Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianOpinionGreen partyThe Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should thinkJonathan FreedlandThe resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism worksFri 2 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareTomorrow I will be in synagogue to say Kaddish, the traditional mourner’s prayer,in memory of my fatherwho died eight years ago this week. If I were a member of the Green party, I would have reason to believe that that simple act could soon see me expelled as a racist.It sounds hyperbolic, butthe warning comesfrom Green party activists opposed to a resolution declaring that Zionism is racism, which will bedebated at the party conferencethis weekend. The motion, which if passed would instantly become party policy, holds that Zionism should be “treated as any other form of racism”. On that logic, given that the Greens do not admit members of self-described racist organisations, they could not tolerate members of self-described Zionist organisations – a category that includes almost every synagogue, or synagogue movement, in Britain and indeed the world. Which is why saying Kaddish could lead to expulsion.All this sounds arcane, but the Greens are no longer a fringe party. They beat Labour in a byelection in February, one of the events that catalysed the eventual removal of Keir Starmer. The Greens’ leader,Zack Polanski, hopes to win Starmer’s former seat of Holborn and St Pancras in next Thursday’s byelection. But the row over Zionism has cast a cloud over his campaign. If he loses the seat, many will conclude that the Green surge is over – which would relieve a significant electoral headache for Labour and Andy Burnham. So the stakes are high.The charitable reading is that this move originates in genuine, and widespread, horror at Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, followed by a series of unfortunate misunderstandings of what Zionism is, who Jews are and how antisemitism works.That, I repeat, is the charitable reading, but let’s go with it. It’s worth saying that if the proposers of this motion had simply wanted to express their revulsion at the catastrophic devastation of Gaza and those who executed it, they could have denounced Israel and the Israeli government. But their admitted purpose is to go much further – to attack Israel’s very existence and the movement that led to it: Zionism.As Polanski, who has been twisting in all directions on this subject, has tried to argue, Zionism means different things to different people. The great Israeli writer and peacenik Amos Oz used to describe it as a family name, an umbrella for a wide range of radically different worldviews. Before Israel’s founding in 1948, you’d have cultural Zionists slugging it out with religious Zionists, Marxist Zionists raging against rightwing militaristic Zionists, all of them wholly at odds with the dominant group: socialist Zionists. What they had in common was the simple belief that Jews had the right of self-determination in their ancestral homeland, the land they had for millennia calledEretz Yisrael, the Land of Israel, and which the rest of the world called Palestine.To this day, that’s essentially what it means to be a Zionist – that you believe in a Jewish national home in some portion of historic Palestine. There are rightwing Zionists who think it should be in all of that land; there are leftwing Zionists who think it should be broadly within the much smaller boundaries that existed before the 1967 war and alongside a Palestinian state. But both groups are Zionists. The racist minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is a Zionist, but so are many of the Jewish and Israeli anti-occupation activists who volunteer to act as a “protective presence”, putting their own bodies between settler extremists and Palestinian villagers in the West Bank. To brand everyone under that one umbrella as a racist shows a deep ignorance of what the word Zionism means and the sheer range of people who identify with it.It also reveals a wilful misunderstanding of Jews andJudaism. Social media has been full in recent days of supposedly progressive non-Jews telling Jews what Judaism is and what it is not – with an arrogance that, I suspect, they would find unacceptable iin a majority group addressing any other minority – and the same error recurs. Breezily, we are told that Zionism is merely a political ideology, wholly separate from Judaism, which means, happily, that one can denounce the former without expressing any animus towards the latter. If only it were so simple.Take that Kaddish prayer I’ll be saying. It refers to “Israel” three times. The Jews were calledAm Yisrael, the people of Israel, centuries before we were called Jews. What’s more, when I say the prayer, I will, following tradition, be facing east – towards Jerusalem. The prayer book in my hand will be full of references to Jerusalem and indeed to Zion, expressing in a hundred poetic ways a yearning to return. This is not some new, political thing. It’s what Jews have been saying and doing for millennia. Many, many centuries before Zionism was a political movement, it was a longing – the need to end a painful exile from the Land of Israel – enshrined in the very heart of Judaism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy BurnhamRead moreWhich is one reason why, incidentally, the language of “settler colonialism”, repeated in the Green motion, fits Zionism so badly. When, say, the French settled in Algeria, they were not returning to the land where the French people were born, where French had been spoken two millennia earlier, and to which the dispersed and lethally persecuted French people had longed to return for 2,000 years. It’s also why, though of course there are plenty of anti-Zionist Jews, you will struggle to find a synagogue beyond the fringes of ultra-orthodoxy that does not identify in some way with Zionism – not, I stress, with this or that Israeli government or policy, but with the idea, the dream, of the Jews’ return to their ancient home. That dream became a matter of basic human survival after a history of bloody persecution reached its climax eight decades ago, in the murder of 6 million Jews by the Nazis and their collaborators across Europe. It’s that need for a refuge from antisemitism – a racism that claimed so many lives, for so long – that the advocates of Sunday’s motion would declare to be racism.A group of Jewish Greens tried to alert their comrades to these dangers, asking for an amendment that might allow Jews to go to synagogue, but they were rejected. When one committedly anti-Zionist Jew rose to speak at a party workshop last week, he wasshouted downwith cries of “Zionist”. Polanski, who is himself Jewish and has called for the motion to be amended, saysthere’s a simple solution: if Jews denounce Israel in the terms demanded, agreeing to condemn “the occupation … the apartheid … the genocide”, they should be left alone. But the resolution itself insists on more. For Jews to comply, they would have to deny all connection with their historic homeland. This has so often been a feature of antisemitism: century after century, Jews are told that if they only disavow this belief or that practice, if they only say these words, they will be admitted into polite society. Where once Jews were told to embrace Christ, now they are told to disavow the world’s only Jewish country. The specific demand has changed; but the impulse is the same.In each generation, those making such demands of Jews believe they are acting in a righteous cause. The Christian persecutors of the Inquisition were sure that they were honouring Jesus; today’s Greens are certain they are advancing the cause of anti-racism, even as they would hound and defame and shame a tiny minority. AnyGreen partymember voting for this motion should reflect on that history and consider the company they are joining. It will be full of people they despise – but they will fit right in.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: For too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Ed Miliband and Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference, Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenEd Miliband and Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference, Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAOpinionAndy BurnhamFor too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that?Andy BeckettThe PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changesFri 2 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTShareHow much can aLabourgovernment change the country? According to many voters, journalists and politicians, including plenty in the party itself, the answer to that stubbornly recurring question has always been: not that much. Labour governments can’t restructure the economy, radically redistribute wealth, truly empower the disadvantaged or adopt a genuinely ethical foreign policy without upsetting too many powerful interests, from the British rich to the US government to global financial markets.This endlessly repeated conventional wisdom – internalised by some on the left as well as centrists and the right – has haunted many Labour governments, from the first, tentative ones in the 1920s to Keir Starmer’s diligent but failed administration a century later. Yet conventional wisdom can be wrong, especially in volatile periods such as the current one, when precedent may count for little.At last year’s Labour conference, Andy Burnham was widely derided for what was seen as a half-launched and clumsyleadership coup attempt. Much of the media and Starmer’s cabinet reckoned his chances of being prime minister were gone for good. Yet, at this week’s unusually packed and perhaps unwisely optimistic gathering, Burnham’s can-do presence was almost as dominant as Tony Blair’s in his early leadership years: a constant point of reference, from the main hall to the merch stands to leftwing fringe events.Moreover, Burnham appears to want to use his personal dominance – which may well be briefer than Blair’s, given Labour’s more fragile position in a more fragmented politics – to open up an array of huge issues that his party has long been advised to keep closed. Electoral reform, social care, public intervention in failing privatised utilities, the pension triple lock, evenrejoining the EU: announcements about exploring or pursuing all these punctuated hisconference speech, in a sequence of softly voiced political shocks.“Change will be difficult,” he acknowledged. But he insisted: “More of the same isn’t good enough.” At an excited fringe event the night before, his ally Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who in that job and his previous one as energy secretary has pioneered Labour’s unexpected recent interest in confronting difficult problems and dangerous interests, summed up the party’s defiant new mood. “All politics is a risk. Progressive politics is a particular risk,” he said with relish. Burnham might have similar charisma and communication skills to Blair in the 1990s, but New Labour ministers did not dare say such provocative things.Defenders of that now remote-seeming political culture would argue that avoiding head-on clashes was one of the reasons Blair was twice re-elected. But Burnham, who served in the Blair government at a formative age, does also have a strong conciliatory impulse, such as his frequently stated keenness to cooperate with other parties. However, as with his reluctance to criticise them by name – his conference speech was almost completely free of the usual party-political attacks – this apparent absence of aggression is in one sense the opposite: a determined attempt to break with the ultra-partisan politics of the post-Brexit decade that has excited many journalists but increasingly exhausted and alienated the public.Burnham might come across as a nice bloke but he is ruthless, wrongfooting opponents and renderingtheir tactics obsolete, as his supposedly formidable Labour enemies such as Morgan McSweeney learned this year. Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage’s perpetual outrage and tribalism suddenly seem rigid and unreasonable next toBurnham’s talk of hopeand national togetherness, and his disarming admission this week that all politicians must do better, that “this country isn’t where any of us would want it to be”.Labour’s modest but persistent rise in the polls suggests that sufficient voters have had enough of the old high-argument, low-achievement politics to make Labour the leading party again for a period, perhaps up to the next general election and even beyond, when many of his ambitious reforms are actually meant to take place. Of course, proposing, let alone implementing, major changes to the status quo such as loosening the triple lock will also make many voters absolutely furious (even if that policy initiallyappears popular), and provide regular targets for Labour’s enemies in Westminster and the media. Yet, with the electorate more divided than ever, and the bar for re-election probably set as low as winning over less than a third of voters, being controversial or unpopular matters less for a government than before – provided it holds its nerve and pleases a large enough core of supporters. Burnham’s sweeping attacks on Labour bogeymen such as the privatised utilities seem likely to achieve that. Meanwhile, his cross-party overtures and support for electoral reform may well lure voters and politicians from the Lib Dems and Greens.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes | Larry ElliottRead moreLike Pedro Sánchez in Spain, another centre-left premier of similar age who has managed to stay in power for eight years, Burnham is a paradoxical politician: both frank and evasive; opposed to populism and good at populist gestures; prepared to echo the left’s critique of capitalism but also pro-business; a self-styled lone saviour who is able to work in coalitions. Photogenic and politically agile – you could say shameless – Sánchez and Burnham seem better suited to today’s world of flux, short attention spans and deep discontent than the previous generation of stiff social democrats such as Starmer. Perhaps the modern centre-left is finally working out how to govern and reshape the societies that its more popular 1990s predecessor never sufficiently reformed.For too long, it has been the right that expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. If Burnham’s barely begun administration is to become a significant one – perhaps like that of Harold Wilson, another slippery, charming Labour leader with Merseyside connections – it will need to enact big reforms as well as talk promisingly about them.Sixty years ago, Wilson won an election landslide, and commemorative items competed with the cult of Burnham on the merch stands at conference in Liverpool. “Wilson’s greatest hits”, said the cover of a souvenir record, “Featuring Creation of the Open University, Equal Pay Act, Abolished Capital Punishment, Race Relations Act, Abortion Act, Decriminalised Homosexuality”. Wilson’s premiership was often unpopular and struggled economically, but it lastingly changed Britain by resolving some contentious social questions. Burnham may have to settle for doing the same.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourPensionsElectoral reformSocial carecommentShareReuse this content

title: AI threatens to destroy so much of our culture. Our greatest loss might be our ability to listen | Shirleene Robinson | The Guardian
description: Australians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019
Content: ‘Listening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing,’ writes Shirleene Robinson.Photograph: Dumitru Ochievschi/Alamy Stock VectorView image in fullscreen‘Listening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing,’ writes Shirleene Robinson.Photograph: Dumitru Ochievschi/Alamy Stock VectorOpinionLanguagesAI threatens to destroy so much of our culture. Our greatest loss might be our ability to listenShirleene RobinsonAustralians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 20.19 EDTShareWe talk a lot about losing our ability to write as a result of AI. I’m convinced our greatest loss might be our ability to listen. Listening to different views and entering into different worlds is integral to our humanity.But Australians are conversing less every year. While rapidly evolving AI tools and chatbots promise faster responses and so-called “empathetic” listening, a recentstudyshowed we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019. That adds up to a staggering loss of 120,000 spoken words per person, compared with the year before.Hanson says Australia has a ‘language problem’ due to immigration. After arriving with little English, Marziyah is now a lawyer with a missionRead moreThis matters immensely. Language is culture. It tells us who we are.As an oral historian, I’ve spent much of my career studying the power of human speech and storytelling. Between 2018 and early 2024, I led a team at the National Library of Australia responsible for the largest oral history collection in the southern hemisphere, which began in 1957 and now consists of more than 58,000 hours of recording. More recently, I’ve immersed myself in listening to hundreds more hours of this collection, working on a new book and an accompanying podcast.The depth of the library’s collection, much of which is available online through Trove, is extraordinary. It holds accounts of First Nations Australians speaking about deep history and first-person memories reaching back into the 19th century.All up, I’ve now listened to thousands of Australians from different eras, places and backgrounds tell their stories in their own words.This has helped me understand exactly what we lose when we stop listening. When I listen to an oral history, I immerse myself in the life of someone I mostly likely will never meet. In a world where our social circles are reducing due to distance, remote work and increasing time online, the gift of hearing from someone different is precious.double quotation markI often hear Australian accents from the past or words no longer spoken, along with many professions described that no longer existDame Mary Gilmore, born in 1865, speaks of tallow candles and life before electricity. An Australian prime minister recalls being elected after their party spent 23 years in opposition. A mother who risked everything shares how she sought refuge here, crossing pirate-infested seas after the Vietnam war. A pioneer stationed in Antarctica reflects on challenges of distance. The next voice may be Dr Ella Stack, a Darwin doctor who survived Cyclone Tracy, stayed to help, recorded survivor memories, then ensured Darwin was rebuilt as mayor.I often hear Australian accents from the past or words no longer spoken, along with many professions described that no longer exist. As I listen, I’ve sometimes cried with laughter because of the ability of some people to share memories with humour.I’ve listened to people remembering times of great social disruption, such as the 1891 Queensland shearers’ strikes or the conscription debates of the first world war. I’ve been deeply moved by the courage of First Nations Australians who shared testimonies of being part of the Stolen Generations.Everything Australians put online could be scraped for AI under proposed new rules. How will you be affected?Read moreListening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing, foster the exchange of information, grow understanding and spark new ideas. It is also deeply linked to building empathy.Empathy is the richest gift listening offers. That will be our greatest loss if we speak and hear less. By engaging with experiences of others without requiring instant gratification and artificial agreement, we enter into other’s lives. We grow to be patient and appreciate difference. We learn we can disagree but in ways not unnecessarily destructive.Mostly we learn that, although a century or more of time may separate us as well as our diverse backgrounds and experiences, we can still connect through moments of shared humanity and experiences of love, loss, change, challenge, joy and resilience. These voices from the past can resonate as powerfully as ever in our present.Dr Shirleene Robinson is an oral historian and visiting fellow at the University of Technology Sydney’s school of communication and social sciences. She editedThe Memory Tapes: Voices from the Oral History Collection of the National Library of Australiaand hosted the accompanyingpodcastExplore more on these topicsLanguagesOpinionHistorySocial historyIndigenous AustraliansAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: Richard E Grant has one hope of lasting on Celebrity Traitors: leaning into his eccentricity  | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: Chats with inanimate objects, farting into Tupperware: this cornered animal must sell his confession as just another quirk
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Chats with inanimate objects, farting into Tupperware: this cornered animal must sell his confession as just another quirk
Content: Genius or idiot? No one has played The Traitors quite like this before.Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenGenius or idiot? No one has played The Traitors quite like this before.Photograph: Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBC/PAThe TraitorsRichard E Grant has one hope of lasting on Celebrity Traitors: leaning into his eccentricityStuart HeritageChats with inanimate objects, farting into Tupperware: this cornered animal must sell his confession as just another quirkFri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTShareAs we all know, The Traitors is a game of deception. The entire point is to conceal your true motivations in order to better carry out a series of murders undetected. This is the way it should be, and the way it always was. And thenRichard E Grantcame along.Grant’s trajectory during the opening episode of Celebrity Traitors was as follows. Step one: be selected as a traitor by Claudia Winkleman. Step two: immediately tell everyone you are a traitor.As a dumbfounded Joe Lycett pointed out in the aftermath of Grant’s revelation, nobody has ever done this in the history ofThe Traitors. The entire system works on a process of elaborate deduction based on a complex matrix of pattern recognition and gut instinct. This, as you will be aware, is much harder to do when the villain straight-up announces that he’s a villain without any form of coercion.13:54Celebrity Traitors: has Richard E Grant blown it already? - The LatestImmediately, you can see why Grant never starred in any episodes of Columbo. This is because his episode would consist of him walking up to Peter Falk, announcing “Hello there, I am a murderer,” and being arrested. It would be 30 seconds long. Nobody would watch it.But let’s look at the positives here. By being so brazen about his identity, Grant has basically forced the game into a place it has never been before. Aside from Jerry Hall – a woman who I am beginning to suspect is wrong about everything – all the contestants this year believe Grant is a traitor. And so it is his job, and the job of his bewildered accomplice, Maya Jama, to frantically throw bodies in his path until suspicion drifts elsewhere. He’s a cornered animal, and they are often the most dangerous.It also means Grant has to play into all his latent eccentricity, to make it seem that erroneously announcing himself as a traitor when he is in fact a faithful is just something he does. To sell it, he has to make everyone around him believe that this is just one bizarre character quirk in an entire ocean of them. From now on, he has to really sell his role as the mad uncle of the castle, by muttering to himself and having conversations with inanimate objects and farting into Tupperware. This is the only way he has any hope of lasting on the show.The big question is how intentional this was, which is to say: was Richard E Grant a genius or an idiot for doing that? Certainly his horrified expression after admitting the truth seems to suggest the latter. And reactions on social media would reinforce that somewhat. Anyone who has watched The Traitors will know that drawing attention to yourself so early on is often a recipe for an early exit.Anita Singh in the Telegraph called Grant “lord of chaos”while Emily Bootle in the i called his outburst “a cock-up”. “This is the only show that could be completely sabotaged in the first episode and for that to somehow make it even better,” Bootle added.But if Grant can survive then he’ll have the freedom to move around knocking people off unbidden. For now, the spotlight is on him and him alone. Though who knows how long that might last.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsRichard E GrantcommentShareReuse this content

title: Should we refuse to give the Bayeux tapestry back to France? Of course not! So why are we keeping the Parthenon marbles? | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to Greece, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to Greece, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: The Parthenon marbles in the British Museum on 11 May 2023.Photograph: Matt Dunham/APView image in fullscreenThe Parthenon marbles in the British Museum on 11 May 2023.Photograph: Matt Dunham/APOpinionParthenon marblesShould we refuse to give the Bayeux tapestry back to France? Of course not! So why are we keeping the Parthenon marbles?Simon JenkinsIt is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to GreeceFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTShareFor the Bayeux tapestry to return to Francewould be a scandal. It is British, probably made in Canterbury by British women, and displays one of the greatest events in British history. The tapestry certainly does not belong in Normandy. It is right that it is now on British soil in the British Museum. Its display is so brief that the herd of visitors desperate to catch a glimpse of the medieval artwork must be jostled to keep moving, as if watching Shakespeare’s Henry V on fast-forward. So let’s keep it. Everybody knows possession is nine-tenths of the law. We can call it a long-term loan.I am joking, of course. This is largely what I assume the British Museum is worriedmight happen if it lent the precious Elgin, or Parthenon, marbles to Athens. In the Guardian last month, the Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, argued that the status of the Bayeux tapestry is parallel to that of the Parthenon marbles. “Both were conceived as single works, intended to be seen and understood as a whole,”he wrote, arguing it was time for the marbles to be reunited.The British Museum director, Nicholas Cullinan, even appeared to agree. He remarked that the Bayeux tapestry loan offered a “glimmer of possibility” of a deal on theParthenon marbles, which were acquired by the British Museum in 1816.Cullinan’s predecessors have long come across as jingoistic hoarders, as if the museum were a lasting memorial to the British empire.In the 1980s, the then director, Sir David Wilson, had an infamous clash with Greece’s then culture minister, Melina Mercouri, who had travelled to London to appeal for the sculptures return. “I want my marbles back,” she demanded to Wilson in front of TV cameras.The debate has since swirled back and forth. But it is as unedifying as watching grownups argue over a bag of sweets. Insofar as the public cares,a majority of Britonsthink the marbles should go back to Greece.There was a refreshing breakthrough in 2022after George Osborne became the museum’s chairand boldly opened negotiations with Athens. He even held a public debate on the matter. The objective was certainly confused. Was it a discreet exchange of some classical artefacts, or was it to be the final reuniting of the Parthenon pediments in the new Athens museum? The latter clearly made sense, both artistically and because of the significance of the Parthenon to Greek national identity.Since then, the prospect of apossible returnof the marbles has been bedevilled by politics and diplomacy. The Greek government rejects any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s “ownership”. But such de-acquisitioning would only be possible if the law were changed. Boris Johnson, once an ardent supporter of the marbles’ return,reversed his position when in office. For his part, Rishi Sunak refused to change the law and clearly wanted the marbles to stay in Britain.Cut to Andy Burnham, who we may have expected to adopt a different stance. During his brief stint as culture secretary between 2008 and 2009, Burnham was reportedly a champion of the marbles’ return. In 2002,he even sponsored a private member’s billon facilitating their transfer back to Greece. His advocacy is longstanding. As recently as 2023, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, declared: “Send them back, no strings attached. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”But Burnham has done a Johnson and Sunak and let it be known hehas reversed his position. Elgin’s ghost seems to spook the Downing Street rafters.The bottom line is there is no agreement on the nature of what a loan could look like. And to make matters worse, the British Museum is lending two minor Parthenon fragments to an exhibition of Greek sculpture opening in November in Frankfurt’s Liebieghaus museum. This has so infuriated Athens that it hasreportedly refused to lendnine fragments of the Parthenon marbles to the exhibition, as if proximity to the British ones would be contaminating. Talks are reportedly back to stalemate. This is desperately sad. I have followed this debate since first visiting the Parthenon with its then surveyor in the 1970s. The temple and its carvings must rank among the founding compositions of western culture.Bringing their sculptural integrity back to life and on the site of its creation should so clearly be the ambition of every historian and archaeologist worth their salt. For museum leaders to go about hoarding, empire-building, nit-picking and point-scoring is frankly pathetic. Modern national museums are outrageous in how they amass collections and then sometimes prevent others from seeing them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen I was chair of the National Trust, we tried to persuade the Tate Gallery and others to lend us paintings from their basements that never saw the light of day. The answer was almost always: “No, they are ours, not yours!” We thought they belonged to the public.As for leaders such as Johnson and Burnham, they demand a course of action in opposition yet lack the guts to do it in power. This has gone on long enough. Greece should drop its obsession with formal “ownership”. London should dispatch its 17 pediment sculptures on indefinite loan to Athens. Then, together, all ofEuropecan rejoice.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsParthenon marblesOpinionBritish MuseumGreeceDisputed artMuseumsEuropeHeritagecommentShareReuse this content

title: There is a way to look after people, the planet – and Britain’s growth. It’s what we call the ‘wellbeing economy’ | Jamie Driscoll | The Guardian
description: Imagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happen, says Green party politician Jamie Driscoll
Author: Jamie Driscoll
Headline: Imagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happen, says Green party politician Jamie Driscoll
Content: A wind farm off the coast of Great Yarmouth.Photograph: NJphoto/AlamyView image in fullscreenA wind farm off the coast of Great Yarmouth.Photograph: NJphoto/AlamyOpinionEconomicsThere is a way to look after people, the planet – and Britain’s growth. It’s what we call the ‘wellbeing economy’Jamie DriscollImagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happenFri 2 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTShareYou’ve just left school. What’s your future?I know a physics graduate making flat whites; a 30-year-old living in his childhood bedroom who feels like a failure; a lad in Blyth who turned down a job 15 miles away because there’s no bus, and for young people his age car insurance is almost £2,000 a year. Britain’s young people are our greatest resource, and we are failing them because capital markets won’t allocate investment where it is needed. Saying “hope”in a conference speechsounds warm. But people need a plan.The first priority of any government is the security of its people. Financial markets are sending price signals thatAI boomsand share buybacks are more important than clean energy or warm homes. We fund aircraft carriers and artillery shells. But wind turbines and council houses are part of our national security, too. Imagine a country with a 20-year investment plan, with retrofitted homes and fast transport connections that leave nowhere behind. That’s a future filled with the potential of proud work for young people.But four words run Britain: “We can’t afford it.” Governments call this mindset “prudence”. My response to it isHostage Nation, my plan to fix Britain. This is a report that lays out how to source the finance, shows what we need to build – and tracks why it would make us more prosperous and resilient. I joined the Green party to achieve this vision. As we approach the party conference, I hope this will become official Green policy that we’ll fight the next election on.Nine sets of fiscal rules have been broken and abandoned since the financial crash. Andy Haldane, a former chief economist of the Bank of England,said current fiscal ruleswere “far from optimal; in fact I’d go as far as to say silly”. TheInstitute for Fiscal Studies saidin 2024 that changing policy based on fiscal headroom projections was “almost literally mad”. What if we’re not really hostages to the bond market? What if politicians have got Stockholm syndrome instead?Bond markets are just complex betting shops. That’s their business model: guess the future, and price accordingly. That price changes when the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates or thestrait of Hormuzcloses. Why do we let bookies decide whether we build railway lines? Give a country nothing to build and struggling people will find someone to blame.Businesses want customers more than they want tax cuts or light-touch regulation. I once asked the chief executive of a global engineering firm if he would invest in green hydrogen. “I’m not investing half a billion in a plant and staff unless I can sell it for 20 years,” he said. No government gave that signal.Provide demand, and supply chains will organise themselves. When I was mayor of the North of Tyne combined authority, I moved our adult training providers from one-year to rolling three-year contracts. Employment training places rose from 22,000 to 35,000 a year on the same real-terms budget. That’s what certainty brings.Markets are great at providing barber shops and burger vans, but markets don’t build reservoirs. The only organisation that can guarantee orders for infrastructure 20 years from now is the state. Public ownership is a must for public planning. We’re not short of need:100,000 council homes a year; fully renewable energy with a storage grid; clean transport; insulating every home; buses and trains that run as one network and are cheaper and more convenient than cars; regenerated high streets with sports centres and warm youth clubs. What George Monbiot callspublic luxury.We can fund it with off-market finance. The government savings bank National Savings and Investments (originally the Post Office Savings Bank) has been goingfor more than 160 years, and 24 million of us use it. The government could offer savers national infrastructure Isas – a fair, safe return for investment in public works. The gilt market carries on; this is a separate channel insulated from tariff antics and international conflicts. No hedge fund has ever shorted a premium bond.We invest£70bn a yearin cash Isas. Our pension pools hold more than £2tn, yetless than 5% is invested in British firms. There is tax relief on both. If you want to speculate on Silicon Valley, that’s your right. But tax subsidies should be reserved for savings that build Britain.As for infrastructure, the state can outcompete private capital. For a business, wages are an expense. For a country, wages lower the welfare bill. The state collects40p in every pound back in tax. Money flows through high streets and pays business rates. A2014 pilot in Sunderlandshowed that a £5,000 investment in insulation and energy-efficient boilers for people with COPD lowered bills and reduced hospital admissions by 25% and GP appointments by 60%. Combine retrofit and clean energy at cost andenergy bills fall by 67%. It turns out the cheapest way to heat a home is also the quickest way to decarbonise a country.This is what awellbeing economy looks like. In the North of Tyne we judged projects on mental health, environmental impact and community wealth before a penny was released.What about inflation? Train the workers, build the supply chains, then release the money. This creates real capacity and builds assets on the public balance sheet. We have the powers. We don’t need new treaties or quangos. We need to wake up the state machinery we already have.In 1946 Britain was so poor we started rationing bread. The national debt was two-and-a-half times the size of the economy. That generation built the NHS. Then anaverageof 126,000 council homes every year for 35 years. Eight prime ministers and two parties kept building. Today our relative debt is under half that. We have machines they could only dream of. They weren’t richer than us. They were braver.I don’t have a crystal ball, but I’ll wager the upcoming budget will tinker around the edges of these issues. Voters already know the Greens care, and with a plan to really fix Britain – and fund it – support will keep growing. Hostage Nation is backed by 134 endnotes that are there to be checked. We can start this plan tomorrow. Values win sympathy, but answers win seats.Jamie Driscoll is a Green party councillor on Newcastle city council and former North of Tyne mayorExplore more on these topicsEconomicsOpinionEconomic growth (GDP)commentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Conservative conference: a party still searching for a purpose | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Kemi Badenoch has a lot to say about Labour and Reform UK but none of it amounts to a coherent alternative programme for government
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Kemi Badenoch has a lot to say about Labour and Reform UK but none of it amounts to a coherent alternative programme for government
Content: ‘To make her party competitive in British politics, Mrs Badenoch needs more serious arguments.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreen‘To make her party competitive in British politics, Mrs Badenoch needs more serious arguments.’Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAOpinionConservative conferenceThe Guardian view on the Conservative conference: a party still searching for a purposeEditorialKemi Badenoch has a lot to say about Labour and Reform UK but none of it amounts to a coherent alternative programme for governmentFri 2 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.45 EDTShareThe Conservative party is far from the margin of British politics, but it has yet to recover the relevance to which it feels historically entitled. The Tories are flattered by their status as the official opposition in parliament. In the wider country, Reform UK has set the agenda on the right, overtaking Kemi Badenoch’s party in opinion polls andpoaching MPsfrom her benches.But Nigel Farage’s progress has stalled. Scrutiny of Reform’sfinanceshas made its leader look shifty. Competition from Restore Britain, an extreme nationalist party, has denied Mr Farage the luxury of taking far-right votes for granted. Pandering to a hardcore audience makes it difficult for Reform to affect the moderation required to capture more Tory and Labour votes.This creates an opportunity forConservativesto reassert themselves as the mainstream opposition to Labour. Many Tories believe the available space has grown since Andy Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.Mr Burnham has abolder agendathan his predecessor, and he communicates it well – qualities that have been rewarded with a poll-ratings recovery. It is also a programme with unapologetic left-liberal ambition – universal social care, free at the point of use; opening the door to public ownership of utilities; dissolving red lines in relations with the EU; electoral reform. Under new leadership, the party has risen out of the defensive crouch from which it fought the election, fearful of offending Conservative sensibilities. Conservatives are duly offended. The vision that Mr Burnham outlined at his party conference last week was a repudiation of Margaret Thatcher’s legacy, and there is no greater heresy in Tory doctrine.Mrs Badenoch will not struggle to articulate a rebuttal at her party’s conference in Birmingham over the next few days. She is a devotee of the Conservativecult of the Iron Lady, committed to low taxes and a smaller state as axioms of political virtue. She believes there are voters who share that conviction, who will be repelled by Labour, and who are deeply wary of Mr Farage. This is the electoral audience she is targeting.It isn’t an irrational strategy, but nor is it a well-developed one. Mrs Badenoch likes to debate the opponent she wants rather than the one she has. She accuses Mr Burnham of taking Britain back to the 1970s, without engaging with his analysis of what went wrong in the 1980s or considering that her own nostalgic ideology might need revision with reference to subsequent decades.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage.Photograph: Scott Heppell/ReutersHer approach to Reform is even more blinkered. The Tories want voters to take a dim view of Mr Farage’s candidacy to be prime minister, but they are selective in their criticism. Mrs Badenoch joins the fray over opaque donations, but has less to say about Reform’s toxic rhetoric around immigration, largely because Conservative policy fits theFaragist mould. The traffic in defections has slowed, but the boundary between the two parties is porous.To make her party competitive in British politics, Mrs Badenoch needs more serious arguments. She needs an answer to Mr Burnham that doesn’t retreat into lazy 20th-century political cliche. And she needs to reject Mr Farage’s brand of national populism in terms that give voters reasons to distinguish between their two parties on points of principle, when at the moment there are none.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Barack Obama’s new podcast: all the president’s books | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: From Oprah Winfrey to Dua Lipa, there is no shortage of celebrity literary champions. But the former US leader is in a class of his own
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: From Oprah Winfrey to Dua Lipa, there is no shortage of celebrity literary champions. But the former US leader is in a class of his own
Content: ‘For Obama, reading helps to create “a moral framework” and is “a way of understanding the challenges of the moment”.’Photograph: Erin Hooley/APView image in fullscreen‘For Obama, reading helps to create “a moral framework” and is “a way of understanding the challenges of the moment”.’Photograph: Erin Hooley/APOpinionBarack ObamaThe Guardian view on Barack Obama’s new podcast: all the president’s booksEditorialFrom Oprah Winfrey to Dua Lipa, there is no shortage of celebrity literary champions. But the former US leader is in a class of his ownFri 2 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.45 EDTShareAt the Labour party conferenceAndy Burnham revealed that Hamlet, Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness and Tony Harrison’s poem V are his favourite works of literature. The UK’s first prime minister with an English literature degree was not the only political figure sharing his book choices last week. Barack Obama, the US’s most literary president since Abraham Lincoln,launched a new podcastin which he discusses six books that shaped him with writer friends.First up was the actor – andrecently turned short story writer– Tom Hanks on Marilynne Robinson’sGilead, a meditation on faith, fatherhood and forgiveness in the form of a letter written by a 76-year-old pastor to his son. It was an unabashedly highbrow start. With the exception of John le Carré’s cold war classic Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, Mr Obama’s selections are American: Toni Morrison’s Song of Solomon, Cormac McCarthy’s All the Pretty Horses, James Baldwin’s essays The Fire Next Time and Robert Penn Warren’s All the King’s Men. Questions of democracy, race, power and violence are all here.The former president’s summer and end-of-year reading lists are known for having an “Obama effect” on sales.This season’s picksinclude the Booker-shortlisted The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout, of whom he has long been a fan. His podcast, A Great Book with Barack Obama, joins a crowded arena. Established celebrity book clubs include those run byOprah WinfreyandReese Witherspoonin the US and Richard and Judy in the UK. These are now competing with starry newcomers, such asDua Lipa’s Service95, appealing to gen Z readers. The British singer’s conversations with bookish heavyweights have seen her hailed as“the best literary interviewer”of our time. Audiences can decide for themselves this month when she is curator and host of theLondon literature Festival at the Southbank Centre, with guests including Zadie Smith.View image in fullscreenDua Lipa.Photograph: Matt Alexander/PAWith reading for pleasure among young people at itslowest level in two decades, high-profile champions have an important role to play – even if celebrity endorsements are sometimes accompanied by a whiff of elitism. Back in 2001,Jonathan Franzen caused a furoreby snubbing an invitation for The Corrections to be featured on Oprah’s Book Club, deriding her choices as “schmaltzy” and “one-dimensional”. The announcement that Lipa would give the Booker prize ceremony speech in 2022raised eyebrows in the industry. Yet a recommendation from Winfrey or Lipa can catapult a novel on to the bestseller lists.You don’t need to be a pop star or president to become a literary tastemaker. Online communities such as BookTok and Bookstagram have democratised the book world. Everyone can be a critic today. Asthe rise of romantasynovels shows, bookfluencers are a powerful new force in publishing.But in a speeded-up world, books podcasts are a balm for the soul. They can boost debuts, resurface old classics and rescue forgotten treasures. The path from politics to podcasting is now a well-trodden one. But an in-depth literary podcast from a former US president is a first, and not likely to be seconded anytime soon. “There are jokes about the Trump library,”Robinson quippedin 2018. “Because there won’t be any books in there.” For Mr Obama, reading helps to create “a moral framework” and is “a way of understanding the challenges of the moment”. Rarely have literary-minded leaders been so urgently needed.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Englishness is not defined by ethnicity | British identity and society | The Guardian
description: Letters: Maariyah Seedat wonders at what point does her family become ‘English’ enough, Mark James Slater has always regarded himself as British and not English. Plus letters from Dr Richard Seabrook and Alan Baker
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Maariyah Seedat wonders at what point does her family become ‘English’ enough, Mark James Slater has always regarded himself as British and not English. Plus letters from Dr Richard Seabrook and Alan Baker
Content: ‘Simply being English is such a restrictive definition, and I am proud to be counted as British as any of my neighbours.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Simply being English is such a restrictive definition, and I am proud to be counted as British as any of my neighbours.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoBritish identity and societyLettersEnglishness is not defined by ethnicityMaariyah Seedatwonders at what point does her family become ‘English’ enough,Mark James Slaterhasalways regarded himself as British and not English. Plus letters fromDr Richard SeabrookandAlan BakerFri 2 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTShareJason Okundaye’s piece on defining Englishness mirrored my own experiences as a member of an ethnic minority (Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone?, 26 September).As a child, growing up in multicultural Leicester in the 1990s and 2000s, I was “corrected” by adults in positions of authority – the vast majority of whom were white – for wanting to call myself English. It was a descriptor that I could not claim and, implicitly, was not my right because of my skin colour. I learned very quickly that referring to myself as British was the better, less objectionable option.It always rubbed me up the wrong way. At what point does my family become “English” enough? How many generations later? I love my country of birth, and when I am abroad my Englishness is never brought into question, so why can my country not accept me as I am?I believe that lived experiences like mine indicate why ethnic-minority adults “prefer an identification with Britishness”: a potent mix of historically being put in one’s place, and a desire to avoid exhausting circular arguments with those who cannot see beyond the colour of one’s skin.Maariyah SeedatToronto, CanadaGiven that my grandparents’ family names are a mixture of Norman French, Dutch and Huguenot French, and we have probably lived within the borders of England from arrival to today, and that I was born in London, is it strange that I have always regarded myself as British and not English?My understanding of being English is either the staid and stuffy upper classes residing in rural isolation or having some background role in an embassy or assurance office or living in a working-class community of very similar people in the terraced streets around a (former) factory.That isn’t me. I am as invested in the other British cultures of Scotland, Wales, Ireland, Cornwall, the West Indies, Pakistan, Australia, India, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Africa and the US, not to mention western Europe and more recently eastern Europe.Simply being English is such a restrictive definition, and I am proud to be counted as British as any of my neighbours.Mark James SlaterHelston, CornwallJason Okundaye asks “Can you be English and non-white?” The answer is no, according to the government’s own system ofcoding ethnicitiesfor the 2021 census. English appears as a subcategory of white, and not elsewhere. Thus it is not possible using this coding scheme to describe oneself as, for example, Black English, whereas you can choose to declare yourself Black British.So the racist implications of “Englishness” are baked into the coding scheme until such time as “English” is moved out of its colour category and treated as a cultural identity (whatever that is) rather than as a consequence of DNA.Dr Richard SeabrookBeckenham, LondonWhile Jason Okundaye claims as a simple truth that “there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s ‘English’ have descended”, he misses a more important general point.While I am able to claim to be a personally responsible agent as a grandfather, father, husband, researcher and writer, I am unable to claim responsibility for the fundamental structure within which I have acted and continue to act. I was born in Canterbury, Kent and thus I am English. My birth certificate, dated 20 October 1938, records my “sex” as “boy”. I am simply not responsible for my nationality or gender.I am accordingly neither proud nor ashamed to be an Englishman: that is just a matter of fact. And this in turn means that I cannot either adulate or castigate others of different nationality or gender on the grounds of those characteristics alone. The right’s fixation based on bloodlines and biological inheritance has no foundation: it is baseless and crass.Alan BakerCambridgeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Pleaseemailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in ourletterssection.Explore more on these topicsBritish identity and societyRacelettersShareReuse this content

title: Utilities are public services – and should not be run as businesses | Utilities | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit
Content: Utilities ‘have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyView image in fullscreenUtilities ‘have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyUtilitiesLettersUtilities are public services – and should not be run as businessesReaders respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that  they could be run for the public benefitFri 2 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTShareWill Hutton and Andy Haldane advocate “turning [utilities] into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim” (Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it, 25 September). So still companies, but with a public interest rather than a profit motive. This is still the wrong approach.Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage.The present government appears to be edging sideways, through metro mayors and joint working, towards governance for city regions. This should be formalised and given a full portfolio of responsibilities, powers and resources for strategic planning, economic development, education, health, transportation, infrastructure and the environment. Infrastructure should include water and sewerage.As an example, urban rainwater needs to be collected and recycled for cooling, which was normal practice for thousands of years in southern Europe. Such practice should be moving north to include water reserves for wildfire control. How could such provisions, urban cooling and wildfire control ever be met through the profit motive?If the present water companies in England have liabilities that exceed the value of their assets, and cannot meet their legal responsibilities, then it is difficult to see why they should be rescued and maintained through public expenditure.Roger ReadFormer secretary general, MetrexWill Hutton and Andy Haldane put forward a poor argument for maintaining private ownership of utilities. Instead of comparing the present situation with how things were when the water utilities were publicly owned – surely the fairest comparison – they cite spurious examples of the alleged failings of other nationalised industries.We are alone in the world (apart from Chile) in having a wholly privatised water industry; is everyone else out of step?SallyThompsonCardiffWill Hutton and Andy Haldane give some interesting thoughts on the public control of utilities. These could also apply across the complete essential services sector, from water companies to dental practices. Few who experienced the performance of the old postwar nationalised industries would wish a return to this failed model. However, why not just keep it simple and legislate to force all essential-services operators to list as companies on the London Stock Exchange?For each sector, further legislation could set maximums for yields and permitted borrowing: two key indicators of company activity. The public would then be more inclined to invest in the companies, just as they do at present with National Grid.Ian GrahamPort Carlisle, CumbriaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Other countries learn from their elders’ wisdom – so could Britain | Older people | The Guardian
description: Letters: A German service matches retired professionals to firms that use their experience, writes Alan Coppin, responding to an article about a 90-year-old Japanese competitive bodybuilder
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: A German service matches retired professionals to firms that use their experience, writes Alan Coppin, responding to an article about a 90-year-old Japanese competitive bodybuilder
Content: Germany’s Senior Expert Service has a pool of more than 14,000 people and has arranged 60,000 placements.Photograph: Peter M Fisher/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGermany’s Senior Expert Service has a pool of more than 14,000 people and has arranged 60,000 placements.Photograph: Peter M Fisher/Getty ImagesOlder peopleLettersOther countries learn from their elders’ wisdom – so could BritainA German service matches retired professionals to firms that use their experience, writesAlan Coppin, responding to an article about a 90-year-old Japanese competitive bodybuilderFri 2 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTShareYour feature on the 90-year-old bodybuilder Toshisuke Kanazawa was a joy (‘I’m 100% natural’: how Japan’s 90-year-old bodybuilder is still winning titles, 25 September), but it’s also a useful provocation. Almost30% of Japan’s 123.7 million people are over 64yet, rather than being written off, people like Kanazawa are still contributing well into their 90s.Britain does the opposite. Between 670,000 and 860,000 people drop out of the UK workforce annually, and by their 60s more than a third of people areeconomically inactive. The loss is a stock of judgment and knowhow that simply walks out of the door.Germany offers one model. Founded in 1983, itsSenior Expert Servicehas a pool of more than 14,000 retired professionals and has arranged more than 60,000 placements by matching engineers, accountants, former military and skilled tradespeople with the small firms, charities and schools that could use their experience. Nothing like it exists here. There’s a second potential beneficiary: the almost 1 million young people not in employment, education or training. It is hard to think of a better use of an elder’s time than helping one of them get a foothold.Modest pilot schemes in one or two sectors, modelled on the German system, would quickly show whether it is worth scaling up.Kanazawa’s story shouldn’t just prompt admiration for one exceptional man. It should trigger a serious look at whether Britain is wasting a resource it already has: the thousands of experienced people it puts out to pasture every year.Alan CoppinAuthor, The Human Capital Imperative: Valuing Your TalentHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Andy Burnham’s ultimate test will be whether people’s lives improve | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services, says Sarah Davidson
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services, says Sarah Davidson
Content: ‘The outcome which all governments should seek is a real improvement to people’s lives, particularly for those with the least.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The outcome which all governments should seek is a real improvement to people’s lives, particularly for those with the least.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAndy BurnhamLettersAndy Burnham’s ultimate test will be whether people’s lives improveMeasures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services, saysSarah DavidsonFri 2 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTShareRe your editorial on Andy Burnham’s conference speech (29 September), the outcome that all governments should seek is a real improvement to people’s lives, particularly for those with the least, and without storing up problems for future generations. But that requires ministers to measure what matters and use that evidence to guide decisions.The good news for the prime minister and his colleagues is that the Office for National Statistics already collects robust evidence about our lives through itsUK Measures of National Well-being Dashboard. Yet there is little suggestion that this sort of data has been driving policy, including tax and spending plans.If improving lives is the goal, measures of wellbeing should carry real weight in decisions about tax, spending and public services.Sarah DavidsonChief executive, Carnegie UKHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves | Oil | The Guardian
description: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Content: Emmanuel Macron said ministers had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks.Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron said ministers had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks.Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/ShutterstockOilG7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reservesLeaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US suppliesJoanna Partridge,Jillian AmbroseandMark SweneyFri 2 Oct 2026 14.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles afterDonald Trumpthreatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.The French President,Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unlessEuropetapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the currentG7chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.Trump said he was consideringa ban on diesel exportsafter the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.9:37Diesel export ban: will Trump push global energy prices even higher? - The LatestTrump said in a post on hisTruth Social platformthat Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September.The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to arecord high of £2 a litreon forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered thelargest release of government oil reservesin its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Explore more on these topicsOilG7Global economyInternational tradeEnergy industryEuropeCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We want action’: Fijian climate activist sends message ahead of UN talks in Pacific  | Fiji | The Guardian
description: Lavenia Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand and is determined to amplify Pacific voices at this year’s pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Author: Sera Sefeti
Headline: Lavenia Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand and is determined to amplify Pacific voices at this year’s pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Content: Lavenia Naivalu hopes to draw attention to Indigenous and Pacific perspectives when Fiji hosts leaders ahead of this year’s climate talks.Photograph: Fiji GovernmentView image in fullscreenLavenia Naivalu hopes to draw attention to Indigenous and Pacific perspectives when Fiji hosts leaders ahead of this year’s climate talks.Photograph: Fiji GovernmentFiji‘We want action’: Fijian climate activist sends message ahead of UN talks in PacificLavenia Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand and is determined to amplify Pacific voices at this year’s pre-Cop summit in FijiSera Sefetiin Yasawa IslandsFri 2 Oct 2026 19.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 19.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom her wooden veranda in Fiji’s remote Yasawa islands, climate activist Lavenia Naivalu remembers when the reefs were once so healthy, her grandfather would walk to the shoreline and return with fish. But life there has changed.“The reefs that the older generation of men spearfished in, no longer provide what they once did,” the 44-year-old says. “Young people … now must travel further out to sea to find fish for their families.”As she looks out at a white sandy beach, eaten away by rising sea levels, Naivalu recounts watching painfully as her three children “feel the brunt of changes in the climate.“I ask myself ‘what did they do wrong?’”View image in fullscreenLavenia Naivalu’s home on Nacula in the Yasawa islands is on the frontline of the climate crisis.Photograph: Sera SefetiThe question is personal, but it’s also part of what drives her pursuit of climate justice for Pacific people, whose way of life is being threatened as the planet warms.At this year’s UN climate talks, known as Cop31, the region will be in the spotlight like never before. Next week,Fiji will host leaders ahead of the climate summit, where Naivalu hopes to draw attention to Indigenous and Pacific perspectives which she says are often relegated in global negotiations.The Pacific Islands are disproportionately affected by the climate crisis, despite accounting for just 0.02% of global emissions,according to the United Nations.As climate crisis threatened her home, Alolita was offered a chance at a new life in AustraliaRead more“One thing that triggers me is when somebody else is speaking on my behalf,” she tells the Guardian. “I want to amplify the voices of my community and the people that I represent directly to all leaders.”Naivalu, an Indigenous representative participating in the Fiji meeting and the Cop31 summit in Turkey, has been a trailblazing advocate for her people.She was Fiji’s first femalemata ni tikina, or district representative, overseeing seven village chiefs under the traditionally male-dominated governance system. Naivalu was also the first Indigenous representative selected to Fiji’s tourism board.A veteran of past Cop summits, Naivalu – who lives on the island of Nacula in the Yasawa islands – says bringing the climate talks home matters, but she wants discussions to move beyond language that people do not see reflected in their daily lives.“We talk about climate change, climate finance, about adaptation and mitigation,” she said. “But my people in Nacula don’t know what climate finance is; what we want to know is action.”On the frontline of the crisisTurkey and Australia agreed last year that the Pacific would host preparatory meetings before Cop31 under acompromise dealto resolve a standoff about where the 2026 summit would be held. The summit will be hosted in Turkey’s Mediterranean resort city of Antalya in November, while Australia will chair negotiations.Sivendra Michael, Fiji’s permanent secretary for environment and climate change, said Naivalu “closes the distance between negotiating room and the reef.“Fiji will go into Cop31 arguing for direct access to finance, for adaptation that is actually delivered at community level, and for Indigenous knowledge to be treated as evidence rather than decoration,” he said.“We are asking the world to trust Pacific leadership. That argument is far stronger when Pacific leadership is not confined to officials like me.”Having grown up in Nacula village, Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand.“Water sources that used to sustain our village are now drying up, while seawater increasingly threatens the hand-dug wells,” she said.Nacula is doing its best to adapt to climate change – families now store drinking water for dry periods and women preserve food.View image in fullscreenWomen in Nacula prepare food. To contend with more severe dry periods, families must now store drinking water and preserve food.Photograph: Sera SefetiVillage chief, Ratu Manasa Naikasowalo, said he sees the value of Naivalu’s advocacy.“Her work has helped bring important connections and practical initiatives back to the community, including food security, salt making, coral planting and food-preservation programmes,” Ratu said.Naivalu knows adaptation cannot be left solely to frontline communities, and has witnessed the gap between Cop discussions and what happens at home.In Fiji next week, she will be bring the lived experiences of Indigenous communities into the Cop31 process, pushing for their voices to be heard as leaders negotiate climate finance, adaptation, loss and damage, and keeping global warming within 1.5C.“I don’t attend Cop to worry about texts and brackets; I attend Cop to forge partnerships with organisations that I believe can help the people of Nacula.”Explore more on these topicsFijiPacific islandsAsia PacificClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham urged by Lib Dems to reveal all meetings with owners of Manchester City | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The prime minister is facing calls from the Liberal Democrats to publish details of all his meetings with Manchester City’s owners
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The prime minister is facing calls from the Liberal Democrats to publish details of all his meetings with Manchester City’s owners
Content: Andy Burnham in conversation with Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium in 2019.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham in conversation with Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium in 2019.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Manchester CityAndy Burnham urged by Lib Dems to reveal all meetings with owners of Manchester CityBurnham should also declare City hospitality, party saysPM said he would be concerned if owners forced to sellExclusive byMatt HughesFri 2 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is facing calls from theLiberal Democratsto publish details of all his meetings with Manchester City’s owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug), and declare all hospitality he has accepted at the Etihad Stadium.The prime minister was widely criticised this week for saying he wouldbe “really concerned”if Adug were forced to sell City after beingfound guiltyof breaching the Premier League’s financial regulations, which led toDowning Street issuing two clarificationsof his position on Thursday.How success of Manchester City helped put Andy Burnham in powerRead moreBurnham also praised Adug’s investment in Manchester, having had close relations with the company, through which Sheikh Mansour bought City in 2008, during nine years as the mayor of Greater Manchester which ended when hereturned to parliamentthis summer.In a strongly-worded letter to
