Burnham the Lib Dems’ spokesperson for culture, media and sport, Anna Sabine, criticised his apparent defence of City as “extraordinary” and invoked Gianni Infantino’saborted World Cup sell-off schemein what she described as a difficult year for football.“As you will know, an independent commission has found Manchester City guilty of 114 charges of breaching financial rules over a timeframe of nearly a decade, including the use of‘sham contracts’ and schemes to disguisemore than £830m of funding,” Sabine writes in a letter seen by the Guardian.“Despite this, your response was to thank the club’s owners for their work and describe the findings as ‘contested’ and that it was ‘wrong to jump to a conclusion’. It is extraordinary that a prime minister would use his position to call into question the findings of the independent investigation, and risk undermining trust in the Premier League’s processes.“This has been a difficult year for football’s reputation. Fifa’s conduct around the World Cup has already raised serious questions about integrity in the game we love. At a moment like this, fans expect their prime minister to stand up for the rules in place, not to appear to side with a club found guilty of breaking them.”Sabine also told the Guardian that Burnham’s ties to Adug should be scrutinised and is planning to write to Downing Street and the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to demand details of their meetings.“Football fans up and down the country deserve to know that the rules apply to everyone, however rich and powerful they are,” Sabine said. “When the prime minister leaps to the defence of a club’s owners within hours of a verdict, people are entitled to ask what their relationship is.“Andy Burnham must come clean and publish details of every meeting and conversation he has had with City Football Group, Abu Dhabi United Group or UAE government representatives, going back to his time as mayor – and that includes any hospitality freebies received.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Burnham, an Everton fan, has been pictured attending City games at the Etihad Stadium in hospitality areas.The extent of that hospitality is unclear because under GMCA regulations the public disclosure of gifts is available for current office holders without the submission of a freedom of information request.A Downing Street spokesperson said Burnham had not met City’s owners since becoming prime minister in July and that his quarterly list of engagements would be published before the end of the year.City’s chair, Khaldoon Al Mubarak, visited Downing Street last month for a meeting with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, but Burnham did not attend.Burnham has not been to a City game since he became prime minister but has attended two Everton matches at Hill Dickinson Stadium, where he was accommodated in the directors’ box despite having a season ticket in the South Stand.City confirmed on Friday thatthey had appealedagainst an independent commission’s verdict. They repeated their assessment that the verdict “contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe”.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityAndy BurnhamLiberal DemocratsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s 100% him’: new video shows police arrest of Luigi Mangione | Brian Thompson shooting | The Guardian
description: Judge unseals bodycam footage from officers who responded to 911 from McDonald’s in Pennsylvania
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Judge unseals bodycam footage from officers who responded to 911 from McDonald’s in Pennsylvania
Content: 3:12Newly released bodycam video shows arrest of Luigi Mangione – videoBrian Thompson shooting‘That’s 100% him’: new video shows police arrest of Luigi MangioneJudge unseals bodycam footage from officers who responded to 911 from McDonald’s in PennsylvaniaAssociated PressFri 2 Oct 2026 18.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 18.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice bodycam footage released Friday shows the moment officers located and arrested Luigi Mangione at aPennsylvaniaMcDonald’s in connection with the shooting death of United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in Manhattan.In one video, officers ask Mangione to lower the face mask he was wearing to hide his identity.“That’s 100% him,” one officer says eagerly as they step outside to speak out of Mangione’s earshot.“I told you, man,” another responds off camera.Later, an officer searches Mangione’s belongings and smiles widely as she pulls out a gun cartridge, seemingly confirming they had found their suspect.The trove of videos comes from Mangione’s 9 December 2024 arrest in Altoona, five days after Thompson, a 50-year-old Minnesota executive, was gunned down as he walked to a midtown Manhattan hotel for his company’s annual investor conference.A Manhattan judge unsealed the recordings Friday after CNN petitioned for their release. Parts of the videos were shown during a December court hearing as Mangione’s lawyers unsuccessfully sought to get key evidence thrown out, including his initial statements to police and items seized at the time of his arrest.Mangione pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking charges and faces life in prison when he’s sentenced in December. He also faces murder charges inNew Yorkstate court, though those proceedings have been postponed indefinitely as his lawyers seek to have the case thrown out.Explore more on these topicsBrian Thompson shootingNew YorkPennsylvanianewsShareReuse this content

title: Hawaii’s centuries-old sea arch collapses into Pacific after series of rough storms | Hawaii | The Guardian
description: Hōlei sea arch, formed 550 years ago by erosion from ocean waves, no longer standing, National Park Service confirms
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Hōlei sea arch, formed 550 years ago by erosion from ocean waves, no longer standing, National Park Service confirms
Content: before and after of Hōlei Sea ArchThe Hōlei arch, left, standing in July 2022, and, right, on Wednesday after it collapsed.HawaiiHawaii’s centuries-old sea arch collapses into Pacific after series of rough stormsHōlei sea arch, formed 550 years ago by erosion from ocean waves, no longer standing, National Park Service confirmsLucy CampbellFri 2 Oct 2026 16.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA famed centuries-old sea arch on Hawaii’s remote and rugged coastline has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean, the National Park Service confirmed on Friday, following a stretch of rough storms in the region in recent weeks.The beloved landmark, Hōlei sea arch, stood at around 90ft high for over half a millennium in Hawaii’s Volcanoes national park, located on the dramatic southern coast of the Big Island. It was naturally formed around 550 years ago due to differential erosion by ocean waves.The exact timing of the collapse is unknown. The National Park Service (NPS)saidthe arch was still standing on Wednesday 23 September, when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo, but had collapsed by Sunday night, on 27 September.“The arch formed in ancient lava flows by removing rock along cracks and weaker rocks,” the US Geological Surveysaidin a description of the arch in 2014. “It will not be here for ever. Every day the ocean crashes against the pillar of the arch, eroding it a little more. One day, it will be gone.”Indeed, the cliffs on either side of the sea arch had shown signs of instability for years amid tropical systems and volcanic activity, the NPS said, meaning the arch’s collapse had long been expected.Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcanic eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs around the arch. Then, in January 2020, new cracks and instability prompted the park to close the original viewing area and open a safer one further from the cliff edge three months later. Later that year, huge surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the arch’s lower portion.The Hawaiian islands have seen anunusually high number of severe stormsthis year, with storm activity in the Pacific running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. Experts say the pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often sees more tropical storms and hurricanes.Nolo, which rapidly intensified into a hurricane on 24 September – causing Volcanoes national park to shutter - was the third major storm to devastate the islands of Hawaii in recent months. Residents were still recovering from hurricanesLala in AugustandLowell in early September, which had flooded homes and roads, toppled trees and caused power outages, when Nolo then battered the islands with heavy rain and high surf.Forecasters have warned there is a high probability thatthis “supercharged” El Niño will reach a historic intensity, with its effects in strengthening the stormscompounded by the broader overheating of the planetcaused by the burning of fossil fuels.Explore more on these topicsHawaiiUS weatherExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like caring for a pet’: the app that lets you know if your neighbourhood tree is thirsty | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Gieß den Kiez app shows trees in critical need of watering and can be adopted by other heat-stressed cities around the world
Author: Emma Snaith
Headline: Gieß den Kiez app shows trees in critical need of watering and can be adopted by other heat-stressed cities around the world
Content: You can see the last time a tree was watered, log a watering, and colour-coding indicates trees in critical need.Photograph: Thanh Thu Nguyen/ CityLAB BerlinView image in fullscreenYou can see the last time a tree was watered, log a watering, and colour-coding indicates trees in critical need.Photograph: Thanh Thu Nguyen/ CityLAB BerlinThe alternativesTrees and forests‘Like caring for a pet’: the app that lets you know if your neighbourhood tree is thirstyGieß den Kiez app shows trees in critical need of watering and can be adopted by other heat-stressed cities around the worldEmma SnaithFri 2 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 04.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmanda Gläser-Bligh sometimes attracts puzzled looks when she goes to water the eight-year-old street tree she has adopted outside her door in Charlottenburg, Berlin.“I named her Linda the linden,” she says. “Berliners are not always known for being super friendly but most people react really positively when they find out what I’m doing.”As summer heatwaves intensify across the city, Gläser-Bligh carries about 20 litres of water to Linda once a week during the hotter months. It takes a couple of trips up and down stairs with a watering can to finish the job, but she has noticed the tree is no longer wilting in the summer heat. Linden trees are a hallmark of Berlin, even lending their name to Unter den Linden boulevard. Their mature, dense canopies offer essential street cooling, while their blooms provide vital nectar for local bees.Planting more trees in cities could cut deaths from summer heat, says studyRead moreGläser-Bligh adopted the tree through CityLAB Berlin’sGieß den Kiez project, which translates to “water your neighbourhood”. An interactive map tracks more than 900,000 trees across Berlin and calculates the water needs of each one based on its age, species and local rainfall. This real-time watering data is what separates the Gieß den Kiez project from other tree maps around the world and allows volunteers to coordinate on a city-wide level.You can see the last time a tree was watered, log a watering, and colour-coding indicates trees in critical need. For instance, saplings lack the mature root networks of older trees and require more frequent watering to survive. Gieß den Kiez also offers advice on the correct watering technique, collecting rainwater and the location of Berlin’s water pumps.“It feels very fun, almost like a video game,” Gläser-Bligh says. “I think many people may want to water the trees, but they might feel weird about doing it or they’re not sure if it’s their responsibility. But, if you have this app encouraging you, you know it’s the right thing to do.”View image in fullscreenA view of the Gieß den Kiez app showing trees in need of water.Illustration: CityLAB BerlinThe Gieß den Kiez project has been running since 2020 and currently 12,000 registered volunteers are using the platform. Their efforts complement those of the district street and green space authorities, which are already watering thousands of trees but cannot always keep up during Berlin’s increasingly hot summers.“I was really surprised at just how deeply people care about trees – for many people it’s almost like caring for a pet,” says Anna Mehrländer, who has been leading the Gieß den Kiez project for more than a year.“Climate change is happening on our doorsteps. But watering a tree is a small action that helps your neighbourhood cope as summers get hotter. It also creates community at a time when people are increasingly working from home and on their phones all day.”Indeed, the biggest annual peak in tree waterings when nearly half a million litres were poured came just after the platform was launched in 2020 at the start of the Covid pandemic. Anna believes this was because watering trees gave people a reason to get back outside and connect with people and nature again. Seasonally, the waterings tend to rise during heatwaves. For instance, on 27 June, when Berlin experiencedan all-time record high of 39.9C (103.8F), people poured 8,000 litres of water over trees across the city.View image in fullscreenAmid the pandemic, watering trees gave people a reason to get back outside and connect with people and nature again.Photograph: Florian Reimann/CityLAB BerlinThere is a growing body of evidence showing the myriad benefits of street trees to counter the effects of the climate crisis. Studies show trees cool the air andbreak up urban heat islands during heatwaves, whilereducing the risk of floodingduring downpours. They also increase biodiversity, reduce air pollution and can improve mental health.Urban forestry expert Dr Cecil Konijnendijk has proposed a 3:30:300 rule of thumb for greening in cities: every citizen should be able to see at least three trees from their home, have 30% tree-canopy cover in their neighbourhood, and not live more than 300 metres from a park or green space.“In the past, trees were thought of as a nice aesthetic element in cities,” Cecil says. “But now we’re starting to see them as critical infrastructure.”He supports citizen initiatives like Gieß den Kiez that complement city efforts to care for trees. Aside from watering, Konijnendijk also highlights the importance of soil volume and underground space to ensure trees can grow a healthy root system.“The question I always ask is ‘how do you take care of your existing trees?’” he says. “It takes 30 to 40 years before a new tree starts delivering the ecosystem services of a mature one… But a lot of trees are now being pushed to their limits during increasingly hot summers – drought is a big issue.”Cecil says that AI and new technologies could help us monitor and maintain the health of city trees better than ever before. He points to increased use of soil sensors and city-wide scanning of tree canopies usinglidar, with cities like Malmo and Singapore at the forefront of innovative urban forestry.The open-source nature of Gieß den Kiez means the map can be adopted by any city in the world. Already residents in Potsdam, Leipzig, Magdeburg, and the 17th arrondissement of Paris have launched their own versions of the platform to coordinate tree watering.“Anyone can copy the code and set up their own Gieß den Kiez,” Anna says. “The main requirement is a data set of all the trees in your city. It’s possible to replicate anywhere, from China to the UK.”Back in Charlottenburg, Gläser-Bligh recently spotted someone else using the map to water a tree on the other side of her local park – a promising sign that word is spreading about Gieß den Kiez.“It’s a small step, a very small step,” she says. “But it has a direct climate impact.”Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsThe alternativesGermanyEuropeClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rare northern bald ibises take flight in human-led European migration project | Birds | The Guardian
description: Micro aircraft used to help guide birds to Spanish stopover as part of efforts to create sustaining migratory population
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Micro aircraft used to help guide birds to Spanish stopover as part of efforts to create sustaining migratory population
Content: The most recent project, in Alt Empordà, Catalonia, has just welcomed the birds from Austria, to join an already established flock.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenThe most recent project, in Alt Empordà, Catalonia, has just welcomed the birds from Austria, to join an already established flock.Photograph: APThe alternativesBirdsRare northern bald ibises take flight in human-led European migration projectMicro aircraft used to help guide birds to Spanish stopover as part of efforts to create sustaining migratory populationDonald ReidFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFifteen new birds have joined a growing flock of bald ibises in northernSpain, guided there by human migration guides in micro aircraft who helped them along the route.The birds are part of the growing European flock of the northern bald ibis (Geronticus eremita), the charismatic and frankly extraordinary bird that had been extinct on the continent for 300 years.By the end of the 20th century, the last major population in Morocco had fallen from 9,000 to 250 individuals in the wild. But then captive breeding and reintroduction plans were launched at various sites in Europe, initially in Austria and in Jerez, Andalucía. This most recent project, in Alt Empordà, Catalonia, has just welcomed the birds from Austria, to join an already established flock.“They are such intelligent birds,” says Bernat Garrigós, a biologist who runs the Alt Empordà project, “very sociable, all with different personalities. They like to check everything that comes into the project with their beaks; your socks, the food, everything.”There is no fear of humans because, as Garrigós explains, the birds do not really know any predators. They are still curious, and trusting.“We started working on the project in 2024, and by 2025 we had a first generation flock of nearly 60 ibises,” he says. “They were released in March 26 here [at Torre d’en Mornau, a converted Spanish army stable]. Currently there are two full-time and two part-time staff on the team, plus 20 volunteers, to manage the flock and site.“The Aiguamolls Park [a protected coastal wetland and nature reserve] is a close collaborator and with whom we maintain a very close, ongoing relationship. The goal is to mitigate risk to breeding, and mortality, until there is have a self-sustaining population.”View image in fullscreenThe northern bald ibis is said to be curious, and trusting, and have no fear of humans, as the bird does not really know any predators.Photograph: Donald ReidIn a year or two, and with some luck, Garrigós’ project should have its first breeding pair. Ibises do not breed until they are at least three or four years old. The plan is to establish a breeding colony, with nests on the towers dotted around the stables. The team will help by partially building the nests. Like most teenagers, they need to be shown how to make their beds.The Alt Empordà group is in constant contact with the projects in Austria and Jerez, and the birds migrate between the groups with the help of the human “foster parents” of the Waldrapp team (Waldrapp is another name for these birds) who guide their path with the help ofan ultralight aircraft. With 20 years of experience, they have helped Garrigós’ group avoid many of the mistakes made early on. So far, as a result, the mortality rate has been much lower.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe plan over the next 10 years is to have a minimum of 50 breeding pairs and about 300 individuals living wild.Photograph: M. Schaef/AlamyOver the next 10 years,Garrigós is aiming to release his ibises into the Alt Empordà, the plan being a minimum of 50 breeding pairs and about 300 individuals living wild. The comarca, or county, which is about halfway between Austria and Jerez, serves as an excellent stopover point in the migration route. The shared goal for the three projects is to establish colonies across Europe. These colonies will be connected by migrating birds, to form breeding pairs of different lineage and creating a robust gene pool to ensure survival.The project in northern Spain is one more piece in a broader European effort to save a species that has been among the most threatened in the world. The charisma of the ibis and the passion of the team are essential for promoting environmental education, raising awareness in younger generations and driving the importance of active conservation.And that charisma is a useful tool for winning over people. Recently, representatives from the Endesa, a large electric utility company, came to visit and were so bowled over by the project that they began retrofitting their pylons to be more visible and less dangerous for birds, with the ibis particularly in mind.“It’s not enough to stop destroying our environment,” says Garrigós. “We need to make a positive, active effort to prevent extinctions and the destruction of habitats where this and many other species live. In the end, it all comes down to having diverse, resilient ecosystems that provide the ecosystem services necessary for the survival of the ecosystem and of humanity itself.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsThe alternativesConservationSpainEuropeAnimalsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Welsh first minister calls on Burnham to deliver ‘new deal’ on devolution | Rhun ap Iorwerth | The Guardian
description: Rhun ap Iorwerth tells Plaid Cymru conference he asked PM to ‘put Wales on equal footing with Scotland as bare minimum’
Author: Bethan McKernan
Headline: Rhun ap Iorwerth tells Plaid Cymru conference he asked PM to ‘put Wales on equal footing with Scotland as bare minimum’
Content: Rhun ap Iorwerth told the annual conference on Friday his government had a ‘clear mandate’ for devolving more powers from Westminster.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenRhun ap Iorwerth told the annual conference on Friday his government had a ‘clear mandate’ for devolving more powers from Westminster.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PARhun ap IorwerthWelsh first minister calls on Burnham to deliver ‘new deal’ on devolutionRhun ap Iorwerth tells Plaid Cymru conference he asked PM to ‘put Wales on equal footing with Scotland as bare minimum’Bethan McKernanWales correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Welsh first minister has formally called onAndy Burnhamto deliver a “new deal” in his first address to a Plaid Cymru annual conference since taking office.Rhun ap Iorwerth told party members during a keynote speech in Llandudno on Friday that his government had a “clear mandate” for devolving more powers from Westminster.The first minister, who beat Labour to lead his nationalist party to a firstvictory in Senedd electionsin May, said he had written to Burnham on Thursday to ask the prime minister for “a new deal to redress the historic unfairness of our fiscal and constitutional settlement and to put Wales on an equal footing with Scotland as a bare minimum”.After being greeted by delegates with a standing ovation, ap Iorwerth said: “A new deal – the first of its kind – whereby a Welsh first minister invites the UK government to genuinely treatWalesnot as a region of England but as a nation in its own right. A new deal to secure powers … not as an end in themselves but as a means of growing our economy and improving outcomes for everyone.”The 2,000-word letter to Burnham made the case for transferring powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure andthe crown estate.Ap Iorwerth recently told the Guardian he had been encouraged by warm initial discussions with Burnham – a stark contrast to his interactions with Keir Starmer. However, the Welsh wing of theLabourparty in Westminster is generally sceptical of devolving more powers to Cardiff, especially now Labour no longer controls the Senedd.The first minister said on Friday: “I do believe the new prime minister and I both want to have a constructive and positive relationship. I’ve looked him in the eyes and said do not undermine Wales as a nation … do not bypass our Senedd, and he looked me in the eyes and promised he would not. I will hold him to that.”Since becoming prime minister, Burnham has made much of his support for regional devolution of power and resources in England, but his approach to the existing devolved administrations in Belfast, Cardiff and Edinburgh is still forming.View image in fullscreenRhun ap Iorwerth meeting Andy Burnham for bilateral talks in Glasgow in July.Photograph: Alastair Grant/ReutersPlaid Cymru’s Welsh election win ended 100 years of Labour dominance in Wales and blocked the momentum of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. Welsh Labour had governed in Wales since devolution began in 1999 but won just nine of the 96 seats in the new Senedd. Support for the party had been ebbing for years, driven by frustration about the management of public services, which havefallen behindthe other UK nations on many metrics.Ap Iorwerth’s win also put nationalist parties in government simultaneously in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland for the first time, althoughPlaid Cymruhas ruled out an independence referendum during its first term.The party’s last autumn conference in Swansea had been full of excitement as members sensedthe tide turningin Welsh politics. Its first as a party of government remained more relaxed and homely than those of rivals with deeper pockets and more seats in Westminster.The first minister’s demands for a “new deal” came a few weeks after alandmark summit of Plaid Cymru, Sinn Féin and Scottish National party leadersduring which they affirmed their respective countries’ right to seek independence from the UK.Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum. Data suggests it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland, and stands at 32% and 36% respectively.Burnham is expected to meet the three first ministers of the Celtic nations at the end of October.A UK government spokesperson said: “This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom.“That’s why our focus is now on working with theWelsh governmentto empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode.”Explore more on these topicsRhun ap IorwerthDevolutionPlaid CymruWelsh governmentAndy BurnhamWelsh politicsLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Polanski says he does not need to win ‘50/50’ byelection to stay Green leader | Green party | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Party leader says outcome of ‘knife-edge’ vote in Keir Starmer’s former seat will not affect his position
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Exclusive: Party leader says outcome of ‘knife-edge’ vote in Keir Starmer’s former seat will not affect his position
Content: Senior Green party figures fear a defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSenior Green party figures fear a defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianGreen partyPolanski says he does not need to win ‘50/50’ byelection to stay Green leaderExclusive: Party leader says outcome of ‘knife-edge’ vote in Keir Starmer’s former seat will not affect his positionAletha AduPolitical correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 11.56 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleZack Polanski has said his authority as leader of the Green party of England and Wales does not depend on winning next week’sHolborn and St Pancras byelection, amid suggestions the party’s popularity may have peaked.Polanski, who is trying totake Keir Starmer’s former seatfrom Labour, described the contest as “probably 50/50 right now” and “really on a knife edge”.Asked in an interview with the Guardian how much his position as leader depended on victory, Polanski said: “It doesn’t depend on it whatsoever.”He said the election had ramifications for politics nationally but “not for my leadership”.“I’ll be completely honest, it won’t surprise you to know that I want to win the seat,” Polanski said. “I think the seat is winnable, and I think it’s probably 50/50 right now. It’s really, really on a knife edge.”SeniorGreen partyfigures privately fear a defeat in Holborn and St Pancras could severely damage Polanski’s leadership, amid concerns the party’s rapid rise in membership and polling has not translated into campaigning strength on the ground.Attempts to concentrate resources on the byelection have caused internal friction, with the Guardian revealing last month that Polanskiwanted the Greens’ annual conference postponedso the party could focus on the contest. That proposal was rejected by its executive.View image in fullscreenDelegates arriving at the Green party’s annual conference in Brighton on Friday.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianPolanski, who has never been an MP, maintained there were “still advantages to being a leader outside Westminster”, while also arguing that entering parliament would offer another way of putting pressure on the Labour government.Polanski is facing a separate test of his leadership at the Green party’s annual conference, where members are due to debate a deeply contentiousmotion declaring “Zionism is racism”on Saturday.Asked about criticism from senior Greens who believe he has failed to provide leadership over the issue, he said: “Leadership is about priorities, and this motion isn’t my priority. My priority is the cost of living. My priority is nationalising Thames Water. My priority is ending the genocide that’s happening in Gaza and freeing Palestine.”Can Zack Polanski win Keir Starmer’s old seat? – podcastRead moreCaroline Lucas, the former leader of the Greens, Adrian Ramsay, the former co-leader, and Rachel Millward, a current co-deputy leader, have distanced themselves from the motion, warning it could be “divisive”.Some Jewish Greens have raised concerns about what the motion could mean for their place within the party.Asked whether he could guarantee that a Jewish member would not face disciplinary action simply for attending a synagogue that identified as Zionist, Polanski said: “I can guarantee that this motion has absolutely nothing to do with disciplinary action against anyone.”The byelection has become an early test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can reclaim progressive voters who have moved towards the Greens, and the result may inform the government’s decisions overexpanding North Sea oil and gas drilling.“I see this election as high-stakes for people in Holborn and St Pancras and high-stakes for the climate crisis,” Polanski said. “We know that … a decision on [drilling projects Rosebank and Jackdaw] has been delayed until after this byelection, because Andy Burnham literally wants to see whether he can get away with drilling for new North Sea oil and gas.”The Guardian has reported that the Jackdaw decision islikely to be held until after the byelection, while a decision on Rosebank is still pending. Burnham has promised a more “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas than his predecessor, as the government balances its climate commitments against pressure over energy security and jobs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoth projects already hold licences granted under the Conservatives, meaning approval by Labour would not amount to issuing new exploration licences.Asked whether Burnham’s surge could win back younger and progressive voters from the Greens, Polanski said there were two possibilities. One was that Burnham “means what he’s saying right now” and would actually “implement action today and not tomorrow, and not after the next general election”. In this case, Polanski said, the country would improve as a result of pressure from the Greens and others.The other, which Polanski called “the more likely scenario”, was that “what we’re getting is talk”. He said Burnham was “promising things after the next general election, but soon we’re going to have a budget that he’s already warning is going to be a difficult budget”.In this case, he said, “more and more people will start to question why would you vote for the Labour party or get involved with the Labour party when the Green party has been growing for over a year now”.He added: “You don’t have to accept the half-fat version. You can join the Green party and actually make sure we have the country that Andy Burnham’s talking about, but not taking the action on.”Arguing that Labour’s climate policy had a gap between rhetoric and actions, Polanski asked: “Does Andy Burnham just not care about the climate crisis? It just feels like such a glaring gap in everything that he’s talked about, not just because of Rosebank and Jackdaw, but in the need to invest in renewables, the need for a clean green revolution, the need for new jobs, and it just feels like this vision is just not there.”He added: “When are we going to see difficult choices for the super rich and the very, very wealthy? Instead, he’s talking about difficult choices for pensioners. So already the action is not meeting his ‘hope’ rhetoric, and I think people are already starting to ask questions.”Referring toarrests of Palestine Action supportersoutside the Labour party conference, Polanski said: “Those people on the doorstep, they can see that Ed Miliband stood on stage and told many of us that we were right on Palestine, but just behind him, outside the conference hall, pensioners were still being dragged off, being arrested for holding signs up saying ‘I support Palestine Action’.”Polanski used his conference speech to introduce new Green party policy, calling for a “three-year emergency brake on private rents”. He said: “No rent rises above CPI wage growth or 2%, whichever is lower. No sudden hikes. No evictions under the guise of rent rises. No more uncertainty, no more fear.”He went further on Palestine Action on Friday, calling for the group to be deproscribed, which led to chants of “free, free Palestine” from Green party members in the hall in Brighton.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiHolborn and St Pancras byelectionLondon politicsLondonByelectionsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tesco is first supermarket to offer paid ‘safe leave’ for victims of domestic abuse | Tesco | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Britain’s largest private-sector employer has also trained managers to spot signs of domestic abuse
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Exclusive: Britain’s largest private-sector employer has also trained managers to spot signs of domestic abuse
Content: Tesco employs 300,000 people in the UK.Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTesco employs 300,000 people in the UK.Photograph: Anna Barclay/Getty ImagesTescoTesco is first supermarket to offer paid ‘safe leave’ for victims of domestic abuseExclusive: Britain’s largest private-sector employer has also trained managers to spot signs of domestic abuseSarah ButlerFri 2 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for victims of domestic abuse, giving staff dedicated time to access support, secure their safety and take steps to move on with their lives.The UK’s largest private-sector employer is offering up to three days of paid leave which can be taken flexibly for activities such as attending court hearings, arranging emergency accommodation, changing locks, securing childcare or separating finances.Managers across the business, which employs 300,000 people, have also been trained to spot the signs of domestic abuse, support those affected and flag them to specialist services.Under the new policy, which was developed in partnership with the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, Tesco will not ask those suffering abuse to provide formal evidence to gain access to the special leave.Tesco is thought to be the first big British retailer to introduce safe leave, but similar policies, such as protected paid leave, emergency accommodation and training staff to spot the signs of domestic abuse, have been enacted at other UK companies, including BP and Vodafone, as well as some local councils.Daniel Adams, an Usdaw national officer, said domestic violence and abuse affected the lives of at least one in five women, and he urged other employers to introduce similar support.“Usdaw has long campaigned for support at work for survivors of domestic abuse and we are pleased to have successfully negotiated this new policy with Tesco. Domestic abuse often has an impact on the working lives of survivors, and it is important that employers understand this and the actions they can take to support and protect them,” he said.“Historically violence against women, and domestic violence in particular, has been hidden, excused and ignored. That needs to change.”Emma Taylor, the chief people officer at Tesco, said:“We believe we have a responsibility to support colleagues in what are likely to be some of the most challenging moments in their lives.“That’s why we’re introducing guaranteed safe leave, ensuring colleagues can access practical support and the time they need without worrying about taking unpaid leave or explaining deeply personal circumstances.“We’re proud to be taking this step and want it to help drive wider action from employers across the UK. No one should have to choose between their job and their safety.”More than 3 million people suffered some form of domestic abuse in England and Wales last year, most of whom were women, according to the campaign group SafeLives. It says eight women a month are killed by a current or former partner in England and Wales, based on 2023 data.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was a sharp increase in abuse incidents during the pandemic lockdowns as victims were trapped at home with perpetrators. The permanent shift to working from home since then is seen to have made some people more vulnerable.The Domestic Abuse Act, which became law in April 2021, includes workplace protection for domestic abuse victims, who can see their place of work as somewhere to seek help and support.A private member’s bill currently before parliament proposes granting 10 days of paid leave for domestic abuse victims in England and Wales to give them time to deal with the practical and emotional steps.In 2020, Northern Ireland passed legislation guaranteeing domestic abuse victims 10 days’ paid leave, and similar laws exist in Australia, New Zealand and the Philippines.Explore more on these topicsTescoSupermarketsRetail industryDomestic violencenewsShareReuse this content

title: Kinky dating app Feeld’s founders share in record £3.8m dividend after sales jump | Apps | The Guardian
description: UK app ‘for the curious’ says users outside the UK account for nearly 90% of its revenues
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: UK app ‘for the curious’ says users outside the UK account for nearly 90% of its revenues
Content: Feeld’s president said people were thinking about connection with ‘greater openness, curiosity and agency’.Photograph: Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFeeld’s president said people were thinking about connection with ‘greater openness, curiosity and agency’.Photograph: Iuliia Bondar/Getty ImagesAppsKinky dating app Feeld’s founders share in record £3.8m dividend after sales jumpPlatform ‘for the curious’ says users outside the UK account for nearly 90% of its revenuesBusiness live – latest updatesRob DaviesFri 2 Oct 2026 05.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFeeld, a UK-based dating app aimed at non-monogamous, queer and kinky users, has reported strong sales growth and paid its largest-ever dividend as it attracts users from more “vanilla” rivals.Revenues jumped by 32% to £64m following a surge in interest from what it called “open-minded people exploring love, desire, and alternative relationships in a safe, inclusive space”.Pre-tax profits grew from £9.3m to £11.4m, and the company’s shareholders – including the couple who founded it – shared in a dividend of £3.8m.Ana Kirova and her partner, Dimo Trifonov, started the business under the name 3nder (pronounced Thrinder), initially targeting couples and singles looking for threesomes.They were forced to change the company’s name to Feeld owing to alawsuit from Tinderbut it has since experienced rapid growth even as larger rivals have faltered.View image in fullscreenAna Kirova, co-founder of Feeld.Photograph: Travis P Ball/SXSW Conference & Festivals/GettyMatch Group, which owns Tinder and other dating apps such as Hinge and OK Cupid, reported a 5% decline in user numbers earlier this year, amid reports offatigue with the experienceof seeking romance or sex via an app.But Feeld, which calls itself a dating app “for the curious”, appears to be scooping up some of those users. While this has promptedreports that its edgy image has been watered downby an influx of people with more conventional or monogamous sensibilities, Feeld’s president, Kyle Brennan, said it reflected changing tastes.“These numbers speak to something bigger than the growth of our business,” said Brennan. “They reflect a broader shift in how people are thinking about connection, with greater openness, curiosity and agency to do things differently.”Accounts filed at Companies House said rising sales reflected “strong global user growth”, particularly outside the UK, with the rest of the world accounting for £56m of its total £64m in revenues, nearly 90%. Mexico and Spain were Feeld’s fastest-growing regions, while New York, Toronto and Paris led the way among cities, each recording an uplift in user numbers of more than 20%, the company said.Feeld makes money via the sale of its Majestic memberships, which give users features such as unlimited opportunities to “like” other members, the ability to see who has liked them, and advanced filters to tailor specifications for a potential partner.It also sells members extra “pings”, a feature that allows members to express interest in someone and send them a message, without having matched with them first.In 2024, it emerged that some of these features were temporarily vulnerable to manipulation due to security “vulnerabilities” exposed by cybersecurity experts.As online dating goes into ‘salvage mode’, can AI solve all its problems?Read moreResearch by the London-basedcybersecurity firm Fortbridgefound that users could have had sensitive data including messages, private photos and details of their sexuality accessed or even edited.At the time, Feeld said it had investigated the problems brought to its attention by Fortbridge on 3 March and fixed them by 28 May that year. It said there was no evidence that any customer data had been accessed. It has invested £10.5m in technological upgrades in the past year.The largest dividend reported in Feeld’s previous accounts was £600,000 in 2024.As well as its dating platform, Feeld runs in-person social events including a “kinky trivia” night and a “pitch your mate” event, at which guests take to the stage to wax lyrical about why people should date their friends.Explore more on these topicsAppsDatingDigital mediaOnline datingnewsShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll | India | The Guardian
description: Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
Content: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) protesting in Mumbai on Friday.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) protesting in Mumbai on Friday.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesIndiaIndia’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter rollThousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rightsHannah Ellis-Petersenin MumbaiFri 2 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are beingunfairly strippedof their vote.The movement, which calls itselfthe Cockroach Janta party (CJP)and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted intens of millions of peoplebeing deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke addresses supporters in Mumbai on Friday.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesOpposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).Millions in India stripped of vote before critical state election, as government seeks to ‘purify’ electoral rollRead moreThe CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured intoresigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the All India Students Association demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar at a protest in Bengaluru.Photograph: Idrees Mohammed/AFP/Getty ImagesLast week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.View image in fullscreenA demonstrator holding a placard wears a mask depicting the face of Gyanesh Kumar.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersThe election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared ​aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.No hope, no vote … how most of Delhi’s sex workers are being struck off electoral rollsRead moreAnger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try to stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election ​commission office in Delhi next week.Explore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows | Spain | The Guardian
description: Opposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Opposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old
Content: Protesters near the Spanish parliament demand 'Fair rents NOW' after lawmakers rejected emergency housing measures on Friday.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/ReutersView image in fullscreenProtesters near the Spanish parliament demand 'Fair rents NOW' after lawmakers rejected emergency housing measures on Friday.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/ReutersSpainSpanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement growsOpposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-oldAshifa Kassamin MadridFri 2 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRightwing lawmakers in Spain have rejected emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against thewidespread protest movementthat has swelled in recent days.On Friday Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.As hundreds of protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.Eviction of 87-year-old puts Spain’s deepening housing crisis in the spotlightRead moreNews of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, wasevicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.Tens of thousands of people heeded the call by housing campaigners to take to the streets, while encampments protesting against the housing crisis sprung up in cities acrossSpain.The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life intoSánchez’s beleaguered governmentand shifting attention away from the lingering impact ofrecent events in Ceuta.On Friday, asa pollsuggested that two-thirds of people in Spain supported the idea of government intervention in the housing market to limit prices, sources told the news site Eldiario.es that the Socialists were mullingwhether to bring forward next year’s elections, potentially to this November.After news broke that several rightwing parties were planning to vote against the proposed measures, Sánchez said the parliamentary vote would go ahead as planned. “You’re with the social majority or with speculators,” the Spanish prime minister said on social media, adding that the vote would reveal the “true colours” of the rightwing parties.View image in fullscreenA sprawling protest camp in Puerta del Sol, Madrid, where demonstrators are demanding affordable housing.Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFollowing five hours of parliamentary debate on Friday, Sánchez made a last ditch appeal to lawmakers to back the measures. “What is behind these decrees is the desire to instil order and a sense of humanity in a market that – if we do not rein it in – will destroy our society,” he said. “Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think.”Across Spain, where rents have surged 80% within a decade and the cost of homes climbed by 63%, the issue of housing has long ranked as one of people’s biggest concerns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier this year, the Youth Council of Spain saidthe average rent in Spain had climbed to €1,176 ($1,323) a month– an amount equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for under-30s.The figures help to explain why the protests that began with Abascal’s eviction have continued even after the investment firm that bought her apartment said it had struck a deal that would allow her to return to her home, with her rent returning to a level closer to that she had paid in the past.It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María RamírezRead moreThe government decrees presented in parliament on Friday were intended to quell some of this public uproar. As they were rejected, campaigners vowed to continue their push to improve access to housing.“They’re not going to stop us,” the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions said in a statement, as it called on people across the country to take to the streets this weekend. “In the face of a parliament that is out of touch, the answer is more organisation and mobilisation. The next step: a general strike.”Saturday will mark one week since a small group of protesters, intent on making their demands heard, set up 10 tents in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol plaza, a short walk from parliament. Since then,the encampment had swelled to more than 1,200 tents– a peaceful settlement in the heart of the capital with its own street names, a medical centre and even a co-working space.As news of the vote reached the camp on Friday, some said it was not what they had expected. “People here are disappointed,” said Marta García. “We had thought that at least one of the decrees would be approved.”Explore more on these topicsSpainHousingProtestPedro SánchezEuropeCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike remains on ventilator after failed execution in Tennessee | Tennessee | The Guardian
description: Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Attorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her system
Content: Emergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tennessee.Photograph: George Walker IV/APView image in fullscreenEmergency vehicles arrive at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tennessee.Photograph: George Walker IV/APTennesseeChrista Pike remains on ventilator after failed execution in TennesseeAttorneys say hospital staff are working to clear pentobarbital she was administered from her systemGuardian staff and agenciesFri 2 Oct 2026 16.26 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChrista Pike remained hospitalized, unconscious and on a machine helping her breathe after herfailed executionin Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing Friday.The attorneys said hospital staff were working to save Pike’s life and clear the pentobarbital she was administered from her system as of late Thursday.Pike received two doses of the drug ina failed attemptby the state of Tennessee to execute her on Wednesday.In the court filing, Pike’s attorneys said they believed problems with intravenous lines caused the pentobarbital to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.“Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms Pike’s body,” they wrote.They also wrote that instead of “remedying this failure” the execution team proceeded to prepare and administer a backup set of pentobarbital syringes.In a statementreportedon X by NewsNation journalist Brian Entin, Pike’s attorneys described her as “critically ill and … receiving medical care for the devastating effects of Wednesday nights events”.“We are working close with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” the statement also said. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”Pike’s attorneys on Friday asked a state court to order Tennessee’s department of correction to preserve all evidence from her failed execution.“Preserving this evidence is essential to understanding what happened, ensuring accountability and protecting Christa’s legal rights,” her attorneys’ statement said.Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 at the age of 20 in connection with the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Pike and her then boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, killed Slemmer at a job training camp in Knoxville, Tennessee.One grim detail about the case is that a pentagram had been carved into Slemmer’s chest.After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, her attorneys said.“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”According to the Death Penalty Information Center, the last execution of a woman in Tennessee was in 1820, meaning Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in more than 200 years.Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Pike has prompted top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community tocallfor a moratorium on the death penalty in the US.The state’s governor, Bill Lee, has ordered a third-party investigation into Pike’s botched execution. He has also paused executions in Tennessee.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsTennesseeUS justice systemCapital punishmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Peter Thiel revealed as secret buyer of Bel Air mansion that sold for $130m | Peter Thiel | The Guardian
description: The 1938 mansion, Casa Encantada, once belonged to Conrad Hilton and was sold at foreclosure auction
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: The 1938 mansion, Casa Encantada, once belonged to Conrad Hilton and was sold at foreclosure auction
Content: Peter Thiel's estate, Casa Encantada, on 1 October 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeter Thiel's estate, Casa Encantada, on 1 October 2026 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesPeter ThielPeter Thiel revealed as secret buyer of Bel Air mansion that sold for $130mThe 1938 mansion, Casa Encantada, once belonged to Conrad Hilton and was sold at foreclosure auctionLucy CampbellFri 2 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe tech billionairePeter Thielhas been revealed as the new owner of a storied Bel-Air estate that quietly sold in July for a staggering $130m.The 1938 mansion, Casa Encantada, was sold at an open-air foreclosure auction in Pomona, with the name of the buyer kept under wraps for months. The winning bid is now revealed to have come from a limited liability company linked to the venture capitalist and PayPal and Palantir co-founder, according to the Wall Street Journal, whichfirst reported the buyer’s identity.The sale of the 40,000sq ft estate is the most expensive inLos Angelesso far this year, though it is far less than the previous asking price. The former owner, late telecom mogul Gary Winnick, wanted $225m for the property in 2019 and $250m in 2023, making it the priciest home in the US at the time. Winnick died in 2023 amid a mountain of debt.View image in fullscreenPeter Thiel in Berlin, Germany on 24 September 2026.Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty ImagesSet on about 8.4 acres of land, the stately property overlooks the Bel-Air Country Club and boasts grand Deco-Hollywood interiors with seven bedrooms, 20 bathrooms, multiple dining rooms and lounges, a walnut-paneled library, a tennis court, terraced gardens, a 60ft tiled swimming pool and a two-storey guesthouse.Other previous owners include the hotel magnate Conrad Hilton, who bought it in 1950, and billionaire David Murdock, who purchased it in 1980 for a record $12.4m. It set a second price record in 2000 when it sold to Winnick for $94m.According to the Journal’s report, Thiel had been considering the mega-mansion for months before the auction, though he does not plan to live there. Rather he sees the property as an investment and plans to upgrade it. The purchase adds to his sprawling real estate portfolio that spans three continents, including compounds in Hawaii and New Zealand, homes in Miami and Washington DC, and arecently acquired mansionin the most exclusive neighbourhood in Buenos Aires. He reportedly relocated his primary residence from California to south Florida last year amid a wealth tax debate in the Golden state.Explore more on these topicsPeter ThielLos AngelesCaliforniaWest CoastThe super-richReal estatenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bosses of three firms that supply trains to UK railways made £3.5m last year | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: Rolling stock companies, which also paid out nearly £400m to shareholders, accused of profiting at passengers’ expense
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Rolling stock companies, which also paid out nearly £400m to shareholders, accused of profiting at passengers’ expense
Content: The government is considering directly owning trains via Great British Railways rather than leasing them from private companies.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe government is considering directly owning trains via Great British Railways rather than leasing them from private companies.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockRail industryBosses of three firms that supply trains to UK railways made £3.5m last yearRolling stock companies, which also paid out nearly £400m to shareholders, accused of profiting at passengers’ expenseGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe chief executives of three firms that rent out trains to Britain’s railways were paid a combined £3.5m last year as they passed on almost £400m to shareholders in dividends.Rail unions accused the rolling stock companies (Roscos) of raking in profits at passengers’ expense.The figures emerged in accounts published this week after ministers announced a new rolling stock strategy for Britain’s railways.The government isconsidering direct ownership of trainsthrough the public body Great British Railways rather than leasing them from the private sector.The latest figures show Porterbrook Holdings paid £80m in dividends and increased the pay of its chief executive, Mary Grant, by more than 10% to £1.44m.Eversholt Rail paid out £200m in 2025 shortly before it was sold by CK Hutchison to Beacon Rail, with its departing CEO, Mary Kenny, paid £1.33m.Angel Trains paid £111m in dividends and a relatively modest £700,000 to its boss, Malcolm Brown.Their pay far outstrips the highest salaries elsewhere on the railway, including the bosses of Network Rail and HS2.The RMT union called for a levy on Roscos after highlighting the dividend payments and salaries. It said the three biggest Roscos had paid out £2.4bn over the last 10 years in dividends.The general secretary of the RMT, Eddie Dempsey, said: “The government’s commitment to explore publicly owned rolling stock for the new trains in the future is welcome but in a cost of living crisis we need action now.“We are calling on the government to use this month’s budget to introduce a ‘cost of travel’ levy on profits to fund a 3.4% fare cut, rather than watching the cash being salted away.”The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, told the Labour conference on Monday that ifGreat British Railwaysowning trains would best serve taxpayers and passengers, then we should do it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to the rail regulator, operators last year spent more than £4bn leasing trains from the Roscos, whose net profit margin was 18.5%.A spokesperson for Porterbrook said it had “deployed over £1bn of capital in new trains, fleet upgrades, traction innovation and rail infrastructure since 2020, and we are actively looking to invest a further £1bn in the years ahead”.They said the group’s companies were UK tax resident, and had paid £82m in the past three years, adding: “It is because of the funding that our shareholders provide that we can make substantial investments in the railway.”Angel Trains is incorporated in Jersey and within the realm of UK taxes. A spokesperson said: “We believe decisions on future fleets should be focused on securing the best outcomes for passengers, while maintaining the conditions and opportunities needed to attract future investment into the railway. We look forward to continuing to work constructively with government and Great British Railways.”Eversholt and its new owner, Beacon Rail, were approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsRail industryRail transportTransportLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Stand on the right side of history’: Starbucks urged to close stores in China’s Xinjiang | Starbucks | The Guardian
description: US lawmakers say operating in region where Muslim minorities face mass detention is ‘morally bankrupt’
Author: Rebecca Bailey
Headline: US lawmakers say operating in region where Muslim minorities face mass detention is ‘morally bankrupt’
Content: People walk past a Starbucks in Beijing, China.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a Starbucks in Beijing, China.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersStarbucks‘Stand on the right side of history’: Starbucks urged to close stores in China’s XinjiangUS lawmakers say operating in region where Muslim minorities face mass detention is ‘morally bankrupt’Rebecca BaileyFri 2 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS lawmakers have urgedStarbucksto close newly opened outlets in China’s Xinjiang, saying it was a “morally bankrupt decision” to operate in a region where Beijing has been accused of widespread human rights abuses against Muslim minorities.The coffeehouse chain, which last year sold a controlling stake in itsChinaretail business to the Hong Kong-based investment firm Boyu Capital, opened two stores in the region on Tuesday.Videos on Chinese social media showed long queues for the flagship store in Urumqi’s Grand Bazaar tourist area, with influencers showing off special edition drinks including “milk-skin-flavoured salty milk tea”.View image in fullscreenStarbucks merchandise on display in its Urumqi store includes dolls in local ethnic dress.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockBut John Moolenaar, the chair of the US House of Representatives’ select committee on China, called the move “morally bankrupt”.“There is no justifiable reason for an American company to do business in a region where the Chinese Communist party has detained more than a millionUyghursand is stripping them of their faith, language and culture,” he said. “Every cup sold in these stores ties an iconic American brand to the CCP’s brutal campaign against the Uyghurs.”Washington is among several governments and rights groups that haveaccused China of genocide in Xinjiang, which Beijing has categorically denied.The United Nations has warned of possible crimes against humanity, including the detention of more than a million Uyghurs and other Muslim minorities in camps.China says these were “education” camps and that crackdowns were necessary to combat terrorism.The World Uyghur Congress advocacy group called on Starbucks to “stand on the right side of history”.“The presence of Starbucks in Xinjiang’s streets … fits in the party state’s narrative, that there’s nothing wrong about the region,” said Human Rights Watch’s deputy Asia director, Maya Wang.Responding to the US comments, the Chinese foreign ministry told Reuters that allegations of repression were “naked lies” and that Xinjiang enjoyed a “stable society, economic growth, ​racial unity and religious harmony”.The Guardian has contacted Starbucks and Boyu Capital for comment.Starbucks Korea raided by police after ‘Tank Day’ campaign sparks public outrageRead moreChina has poured resources into developing Xinjiang as a tourism destination in recent years.Starbucks is far from alone in seeing the commercial appeal there: other major western brands such as Hilton and InterContinental Hotels Group have been criticised for their operations too.Critics have characterised Xinjiang’s development as “Disneyfication” – commodifying the region’s heritage even as its inhabitants’ ability to practise their culture on their own terms has been restricted.On Chinese social media, excited visitors posted pictures of Starbucks-branded merchandise, including patterned flasks and teddy bears in outfits based on local ethnic dress.When the deal with Boyu Capital was announced, Starbucks said it would bring “deep local expertise”, with analysts noting the US behemoth had been losing ground to domestic competitors for some time.The move by Starbucks makes “commercial sense”, said Yaling Jiang, the founder of the research and strategy consultancy ApertureChina.“What is politically correct in China is not necessarily politically correct in the rest of the world, and this is a prime example,” she said. “Starbucks in China is now operating from a Chinese perspective rather than a US perspective, and that is ultimately how they can win in China.”Explore more on these topicsStarbucksUyghursChinaHouse of RepresentativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia  | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday
Content: OpenAI has disclosed an attack on a NSW government department.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOpenAI has disclosed an attack on a NSW government department.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpenAIOpenAI disclose another hack on government department in AustraliaAttack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until ThursdayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotFri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtificial intelligence companyOpenAIhas disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia.In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into aNew South Walesstate government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.The breach, which comes weeks after news ofa similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data, was not reported by the US based company until Thursday.The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach.The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service.OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available.The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office.“The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences.“We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said.Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week.“We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said.On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date.The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June.The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent.An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools.AAP contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsOpenAINew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Would a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs? | Tax and spending | The Guardian
description: Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a year
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a year
Content: The are calls for the government to hike machine games duty from 20% to 40%.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe are calls for the government to hike machine games duty from 20% to 40%.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianTax and spendingExplainerWould a gambling tax rise in the budget really shut shops and cost jobs?Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a yearRob DaviesFri 2 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 03.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGambling industry kingpins are fuming about reports that the chancellor, John Healey, is considering increasing taxes on high-street slot machines in his first budget.The influential Social Market Foundation thinktank, the most vocal advocate for a rise in machine games duty (MGD), from 20% to 40%,thinks the measure could raise between £275m and £460m annually, on top of the roughly £610m collected last year.Its proposal is likely to meet with sympathy from Andy Burnham, avocal and repeated critic of slot machines, who has already moved totighten licensing lawsso that gambling firms find it harder to open up new shops.The billionaire owner of Betfred, Fred Done, is among industry bosses who say such a policy would force shop closures, cost jobs and ultimately fail in its objective, depriving the Treasury of taxes.But not every figure in the gambling world agrees. Stewart Kenny, the co-founder ofPaddy Powerwho has become a critic of his erstwhile industry, accused Done of “scaremongering”.So who’s right? It’s complicated …What does the industry say?Bookies might be best known for bets on horses or football but they make big money from slot machines.
