The Betting and Gaming Council, an industry lobby group, commissioned a report from the accounting firm EY that estimated a duty rise to 40% could close up to 1,470 betting shops (nearly a third of the total 5,617), resulting in 15,900 job losses and a net loss to the exchequer of about £120m. Horse racing, which receives a levy from bookies’ profits, would also take a hit.Done said he alone would be forced to close about 495 betting shops, nearly half of Betfred’s estate, with the loss of 2,475 jobs and £67m in taxes.Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes and Coral, has written to Burnham saying it would have to make job cuts across its nationwide estate of 2,300 shops, were the policy to go ahead. Casinos and bingo halls are in the firing line too. Rank Group, which owns Mecca Bingo and Grosvenor Casinos, cautioned that a third of its venues could close, affecting 2,000 staff.Are they crying wolf?When dealing with bookmakers, it is wise to be sceptical.Back in 2019, Betfred had about 1,620 shops. Since then, the company has threatened to close nearly 1,000 in response to tougher regulation or taxes. While most of the policies it objected to have come to pass, the number of shops has decreased by only about 330. Some of that is down to a broader shift to the web that has led to soaring online gambling revenues.In one Betfred TV ad, Done encourages punters to “come and see me”. In your neighbourhood bookies? No, at Betfred.com. Meanwhile, the Done family has taken out tens of millions of pounds in dividends, including£50m in 2022 alone.Any other examples?Bet365 does not have high street shops, operating only online. But it recently cited anincrease in gambling duties in the former chancellor Rachel Reeves’s budget last yearas it announced plans to cut about 300 jobs at its Stoke-on-Trent headquarters.What it failed to mention is that it has been increasing its use of AI within the business since well before the tax rise. Some staff at Bet365’s Stoke HQ are understood to feel that government policy is a convenient smokescreen for good old-fashioned corporate cost-cutting.A spokesperson said Bet365 was responding to a “highly competitive trading environment, plus increased regulatory and tax-related costs”.So it’s all a bluff?Well, no. The UK’s biggest gambling companies, including Betfred, Entain, Flutter and more, have all announced cuts since Reeves’s duty rise. It is impossible to say how much of this retrenchment might have happened anyway, given economic worries and structural shifts within the sector. However, it makes sense that any further increase in costs, in the form of higher taxes on slot machines, will negatively affect the gambling sector.Simon Thomas, the chief executive of the Hippodrome Casino in London, says that fear of the tax is already hurting investment.“We have a £6m rooftop expansion plan with full planning permission, ready to go. With MGD up in the air, we’ve had to shelve it,” he said, adding that if MGD goes up to 40%,  a third of bingo halls and a third of casinos could close.Does the government want a smaller gambling sector?Burnham has already moved to limit the opening of new gambling premises. He has voiced particular concerns about 24-hour adult gaming centres (AGCs), high street venues packed with the sort of machines that would be more heavily taxed by an MGD increase. The rise of these “slot farms” is understood to be the main driver for any such move.But there are question marks over whether AGCs would actually take the hit. They already have much lower overheads and looser regulation than casinos and bingo halls, which have experienced negligible growth. Last year, AGCs managed to increase their takings from £528m to £613m by packing more machines into larger venues.So if slot machines taxes go up, in theory AGCs are best placed to survive the impact. The AGC operator Merkur has already offered to buy some of the 132 shops that Betfred put up for sale, indicating it is unruffled by the prospect of a tax rise. If others follow suit, just as bookies retrench, an MGD rise could simply lead to bookies being replaced by 24-hour slot farms.As Treasury officials weigh up duty rises, they will have to consider the law of unintended consequences.Explore more on these topicsTax and spendingGamblingBudget 2026Economic policyBudgetBetfairPaddy PowerexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touring | Erasure | The Guardian
description: Returning for a 20th album of sumptuous synthpop, Andy Bell and Clarke open up about supporting one another through bereavement, being happily uncool and battling the resurgence of homophobia
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: Returning for a 20th album of sumptuous synthpop, Andy Bell and Clarke open up about supporting one another through bereavement, being happily uncool and battling the resurgence of homophobia
Content: ‘I just love listening to you, man’ … Vince Clarke (right) and Andy Bell.Photograph: Travis ShinnView image in fullscreen‘I just love listening to you, man’ … Vince Clarke (right) and Andy Bell.Photograph: Travis ShinnErasureInterview‘It’s a deep soul connection’: Erasure on how 40 years of friendship got them through grief – and why Vince Clarke has quit touringTim JonzeReturning for a 20th album of sumptuous synthpop, Andy Bell and Clarke open up about difficult recent years, being happily uncool and battling resurgent homophobiaFri 2 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Bell is rabbiting away on multiple topics. There’s his farm in Mallorca, where he and his husband Stephen Moss have had a fine year harvesting pomegranates, kiwis and lemons. Then there’s theErasurefrontman’s fascination with clowns (“Would the makeup help you avoid facial recognition technology?”), memories of 90s nightclubbing (“You could do anything and get away with it!”) and a worry that he’s turning into “a fussy old grandpa”. Suddenly, he catches himself: “But what aboutyou, Vince? You’re being very quiet!”Bell’s bandmate, whose only contribution since joining the video chat from his San Diego home has been to say hello, smiles. “No, no, I justlovelistening to you, man. I’m really enjoying this.”This has always been the pair’s dynamic. Ever since they formed in 1985, Vince Clarke has preferred to remain in the background, unleashing precision-tooled electronic bangers while hidden behind a bank of synths. Bell, meanwhile, spun around centre stage in sequins and angel wings, his vocals adding lovelorn melodrama to the melodies. The combination has served them well. In the 40 years since their debut album Wonderland came out, the band have never split up, gone on hiatus or – if you take their word for it – fallen out. “We’ve never been one of these ego-driven bands bringing their drama to the band every five minutes,” says Bell.View image in fullscreenAndy Bell on stage in Dublin in 2005.Photograph: ShowBizIreland/Getty ImagesRecently, their deep friendship has proved its mettle. In January 2024, Clarke’s wife Tracy Hurley Martin died from stomach cancer. A taciturn man at the best of times, Clarke still finds the experience difficult to talk about, but he’s on easier ground praising his bandmate’s support.“He was amazing,” says Clarke. “Andy gave me all the love and support I could possibly ever want. I don’t think I could have gotten that from anyone else. Because he’s been through shit as well.” Bell lost his partner Paul Hickey in 2012. “He’s coming from a similar perspective. So, yeah, I’m truly grateful.”“You have to look after your friend,” says Bell. “It sounds corny, but we’ve been through so many things together. We all have misgivings when we lose a partner – that we couldn’t do the best for them when they were here or whatever. But that’s just normal life. So we have to hold each other up.”The experience of being there for each other has fed into a new Erasure album – amazingly, their 20th – called Radio!! Radio!!. The record will accompany an arena tour across the UK and Europe, although with one significant difference: for the first time in the band’s history Clarke won’t be in attendance. Instead, he will serve remotely as the tour’s musical director, leaving keyboard technician Howard Rider to work the synths on the night.“I was really panicking last night, Vince, thinking: oh God, I’m going to be on tour on my own,” says Bell.“That’s not true,” reassures Clark. “You’ve got the whole crew with you!”“I know, but it’s still not gonna bethe samethough,” says Bell, amusingly off-message. “But it’s your music and we can’t do it without your music.”When I ask if Tracy’s death is the main reason Clarke is stepping back, there’s a long pause before he replies simply: “Yes.”How has he been getting on?“I’m OK,” he says. “Obviously everything’s changed but … yeah … it is what it is …”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Travis ShinnBell, realising his friend is struggling, pipes up: “Vincent, I have to say, you lookamazing. You do!”“Ah thanks,” he says. “I had a shave this morning and everything. I had a bath!”Do they consider each other best mates?“It’s much deeper than mates,” says Clarke.“Yeah, I wouldn’t even say mates,” says Bell. “It’s more a family thing. A deep soul connection.”“Can I just say something?” says Clarke. I’m expecting another moving paean to their friendship. “When you’re talking in front of that [red feather plate on Bell’s wall] you look just like Ronald McDonald!”They’re both laughing now. “Well, I am thinking of putting a Babybel on my nose and going on stage like a clown,” says Bell.Radio!! Radio!! acquired its four exclamation marks because Bell wanted a title with a sense of urgency. What’s the emergency he’s warning us about? “I suppose it’s technology, rushing too fast,” he says. “The album is a call to more peaceful and relaxed times.”Is it hard to write about that without sounding like a bit of a boomer?“Iamquite surprised by how moral I’ve become!” he says. “I don’t want to be telling young people, ‘You can’t do this, you can’t do that,’ because I’ve never been like that myself – especially not on stage. But [as you get older] you do start seeing the world in a different way.”Perhaps this maturing viewpoint inspired the album’s shift away from the synth sound of 2020’s The Neon and towards piano and guitar. Bell and Moss made it their personal mission to buy a “perfect Spanish guitar” for Clarke before he arrived in Spain for the sessions, chatting to a local instrument shop owner about everything from his specific body measurements to the most common guitar lines used in classic Erasure songs.Bell happily admits to an ignorance of technology. He still uses the term “ghetto blaster” and his knowledge of Clarke’s synth collection seems to extend to: “Do you still use that one with the little bulbs inside it?”View image in fullscreen‘Vince’s persona has always been very cool’ … Clarke and Bell in 1988.Photograph: BSR Entertainment/Gentle Look/Getty ImagesThe pair of them reminisce about the very early days, working on Wonderland, when Clarke would roam the studio asking people to shout out random three-digit numbers. As Bell recalls: “I’d shout, say, 246 and he would input that into his synth and that would create the arpeggio for the song!”“That was before randomise functions,” smiles Clarke. “I’d go around asking the tape operator, the engineer.”Wonderland struggled, but soon afterwards the band released the single Sometimes and entered an imperial phase: between 1987 and 1991 their hits included Ship of Fools, Chains of Love, Stop!, Drama! (from their 1989 album Wild! – they’ve always loved exclamation marks), Blue Savannah, Chorus, Love to Hate You and plenty more. A Little Respect in particular has taken on a life akin to Dancing Queen or Come on Eileen – a song guaranteed to pack the dancefloor.Bell tells me the young people in the village where he lives often ask him if he knew the song was going to be such a hit when they wrote it. “And of course, no, we didn’t, we didn’t even think about it.”“I’m chuffed that they’re singing it at football matches – and rugby too,” says Clarke.“To have a calling card in your life is amazing,” says Bell. “And Vince has three!”He’s talking about Clarke’s former life as a founding member of Depeche Mode, and then a partner to Alison Moyet in Yazoo – during which time he penned the enduring hits Just Can’t Get Enough and Only You. Bell seems just as proud of Clarke’s pre-Erasure smashes as he does the ones they wrote together.“There’s a lot of programmes on here in Spain about Vince, about the making of Only You or the breakup of Depeche Mode,” he says. “I’m always like: wow, whoisthis guy?”Bell was a huge fan when he answered an advert in the music press seeking a singer, so seeing Clarke in the room was an understandably nerve-racking experience. Still, he threw himself into the songs. Clarke liked that he interpreted them in his own style. “It wasn’t like: this is the guy I’m going to be with for 40 years,” he says. “It was: this is the guy who can sing this one song. We weren’t planning for 10 years ahead, we were planning for what was going to happen next Thursday.”View image in fullscreenPerforming in Germany in 1986.Photograph: Galuschka/Ullstein Bild/Getty ImagesDespite their success – more than a dozen Top 10 hits, the best British group award at the 1989 Brits – Erasure were often treated a little suspiciously by critics. “Vince’s persona has always been very cool,” says Bell, “but when I came along I ruined it for him. I’d get him to dress up onstage as a cactus” – as he did during their 1997 Cowboy tour – “and then expect us to be taken seriously by the music industry! But to me that’s more punk than punk, right?”Most famously, the pair recorded the video for their chart-topping Abba cover Take a Chance on Me in drag as Frida and Agnetha. Looking back, was there something subversive about Clarke, a proper working-class geezer, throwing himself into camp abandon like this? “It was always funny to me,” he says. “If you’re dressed as a cactus on stage, people relate to that – don’t ask me why! I think they just see you and think: ah, he’s a silly bugger.”Radio!! Radio!! might have emerged during a traumatic time, but it’s a more positive record than that suggests. “I’m a bit of a doom merchant and a spiraller,” says Bell, “but I always have this internal optimism.”‘Work is therapy’: synth-pop icon Johnny Jewel on David Lynch, Chromatics and near-death experiencesRead moreThe song Holy! is a good example. It deals with LGBTQ communities under increasing attack, from the perspective of showing up as a friend: “When you’re falling / I will shield you.” Bell was one of the few out gay pop stars in the 1980s, and has lived through decades of social progress. Is he shocked at the way things have fallen backwards over the last decade?“I am, but I shouldn’t be, because politicians always pick the supposedly ‘weakest’ group to attack,” he says. “Really, it’s because they’re the strongest.”How does it compare to the 1980s? Was there more acceptance then in some ways? “I don’t think there wasmore, it was just different. Back then was the first time things were sort of laid out. We were just showing people there’s nothing to be scared of.”Ultimately, says Bell, whether it’s gay rights, a friend’s grief or performing a huge pop show without your trusted partner, the solution is always the same: “All you need to do is put your arms around people,” he says. “You bring them all in – and that’s what music does best.”Radio!! Radio!! is released via Mute on 12 March 2027Explore more on these topicsErasurePop and rockFriendshipinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If you can’t hold it, you don’t own it’: why media fans want to escape algorithms with CDs, DVDs and vinyl | Media | The Guardian
description: People describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choices
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: People describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choices
Content: Some people have begun to buy secondhand CDs and DVDs from charity shops to wean themselves off subscription services.Photograph: Charday Penn/GettyView image in fullscreenSome people have begun to buy secondhand CDs and DVDs from charity shops to wean themselves off subscription services.Photograph: Charday Penn/GettyMedia‘If you can’t hold it, you don’t own it’: why media fans want to escape algorithms with CDs, DVDs and vinylPeople describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choicesJane ClintonFri 2 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor some, it is the security of knowing they have a physical copy of their favourite films and music, free from algorithms, interruptions and the vagaries of streaming. For others, it is the sound of needle on vinyl, the click of a cassette player and the ability to interact with a physical format.We asked people if they were moving back to CDs, DVDs, vinyl and older formats to escape algorithmically curated content. Here are some of their responses.‘I missed the physical connection with music’View image in fullscreenAsh says discovering new music for yourself requires more work and effort.Photograph: Dylan Odedra/Guardian CommunityAsh, 52, a university lecturer from Cornwall, says he initially embraced streaming but has since tempered that enthusiasm.“Algorithms make great suggestions, but it feels like you catch a lot of small fish (OK, bands),” he says. “Reading music magazines and artist recommendations and discovering new music for yourself requires more work and effort … it feels like catching the bigger fish.”Recently, he has returned to buying and listening to physical media. He says he has amassed more than 5,000 records and CDs from 1990 to 2009.“Technology and streaming felt liberating for a person who has a deep and wide music collection and a bad back. I stopped buying and streamed,” he says, but adds: “I spent more time making playlists than listening to music; I lost the ability to listen to a whole album and missed the physical connection with music.“I listen to records as an activity, but listen through tech more passively. It’s more like wallpaper than a work of art.”‘We scour flea markets and secondhand shops for shows and movies’CJ, 55, a compliance manager from Atlanta, says she decided to return to physical media when shows she liked began disappearing from streaming services.“HBO removed about 200 episodes of Sesame Street in 2022, so we realised any media we wanted to continue to watch or listen to could be gone, and we’d have no way to get it back,” she says. “As the saying goes, if you can’t hold it, you don’t own it, and we firmly agree with this.“There are so many shows that aren’t on streaming platforms that we want to rewatch. We scour flea markets and secondhand shops for shows and movies that are hard to find. We have also continued to buy CDs.“When access to media is so easy to cut off, it makes sense to return to owning what you can, so no one can take it away from you.”‘I wanted to support musicians’View image in fullscreenRuth’s CD collection has its own ‘walk-in closet’Photograph: Ruth/Guardian CommunitySpotify quickly “bored” Ruth, 67, a retired professor from Michigan, but there were other reasons behind her move to CDs and DVDs.“Most of all, I wanted to own my music and support the musicians, so I own 5,300 CDs; they have their own walk-in closet,” she says. “Owning my own books, music, and photos (no iCloud) has always seemed normal to me, and, increasingly, prudent.She adds: “No algorithm is as creative as a well-stocked human brain alive to its actual surroundings.”Ruth also rents physical film titles by mail from a store in Seattle. “We retired to a rural area with internet unreliable for streaming that wouldn’t sustain a movie without interruptions and buffering. We can stream music from the internet, although even then the connection will conk out every once in a while.”‘Now I don’t have to share my data with a company’This summer, Antonio, 40, began buying secondhand CDs from a charity shop in an attempt to get off music subscription services.“I have a ritual now,” says the software engineer, who lives in Reading. “Twice a month I buy between one and 10 CDs – depending on what is available.“I decided I didn’t want to rely on a subscription any more and have to deal with price rises, and now I don’t have to share my data – both personal information such as my name, bank account details, location, and my listening history – with a company.“Nowadays we hand over so much of our data (intentionally or unintentionally) to big corporations that, if I can reduce it in any way, I’m more than happy to do so.”‘Sometimes I’m ‘out of the loop’, but I prefer it’View image in fullscreenQuinn buys tapes from bands to support the artists.Photograph: Quinn/Guardian CommunityQuinn, 26, began collecting cassette tapes last year and “quickly fell in love with it”.He works nights and weekends, leaving him little time to go to concerts. “Buying tapes from bands gave me a way to engage with and support them, despite not being able to see their shows,” says Quinn, who works in food delivery and lives in Washington.“I really appreciate the format’s restrictions. There’s the routine of interacting with the tape and equipment to play it, the quirks that come with analogue tech and, of course, being able to share music with people by handing them a tape rather than a Spotify link.“My switch has definitely come with the desire to choose what I’m engaging with. Rather than having content presented to me, I’m seeking it out for myself, or finding it through friends, and that’s a huge part of being low-tech. Sometimes I’m ‘out of the loop’, but I prefer it.”‘I love the slowness of the setup to see the films’Tim’s young and adult children all enjoy watching films on older formats.“In Sweden many people have a summer house,” says the 61-year-old academic, who lives in Stockholm. “Ours, on the mainland, a 45-minute drive from Stockholm, located in the southern end of the Swedish archipelago, contains a video projector from around 2010, a DVD player, and the collection of DVDs watched by my big kids when they were small.“The biggest luxury for my small kids is when the cables are rigged, the choice of DVD made, and they sit through five minutes of ‘coming soon on Disney’ before we press play on Shrek or whatever the film is.”Tim says the “aged DVDs” often need a clean, as sticky fingers over the years have left their mark.“I love this middle stage between the digital and the analogue, and the slowness of the setup to see the films. Next step is to open the trunk containing my (younger) partner’s childhood VHS collection. We’ll see where that goes.”‘I feel less controlled’View image in fullscreenSophie says she feels less analysed watching DVDs and listening to CDs.Photograph: Sophie/Guardian CommunitySophie, 32, a librarian from Los Angeles, does stream music, but “mostly listens to CDS”. She also often watches DVDs from her own collection or checks them out from the library.She is “not a fan” of algorithms, something that informed her move to CDs and DVDs. “I enjoy watching DVDs and listening to CDs because nobody sees what I’m doing and they’re not analysing it. It feels less overwhelming to browse physical versions. I also feel less controlled.”Explore more on these topicsMediaMusic streamingTV streamingSpotifyDigital music and audioTelevisionInternetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classic | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The Geese frontman mesmerizes in a concert film that is both swoony and austere
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The Geese frontman mesmerizes in a concert film that is both swoony and austere
Content: A still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.Photograph: Courtesy of Janus FIlmsView image in fullscreenA still from Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall.Photograph: Courtesy of Janus FIlmsFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewCameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classicNew York Film Festival:The Geese frontman mesmerizes in a concert film that is both swoony and austereAdrian HortonFri 2 Oct 2026 16.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne night last December, weary from a busy week and the impending doom of winter, I hurried into Carnegie Hall to witness Cameron Winter. TheGeesefrontman was marking the end of abreakout yearwith a series ofrapturously receivedsolo acoustic shows, drawing the penitent for whom the 23-year-old’s primordial voice struck some kind of destabilizing natural frequency. I had bought the ticket months earlier, after being hypnotized by Winter’s beguiling debut solo album, Heavy Metal, and sat transfixed in the rafters, far from the Brooklynite’s lanky, stygian presence before a single piano.So far, in fact, that I assumed the maybe-camera that came on stage at one point was a bit, perhaps a jab at our incessant need to film things from a very deadpan celebrity whose only non-music interlude that evening was to wordlessly stand, stretch and mockingly fight with the stage door, as if trying to escape his own momentous show. I emerged from the event teary, charged by what felt like a communion across time, and confused by a friend’s text: “can’t wait for the cameron winter PTA doc”.Cameron Winter review – Geese wunderkind whittles confident rearrangements in an intimate showRead morePTA, of course, isPaul Thomas Anderson, the acclaimed film-maker and, it turns out, one of five camera operators (including Benny Safdie) working that evening to capture Winter’s masterly performance on film. The resulting project, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall, which premiered this week at the New York Film Festival, is very much not a bit. Shot on 35mm, with coloring so luscious even the scaffolding outside Carnegie Hall looks dignified, this 75-minute concert film manages to preserve most of what made that evening so special — the stark contrasts of Winter’s music, the mesmeric force of his baritone vibrato, the vanishingly rare power to make an audience implicitly agree to collectively ignore their phones and focus, for as long as necessary. The auteur’s second concert film is an immediate classic, memorializing, in the medium of said classics, a performance that felt less like a concert than an ancient ritual and proclamation, a stake in the ground of a young but blazing career.Fittingly for a subject whose only address all evening was a post-encore “thank you for coming, everybody,” Anderson dispenses of virtually all bells and whistles; save a minute of exterior shots and ticket scans plus a couple of finely wrought transitions, Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is, well, just that – the concert, straight up and gorgeously recorded, Winter’s woozy vibrato and intensity on the keys so seemingly unmediated that I felt compelled to applaud after each of the 12 songs. (The film’s brilliant music production was done by Ariel Rechtshaid, a Grammy winner for his work on albums by Vampire Weekend and Adele; a live album is soon to be released.)View image in fullscreenCameron Winter.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianThe on-stage camera notwithstanding, Anderson et al largely stay out of the way, appearing to lurk throughout the cavernous theater, from my rafter seat to the aisle to the piano bench, like one of Winter’s many shadows, themselves filmed to haunting effect. Depending on the scene, the stark shifts in light, and the angle of piercingly close shots on his face, Winter appears either 20 or 60 – all the better to get hit by his absurd yet evocative lyrics, such nonsense as “the beach ball cathedral dimpled like a sea fly swarming”, “until the conga line behind me is a thousand chickens long” and, most evocatively for a largely secular New York audience, “god is real.”‘People think I’ve gone crazy’: indie sensation Cameron Winter on leaving crowds in tears with his wild lyrics and supernatural voiceRead moreSome elements of the show did not fully translate to film – the ecstatic, slyly humorous decision to bring the lights up on that “god is real, I’m not kidding this time!” so one could see other beaming faces, was the show’s acme but a film footnote – though Anderson and co were able to capture the quiet that Winter wields to such seismic, spellbinding effect, as well as the rapt audience receiving it. Like Winter’s music, the film itself appears at once sumptuous but austere, raw and intuitive yet precise.This is, of course, a document for the faithful, the people who either already adore Winter’s singularly striking voice or are naturally predisposed to. Those who don’t will find no other hook – no interview nor testament nor voiceover nor crowd work – to bring them in. But those who do enter will find a exquisitely rendered version of something old and timeless — an interplay of light and shadows and a communion of generations, summoned by a figure of gifts beyond his age, captured for the ages.Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall is screening at the New York Film Festival and will be released in the US on 20 November with UK and Australia releases to follow in 2027Explore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewPaul Thomas AndersonGeesePop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The singer’s hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old self
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: The singer’s hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old self
Content: Teen spirit … Hayley Kiyoko.Photograph: Grace ScuittoView image in fullscreenTeen spirit … Hayley Kiyoko.Photograph: Grace ScuittoMoviesInterview‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’Lucy KnightThe singer’s hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old selfFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlot of Hayley Kiyoko’s teenage summers were spent waiting, bored and pining, as she sat at the computer willing her crush to message her back on AOL instant messenger. Like Coley, the 17-year-old protagonist of Girls Like Girls, the film the pop star has co-written and directed, Kiyoko fell hard for a girl who “put me through my own heartbreak and haunted me for a long time”, she says.Although the 35-year-old singer became known by fans as “lesbian Jesus” following the release of her breakthrough single Girls Like Girls in 2015 (the film is an extended version of the story first told in the song’s music video), feeling comfortable in her sexuality didn’t actually come until after its release. Her gay identity was, at the time, the topic she was “the most scared of writing about”, and the song’s confident refrain “Girls like girls like boys do, nothing new” came from wanting to “manifest feeling confident”.View image in fullscreenPool cute … Maya da Costa and Myra Molloy in Girls Like Girls.Photograph: Dan Power/Focus Features“Once I released Girls Like Girls, not only the song but the music video, and saw that so many people in the world felt the way I felt, and that I could still be loved for who I was, that was a big indicator of allowing myself to feel that type of love,” she says. After directing the music video, in which two teenage girls, one of whom has a boyfriend, develop romantic feelings for one another, Kiyoko became “very fixated on being able to tell this story on a feature film level”.It took just over a decade to make that happen, with a “pivot” to a different form in between, via the publication of Girls Like Girls the YA romance novel in 2023, which helped to get the film greenlit. The film is “definitely a love letter to my younger 16-, 17-year-old self who desperately was seeking that kind of love,” Kiyoko tells me via Zoom, dialling in from Bangkok where she has been celebrating the film’s Thailand release. The sun is shining on her and her eyes are bright as she excitedly tells me about meeting her Thai fans for the first time.double quotation markWe watch movies to dream and to see representation that maybe we lack in our livesThe Bangkok screening was “super-special” because one of the film’s stars, Myra Molloy, who plays Coley’s love interest Sonya, is from Bangkok, Kiyoko says. The Canadian actor who plays Coley, Maya da Costa, has Vietnamese heritage: it was important to Kiyoko to create not just a queer love story, but one that reflected her Asian heritage, too. Growing up in Los Angeles, “I never was able to buy a ticket at a cinema and see myself reflected back to me in my own experience as a queer person, as a mixed-race Asian person,” she says (Kiyoko is of Japanese descent on her mother’s side). “I never believed that my stories really mattered, because I never got to see them.”Born Hayley Kiyoko Alcroft, the singer grew up close to the limelight. Her father, Jamie Alcroft, is an actor and comedian, while her mother is the figure skater and Emmy award-winning choreographer Sarah Kawahara. Kiyoko herself has been performing since she was five, initially as an actor in commercials and later Disney Channel and Nickelodeon shows. She started learning the drums at six years old and wrote her first song at eight. In her late teens, she was part of the all-girl band the Stunners, which supported Justin Bieber in 2010 but broke up a year later without having released an album.View image in fullscreenLike the clappers … Hayley Kiyoko on the set of Girls Like Girls.Photograph: Dan Power/Focus FeaturesKiyoko’s solo career took off after she released Girls Like Girls as a single, which happened to be just days before same-sex marriage was legalised by the US federal government in June 2015. Back then it felt like an appropriate anthem for a time full of hope and steps forward for the LGBTQ+ community. Now, however, the picture is less positive: there has been a major increase in the number of anti-LGBTQ+ policies across the US in recent years, with the American Civil Liberties Uniontracking more than 500 anti-LGBTQ+ billsbeing considered so far in 2026 alone.Kiyoko describes the current political climate as “heartbreaking”, and though she is keen to make clear that she is “not the spokesperson for what’s going on in the world”, she says: “It’s not safe for our community, and we are continually fighting for pride events and pride festivals to continue to be funded.” Reflecting on the video for her 2016 song One Bad Night, in which she highlighted the violence transgender women experience, she says she would go about making it differently, were she to make it now.View image in fullscreenDaddy daze … Zach Braff as Coley’s father in Girls Like Girls.Photograph: Focus FeaturesShe stands by it being “really important” to spotlight trans people’s stories, but now thinks it’s more important, rather than focusing on the violence queer people experience, to “create art that is more queer joy and showing us in spaces where we are thriving … How radical is it that right now in this awful political climate, we get to release a movie called Girls Like Girls in cinemas and to remind the world that our stories and our love matters and that we will never go anywhere?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe queer couple at the heart of the Girls Like Girls film do face adversity, with Sonya describing her relationship with Coley as “wrong” at one point, but for the most part it’s an intentionally positive portrayal of self-discovery. In particular, Coley is unequivocally accepted by her father, without fanfare. Kiyoko, who has spoken previously about how her parentsinitially dismissed her sexuality as “a phase”, says “everyone has their own journey with their family dynamics”, but says it felt important to show an accepting father figure in the film. “We go to watch movies to dream and to fantasise and to see representation that maybe we lack in our lives.”Kiyoko says “it’s been really healing” to promote Girls Like Girls right after getting engaged earlier this summer, “celebrating this traumatic moment of my teens” while also being able to show her fans that she now has “a partner who makes me feel so seen and loved”. The singer’s fiancee, Becca Tilley, is a former contestant on the dating show The Bachelor. The pair met in 2018 when the reality TV star was trying to set Kiyoko up with her younger sister, but Tilley’s sister “bailed, and she ended up going instead”, Kiyoko says. “We’ve been together ever since.” Wedding plans are on hold as “I’ve been in Girls Like Girls universe”, she says, but she hopes that soon “we’ll be able to get into that”.Certainly, Kiyoko’s career seems to be in full flow right now: she will be headlining the 35th iteration of the famed lesbian music festival The Dinah, which she is “very excited” about, particularly at a time when lesbian spaces are not “very accessible or available to people”. After that, she hopes to continue developing herself as a film-maker, and wants to take on more film and TV directing jobs. Music “will always support my storytelling”, she says, but she has “no idea” if she will continue to release new albums and go on tour.While Kiyoko rides the high of her first feature film finding global audiences, where is her own personal Sonya, the girl who broke her teenage heart, now? She doesn’t know, “but I’m grateful for the trauma because it led to my directorial debut”, she says with a grin. “I really do feel like I finally found my home, which is directing,” she says. “And I hope to continue to do that for ever.”Girls Like Girls is in cinemas2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive’: how Ross McElwee made a film about unimaginable loss, grief and guilt | Movies | The Guardian
description: When his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary project
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: When his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary project
Content: Adrian as a boy in Venice, as seen in Remake.Photograph: Giant Squid FilmsView image in fullscreenAdrian as a boy in Venice, as seen in Remake.Photograph: Giant Squid FilmsMoviesInterview‘I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive’: how Ross McElwee made a film about unimaginable loss, grief and guiltXan BrooksWhen his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary projectFri 2 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoss McElwee is the film-maker who spun home movies into art, framing himself and his friends and his son Adrian. The director used to film Adrian for a few minutes each month. He tracked the kid from infancy to adulthood, trying to catch the significant turns of his life. When tragedy struck it back-shadowed the footage. Maybe every home movie is a ghost story at heart.It feels crass to compliment McElwee on his latest documentary, Remake, because it isn’t the picture he’d ever have chosen to make. It is instead a grief-struck tour-de-force: a magnificent film about film-making and its real-world repercussions. McElwee filmed Adrian because he loved him, but now fears he might have hurt him. So he sifts through the material in search of clues, addressing his son as though he’s still in the room. “I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive,” he says. “But also to convince myself that you’re gone.”The plan, he explains, was for a completely different film. A Hollywood producer wanted to shoot a fictionalised version of his 1986 documentarySherman’s March. McElwee decided to follow the process – to make a new documentary about adapting an old documentary. That might be funny, he thought. But events overtook him. Adrian’s mental health was deteriorating. He became addicted to opioids. He died from a fentanyl overdose at the age of 27, in the bathroom of McElwee’s Boston home.“Everything immediately ground to a halt,” the director recalls. “My son was gone. I was devastated. And compared to everything I was facing, the film seemed banal and frivolous.” He took a year to regroup and plotted a new course.A more traditional film-maker would have junked the original idea. McElwee has audaciously chosen to preserve it, so that the remake plays as a kind of absurd counterbeat to the anguish of Adrian’s death. The film would have been too depressing otherwise, he says. “And in a sense I’m remaking my life by picking up the camera again. I’m reconstructing the life of my son from the scraps and pieces that had ended up being filmed.”Adrian, we learn, was gung-ho for a Hollywood version of Sherman’s March. Remake shows him discussing the project at length. He feels that his dad should be making more mainstream movies. He says, “Why not just do some big blockbuster hit?”View image in fullscreenCharleen Swansea at McDonald’s, as seen in Sherman’s March.Photograph: Little Field FilmsAfter seeing Remake, I rewatch Sherman’s March. It’s a joyous, insightful, free-ranging affair; a film that delights in taking the road less travelled. McElwee is ostensibly making a civil war documentary, but he keeps being set up with various “nice southern girls”. In one scene, Charleen Swansea – his voluble former English teacher – demands that he turn off his camera before a big date. “This isn’t art,” she roars. “This is life!”The success of Sherman’s March made Swansea a cult celebrity. A poll of American critics named her “the greatest documentary character of all time”. But when McElwee revisits Swansea for Remake, he finds she is now in the grip of dementia. She has no memory of the movie, or of teaching him English. “Things just disappear,” she says with a frown.View image in fullscreen‘There is a possibility that I was in denial’ … Ross McElwee.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesPeople disappear, that’s the tragic logic of life. Except that on the screen, in the footage, Adrian still feels alive, which is both a comfort and a torment. McElwee dips back through the archive to show him as a gorgeous, earnest little kid, netting crayfish on the rocks (“I just love the deep surprise of the ocean,” he says). Now here he is again as a tense, watchful teenager, raising his hand to block the camera lens. “There was no evidence for me that my films were a problem for him,” McElwee tells me. “Overall I would say that they were more a plus than a minus.” All the same, he can’t help but wonder.Might the issue be one of divided loyalties? McElwee has a set of responsibilities as a parent and a set of responsibilities as an artist. But maybe these are always going to be at loggerheads.McElwee nods. “Yeah, they’re antithetical. And when it works, the antithesis is what gives a film its creative friction. Because it never resolves itself. It’s always part of the problem. You have the camera, which means you have the power and other people don’t. And that’s the big responsibility. You can’t push your subject to say what you want them to say. You have to keep that in mind when you shoot and you edit.”View image in fullscreen‘They recognise what it means to you’ … Victoria Mapplebeck and her son, Jim.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianIf McElwee has a British counterpart, it might be the film-maker Victoria Mapplebeck. OnMotherboard, her fabulous 2024 documentary, Mapplebeck condensed two decades of life as a working single mother alongside her phlegmatic son, Jim.After speaking with McElwee, I call Mapplebeck. She says she relates to Remake and the ethical issues it raises. It’s about the compulsion to film and its effect on a family; the granting of consent and how that is understood by both parties.‘Mum, I can’t think straight any more’: the mother who filmed her son’s entire childhoodRead more“Watching it,” she says, “I felt both ashamed and moved. Because the thing with both Jim and Adrian is that at times they do provide consent [to film] because they recognise what it means to you. I think Jim definitely got more from the process than Adrian did. It was a useful way to get us talking. But fundamentally I needed to do it more than Jim did.”In his 2011 film Photographic Memory, McElwee painted Adrian as a troubled but basically resilient young man. The pair promoted the picture at the Venice film festival. Adrian posted pictures of speedboats, gondolas and wild parties. It should have been a triumphant moment. But McElwee now worries that his film got Adrian wrong and that the subsequent fuss turned his head and caused problems.“Did I give him a false impression of who he was? That he was more or less invincible and could therefore keep doing drugs?” He doesn’t know; he fears the worst. “For a child to see himself in a movie that his father has made and to then travel with him to festivals – often that would be wonderful for both father and son. But then all these other things arose from that. So there is a possibility that it had a corrosive effect on him and that I was somehow in denial about that. It was only later – after he got into trouble and then after he died – that I began to see the film in a different light.”View image in fullscreenAdrian in Remake.Photograph: Giant Squid FilmsI’m glad McElwee has made space for his unquiet old work. It speaks to Remake’s themes of representation and memory, and suggests that a film is never truly finished. The Sherman’s March remake, for instance, is initially billed as a comedy feature from the director of Paul Blart: Mall Cop. We then see it redrafted as a dramatic miniseries and a TV sitcom before it’s finally rolled out as a verbatim live opera. McElwee wonders what his son would have made of all that.What, for that matter, would he have thought of Remake? That’s the unanswerable question; the director can’t say. “I’d like to think that he came out the other side sober, and that he would think it had honoured him and was honest, and also that I was admitting the mistakes I’d made. But I’ll never know for sure.”Another thought strikes him. “It’s also possible that he’d say, ‘Yeah, this is good but you need to get a proper Hollywood deal.’ He was relentless about that. He liked my films, but I could tell they were never quite up to snuff in terms of the interest they generated and the money they made. He saw them as interesting exercises but a waste of time when I could have been doing something else.”McElwee is 79 and slowing down. Ideally, he’d like to make one last documentary – something light, warm and funny. But something is missing: the old itch, the compulsion. “I’ve been to family reunions in North Carolina,” he says. “Also, I had a nephew who got married. Each time I thought, ‘Gosh, I should be filming this.’ And I just can’t do it. This whole past year. I want to take a break and let life be life without me trying to turn it into art.”It reminds him of what Charleen said in Sherman’s March: “This isn’t art, this is life.” That’s four decades ago now. McElwee almost smiles. “I’m a slow learner,” he says.Remake is out nowIn the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393.
