title: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’ | Thrillers | The Guardian
description: In the film-maker’s Houston-set film, Ali stars as a devout Muslim who moonlights as a vicious hitman
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: In the film-maker’s Houston-set film, Ali stars as a devout Muslim who moonlights as a vicious hitman
Content: Bassam Tariq at Toronto Film Festival, September 2026.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbView image in fullscreenBassam Tariq at Toronto Film Festival, September 2026.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbThrillersInterviewHow Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’Radheyan SimonpillaiIn the film-maker’s Houston-set film, Ali stars as a devout Muslim who moonlights as a vicious hitmanFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMahershala Aliis swinging around a blade inYour Mother Your Mother Your Mother. That’s not a nod to Ali’s previousattachmentto Marvel’s Blade. It’s of a piece with Ali’s character, Latif, a devout Muslim who also happens to be a contract killer, though he fashions himself a righteous killer. Latif justifies his violence as divine retribution, dispensing victims he believes to have offended God. His sword, according to writer and director Bassam Tariq, is a part of Latif’s code, a negotiation with his faith.“You are forced to strike with intention when you use a sword,” Tariq says, speaking in a recent interview in Toronto.Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review – Mahershala Ali is a grieving hitman in soulful thrillerRead moreThe film-maker seems equally purposeful in our conversation as we dive deep into his pulpy samurai-coded neo-western. In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, he grapples with grief, spirituality, violence and the culture in America writ large. The movie is a visceral and stylish genre thriller – think Steven Soderbergh’s The Limey by way of Nicolas Winding Refn’s Drive. It’s also a textured portrait of Houston, navigating the city’s cultural tapestry, but also the hostility and tension between its siloed faiths and ideologies. That’s the conflict playing out between Ali’s Latif, who’s struggling to raise three kids on his own, andJon Cho’s Pastor Hwan, a militant evangelical Christian posting fire-and-brimstone sermons online while waging a heavily armed and indiscriminately brutal religious crusade.“It feels a little different in Texas right now,” Tariq says. He describes a palpable contrast between what he refers to as the “Mamdaniera” in New York, where he lives, and Houston, where he grew up. “Something that I found particularly in Texas, where I started writing [this] is, whether they’re religious or not, people are connected to the third spaces that are religious. All the social services are cut. So, if you’re going to go hang out or play basketball, it’ll probably be at a mosque or a church. You end up being a part of those communities. At the same time, you can start building dogmatic ideas, [like,] ‘We’re better than other people’. The nature of it has been really politicized. I think it’s a dark moment right now.”Mahershala Ali on Marvel’s collapsed Blade reboot: ‘If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it’Read moreYour Mother Your Mother Your Mother fearlessly cuts through that tension while capturing what makes those communities so vibrant and inspiring, and searching for a sense of hope in its heartfelt and intimate interrogation of faith and fatherhood. Those themes were especially important to he and Ali, Tariq says.“We connected on these things while we were on this [other] movie together,” says Tariq, referring to Marvel’s Blade. “You might have heard of it.”He’s being cheeky. The fallout from the aborted Blade reboot, which Tariq was set to direct, has become an intricate part of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’s lore. Ali was attached for several years to star as Marvel’s vampire-slayer, once played byWesley Snipes. He only recentlyconfirmedthat the long-delayed reboot is simply not happening.“We were very close to shooting when the pencils went down,” says Tariq, describing the moment before he departed Blade in 2022. “Even though we had no script, which is why it shut down.”View image in fullscreenMahershala Ali in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosTariq says they had their action sequences all planned out, following a year and a half of prep that included extensive fight training and choreography for Ali. That was Marvel’s process at the time: the action comes first, allowing time for VFX and set design, and the rest comes after.“It was like Bollywood, dude,” he says today. “You have dance scenes. Figure out all the choreography. And then we’ll figure out what the story is later … Now [Marvel’s] not moving forward until they have a great script.“I’m not trying to throw any shade on the writers,” Tariq adds, adding that they had big shoes to fill given that theearlier Bladein his mind was a near-perfect movie. “They worked really hard on it. It’s just a very tough thing to crack.”Tariq says he’s more than at peace with how everything turned out. He’s actually a squirrelly mix of nerves and excitement when I speak to him, the evening before Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother premieres at the Toronto film festival, his whispery voice barely containing that mix of emotion. He’s taking a moment for this interview before settling back in with his family, including two kids aged 12 and nine.They’re in town for the occasion. They’ve been along for the whole ride, from the writing process in Houston to production in Atlanta, observing onset, during ADR and the sound mix. “I’m trying to just keep everyone close,” he says, before tying that ethos to the story of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which is ultimately about a father’s wayward journey back to his kids. “You live the movie that you make.”View image in fullscreenAli, Tariq and Jahleel Kamara on the set of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.Photograph: Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon MGM StudiosThe seeds for the film were planted after Tariq’s own harrowing experience following the birth of his first child in 2014, when his wife had an infection that sent her to the emergency room. “My son was only breastfed at the time,” says Tariq. “So I had to go around New York City trying to find breast milk for my son. I couldn’t find it anywhere.”He poured that frantic search into the earliest iteration of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which opens with Ali’s Latif scouring for breast milk after his wife passes, while having the same crisis of faith that Tariq experienced.“I remember that frustration,” says Tariq. “I felt like that anger towards divinity. And then, of course, my son was fine. I realized all he really needed at that moment was just for me be present as a father. To have that miraculous moment when you hear your kid wanting you, that’s something that I think about. I’ve been trying to contemplate: how do I put that in a story that’s propulsive and exciting?”You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead morePart of the solution came from working on Blade, where Tariq connected and collaborated with Ali, and mapped out those elaborate fight scenes, which would have been abandoned after Marvel pulled the plug. Instead, Tariq and Ali were able to salvage what they prepared for the superhero movie, and bring it all over to their more intimate film about a father discovering that his kids are his superpower.“I’m a lot happier that I made this movie,” says Tariq, comparing working within the Marvel machine versus having the freedom to really explore and express himself on Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.“As you know, with all these things, there are these massive systems, and they have so many stakeholders to please. It’s just the nature of these things where they have to gross a certain [amount], and they have to look a certain way. There’s a glossiness. And that’s fine. I think some people have thrived in it and made some incredible films. For where I am right now, this feels like the right space. My mind and heart feel very much at ease.”Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is out now in the US, in Australia on 9 October and in the UK on 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsThrillersAction and adventure filmsMahershala AlifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio | Music | The Guardian
description: When a rarity blew up on TikTok, the solitary ambient artist had fraudsters trying to steal her royalties. It reinforced her DIY mentality – until reforming her band Helen reminded her of the beauty of collaboration
Author: Jenn Pelly
Headline: When a rarity blew up on TikTok, the solitary ambient artist had fraudsters trying to steal her royalties. It reinforced her DIY mentality – until reforming her band Helen reminded her of the beauty of collaboration
Content: ‘I get to show a side of myself that doesn’t always show through, which is that I like having having fun’ … Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.Photograph: Colin SmithView image in fullscreen‘I get to show a side of myself that doesn’t always show through, which is that I like having having fun’ … Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.Photograph: Colin SmithMusicInterview‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trioJenn PellyWhen a rarity blew up on TikTok, the solitary ambient artist had fraudsters trying to steal her royalties. It reinforced her DIY mentality – until reforming her band Helen reminded her of the beauty of collaborationFri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn mid-September, I watched as Liz Harris soundchecked to 1,500 empty seats at midtown Manhattan’s historic Town Hall theatre. Soon each plush red chair would be filled for the second of two sold-out nights, but this ornate seclusion felt oddly perfect. It is fair to infer that most of her concertgoers generally listen to the uncanny experimental music she makes as Grouper alone, just as she creates it.Harris started Grouper in 2005 in the DIY noise warehouses of Oakland, California. At 46, she now lives farther north, in coastal Astoria, Oregon, where she creates densely tessellated visual art and spare, lucid albums that have made her a titan of modern ambient music. Painfully beautiful and often inscrutable, hers is a sonic language all its own, creatingthickets of sound using little more than guitar or piano, voice and space; her angelic and alien songs have influenced artists as disparate asPhoebe BridgersandMk.gee, and been sampled by Lil B and 100 Gecs. It is intensely solitary work, often characterised as sad but full of profound relief. “Like a bloodletting,” Harris offers.Harris reflects on its origins in the abstract drone of her 2005 debut Way Their Crept. “I thought there was some really dark part of me, and I was trying to understand it and incorporate it,” she says now. She is uneasy being the face of her music and generally keeps herself at arm’s length from the industry. “I’ve always been backing away from that,” she says, preferring to remind herself before shows “that we’re all in the room together”.View image in fullscreenHelen … l-r Jed Bindeman, Scott Simmons, Liz Harris.Photograph: Colin SmithWhen Harris and I meet at her Williamsburg hotel prior to the show, she’s wearing a T-shirt that says “Birth Ends in Death”, merch from her friend and occasional collaborator, the ambient musician Jefre Cantu-Ledesma. In addition to these milestone Grouper shows – coming five years after her last album, Shade – we’re speaking in light of the second record by Helen, the dream-pop trio in which she sings and plays guitar alongside drummer Jed Bindeman, who runs Portland shop Little Axe Records, and bassist Scott Simmons, also of lo-fi bandthe Lavender Flu. Their new album, Linda’s Head, like their 2015 debut The Original Faces, evokes scrappy Flying Nun indie-pop remade in their own stark Pacific Northwest image. But there’s a striking clarity and weight to the new one. If Grouper is the sound of a woman singing to herself, on Linda’s Head, she sings out.Helen’s appeal, for Harris, is in part its collectivity. “I get to relax more in Helen,” she says. “It feels as if I get to show a side of myself that I’ve always had, but that doesn’t get to show through Grouper, which is that I like having fun and I like my friends. I’m not just in the corner crying,” she says with a hearty laugh. Helen has a “bright energy”, she says, but, as with Grouper, a darkness gently haunts the music and Harris’s beguiling layered harmonies. The band’s name references Washington’s Mount St Helen, the site of a deadly volcanic eruption shortly before Harris was born in 1980, and it also alludes to a childhood spectre. “When I was a total loner social reject in junior high, I was trying to talk to ghosts all the time,” says Harris. “I thought I was talking to a ghost named Helen that lived in my house.”The songs consider what Harris calls “ecstatic nihilism” in a brutal world. “We’re all going through this time where things are really fucked up – it’s the war on Gaza and straight-up fascism in this country,” she says of the US. “There’s this urge to escape, but at the same time, a very pressing urge to be present and have community.” She hears both on Linda’s Head, and says the collaborative process of making the music lifted her spirits during a time when she was navigating medical difficulties. “Jed would be like, ‘Come on, let’s practise,’ and I’d drag my feet there. I’d always leave thinking, ‘Thank God I did that.’ It was really restorative.”In conversation, Harris is gracious and direct – she sounds as comfortable discussing her art, process and many tattoos as she does politics and music-industry corruption – which may surprise those who know her through her often cryptic music. Touring and performing like this is daunting for her, but she’s enjoying it. She says she’s been feeling more “integrated” lately, which she hears in Helen.A pair of songs on Linda’s Head, Dead Shark and Dead Shark II (alternate versions of the same tune), are disarmingly vibrant for Harris, despite their morbid origins. They were inspired by an actual shark Harris saw one day at the coast when she was feeling especially low. She observed its large, lifeless body floating by. “It distracted me from my own shit, and took me out of my headspace, this poor creature,” she says. “The song is about connecting and the process of feeling bad and going out into nature and letting it change you.”Helen: Dead Shark II – videoThe macabre titles recall Harris’s 2008 breakthrough, Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill, when she pivoted from abstract noise to acoustic, subtle art songs. That earlier title derived from a core childhood memory: Harris encountered a dead deer in the woods with a friend who dared her to hoist it up a hill. It incited a realisation about her agency in the world, and later inspired a title about the process of unburdening yourself of the past.When she was two years old, Harris’s parents were among the many seeking structure after the chaos of post-hippy late-60s San Francisco. The family moved from nearby Bolinas, where her father built houses with back-to-the-lander Lloyd Kahn, to a Fourth Way commune in Sonoma County. They joined a spiritual group – called the Group – where kids defiantly referred to the initiated as “groupers”. Harris still has friends from then: “There was a grouper at the show last night.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m pretty happy at the place I’ve landed’ … Liz HarrisPhotograph: Kait De AngelisThe adults enacted the Group’s dogma on to children who were shuffled between households. Theoretically, they followed the teachings of famed mystic Gurdjieff. Harris was told that they wererealpeople, but most of the world was asleep. “It was so confusing, and actually just instilled terror in me,” she says. “It made me terrified of other people, but also terrified of, how do I make sure that I stay real? I can’t become one of thesleepers.” I ask if this affected 2008’s Heavy Water/I’d Rather Be Sleeping, still her signature song, but she says that was about a depressive period and retreating into her “very active dream world”.Making music in her 20s was a way to begin processing it all. “I would still call it a cult,” she says of the Group, “and what happened was exploitative. But it’s not holding my focus in the way that it used to. There were enlightening things and shitty things – all of it led to where I’m at now. I still have my existential crises, but I’m pretty happy at the place I’ve landed.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHarris helps to maintain that balance by avoiding the music industry, but during the pandemic, she became caught in the undertow of a uniquely modern phenomenon when her 2008 rarity Poison Tree went viral. Harris wrote the gothic hymn in her mid-20s after relocating to Portland and feeling intensely isolated. “I went dark with it:I’ve never been able to connect with people. There’s something wrong with me, and people can see it,” she recalls. “I was having self-punishing thoughts and then trying to process it and turn it into something more expansive or rational-minded.”The song’s unlikely TikTok moment means “there’s this younger generation of really sweet, rad, open-minded kids” newly discovering Grouper, says Harris. She delights in recounting how her friends’ teenage children are now independently getting into her work.This current Grouper tour has been Harris’s first time “out in the world” since the song “fluffed up, or whatever you want to call it”, she says. “I hate saying ‘gone viral’.” She was late to learning about Poison Tree’s second life; she pays little attention to stats and doesn’t know how to look them up. When Brian Foote, general manager of her label Kranky, first told her that Poison Tree had accrued 20m plays (it now has more than 300m on the world’s biggest music streamer) she told him, “‘Well, that’s weird because I haven’t even put that on digital.’ He was like, ‘Yeah, that’s why I’m telling you.’”The song had been fraudulently registered and uploaded by someone else and had already earned around six figures. Fortunately, since that person used the same distribution platform as Harris, she and Foote were able to shut down the scammer and get back what she was owed.‘A sacred kind of sound’: inside a solar-powered journey to preserve the music of church organsRead moreAs an independent artist, Harris has learned first-hand that an elevated digital profile comes with a range of new concerns – like fake remixes and songs posted with the same titles as hers by bad actors trying to skim whatever royalties they can. “You have to spend all this stupid energy whack-a-mole-ing” these infringing tracks, she says. “I have learned that people think [streaming] platforms are a lot more regulated than they are. It is not regulated. I think it’s rational that I have a fear of immersing myself more into the music industry.”As Harris’s self-contained world expands – her label YellowElectric, her zine Presence, plus the gallery, Anita, she occasionally runs from her studio – her independence feels heroic. She carries a sweatshirt repping Portland punk legends Dead Moon to our interview, a fitting nod to her regional DIY forebears. Those ideals feel of a piece with Helen’s graceful, threadbare sound, too. “I’ve always adamantly wanted to be a balanced person,” she says. “In my 30s, I toured too much and got burnt out. I thought, ‘I want to have other things I’m doing. I don’t want to get stuck in a corner.’ In some ways, that still happens, but I’m intentional about having a full life.”On her current tour, she channels older material through this light. The first song of her set is Invisible, a downcast and tactile acoustic ballad from 2008. The incantatory lyrics – “I’ve become invisible” – seem to temper an innate shyness with the texture of a devotional. When she sings it now, glowing and a cappella, it becomes a “ritual chant” to ground herself.“It feels more like singing about a special quality, or a superpower,” she says. “I can turn myself invisible – like a person who’s here but isn’t. That could be really dark. Or it could be that I have the power to retreat as I need.”Linda’s Head is released via Kranky on 2 October. Grouper tours Europe and the UK from 29 October, including sets at Club 2 Club festival, Turin (1 November) and Le Guess Who? festival, Utrecht (7 November)Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Greg Freeman: All Set the Bone review – ambitious alt-country double album spreads its talents a touch thin | Music | The Guardian
description: The Maryland singer-songwriter’s third album has an impressive sense of scale compared to last year’s breakout Burnover, but is less immediately appealing
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: The Maryland singer-songwriter’s third album has an impressive sense of scale compared to last year’s breakout Burnover, but is less immediately appealing
Content: Lyrical anxieties … Greg Freeman.Photograph: Nat CambellView image in fullscreenLyrical anxieties … Greg Freeman.Photograph: Nat CambellMusicReviewGreg Freeman: All Set the Bone review – ambitious alt-country double album spreads its talents a touch thin(Transgressive)The Maryland singer-songwriter’s third album has an impressive sense of scale compared to last year’s breakout Burnover, but is less immediately appealingShaad D'SouzaFri 2 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreg Freeman’s third album All Set the Bone feels, at its best and most nervy, like an off-brand pressure cooker: too hot, bursting at its seams, rattling with kinetic energy. The Maryland-born singer-songwriter has a voice that often sounds like it’s straining at its limits, and although he is ostensibly part of agrowing indierock revivalthat’s been taking hold over the past few years – a cosy perennial – there’s nothing particularly comfortable about the songs on this double album. On Marooned, frantic stabs of guitar and drums create queasy unease; opener Cahokia muddles up the catharsis of a great American road song, descending into proggy bedlam. And his lyrics most often drum up anxieties big and small: “Who do you look to when you’re all on your own?” he asks on Culture. “When all your heroes lost their microphones?”View image in fullscreenGreg Freeman: All Set the Bone albumFreeman broke out with last year’sBurnover, a set of taut story-songs that were at turns witty, delirious and devastating. Freeman’s secret was in his ability to weld that literary streak to loud, bolshy, riff-heavy music that wouldn’t sound out of place on mainstream rock radio. All Set the Bone is several orders more ambitious in its scale, and its songwriting, which is more imagistic and diffuse. The result is an impressive record but one that’s less immediately appealing. Freeman wrote it while travelling through the US and reckoning with “a lot of change in my personal sense of … everything”, and you can hear that searching quality in the final product. All Set the Bone contains fewer fireworks than Burnover, but Freeman still has plenty of spark.Explore more on these topicsMusicIndiealbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: His hyperactive stylistic shifts and high-speed rhythms have a delirious, head-spinning beauty of their own
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: His hyperactive stylistic shifts and high-speed rhythms have a delirious, head-spinning beauty of their own
Content: Hallucinatory … Chidi Obialo AKA Heavensouls.Photograph: AUTHKS/PRView image in fullscreenHallucinatory … Chidi Obialo AKA Heavensouls.Photograph: AUTHKS/PRAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracksHis hyperactive stylistic shifts and high-speed rhythms have a delirious, head-spinning beauty of their ownLaura SnapesandBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromBiafra, Nigeria/Texas, USARecommended if you likeLos Thuthanaka, Jpegmafia, DJ Sabrina the Teenage DJUp nextAlbum Cantu of the Sower released via NTS Recordings on 7 OctoberMany listeners might find blown-out noise, hyperactive stylistic shifts and breakneck rhythms a hellish prospect, and fair enough. But for a certain stripe of sensory freak, such swarming intensity can tip over into a state of heady relaxation. The ultra-prolific Heavensouls’ latest project scratches that itch: the six songs on Cantu of the Sower glitter like rich seams of rare crystal, billowing from arcade glitter to compression-straining bass, sprite-like playfulness to warm, rushing brass. Languid trumpet lines float around trash-compactor crunch; sugary breakbeats reach tweaky maximalist peaks. I don’t know about you, but I could bathe in it.This isn’t shitpost music, fidgeting for its own sake. Cantu … glows with wonder at its own abundance, and the found-sound snippets of chatter ground its sense of an observant musician full of love for his fellow man. A sample of civil rights activist Stokely Carmichael makes 20-year-old Chidi Obialo’s mindset explicit: “I want my liberation more than I want anything else.” You hear it as Fela Kuti-worthy hand percussion is swept away by a hallucinatory, howling tide of guitar.Obialo was raised in Nigeria and moved to the US age seven. As a teenager, he started putting out wildly varied, collagist music, aiming to create a “rabbit hole” for listeners to get lost in. If you are of the shitpost sensibility, there’s the Sidepeices, his funny, glitchy duo with Atlanta’s Stickerbush. (Not for nothing is Obialo wearing a Captain Beefheart shirt above.) But then this year’s Westside Trapped, his gorgeously heavy love letter to Nigeria, is more approachable, in keeping with Sault’s luxuriant spirituals. Already 15 releases in to a brief career, Obialo’s talent for delirious, head-spinning beauty is clear, whichever way he chooses to express it.Laura SnapesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenDizzy dance .. Mei Semones.Photograph: Saeka ShimadaMei Semones – HowlUndeterred by unrequited love, the Japanese-American jazz-popper swears she’d “rather chase ’til I die and so / I’ll never have to learn to be still” – borne out in her gorgeous, dizzy dance of bossa nova guitar and strings.LSAngèle – Love Triangle (ft Caroline Polachek and SebastiAn)A malevolent electroclash beat by SebastiAn builds the drama in this menage-à-trois tale, where two of pop’s best bilingually vie with each other to see who walks away with their heart intact.BBTRomy Mars – The RageMars uses a gorgeously drowsy, wordy slow jam to taunt an ex. “Now you’re in film school studying movies / When they talk about my family do you lose sleep?” That’s mum Sofia Coppola and grandpa Francis Ford, FYI.LSMadra Salach – Ribbon FactoryTaut, insistent and wracked with pain, this is a gothic nightmare from an Irish folk band who keep turning up the volume on their word of mouth with every impassioned live performance.BBTBlackhaine – ConsumerAfter reworking rage rap under dull moorland cloud – and doing devastating choreo with Playboi Carti – the north-west rapper and dancer has announced his debut album with this symphonic, slowly syncopated stunner.BBTRyley Walker – CarrierThe Illinois guitarist signs to label du jour AD93 for a teeth-gritted turn to distortion that brings to mind fellow travellerWilliam Tyler’s Time Indefiniteand Sunn O)))’s glistening noise.LSHodge – Moments of JoyFull of body-high synth melodies and bird-call detailing, this track taken from the Bristolian producer’s new album, Big Splash, will have you mulling a last-minute dash to Ibiza’s closing parties.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistHip-hopExperimental musicElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trá Pháidín: Cloch’s Claí review – giddy Galway gang burst the boundaries of folk music | Folk music | The Guardian
description: With musical ideas spanning mariachi and motorik beats, and lyrics with Kneecap-grade rage, this brilliant collective evolve tradition with stinging, joyful songs
Author: Jude Rogers
Headline: With musical ideas spanning mariachi and motorik beats, and lyrics with Kneecap-grade rage, this brilliant collective evolve tradition with stinging, joyful songs
Content: Psychedelic rurality … Trá Pháidín.Photograph: Sara LeslieView image in fullscreenPsychedelic rurality … Trá Pháidín.Photograph: Sara LeslieFolk album of the monthFolk musicReviewTrá Pháidín: Cloch’s Claí review – giddy Galway gang burst the boundaries of folk music(World of Echo)With musical ideas spanning mariachi and motorik beats, and lyrics with Kneecap-grade rage, this brilliant collective evolve tradition with stinging, joyful songsJude RogersFri 2 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQuicksilver and giddy in its exploration of Irish music, language and identity, Trá Pháidín’s second album bursts open the idea of a 21st-century traditional folk record. It woos you with the reverb-smothered guitars and birdsong-like flutes of Tí Mhichael Phaddy (Michael Paddy’s House, an opener suggesting a psychedelically perfect rurality) before an Irish woman cuts in, bigging up her countryside Airbnb on the phone. A shouty local then comically interrupts her.Trá Pháidín (Paddy’s Beach) are a six-strong collective of brilliant musicians from Galway, Ireland’s largest Irish-speaking county, and their album’s title, Cloch’s Claí (Stone and Dry Stone Wall), suggests that each track plays its own scabrous, weight-bearing part in the whole. The 45 minutes unfold as an interrupted sequence, full of improvisation, texture and ornament, the band freely roaming other genres, revealing them as connected neighbourhoods.View image in fullscreenTrá Pháidín, Cloch’s Claí album artworkPhotograph: PRMariachi and a fantastic motorik beat blast into the brilliant Garbhóg (The Rough One), before pastoralism returns. On Fothrach an Cheirtleáin (The Ruin of the Conurbation) the band strut like a disconsolate Mogwai, before To Hell or to Connacht’s intricate flutes, full of elegant, menacing repetition, swirl us into their undertow.The lyrics throughout are full of Kneecap and CMAT-grade rage. Named after Flann O’Brien’s brilliant parody of Gaelic poverty memoirs, An Béal Bocht (The Poor Mouth) drops in rhythmic passages of words about people living in crumbling concrete, dreaming of the Celtic tiger and its tail. Seachtain na Gaeilge (Irish Language Week) is sharper still: over a slow dance, facts about the magic of the country are followed by English translations, delivered in a sinister whisper, that reveal the ridiculousness of tourism lingo (“this ancient tongue is over 10 years old”). Trá Pháidin also mock themselves for “being an Irish language band but speaking English on the sly”. Stinging, musically all-enveloping and often unexpectedly joyful, Cloch’s Claí suggests new foundations for folk with every listen.Also out this monthCladach/Mullach (Chamber Music Scotland) is the gorgeous debut fromPeaks, a new duo of violinist George Smith and cellist Duncan Strachan. Exploring legends from Scotland’s Western Isles, its first five tracks showcase their pretty playing, before the story unfurls of a mother who exchanged her soul for her son’s ability to play a magical harp. Brìghde Chaimbeul provides spoken-word vocals over the ambient meditations. Two contemporary US masters also release ambitious albums.Rhiannon Giddens’ Hope Is the Thing With Feathers (Nonesuch) features a rousing band, made up of family and friends, playing full-blooded versions of Elizabeth Cotten’s Freight Train and folk songs such as Cluck Old Hen and Walk With Me.Jake Xerxes Fussell’s The Old Beloved Path (Fat Possum) is his most moving album yet: a gentle journey through traditional songs he adores, including Boney and Boll Weevil, and a surprising, delicate take on Lonnie Donegan’s Rock Island Line.Explore more on these topicsFolk musicFolk album of the monthExperimental musicreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best recent poetry – review roundup | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Have It by John Cooper Clarke; The Dodo Stories by Mary Mulholland; Red River Valley by Ian McMillan; Some Sacred Harbour by Roger Robinson; Otherwhere by Carolyn Forché
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Have It by John Cooper Clarke; The Dodo Stories by Mary Mulholland; Red River Valley by Ian McMillan; Some Sacred Harbour by Roger Robinson; Otherwhere by Carolyn Forché
Content:
John Cooper Clarke.Photograph: Ki Price/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Cooper Clarke.Photograph: Ki Price/Getty ImagesPoetry roundupPoetryReviewThe best recent poetry – review roundupHave It by John Cooper Clarke; The Dodo Stories by Mary Mulholland; Red River Valley by Ian McMillan;  Some Sacred Harbour by Roger Robinson; Otherwhere by Carolyn ForchéJennifer Lee TsaiFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenHave Itby John Cooper Clarke(Picador, £16.99)The latest collection from the original “people’s poet” displays his characteristic swagger, delivered with a distinctively northern humour. Merging blistering social satire and brash wit, Cooper Clarke irreverently tackles themes from the ridiculous to the sublime, including the malaise of contemporary urban life, the erosion of nature and the environment, money and the prospect of a cashless society, death and ageing, fascism, bachelorhood, popular culture and the NHS. His punk rock values caustically underpin the collection: “Me and my shrinking crowd / Each under our own personal cloud”; “We wish you no serious harm/ However, everybody sucks but us”. There’s heavy use of doggerel and jokes as he stridently proclaims his passion for writing. “It’s a meaningless job but someone’s got to do it / Thank God it’s me”. Overall, Cooper Clarke’s consummate performance skills in playing to the crowd demand applause as he advocates for the “blood royal of the working class”.The Dodo Stories by Mary Mullholland (Nine Arches, £11.99)Mulholland’s compelling debut collection explores complex questions of inheritance, migration and colonialism. “i go to the old country we’re from, / long to belong, to be like that fennel-lapping lizard in funchal”. She delves into personal and public archives, memory, dreams and the unconscious to uncover her family histories, stretching back to her great grandparents and the silenced stories of Portuguese indenture to the Caribbean. Her descriptions of wildlife and landscapes are skilfully rendered: “the three-night flower smells of pineapple and banana, scarab beetles hurry to the feast and stay like lovers”; “purpleheart, greenheart, spiny fiddleheart, and palms that walk by themselves, shift-shape”. At the heart of this richly evocative book is a moving tribute to her “exotic morpho mother”, the eponymous Dodo, and a desire for healing from the effects of intergenerational trauma. “May she receive this / benediction, an invocation to wish her well”.View image in fullscreenRed River Valley by Ian McMillan(Carcanet, £12.99)McMillan’s latest is inspired by his family life, living in a village near Barnsley as a poet and broadcaster in the community. These clear, accessible poems blend the surreal with the quotidian, as in the opening, Sudden Memory of My Dad Wearing Shorts, which reimagines his father singing his favourite song, “Red River Valley”. There is a madcap, maverick energy to the book, which explores encounters with people and familiar places such as the barber’s, a cricket club, a train station, the motorway, a bookshop. McMillan often engages in wry commentary to reflect on societal inequalities  and austerity in Britain. Overall, his compassionate outlook finds solace and the possibility of transformation in the everyday, where “It’s moments like this when all the stars align. / Evening games in winter; a touch of the sublime”.View image in fullscreenSome Sacred Harbour: New and Selected Poemsby Roger Robinson (Bloomsbury, £12.99)A testament to a lifetime’s work from the prize-winning poet, educator, performer and musician. The title piece is an artistic manifesto on survival and the vital importance of creativity in society. Robinson elucidates this philosophy as “creating a platform where sacred stories – the moments that define a life and its joys, traumatic hurts and recoveries – could be told. Something about bringing the margins to the centre”. These exquisitely crafted and dextrously lyrical poems centre around Black Atlantic and Black British identity, grief, migration, racial tragedies and injustices, family, music. Robinson emphasises a shared communal consciousness, “praise for these moments of quick recognition, / miracles of synchronicity and signalled kinship”. Sonically resonant and often biblically charged, the collection illuminates the breadth and depth of human experience, where “the shoots of spring always bring hope / and a chance for renewal”.View image in fullscreenOtherwhere: New & Selected Poems 1976–2026
by Carolyn ForchéOtherwhere: New and Selected Poems, 1976-2026by Carolyn Forché(Bloodaxe, £14.99)A landmark retrospective spanning five collections across five decades, this impressive volume opens with an eloquent preface, Older Than Glass, Younger Than Music, which delineates Forché’s poetics. What is remarkable about her work is a visionary ability to merge poems of personal intimacy with geopolitical realities, distinguishing her as a “poet of witness”. War, displacement and genocide are juxtaposed with elegiac meditations: “The word forwindis, in another language, the word forsoul”. The collection includes a new sequence entitled If There is Ink, addressing contemporary global crises. The title poem focuses on the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine and questions the limits of language: “if there is something to write that would raise the cities/ from the ruins the apartment blocks hospitals schools/ that would put the cities back as they were/ I would give everything to fill this pen with it”.Explore more on these topicsPoetryPoetry roundupreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rhapsody: A Manifesto by Alice Oswald review – a history of the spoken word, from Homer to Ted Hughes | Literary criticism | The Guardian
description: A twisting, beguiling investigation into the art of poetry that ends in a call to arms on behalf of the natural world
Author: Fiona Sampson
Headline: A twisting, beguiling investigation into the art of poetry that ends in a call to arms on behalf of the natural world
Content: Alice Oswald.Photograph: Jeff Morgan 13/AlamyView image in fullscreenAlice Oswald.Photograph: Jeff Morgan 13/AlamyBook of the dayLiterary criticismReviewRhapsody: A Manifesto by Alice Oswald review – a history of the spoken word, from Homer to Ted HughesA twisting, beguiling investigation into the art of poetry that ends in a call to arms on behalf of the natural worldFiona SampsonFri 2 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe poetAlice Oswaldis no stranger to thinking in public about her art. She was Oxford professor of poetry until 2023, and her lectures are available online. But this is her first full-length book, and as such is something of an occasion.So what exactly is it? For a work of prose it contains a lot of poetry, much translated or composed by Oswald herself. Shakespeare, Donne, Shelley and Ted Hughes also feature. Though nonfiction, the book is full of stories, particularly retellings of Homer and Aeschylus. It is billed as “genre-defying” and there is much formal experimentation. But at heart it is an exploration of the oral tradition, and the writer’s own subtitle is A Manifesto, which feels exciting and urgent, pointed at the contemporary world with its pressing realities.Sure enough, the first chapter invokes both Homer and the spoken word as a living phenomenon, through Oswald’s encounter with a Ukrainian heart transplant recipient who tells her his story; references to David Bowie and Nat King Cole; Catalan folksong; and Badia Obaid, “a still-breathing Mesopotamian storyteller who was born in Baghdad”. This is important, for there aren’t so many passages in the rest of this book that engage with individuals or suggest real-world stakes for poetry.double quotation markA fabulous phrasemaker, Oswald fills this book with revelatory linesInstead, the following nine chapters take us on an often fascinating, frequently beautiful path through poetry. A fabulous phrasemaker, endlessly able to transfigure the natural world, Oswald fills this book with revelatory lines: “woodland at night, when every tree gives off an applause of frightened birds”; reflections in water as a “liquid, impermanent, unstable gift of similarity”.But where exactly do they lead? The final chapter offers a series of historical definitions of “rhapsody”, moving from “exalted expression” (1639) to “literary … miscellaneous or disconnected” (1764) and, by 1880, “an instrumental composition enthusiastic in character but of indefinite form”. In classical Greece, the rhapsode was the performer of oral poetry, and often peripatetic.This Rhapsody isn’t just wandering about, however. It’s going in search of those moments beyond fashion, bluster or rhetoric where poetry really happens. This is the most controversial and elusive of quests: every poet since time began has felttheypossess the secret, which is, on the contrary, the proverbial needle in a haystack. At one point Oswald even finds it in the space between two lines of verse.This isn’t as ridiculous as it might sound. She’s looking at Shakespeare’s Sonnet 87. For Oswald, the essence of this poem is in the tiny breath implied by a full stop and line break before a change of pace. “An apparition floats up, the same shape as the original speaker’s lungs,” she says. Oswald, herself a virtuosic performer, understands that something takes place when an audience is present that is about more than just words.Perhaps this is why she frequently declares disdain for “scholars” and “academics”, though they’re all there in a chunky 40 pages of endnotes. Sometimes, though, the effect is of Oswald “alone of all her sex”, conversing with the great men of poetic history. Though she includes a poem by the late Nobel laureate Louise Glück, living poets are less present. Does this matter? Every writer has their own imaginative territory, after all. I think it may, for if poetry being composed right now is not addressed, we’re left with a manifesto not for poetry itself, but only for the performance of existing work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s also disappointing that, echoing her fine early poetry in Dart and A Sleepwalk on the Severn, Oswald slips once again into using a running river as her default literary form. For in its very last pages Rhapsody turns out to be a call to arms on behalf of the natural world. Oswald understands this to be the true source of poetry as well as of our physical existence. As she will know, having edited an anthology of his work, Ted Hughes came to the same conclusion decades ago. That doesn’t stop it being true, of course. And important truths, like poems, bear repetition.Rhapsody: A Manifesto by Alice Oswald is published by Jonathan Cape (£20). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsLiterary criticismBook of the dayAlice OswaldPoetryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral review – Beethoven explodes into bright bursts of gorgeous dance | Dance | The Guardian
description: Spinning off from the classic symphony with composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner, Tanowitz’s dancers find fresh thinking space
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Spinning off from the classic symphony with composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner, Tanowitz’s dancers find fresh thinking space
Content: Every angle planed to the exact degree … Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEvery angle planed to the exact degree … Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewPam Tanowitz: Pastoral review – Beethoven explodes into bright bursts of gorgeous danceBarbican, LondonSpinning off from the classic symphony with composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner, Tanowitz’s dancers find fresh thinking spaceLyndsey WinshipFri 2 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePam Tanowitz’s work is the antidote to the trend in dance for dark and shadowy stages, buckets of theatrical haze, claustrophobic soundscapes and gloopy movement. This stage is so bright and clean, like a sharp palate cleanser, and full of white space – literally, and in a more figurative manner. Tanowitz’s dance can be eccentric, odd even, but it’s also seriously thought-through and specific, every choice utterly distinct and deliberate, every angle planed to the exact degree.This UK premiere of Pastoral is a collaboration between New York choreographer Tanowitz, Pulitzer prize-winning composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner. Inspired by Beethoven’s Pastoral Symphony and the idea of the pastoral in art, Shaw pulls apart and deconstructs the Beethoven, with three live musicians (on various reed instruments) and excerpts of orchestral recordings that emerge like echoes or memories, plus real-world sounds of the street, the skies and the city.Tanowitz likes a bit of deconstruction too, taking apart or adding to phrases and motifs, with flashes of wit and eccentricity. Her style, simplistically speaking, nods to Merce Cunningham’s mid-century abstraction, with flattened lines and pleasing symmetry. Crowner’s work also harks back to the 1950s and 60s (to geometric abstraction and so-called hard-edge painting). She’s designed a floor-to-ceiling curtain and a vast canvas, with pale pink slices cutting through deep greens. They divide the space, creating “rooms” amid otherwise white walls. Reid Bartelme’s costumes have the dancers in ombre chiffon, an offbeat spectrum through coral-pink-red-lilac-chartreuse. The colours hum, on the edge of concord and discord.View image in fullscreenThe colours hum … Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThere’s something refreshing and challenging in the sparseness of the score, the dance and the stage, with all its thinking space. There’s zero fuss, even when the dancers have to execute fiendishly tricky balances. When Anson Zwingelberg suddenly dances a gorgeous phrase, like an exquisite miniature, it appears and evaporates with no fanfare.In the same way Beethoven’s music will unexpectedly slide into view, images and associations make fleeting impressions. When the dancers gather against the green, for example, as if picnicking in a 19th-century painting. Or when the pastoral idyll is interrupted by an angry red square canvas and the sound of a bird call like a siren – a threat against nature, perhaps. It’s a dance full of curiosity, and curiosities; a tangy conversation between three distinctive artists.At theBarbican, London, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDancePam TanowitzBarbicanLudwig van BeethovenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Parsifal review – bunkers, CCTV and fembots in elusive vision of Wagner’s mystical masterpiece | Opera | The Guardian
description: Evgeny Titov’s brutal and powerful new staging of Wagner’s final opera explains as little as possible. Christian Gerhaher is a compelling and wild-eyed Amfortas and Jakub Hrůša and the Royal Opera’s orchestra are superb
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Evgeny Titov’s brutal and powerful new staging of Wagner’s final opera explains as little as possible. Christian Gerhaher is a compelling and wild-eyed Amfortas and Jakub Hrůša and the Royal Opera’s orchestra are superb
Content: An appalling, wild-eyed must-see … Christian Gerhaher as Amfortas in Parsifal at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenAn appalling, wild-eyed must-see … Christian Gerhaher as Amfortas in Parsifal at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Marc BrennerOperaReviewParsifal review – bunkers, CCTV and fembots in elusive vision of Wagner’s mystical masterpieceRoyal Opera House, LondonEvgeny Titov’s brutal and powerful new staging of Wagner’s final opera explains as little as possible. Christian Gerhaher is a compelling and wild-eyed Amfortas and Jakub Hrůša and the Royal Opera’s orchestra are superbFlora WillsonFri 2 Oct 2026 07.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrail, wound, spear: some of the narrative trappings of Wagner’s final opera are immediately recognisable as symbolic. Others – woman, saviour, chastity, seduction, suffering, death – are harder to pin down, lodged in the half-light between the literal and the metaphorical. Wagner’s score is his most beguilingly luminous; its critics have pored over the work’s commitment to racial purity, its misogyny, its religiosity. The question thatEvgeny Titov’s debut production for the Royal Opera poses is whether we really believe in the story Parsifal tells – the fall, the curse, the redemption through purity – and what it means if we want to.View image in fullscreenThe pure fool? … Stanislas de Barbeyrac as Parsifal at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Marc BrennerTitov’s staging explains as little as possible. In Etienne Pluss’s sets, the grail realm is an underground bunker hewn from monumental stone blocks that trundle slowly around the stage. There are CCTV screens and a grimy washroom where Amfortas – the fallen King – is scrubbed down by Grail Knights in breathing apparatus. Costume designer Esther Bialas has the Knights in anoraks. Kundry (the virgin-whore dichotomy incarnate) wears black leathers at first, virginal white later. In a rare moment of literal-mindedness, Titov has Parsifal arrive holding the swan he has shot, which twitches gawkily until the orchestra heralds its demise.Evil Klingsor’s kingdom is another bunker – no enchanted garden here, just a loud suit, a telephone for barking orders, more screens with wiring that curls serpentlike across the floor and cabinets displaying his treasures: an Egyptian mummy, a crown, the sacred spear. (In another of the production’s less convincing details, Parsifal breaks the “glass” to retrieve the spear with an unsatisfying plastic crunch.) We first encounter the flower maidens as a disturbing gaggle of little girls chasing around Klingsor’s lair. Their grown-up counterparts are fembots in headdresses and silver hot pants, part chorus line, partHandmaid’s Tale. The effect is grotesque – but how could it be otherwise in 2026?Some of the stage pictures and much of the subtle lighting designs riff on the language of religious painting. Other details raise questions rather than answering them: the leather restraining straps used on Amfortas during the grail ritual, the metal gynaecological chair in which Kundry cowers. Moments of physical tenderness stand out, shocking amid so much implied and – in Titov’s remarkable closing coup de théâtre – explicit violence.View image in fullscreenFlower maidens recast as fembots … Evgeny Titov’s production of Parsifal for the Royal Opera.Photograph: Marc BrennerThis production’s power also depends on the musical performance, which threaded beauty and emotional intensity through so much equivocation. ConductorJakub Hrůšacharted long lines through Wagner’s enormous score, taking time between some musical paragraphs and pushing precipitously onwards elsewhere. The orchestra was on superb form – woodwind featherweight or saccharine or keening painfully, the strings producing sound alternately in reams of satin and razor-sharp shards, the brass foundry-fresh – at times blending into a single, majestically organ-like tintinnabulation.Brindley Sherrattwas a moody, complicated Gurnemanz – some nasty high notes standing out against his granite lower register – but his storytelling was as compelling as ever.Ekaterina Gubanovawas a constantly shapeshifting Kundry, her tone reactive, from shrieks to quasi-speech, via finely sculpted phrases that seemed to skim the orchestra’s surface.Mark Stone’s Klingsor managed to be both oleaginous and fierce,James Platt’s Titurel appropriately stentorian.Stanislas de Barbeyracwielded his gleaming steel of a voice on the title role, his earlier fragmentary mode blossoming into potent, supple declamation in the final scene. But it isChristian Gerhaher’s appalling, wild-eyed Amfortas that makes this production a must-see. In this bleak portrayal of self-obsession, every note he sang oozed misery, every phrase felt unmissable.At Royal Opera House, London, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsOperaRoyal Opera HouseClassical musicRichard WagnerreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ravishing Renoir, cool Britannia and mighty Aphrodite – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Swoon at immaculate impressionism, ’ave it large with 90s Brit art and fashion and head to the beach with Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Swoon at immaculate impressionism, ’ave it large with 90s Brit art and fashion and head to the beach with Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse
Content: Joyful and sumptuous … Dance at Bougival by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1883.Photograph: © Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Picture FundView image in fullscreenJoyful and sumptuous … Dance at Bougival by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1883.Photograph: © Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Picture FundArt Weekly newsletterArt and designRavishing Renoir, cool Britannia and mighty Aphrodite – the week in artSwoon at immaculate impressionism, ’ave it large with 90s Brit art and fashion and head to the beach with Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 2 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekRenoir and LoveJoyful and sumptuous, yet realist and raw, Renoir’s impressionist paintings glow in this immaculate exhibition.National Gallery, London, from 3 October until 31 JanuaryAlso showingThe 90s: Art and FashionThe fin de siecle decade gets a fresh look that puts fashion alongside art to take us back to when Britannia thought it was cool.Tate Britain, London, from 8 October until 14 FebruaryAphrodite: The Making of a GoddessThe ancient god of love and desire, often known by her Latin name Venus, returns on her shell in the art of Botticelli, Michelangelo Pistoletto and more.Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, from 8 October until 11 AprilMike Nelson: Double Negative (The Clown)Another soul-harrowing installation by the sculptor of urban labyrinths.Modern Art Oxford, from 3 October until 11 AprilPainting the French RivieraThere are masterpieces here by Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse, but it’s a weary slog and the beach is miles away.Royal Academy, London, until 31 JanuaryImage of the weekView image in fullscreenDavid Hockney, Dog Painting 17, 1995.Photograph: David Hockney/Christie’s Images Ltd. 2026How much is that doggy in the window? Well, if it’s a rare painting of Hockney’s adored dachshund Stanley, you’re looking at an estimated £1.5m-£2.5m. The painting will be sold at auction on 14 October during the Frieze art fair, but anyone cansee it for free at Christie’s in London from Thursday.What we learnedSome art seems better when it’s brokenBalraj Khanna paints biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacleCeleb set designer Es Devlin’s studio has a lot going onA row has erupted over a Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun with dark skinA Van Gogh is up for grabs, alongside a Cézanne and a Monet as an ‘almost mythical’ private collection goes on saleskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMasterpiece of the weekFête Galante by Jean-Baptiste Pater, probably about 1721-5View image in fullscreenPhotograph: © The National Gallery, LondonPeople are picnicking on the grass, in a woody parkland that’s given extra mystery by classical sculptures and urns, even though a view through the trees reveals ordinary rural buildings rather than a great house. This is the ambiguous pleasure-world of the fête galante, a genre of painting invented by Pater’s teacher Antoine Watteau, in which lovers dance and talk and sometimes go off together into the woods, in an enigmatic, timeless and softly brushed fantasy realm. Pater is nothing like as poetic as Watteau, but still, you get the idea in this typical example of his work: women in silk dresses that catch the light and men in archaic, Renaissance-style costumes have escaped the cares of the city and the everyday to gather and celebrate love in this clearing under the gentle, feathery trees. title: ‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom? | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’
Content: Familiar face … the Skanderbeg Tower is designed to echo a bust of Albania’s national hero.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/AlamyView image in fullscreenFamiliar face … the Skanderbeg Tower is designed to echo a bust of Albania’s national hero.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/AlamyArchitecture‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom?Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’Oliver WainwrightFri 2 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast autumn, I was sitting with a prominent architect in New York, when their phone wouldn’t stop buzzing. They finally checked the messages and chuckled. “Oh, the AlbanianArchitectureArmy chat is blowing up again,” they said. “It looks like Edi has some new projects for us.”Edi was Edi Rama, the prime minister of Albania since 2013, who has been presiding over the rapid transformation of the former communist country with a fleet of glamorous building projects. There are twisting towers in Tirana, along withprize-winning public spaces, striking coastal resorts, and many more dazzling visions on the way – all now brought together in a hefty new book,The Albanian Files.double quotation markCritics see the 800-page book as a 2.2kg dossier of evidenceThe country’s makeover, it turns out, is partly coordinated via a WhatsApp group (“Albanian ArchArmy” for short) which includes some of the most famous architects in the world. It is a forum where achievements are shared, new projects celebrated, and the great prime minister-patron showered with praise for his bravery and boldness. The New York architect describes the situation in the manner of a superhero movie: Rama sends out the signal and the world’s starchitects rally to the rescue with their daring designs. Look hard enough and you might even see theAlbanian double-headed eagleprojected into the night sky.View image in fullscreenHub … Saranda port development plan by XDGA, shown in The Albanian Files.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller PublishersThe WhatsApp chat might be confidential, but The Albanian Files is the next best thing. It is a remarkable document, in ways that are both intended and not. In his foreword, Rama describes the book as “a precious behind-the-scenes record” of a process that is “liftingAlbaniain a way that nobody saw coming”. It is an eye-opening directory of dreams, in which 60 international practices (and not a single Albanian one) lay out their plans for over 500 projects up and down the country.To Rama’s critics, however, the book is an 800-page, 2.2kg dossier of evidence. They point to theopacity of decision-making, thedestruction of heritage, theforced evictions, thetrampling of protected landscapes, and therole of Albania’s construction industry in laundering money for organised crime. The publication is full of first-hand testimonies by architects documenting their experiences, andone opposition MP has called it the “smoking gun”– although there is no suggestion that the architects have been involved in any wrongdoing. Rama is right that nobody saw it coming: most of the projects in the book’s pages are news to the local population, which has reacted with fury.“Starchitects go home!” read one placardat a noisy protest in June, outside a venue in Tirana, where many of the architects in the book were gathered for an exclusive event to celebrate their work and launch the publication. “Where is the public?” read another. Tickets for the architecture festival, titledLandscapes of Abundance, cost up to €200, in a country where the median monthly wage is €700. It came at a charged moment, just a few weeks after huge national protests were ignited by the multibillion dollar plans todevelop Zvërnec nature reserve and the nearby island of Sazan into a luxury resort, backed by the Trump family.Dubbed theflamingo revolution, in reference to the fragile habitats critics say will be trampled by the project, the protests have now continued for over 120 days, with ever-louder calls for Rama’s resignation. Architecture has found itself unexpectedly in the firing line.View image in fullscreenAnger … Albanians protest at development of coastal nature reserve in June this year.Photograph: Armando Babani/Getty Images“It feels like living in an autocratic kingdom,” saysLorin Kadiu, director of Citizens.al, an investigative news platform that has been tracking construction projects in Albania since 2018. “Not just the lack of transparency, but the fact that we must all be subjected to the aesthetic tastes of one person. The whole country must be painted the way he wants.”Rama, who trained as a painter, first rose to prominence as the mayor of Tirana in the 2000s, when he made international headlines with his programme of painting thedreary soviet blocks a rainbow of jaunty colours. The cheap and cheerful makeover worked, and Rama was hailed for his maverick artistic approach.But, now, many of his former supporters feel like his architectural ambitions have gone too far.An open letter, handed out at the protests, denounced the “art-washing of bulldozer politics,” and asked the assembled architects if they enjoy “the freedom to do here what would be forbidden, challenged, or otherwise made impossible in your own countries?” Of the architects contacted by the Guardian, only one responded, to say they do not do anything in Albania that they would not be allowed to do in another place. They added that “the freedom in Albania is certainly alluring and as such the personal responsibility is greater”.As Rama writes pointedly in his foreword to The Albanian Files, the architects are attracted to work in Albania by the “freedom from ‘no’ in all its forms”. The pages are studded with visions for virgin coastlines, verdant forests, and pristine dunes and lagoons. In Gjipe, a bay that many consider the last virgin beach in southern Albania, Dutch firm MVRDV hasproposed a mirrored glass hotel that would span the gorge, “like a jewel on the coastline”.It comes hot on the heels of their apartment towerin Tirana shaped like the head of Skanderbeg, Albania’s national hero (which also bears a striking resemblance to Rama). In the protected dune area of Rana e Hedhun, the venerable Portuguese architectÁlvaro Siza has masterplanned a hillside development with a cable car and a tower-block on the beach.A few pages later, Swiss maestro Valerio Olgiati proposes a cluster of concrete towersrising from the sand, peppered with defensive windows. It looks as if he might be preparing to fend off an invasion from the sea.The coastal glow-up continues with the Florentine luxury yacht designerLuca Dini(studio mission: “to astonish even the most discerning”). He presents an illustrated voyage through his 17 projects, including the Life Marina Complex, spanning seven kilometres of virgin coastline near Saranda, and the Atara resort, with a golden “crown” that hovers above the cliffs like another military lookout post. It almost reaches parody when his comic-style illustrations conclude with an image of a super-yacht hurtling above a skyline, with the designer himself declaiming from the deck: “[we] create spaces that harmonise with the environment.”View image in fullscreenComic-style illustrations … Luca Dini’s section in The Albanian Files.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller PublishersThe book’s editor, Anneke Abhelakh, asked the architects to submit their own texts, and they are striking in their honesty. At times it reads like a hot-mic transcript. “Because there are not many rules and my clients care very little for the context,” writes Berlin-based architect Sam Chermayeff, “we are forced to think through our own values.” He recounts the “truly wild” experience of working in Albania, including how he was called, out of the blue, by one of Rama’s associates, and soon asked to designtwo towers in Tirana, totalling 45,000sq m – quite something for a designer better known for experimental kitchens.“Of course I agreed,” he adds, “not really understanding what was happening.” Contacted for comment, Chermayeff responded: “I do ask Albanian clients the same questions that I ask of clients in any country and am equally assured,” adding that “as in Germany or the US, I really do not know more than what I am told,” and that he does not work in or near protected areas. “I do not do anything,” he added, “I would not do at another place.”Austrian architect Chris Precht describes how he was approached on Instagram by Rama himself, “asking if I would be interested in working in Albania”. He now has 29 projects to his name, including a €4m “Garden of Eden”, built in the courtyard of the prime minister’s own office.“It is an unimaginable reality,” says a campaign group of Albanian architects and urban planners,Arkitektët Shqiparë, which has created an online database of all of the projects – published in Albanian, unlike the book. “A narrow group of foreign architects is contacted directly by the prime minister’s office and receives projects without a competitive procedure.”View image in fullscreenBeside the seaside … Olgiati’s proposal for concrete towers on the beach in Lezha.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller PublishersThe foreign architects describe it differently. “Rama never appoints the architects himself,” one member of the ArchArmy group tells me. “But he makes introductions to developers. And it is understood that, if they choose one of his architects, they [the developers] will get permission to build what they want.”Rama has consistently denied the allegations. In a furious interview with CNN in June, he denounced the claims of corruption as “fake news”. He has long maintained that the wider protests have beenstoked by the US president’s enemies, including Iran. “If it were not Jared Kushner,” he said, “nobody would give a shit about flamingos, about Albania, about nothing. It’s the whole hate against Trump that creates all this scrutiny.”Contacted by the Guardian, the prime minister’s office did not respond to requests for comment in detail but called the allegations “hearsays” and “bitter assessments”. During a speech this week to launch the competition for a new tower,Rama insistedthe competition juries are “mostly architects, urbanists and academics who are entirely free,” that “the Albanian side is in the minority” and that there is “never any orientation or influence” on the jury. He added that today Albania “is the largest open ‘university’ in architecture,” as young Albanian architects have the opportunity “to meet, to follow, to work concretely with masters”.The book’s subtitle is Freedom and Architecture, and there is an air of carte blanche to many of the designs. “Working as an architect in Albania is liberating,” writes the Belgian Xaveer De Geyter, alongside his proposal for a colossal trio of M-shaped towers for the port of Saranda, “provoking a degree of freedom that sometimes leaves us in a cold sweat.” Spanish studio Arquitectura-G praises Albania’s permitting process as “significantly faster and less restrictive” than elsewhere, driven by “a clear vision coming from the prime minister.” Portugal’s Manuel Aires Mateus concurs: “There are times when things have to be top-down.”The palpable thrill of building on virgin terrain is also evident. Japanese doyen Kengo Kuma describes the exhilaration of flying over Albania in a helicopter. “I found it very exciting,” he writes, “as most of the nature is untouched.” In Asia, he adds, “it is very difficult to find a project in such ‘virgin land’”. The Berlin-based Indian architect, Anupama Kundoo, talks of the opportunity to create, “free from the baggage” ofEuropeand other “developed countries”.Kundoo is working on a masterplan for a “laboratory settlement” of 50,000 people in the protectedDivjakë-Karavasta national park. Such a project has only been made possible by a controversial 2024 law, which allows the construction of five-star resorts in protected areas, from which the Trump-backed plan in Zvërnec also benefits.There is no suggestion that any of the architects named in this article are breaking any laws.“The developers are in a hurry,” says Kadiu. “There is a sprint to build as much as possible before these laws are repealed.” Pressure is growing. Albania has entered the concluding phase of its EU accession negotiations, but these lax regulations remain an obstacle. Both the 2024 law, and 2015 legislation that gives preferential treatment to “strategic investors”, were criticised byan EU report last yearas being in conflict with its standards.A European Parliament resolution in June this year “expressed serious concerns” and called for an “immediate moratorium on new permitting procedures, construction works and development interventions” within protected areas. Rama continues to defend both laws as pragmatic, modernising policies that balance environmental conservation with high-value economic development.Beyond fears for the environment, and the opaque permitting and procurement processes, another burning question remains: how can one of the poorest countries in Europe afford to build these extravagant schemes? There has been an astronomical rise in property prices, but no comparable increase in wages or bank mortgages being issued, leading critics to suspect that dark money is involved.The Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime identifies Albania’s real estate and tourism sectors as major sites of money-laundering, noting that the construction sector is “heavily infiltrated by illicit funds”. Its 2020 report estimated that€1.6bn of “dirty money” had been laundered through Albanian real estatein the previous three years.As I reported in 2022, leaked wiretaps revealed Italian mafia figures discussing how Tirana’s high-rise boom was a prime opportunity for laundering their cash, with construction prices of roughly €500 per sq m paling in comparison to the listing prices of up to €4,000 per sq m.Albania’s own Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organized Crime, SPAK, is making progress. InJune, it seized €150m of assets, including apartments, villas and commercial properties, tied to an alleged cocaine trafficking network. The same month, Pëllumb Gjoka, once named a “strategic investor” by the Albanian government with approval to build a €52m resort on the coast,was sent to prison for ordering mob hits.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a classic example of what happens when you think you’re the benevolent leader’ … Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama.Photograph: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesResearch by Citizens.al shows that several projects in The Albanian Files are linked to ongoing SPAK investigations (none of the architects named in this article are implicated), alleging criminal capital has been funnelled throughshell companies, construction contracts and property transactions. Over 40% of the projects in the book don’t even mention who the client is, leading many to ask: why the opacity?One former member of the ArchArmy is rueful about the way things have turned out. “Like the others, I joined with a real conviction that this could be a positive change for the country,” they tell me. “Rama knew Albania was going to develop very quickly, and he didn’t want to fuck it up. It’s better to have some good architects involved to make sure it turns out halfway decent, rather than people building generic apartments along the coast without any control.” The architect says they backed out after being part of a competition jury that “didn’t feel democratic” and the fact that issues around land ownership “always felt very vague”.They add: “Rama still very much believes that he’s doing the right thing for the country. It’s a classic example of what happens when you think you’re the benevolent leader, but you stay in power too long.”This sentiment is echoed in one of the most revealing contributions to the book. Reinier de Graaf, of Dutch firm OMA, writes an open letter to Rama – intended as a parody, but the humour is moot. “Given Albania’s enduring status as an enlightened architectural patron,” he writes, “our profession would benefit greatly if the country never had another election again, and if you … would just continue as president for life – maybe even king.”He adds: “In a world of autocracies, may we have one benevolent autocrat with taste?”Explore more on these topicsArchitectureAlbaniaOrganised crimeEuropeConstruction industryfeaturesShareReuse this content
