title: No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitude  | Metal | The Guardian
description: As frontman of Venom, Conrad Lant made an impact on metal to rival Black Sabbath, inspiring a whole new subgenre with his diabolical grandstanding, unruly spirit and heretic noise
Author: Matt Mills
Headline: As frontman of Venom, Conrad Lant made an impact on metal to rival Black Sabbath, inspiring a whole new subgenre with his diabolical grandstanding, unruly spirit and heretic noise
Content: ‘I’m in league with Satan!’ … Cronos pictured in 1985.Photograph: Fin Costello/RedfernsView image in fullscreen‘I’m in league with Satan!’ … Cronos pictured in 1985.Photograph: Fin Costello/RedfernsMetalNo one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitudeMatt MillsAs frontman of Venom, Conrad Lant made an impact on metal to rival Black Sabbath, inspiring a whole new subgenre with his diabolical grandstanding, unruly spirit and heretic noiseConrad ‘Cronos’ Lant, frontman of UK heavy metal band Venom, dies aged 63Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTShareWhen Venom’s first blasts of ungodly racket emanated from Newcastle upon Tyne in the late 1970s, metal was enduring its awkward adolescence. Black Sabbath and Deep Purple had respectively slipped down the charts and broken up, and young guns Iron Maiden and Judas Priest were years away from reaching their commercial heights. Frontman Conrad “Cronos” Lant decided that the genre had become “lame”.“There could only be one new way to do this,” herecalled to Guitar Worldin 2008. “For metal bands to get some fucking balls again.”It wouldn’t take long for Lant and his bandmates to reintroduce the kind of danger that their singer/bassist thought was missing. They dragged the unruly, DIY spirit of punk to heavier turf, smashing hoarse vocals against basic yet hammering riffs, unconcerned with the notion of harmonies. The lyrics took the occult fascinations of Black Sabbath and made them confrontational, rather than ominous. “I’min league with Satan!Iwas raised in hell!” Lant declared on 1981 singleIn League With Satan, with the hellhound bark and ground-rumbling low end to back it up.Critical feedback was harsh: Kerrang! dismissed In League With Satan as “a pompous piece of horrifying power plod”. But the disdain only made Venom’s ferocity scream further, inspiring its own subgenre, black metal, plus a host of future giants – and a school of musicians who wanted to look, sound and terrify just like he did.Born in Chelsea in London in 1963, Lant moved up north with his family when he was eight years old. Although his London accent made him an instant target at school, he gave as good as he got. “We used to beat the shit out of each other as part of the curriculum!” hetold Metal Hammer. “You learn to stand up for yourself, and I think that’s something I carried into Venom with the attitude: if you don’t like it, fuck you!”Venom: Black Metal – videoAfter he joined Venom aged 16, it took only a few seconds of watching Lant on stage to see that attitude in action. Tongue out like Gene Simmons, bass in hand as he snarled into an overhead mic like Lemmy, he was a conglomeration of rock’s most intimidating figures to date. At the same time, his gravel-throated insistence on how diabolical he was, plus his gauntlets and lashings of leather, made him more than the sum of those parts. His grandstanding was soon mimicked by Slayer’s Tom Araya, Hellhammer/Celtic Frost’s Tom G Warrior, Kreator’s Mille Petrozza and countless underground metal singers.These baying frontmen were just one subsect of the legions who owed themselves to Venom. The notorious Norwegian “black metal” scene took its name from the band’s 1982 second album and attempted to exceed their idols’ monstrousness, with certain members burning down local churches and even committing murder. Lant never endorsed the violence, tellingthe Quietus: “What a fucking shame that those guys are known for that and not for their music.”On the other side of the Atlantic, Megadeth guitarist Dave Mustaine (also ex-Metallica) wore a T-shirt on stage that depicted the artwork to Venom’s 1981 debut album Welcome to Hell. Anthrax leader Scott Ian hailed the same album as “a new kind of insanity”, referencing how raw and savage the recording was (the band intended the recordings to be demos for the label, who decided to release them as they were). With the same self-assuredness that he brought to his live shows and old schoolyard scraps, Lant expressed pride in many, many interviews over his music being so different from the glossiness of other early-80s UK metal acts.View image in fullscreen‘A new kind of insanity’ … Lant performing with Venom in Oslo in 2022.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/Alamy“I would never, ever have wanted to be in a band like Iron Maiden or Saxon, and I didn’t want to be commercial or sound like anyone else,” he told Classic Rock. “We wanted to create music that scared people. And we succeeded.”‘I want to go further’: Justin Broadrick on retiring Godflesh, playing with Phoebe Bridgers – and his new bandRead moreBut the public persona was only one side of him. As Classic Rockobservedin a profile earlier this year, “there are two versions of Cronos”. At home, he listened to the usual suspects such as Led Zeppelin and Status Quo, but also Joni Mitchell and Kate Bush. He liked birdwatching in his spare time. He left Venom from 1987 to 1995, after record sales started to dwindle. During that self-imposed exile, he became a fitness instructor.Following his return to Venom, Lant steered the ship through a number of personnel changes and stayed committed to the heretic noise that had made his band so striking early on. Even though repetition naturally dulled the scariness, he became regarded as a beloved elder statesman, enjoying guest spots including on Dave Grohl’s metal tribute Probot. Mark Tremonti, guitarist of radio-rock institution Creed and unsung extreme metal connoisseur, told me in 2022 that Venom rivalled Black Sabbath in terms of their impact on metal. Lant’s vehement drive to stop the genre from going soft almost 50 years ago had ensured its survival.Explore more on these topicsMetalPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Obsession is a terrifying, violent nightmare of lovestruck madness – but the Globes’ rigid awards categories have forced it into an absurd choice
Author: Tom Beasley
Headline: Obsession is a terrifying, violent nightmare of lovestruck madness – but the Globes’ rigid awards categories have forced it into an absurd choice
Content: Musical or comedy? Obsession.Photograph: Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenMusical or comedy? Obsession.Photograph: Toronto film festivalHorror filmsHorror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comediesTom BeasleyObsession is a terrifying, violent nightmare of lovestruck madness – but the Globes’ rigid awards categories have forced it into an absurd choiceFri 2 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 05.55 EDTShareWhat do this year’s wish-gone-wrong taleObsession, gross-out transformation bloodbathThe Substance, and Jordan Peele’s generational masterpieceGet Outhave in common? Well, they’re all modern horror success stories, with critics and at the box office, and they broke free of genre snobbery to become awards-season contenders.They’re also toe-tapping laugh riots. At least that’s what theGolden Globeswould have you believe.The Globes present a conundrum for horror. Its major categories are split into either “drama” or “musical or comedy” and it’s fair to say neither of those is an obvious home for throat-ripping gorefests or white-knuckle ghost-train rides. So if you’re managing an awards push for a hotly tipped horror, what road do you take? The answer, often, is titters and tap-dancing.That’s what has happened with Obsession. Perthe Hollywood Reporter, Focus Features will submit it for consideration in the musical or comedy categories. This is despite the fact the movie is a pitch-dark story about what happens when a lonely man Bear (Michael Johnston) uses a magical trinket to force female pal Nikki (Inde Navarrette) to fall devotedly in love with him. The consequences are stark, with a descent into madness that includes Navarrette delivering some of the most terrifying facial expressions since Gordon Brown attempted to smile. The closest thing Obsession has to a knock-knock joke is when someone is graphically bludgeoned to death with a brick. Not exactly a zinger worthy of the Apollo.But it’s easy to see how this impulse towards category chicanery arises. Traditionally, the drama category is where the big-hitters duke it out. This year, it’s likely to be a straight fight between Christopher Nolan’s exceptional take onThe Odysseyand the Spanish LGBTQ+ epicLa Bola Negra. That’s not to mention Dune: Part Three, which could ride a Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King-style wave if Denis Villeneuve can bring Frank Herbert’s books to a satisfying conclusion.While the musical or comedy category looks uncommonly formidable this year – with Martin McDonagh’s fast-talkingWild Horse Nineset to battle Olivia Wilde’s summer hitThe Inviteand the small matter of the Michael Jackson biopic – it’s less intimidating than a straight fight with Nolan’s Homeric juggernaut.As horror doesn’t fit neatly, it’s able to tactically pick its battles. In actuality, though, this makes it very difficult for horror to ever emerge victorious. Most horror fits more suitably into the drama category. The Exorcist won as a drama back in 1974, despite the fact it would go on to lose to The Sting at theOscars, but even The Silence of the Lambs – the last film to complete a clean sweep of the Academy’s Big Five – struggled at the Globes, having been pitched as a drama. The only one of its Oscars it replicated at the Globes was for Jodie Foster.Horror hasn’t fared too much better in the musical or comedy category. Tim Burton’s gothic bloodbathSweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Streetdid win in 2008, but that one genuinely had some Sondheim warbling amid the slashed throats.It’s a sticky wicket for horror movies at the Globes. They are seldom seen as “worthy” enough to compete as dramas, but they feel like too much of a square peg in a round hole to be considered as viable musical/comedy winners. They’re essentially pushed aside like a lonely kid on Halloween with eyeholes cut into a bedsheet, desperate for someone to trick or treat with.You may well argue that the Golden Globes don’t matter. The ceremony has often been dismissed as more obsessed with A-list stars than celebrating cinematic excellence and the whole thing almost went the way of the dodo in 2021 amid controversy around the lack of diversity in its voting body. So while it’s true that the Globes aren’t the be-all and end-all when it comes to awards season, they set the tone for the months to come. They’re often the first major awards to be handed out, giving momentum to winners and stalling the campaigns of those who lose out. And given the uphill struggle involved in getting horror even nominated at the Oscars, this sort of early-season momentum can be pivotal.There’s one case, though, that the Obsession team might be looking at. Navarrette’s remarkable central performance is believed to be the movie’s best chance at scooping a statuette and there’s a recent precedent that may go in her favour. While The Substance’s status as a “musical or comedy” might have cost it a chance at the top prize, it did enable Demi Moore to win for best actress. And while a topsy-turvy race in that category would ultimately hand the Oscar to Anora’s Mikey Madison, Moore’s victory was a big moment for horror that Navarrette will hope to repeat.Still, awards season remains an inhospitable place for horror movies. Obsession is a true breakout hit, cementing a new star in Navarrette and minting a directorial hot prospect in Curry Barker. But none of that will help it when it comes to the Golden Globes. title: They’re delicious, popular and versatile – but how healthy are berries? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you are benefiting
Author: Adrienne Matei
Headline: Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you are benefiting
Content: Berries bring a meaningful dose of antioxidants to the table.Photograph: fcafotodigital/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBerries bring a meaningful dose of antioxidants to the table.Photograph: fcafotodigital/Getty ImagesWell actuallyThey’re delicious, popular and versatile – but how healthy are berries?Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you are benefitingAdrienne MateiFri 2 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSprinkled on top of yoghurt, blended intosmoothiesor baked into crumbles, berries are among Americans’favoritefruits.Luckily, berries are as healthy as they are delicious and versatile: low in calories, full of vitamins and antioxidants, and a goodsourceof fiber. Research shows that, depending on the type, berries supportcardiovascular health, may boostgut healthand fight inflammation and show promise as part of a “healthy dietary strategy for diabetes prevention and management”, to quoteresearchers.Meta-analysesalso link compounds in berries with improved cognitive health.Here’s what experts say about the health benefits of berries.Why are berries good for the brain?Berries bring a meaningful dose of antioxidants to the table.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’“Berries’ high polyphenol content is what we think makes them so protective” when it comes to mental processes such as memory and attention, said Maggie Moon, a registered dietitian.Polyphenols are a broad category of plant compounds; in berries, the most active and proportionally meaningful of them are anthocyanins, which also give many berries their blue, purple and red pigments.Researchers areinvestigatingwhether berry polyphenols and the metabolites produced when gut microbes process them may influence inflammation and blood-vessel function. Because the brain depends on an extensive blood supply, better vascular function is one plausible route by which berries could support cognition.“In simple terms, the anthocyanins are likely creating a healthy working environment for brain cells by improving blood flow into the brain, which improves oxygenation and nutrient delivery,” said Tim Crowe, a nutrition scientist who closely follows anthocyanin research. “What’s good for our blood vessels is also good for our brain.”A scientist said bananas ‘kill’ the benefit of blueberries. Is that true?Read moreThe equivalent of a daily cup of blueberries was linked to slightly improved speed of information processing relative to a placebo in older adults with mild cognitive impairment over a six-month period, according toresearchby Mary Ann Lila, a professor in the department of food, bioprocessing, and nutrition sciences at North Carolina State University. That suggests berries could not only be neuro-protective, but an intervention for those already experiencing cognitive decline. “A pretty amazing result,” said Lila.A particular pattern of eating called the Mind diet – a version of the Mediterranean diet geared toward supporting cognitive health – involves berries.“We have a strong indication that diets that are higher in berries over many years tend to have slower cognitive decline and delaying of cognitive ageing,” said Moon, who has written abookabout the Mind diet.In the 2015studyinforming the Mind diet, researchers observed 923 participants. They found those who prioritized whole foods including berries,leafy greens, nuts and seeds,beans, fatty fish and olive oil – while avoiding sweets,ultra-processed foodsand red meat – for an average of 4.5 years had a 53% lower risk of developing Alzheimer’s compared with those who did not.Which berry is the healthiest?Experts say that if you’re eating any berry – strawberries, blackberries, currants, raspberries, blueberries – you’re benefiting.“All berries are good. We should eat a heck of a lot more than we do,” said Lila.View image in fullscreenEach type of berry has its own valuable nutritional fingerprint.Photograph: Xiu Huo/Getty ImagesHowever, some studies suggest wild berries may have a bit of a nutritional leg up on their conventionally grown counterparts, because they develop an “abundance of phytochemical resources” to “defend them against the environment”, Lila said. “Those are the same phytochemicals that when we consume them … dispel human chronic diseases.”Each type of berry has its own valuable nutritional fingerprint. Some punch above their weight in particular categories. For instance, cranberries are the only commercially cultivated berry with a significant amount of “a particular kind of polyphenol called an A-type proanthocyanidin” which helps prevent recurrent urinary tract infections, said Lila.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlackcurrants, meanwhile, provide themostvitamin C per cup of raw berries – about 190mg, compared with only 15mg in blueberries. Raspberries are fiber champions, with 8g, or about a third of your daily fiber needs, per cup.Blueberries contain high levels of anthocyanins, and are colloquially lauded as asuperfood– but that doesn’t necessarily mean that blue is best. Other varieties could have similar benefits, but blueberries are “the well-studied one” because they are known to produce positive findings in nutrition research studies, said Crowe.Moon recommends eating a cup of berries a day, though she notes that any amount you add to your diet regularly is a net positive. “The more people are eating fruits and vegetables, including berries, the better,” she said.Should we be worried about pesticides on berries?Berries usually appear onthe Dirty Dozen, an annual list made by the non-profit Environmental Working Group. The EWG tests produce for pesticide residue and the results often make headlines, causing people to wonder whether they should be avoiding certain fruits and vegetables.Are you taking supplements correctly? Here’s a guide on their dosage limitsRead moreIt is important that pesticide residue on organic and conventional produce remain below the regulatory limits. In the US, these are set by the Environmental Protection Agency, and monitored and enforced by federal regulators such as theFoodand Drug Administration and the US Department of Agriculture. But mere detection of a substance doesn’t automatically translate to a dangerous concentration.“The dose makes the poison, and detection is not the same as harm. The very real benefits of eating a variety of any produce, including berries, outweigh theoretical risks,” said Moon. “No major scientific or public health organization recommends avoiding conventionally grown produce, including berries.”“You’d need to eat hundreds of servings of each food to even hit the safety threshold, which is already 100-1,000 times lower than a level that could theoretically cause harm,” writes science communicator, microbiologist and immunologist Dr Andrea Love in her 2025assessmentof the Dirty Dozen.What are the best ways to eat berries?“Fresh and frozen berries have fairly similar nutrient profiles,” said Moon. Frozen berries are flash-frozen soon after being harvested, meaning they retain their nutrients well. Frozen berries are convenient and potentially cheaper than fresh ones, added Crowe. Freeze-dried berries alsoretaintheir nutrients.However, anthocyanins are heat-sensitive, andresearchhas found that they can be reduced in berries by up to 80% in prolonged, high-heat processes such as jam-making.Berries aren’t just forbreakfast or sweetpreparations, either. “One of my favorite ways to eat berries is a wild berry salsa – all the ingredients of a salsa minus the tomatoes, with wild blueberries standing in,” said Lila. “It’s a beautiful blue, cold dish you scoop up with chips, and since it’s raw, you’re not losing any potency to heat.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyFruitFoodHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Brimful of personality: the rise of fashion’s ‘silly little hats’ | Hats | The Guardian
description: From pillboxes and boaters to bicornes and buckets, characterful hats are making their way from the catwalk to the high street
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: From pillboxes and boaters to bicornes and buckets, characterful hats are making their way from the catwalk to the high street
Content: A model at the Bottega Veneta fashion show in Milan.Photograph: Nowfashion/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA model at the Bottega Veneta fashion show in Milan.Photograph: Nowfashion/ShutterstockHatsBrimful of personality: the rise of fashion’s ‘silly little hats’From pillboxes and boaters to bicornes and buckets, characterful hats are making their way from the catwalk to the high streetEllie Violet BramleyFri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Here goes – an order for a million hats,” wrote Jackie Kennedy to Bergdorf Goodman before moving into the White House in the early 1960s. It’s a line that could have been uttered by any number of people working in fashion today, because the hat – and not just the ubiquitous baseball cap – has been enjoying a very characterful resurgence.View image in fullscreen‘Showing off, but only a little bit’ … A Chloé sailor hat, Paris fashion week.Photograph: Gonzalez Alain-Gil/Abaca/ShutterstockThis season at the turbo-high-end brand Loro Piana, whose clothes are beloved by tech bros and Kendall Roy,almost every model was wearing a hat. At Thom Browne, straw boaters came shrouded in colourful mesh. At Chloé there were see-through hats to match see-through trenchcoats and white sailor hats atop all-white outfits. Courrège’s hats were space-age, Burberry had big buckets, Bottega Veneta had hats brimming with charisma.Some are calling them “personality hats”, others, affectionately, “silly little hats”, but hats that foreground character over practicality are enjoying time spent on heads fromMilan fashion weekto the shops. It’s not about a sou’wester in a storm but a creative punctuation point to an outfit, meant to draw the eye upwards.Hats are a great expression of personality. According to David Long, the author of TheHatsThat Made Britain: A History of the Nation Through Its Headwear: “Excluding beanies and baseballs, hats are a rare opportunity for display, so I think the wearers are trying to say: ‘I’m not like everyone else, even though we all wear the same clothes nowadays.’ They’re showing off, in other words, but only a little bit.”Noel Stewart, a millinerwho has created hats for Mulberry, JW Anderson and Valentino, said: “Hats can be a major signifier of personality and intent, whether it is shouted or whispered is up to the wearer.”View image in fullscreenJackie Kennedy arriving at Love Field in Dallas in 1963.Photograph: APConsumers of high-street fashion have also been “showing off a little bit”, as personality hats have trickled down toAsosand H&M, where iterations of wool and pillbox hats are on sale, giving off Jackie Kennedy vibes.As part of John Galliano’s new collaboration with Zara, there are Napoleonic-style bicorne hats, as well as one hat that looks like a fashion take onthe millinery of the woman feeding the birds at the end of Mary Poppins.‘Vessels for joy and play’: Sarah Jessica Parker cements big hat momentRead moreAt Copenhagen fashion week, pillbox hats were a common sight on the streets of the Danish capital. “People want to be chic without being too forced (and expensive) about it. This soft pillbox is a very good way of doing that,” said Stewart.Some might see these “personality hats” as a way to stand out from the baseball-cap-wearing masses. For those fluent in hat, such as Stewart, there’s a time and a place for all hats: “I am wearing a baseball cap at the moment, but it’s not all I wear and we all need different hats for the different moments in our lives.”But for many, such characterful hats will still take some bravery to wear on a random Tuesday. Even Kennedy, arguably the most famous pillbox hat wearer of the 20th century, once wrote: “Oh dear, it was so pleasant when I didn’t have to wear hats! They will pauperise me and I still feel absurd in them.”Explore more on these topicsHatsMilan fashion weekAsosH&MZaraAccessoriesnewsShareReuse this content

Headline: From bullets to rabbits to wand vibrators, our sexual wellbeing expert demystifies what’s available and rates her top 17 models (she tested 67)
Content: Intimate toy ownership has been linked to greater satisfaction – not only with sex but also with life.Photograph: Hans Neleman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIntimate toy ownership has been linked to greater satisfaction – not only with sex but also with life.Photograph: Hans Neleman/Getty ImagesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSexReview‘It could get an orgasm out of a cabbage’: the best vibrators, testedFrom bullets to rabbits to wand vibrators, our sexual wellbeing expert demystifies what’s available and rates her top 17 models (she tested 67)26 easy ways to spice up your sex lifeAlix FoxFri 2 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJump toWhy you should trust meTypes of vibratorThe best bullet vibratorsThe best rabbit vibratorsThe best wand vibratorsHow I chose vibrators – and what you should considerCan vibrators decrease your sensitivity?What to do when your old toys finally dieIcould write here about how almost a fifth of women surveyed by Durex said using a sex toy was the most dependable way for them to climax. Or I could point out howKinsey Institute researchsuggests regular masturbation can help relieve and prevent symptoms of menopause, such as vaginal atrophy. I could even tell you thatstudies demonstratea significant correlation between intimate toy ownership and greater satisfaction – not only with sex but also with life itself.But the potted version is that orgasms and erotic pleasure are glorious, and top-class toys can help you savour more of both. So here are the best vibrators available. I’ve worked as an expert independent research and development consultant for more than a dozen adult product companies; I’m a board member of theVagina Museumin London; I’m a campaigner for sexual health and gynaecological charities, includingTerrence Higgins Trustandthe Eve Appeal; and I helped write many of your favourite characters’ lines about dildos, douching and desire in the hit Netflix series Sex Education. All this means I’m well qualified to assess whether these devices have been crafted decently.I’m also a freelancer who works from home. I’ll leave it at that.Types of vibratorView image in fullscreenThe Satisfyer Air Pump Bunny 1Asking, “What’s the best sex toy?” is a bit like asking, “What’s the best tool?”: a plethora exists, and selecting the most suitable one is influenced by what you want it to do. Here, I’ve examined three popular styles of vibrators.BulletsSmall, versatile vibrators for external use only. They’re primarily designed for targeted clitoral stimulation but can be used to tickle nipples, glide up the insides of thighs, or take on a tour practically anywhere on the body (except inside the anus – that’s not safe).WandsLarge vibrators with broad heads, again typically designed for external use. Wands deliver the most powerful vibrations over a wide area – this sector is where you’ll find the most bone-shaking master blasters on the market. Fantastic for people who need intense stimulation, and good for deep body massage, too.RabbitsThese vibrators have two parts: an insertable shaft, designed to stimulate inside the vaginal canal and excite the G-spot, and an external head that stimulates the clitoris. This “dual stimulation” is intended to provoke a “blended orgasm”: a climax induced by mixing multiple forms of simultaneously delivered sensation.The best bullet vibratorsAt a glanceBest bullet vibrator overallWe-VibeTango X£79 at We-VibeBest bullet for innovationLovenseAmbi£55 at AmazonBest sustainable bulletLove Not WarMaya£54.99 for base at SheSpotBest soft and sensual optionSmile MakersThe Firefighter£39.95 at Beauty BayBest budget bulletRocks OffRO-90£15.99 at BootsBest bullet vibrator overall:We-Vibe Tango XWe-VibeTango Xfrom£79£79 at We-Vibe£79.99 at LovehoneyWhat we loveImpressive, deep, rumbly vibrations for a bulletWhat we don’t loveIts magnetic charger has a weak connectionView image in fullscreen£79 at We-Vibe£79.99 at LovehoneyThe original Tango came out about 16 years ago, and it’s consistently remained so high up in expert rankings that by this stage it might have altitude sickness.Why we love itIts Goat status is justified: while many bullets offer “buzzy”, high-frequency vibrations that don’t travel far into the body, the Tango is satisfyingly “rumbly” for its size, providing additional lower-frequency stimulation that carries deeper into tissues and awakens more nerve endings. It packs a lot of oomph into its small size.This latest incarnation features a silicone grip to make it less slippery to hold, while the business end remains hard and glossy. There’s nothing to muffle the vibrations: they’re full-on and focused, which isexactlywhat tickles many people’s pickles. Others may find the feeling too “sharp”, however.Three separate buttons to increase/decrease power and change pulse patterns make it easy to find the exact output to suit you. There’s excellent variety between the settings, the lowest of which is more a brisk twitch than a vibration. Plus, a travel lock means you won’t have to trot out the “it must be my electric toothbrush!” line when your handbag starts humming.It’s a shame that …the magnetic charger can be accidentally knocked off its connections, but it’s more hygienic than a lead that needs to plug into a hole in the toy.Speeds:eightVibe patterns:sevenPower:rechargeableRun time:two hoursCharge time:one hour and 30 minutesWaterproof:yesWarranty:two yearsWe-VibeTango Xfrom£79£79 at We-Vibe£79.99 at LovehoneyWhat we loveImpressive, deep, rumbly vibrations for a bulletWhat we don’t loveIts magnetic charger has a weak connectionBest bullet for innovation:Lovense AmbiLovenseAmbifrom£55£74.99 at Boots£55 at AmazonWhat we loveShape offers diffuse vibrations and precisionWhat we don’t loveVibrations travel up handle; charger is fiddlyView image in fullscreen£74.99 at Boots£55 at AmazonA palaeontologist friend told me the Lovense Ambi is shaped exactly like a Parasaurolophus’s head. I Googled it; they were right. But while its form may hint at the prehistoric, its function and features are futuristic.Why we love itThe Ambi’s ingenious architecture means it can be angled so its pointy tip provides pinpoint pleasure. The broader head delivers more diffuse vibrations, or it can be nestled lengthways between labia. You can change speeds and patterns manually using a button on the base, but it really comes into its own when paired with the Lovense Remote app. This allows you to set it to respond in sync with music or voices, hand over control via mobile phone to a playmate anywhere in the world or adjust the power in itty-bitty increments all the way up to a top strength reminiscent of that T-Rex shaking the water glasses scene in Jurassic Park.It’s a shame that …those meaty vibrations do transfer significantly into this toy’s handle, too, so your fingers can start feeling fizzy and numb after a short period of holding it. And like much of the Lovense range, the Ambi is solely available in shocking pink: fabulous for those who love a kitsch Barbie Dreamhouse aesthetic, but less so if you harbour refined Architectural Digest aspirations.I’d also like to see the magnetic charging stand improved: it’s rather wibbly-wobbly, and the Ambi only seems to power up when it’s facing forward despite also clicking neatly into the dock the other way around, so you need to pay close attention to the red charging light to check it’s fitted correctly and actually charging.Speeds:three intensity and four vibration patterns in manual mode; almost infinite increments when using the appVibe patterns:unlimited, as you can program it via the appPower:rechargeableRun time:up to two hoursCharge time:70 minutesWaterproof:yes, to IPX7 standardWarranty:one yearLovenseAmbifrom£55£74.99 at Boots£55 at AmazonWhat we loveShape offers diffuse vibrations and precisionWhat we don’t loveVibrations travel up handle; charger is fiddlyBest sustainable bullet:Love Not War MayaLove Not WarMayafrom£54.99£54.99 for base at SheSpot£54.99 for head at SheSpotWhat we loveRecycled aluminium build; interchangeable headsWhat we don’t loveAlternative heads are expensiveView image in fullscreen£54.99 for base at SheSpot£54.99 for head at SheSpotIf you want to feel the earth move without harming the planet, Love Not War is your friend with benefits. Its Maya bullet is made from recycled aluminium in a hydroelectric-powered factory, and minimally packaged in a brown cardboard box printed with soy ink.Why we love itSeven different screw-on heads are sold separately to convert the bullet into, say,a rabbitora G-spot probe. Interchangeable efforts I’ve tried in the past have suffered from insufficiently strong motors, so they haven’t been able to successfully transmit vibrations throughout each attachment, especially longer/larger ones. Love Not War is mounting an admirable battle against that challenge, however.It’s a shame that …at more than £50 a pop, amassing a collection of heads will cost you a pretty penny – although the brand will plant a tree for each one sold.Speeds:fourVibe patterns:sevenPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:two years, and Love Not War will repair toys to keep them alive for as long as possibleLove Not WarMayafrom£54.99£54.99 for base at SheSpot£54.99 for head at SheSpotWhat we loveRecycled aluminium build; interchangeable headsWhat we don’t loveAlternative heads are expensiveFor more, read19 self-care treats for the perfect pick-me-upBest soft and sensual option:Smile Makers the FirefighterSmile MakersThe Firefighterfrom£39.95£39.95 at Beauty Bay£49.95 at Victoria HealthWhat we loveFlickers gently but has a pointy end to do the jobWhat we don’t loveIts pink colour won’t be for everyoneView image in fullscreen£39.95 at Beauty Bay£49.95 at Victoria HealthBullets are often designed to treat the genitals like a game of darts: if the clitoris is the bullseye, they aim to hit it dead on. The Firefighter instead approaches stimulation more like a curling match: gently brushing, sweeping and edging towards a climax.Why we love itThe fluttering, flickering flame-shaped head will suit those who prefer a slow, delicate buildup before switching to the more traditional, targeted “pointy finger” part of the toy.It’s a shame that …it only comes in pink.The Surfer, another Smile Makers bullet, is a refreshingly unusual zesty orange.Speeds:fourVibe patterns:twoPower:rechargeableRun time:three hoursCharge time:two to two-and-a-half hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:two yearsSmile MakersThe Firefighterfrom£39.95£39.95 at Beauty Bay£49.95 at Victoria HealthWhat we loveFlickers gently but has a pointy end to do the jobWhat we don’t loveIts pink colour won’t be for everyoneBest budget bullet:The Rocks Off RO-90Rocks OffRO-90from£15.99£15.99 at Boots£17.99 at SinfulWhat we loveAffordable; wide range of shapes and coloursWhat we don’t loveOne-button controls are tediousView image in fullscreen£15.99 at Boots£17.99 at SinfulRocks Off makes a whole shooting range of cheap-and-cheerful battery-powered bullets. Take your pick of pointed, rounded, angled or lipstick-shaped tip; select a slick gloss, powdery matt or silicone finish; and choose from more colours than the fabric of Joseph’s dreamcoat, including one that changes from purple to pink in response to body heat.Why we love itIt’s a fair amount of bang for very few bucks. I singled out the RO-90 as my best budget buy because the AAA battery it takes is much easier to source than the N-size variety insidethe smaller RO-80 model. The slightly longer shaft makes it better suited to use for penetrative play, too, if that’s your bag.Hats off to Rocks Off as well for its collaboration with disability charity Enhance the UK to developa truly accessible toy range, Quest. A 5% share of sales from that collection goes back to the charity.It’s a shame that …single-button controls mean you have to cycle all the way through speeds/pulses to change them. Many toys are too rigid to allow sufficient bending and angle adjustment to solve this issue.Why we love itThis Je Joue genius solves that: it’s as flexible as a yoga master, and both parts of it are poseable, allowing you to easily customise how it curves to fit your bits. Another irritating rabbit habit is that the “ears” intended to tickle either side of the clitoris can pinch, poke or catch against sensitive flesh, depending on how your body happens to be built. Here, the Hera is a hero once more, replacing the traditional bunny head with a plush, spongy, smooth “thumb”. If you’re someone with a more frilly clitoral hood or labia that gets painfully pulled by rabbit ears, this could be a real thumbs up. A quality, thoughtfully re-engineered rabbit reboot.It’s a shame that …there’s a bit of a jump between the first two power levels. A steadier climb would be preferable. The squishiness of the Hera Flex won’t suit folks who prefer firmer pressure on their hotspots, either. But as so often in the world of sex toys, that’s rather like saying, “people who prefer raspberries shouldn’t choose this banana”; it’s a question of taste, rather than a product being bad.Speeds:fiveVibe patterns:sevenPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:one hour and 30 minutesWarranty:one yearJe JoueHera Flexfrom£99£99 at Je Joue£115 at SuperdrugWhat we loveFlexible and poseable to fit every bodyWhat we don’t loveBig jump between lowest power levelsBest for temperature titillation:Lovehoney Glow BunnyLovehoneyGlow Bunnyfrom£51.99£79.99 at Lovehoney£51.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid rabbit with unique temperature play tipWhat we don’t lovePower levels won’t knock your socks offView image in fullscreen£79.99 at Lovehoney£51.99 at AmazonIf you just want to use this toy as an old-school rabbit, it’s a solid choice … but it also has new-fangled tricks up its sleeve.Why we love itThe temperature-play plate on the top of the shaft heats to 38C in less than two minutes, feeling almost like a warm tongue, and swiftly cools to 18C, giving a whole new meaning to “Netflix and chill”. I imagine the cold setting could be particularly enticing during sweltering summer nights, and it works nicely for nipple play, too.It’s a shame that …the power is perfectly acceptable, but not perfect for the power-hungry.Speeds:threeVibe patterns:fourPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:three hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:100 daysLovehoneyGlow Bunnyfrom£51.99£79.99 at Lovehoney£51.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid rabbit with unique temperature play tipWhat we don’t lovePower levels won’t knock your socks offBest for air pulse stimulation:Womanizer Duo 2WomanizerDuo 2from£189£189 at Womanizer£189 at BootsWhat we loveDual-action air pulse tech; clever automatic modesWhat we don’t loveTakes more practice than similar, cheaper productsView image in fullscreen£189 at Womanizer£189 at BootsAdmittedly, this looks more like something Star Trek’s Captain Picard should be at the helm of than a conventional rabbit. Rather than stimulating the clitoris with vibrations, the Duo 2 uses pulses of air to create a throbbing, sucking effect. Womanizer was the first to introduce this technology to the adult market in 2014, when it represented one of the most groundbreaking innovations in years.Why we love itThe firm continues to be a pioneer. This toy boasts multiple proprietary features, including “Smart Silence”: it will only turn on when in contact with skin. This means the battery life is preserved,andyou don’t have to fumble to switch it off in a panic if your intimacy is interrupted.An Autopilot mode alternates between surprise pulse patterns and intensities to prevent masturbation from becoming predictable, while the Afterglow setting helps you gradually wind down post-climax, rather than simply switching off.It’s a shame that …the shape takes getting used to, and there are now more intuitive (and affordable) suction and vibration rabbit toys available. That said, I believe the Duo 2 is worth mastering due to its god-tier-level exclusive features.Speeds:14Vibe patterns:10Power:rechargeableRuntime:two hoursCharge time:two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:five yearsWomanizerDuo 2from£189£189 at Womanizer£189 at BootsWhat we loveDual-action air pulse tech; clever automatic modesWhat we don’t loveTakes more practice than similar, cheaper productsBest for an innovative shaft:Satisfyer Air Pump Bunny 1SatisfyerAir Pump Bunny 1from£36.99£49.99 at Sinful£36.99 at AmazonWhat we loveInflating shaft with a whopping warrantyWhat we don’t loveLoud inflating noises may have deflating effectsView image in fullscreen£49.99 at Sinful£36.99 at AmazonSatisfyer is known for two things. First, making excellent-quality, more affordable “dupes” of aspirational high-end sex toys – almost like an Aldi version of Lelo and co. Second, and in contrast to the first, rolling outvastmultitudes of its own novel inventions, including this Air Pump Bunny.Why we love itIt sports an inflatable shaft that can be enlarged by up to 15mm in diameter at the touch of a button, producing a “filling” sensation that some find mind-blowing. This could be just the ticket if your orgasm is intensified by the presence of a girthy internal toy, giving your vaginal muscles something to clench around as the waves of climax hit (more common than is discussed), especially if you need to build up to having something wide inside you. Magnetic charging, smart buttons and a walloping 15-year warranty show this toy is more than just hot air.It’s a shame that …it makes a noise like a car tyre inflator while it’s pumping up, and sounds like your vagina is sighing mournfully as it deflates. But now the Natural Love Company is making beautiful, talented toys, with eco credentials, including the incorporation of reclaimed ocean plastics and carbon-neutral delivery.Why we love itI was intrigued to check out the Senna after being impressed bythe Yarrow: a willow-green rabbit with a thrusting head that’s far more graceful-looking than this kind of gadget has any right to be. It takes a while to find your way around a toy this curious, but the payoff is worthwhile.It’s a shame that …the buttons are a fraction fiddly, and don’t think about trombones during use, or you won’t be able to stop laughing.Speeds:five for each motorVibe patterns:five for each motorPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:two yearsSnail VibeCurvefrom£109.99£114.99 at Boots£109.99 at AmazonWhat we loveConstant clitoral contact; two independent motorsWhat we don’t loveFiddly button controlsBest budget rabbit:Ann Summers Self Love Dual SimulationAnn SummersSelf Love Dual Simulationfrom£55£55 at Ann Summers£55 at BootsWhat we loveClassy vibe; high-end specs at an affordable priceWhat we don’t loveAnn Summers’ trend-driven range sells out quicklyView image in fullscreen£55 at Ann Summers£55 at BootsRabbit-style vibrators emerged in Japan in the early 1980s, and the inaugural model had a trio of creature cousins – a beaver, a turtle, and a kangaroo. The zoological designs were a way of circumventing strict obscenity laws of the time, but as buyers realised how well the rabbit’s ears in particular were suited to their X-rated job, demand soared and word spread internationally. Ann Summers launched its own “Rampant Rabbit” in 1991 – and the store remains an excellent place to bag a bunny.Why we love itThis rabbit feels far posher and more well-bred than you might expect for the price. It has a flexible shaft to help it better fit different anatomies. The Tiffany-blue diamond-textured silicone has a high-class aura. Is it rechargeable and waterproof, with a respectable degree of horsepower and plenty of speed and pattern options? Tick, tick, tick – and all without making your bank manager cross.It’s a shame that …Ann Summers’ offering is trend-driven, with a lot of seasonal, once-they’re-gone-they’re-gone toys. It recently stocked some especially slender, petite rabbits I would have loved to recommend to people seeking smaller-than-average dual-stimulation toys, but they were gone in a heartbeat. TheRampant Rabbit Slimis a decent option from its core range for anyone who finds the Self Love’s shaft too thick.Speeds:three in both the shaft and ears, separately controlledVibe patterns:seven in both the shaft and ears, separately controlledPower:rechargeableRun time:60-90 minutesCharge time:about two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:one yearAnn SummersSelf Love Dual Simulationfrom£55£55 at Ann Summers£55 at BootsWhat we loveClassy vibe; high-end specs at an affordable priceWhat we don’t loveAnn Summers’ trend-driven range sells out quicklyBest old-school throwback rabbit:Lovehoney Jessica RabbitLovehoneyJessica Rabbitfrom£34.98£39.99 at Lovehoney£34.98 at AmazonWhat we loveNostalgic design; lots of pleasing featuresWhat we don’t loveIts soft plastic build can become stickyView image in fullscreen£39.99 at Lovehoney£34.98 at AmazonThere’s a Y2K revival under way, and to me, the Lovehoney Jessica Rabbit screams “millennium” at least as much as flip phones, inflatable furniture and wearing high heels with cargo pants. It’s wonderful that many modern toys are so sophisticated, but since eroticism can have strong associations with past pleasurable experiences, the lure of “the old faithful” shouldn’t be discounted.Why we love itJessica: she’s a camp icon. The translucent bubble-gum pink soft-plastic material. The swirling pearl beads in the shaft. The fact that the head rotates clockwise and anticlockwise. Lovehoney has sold versions of the Jessica since 2008, so for many people, a rabbit like this one will have been their first foray into sex toys.It’s a shame that …soft plastic can quickly get grubby, and if the material degrades, it can become harder to clean hygienically. Keep this rabbit away from silicone-based lubes and anything oily, as these may damage the material and make it sticky – although Jessica will always be delightfully tacky.Speeds:three speeds in the ears; three speeds and reversible rotation in the shaftVibe patterns:seven patterns in the earsPower:3 x AA batteries – not includedRun time:about 60-90 minutesWaterproof:no, splashproof, IPX4Warranty:one yearLovehoneyJessica Rabbitfrom£34.98£39.99 at Lovehoney£34.98 at AmazonWhat we loveNostalgic design; lots of pleasing featuresWhat we don’t loveIts soft plastic build can become stickyThebest wand vibratorsAt a glanceBest wand vibrator overallDoxyDie Cast Max Plug-In£160 at Ann SummersBest classy all-rounderLeloSmart Wand 2£159 at SinfulBest for long-distance loversKiirooProWand£75 at KiirooBest budget wandSo DivineWicked Game£54.99 at AmazonBest wand vibrator overall:Doxy Die Cast Max Plug-InDoxyDie Cast Max Plug-In£160£160 at Ann SummersWhat we lovePunchy plug-in power that can take proper pressureWhat we don’t loveIt practically needs its own roof rack if you want to travel with itView image in fullscreen£160 at Ann SummersAs they say: go hard, or go home. The mains-powered Doxy Die Cast Max Plug-In is arguably as hard as you can go. It’s not for the faint of heart (or parts), but it’s so mighty that it can probably conjure up an orgasm through walls. And speaking of your hopefully thick walls, you don’t get up to 9,000 revs a minute without noise, so be aware that even though the metal body rattles less than plastic wands, this is still loud enough to sound like you need a licence to drive it. Heck, though – what a ride.Since Doxy launched more than a decade ago, its products have been revered for their tectonic-plate-juddering strength and have gained a fervent fandom – all of whom must have supreme confidence in their dental health, because I swear these wands could shake your teeth right out of your head. Earlier in 2026, the brand gathered feedback from more than 1,300 devotees and relaunched with an Alien-esque neon-green-and-black logo and a streamlined suite of hotly anticipated, improved toys.The new edition of the Die Cast Max Plug-In model features a reinforced, flexible neck that can withstand greater pressure, so you can back your thang up on it and push against it with some serious welly. The buttons have also been redesigned to feel more tactile, and the packaging has been upgraded so it serves as long-term storage.Why we love itThe reworked Doxy range now includes several less behemothic, cordless, USB-C rechargeable wands, including the smaller-but-still-seriousDie Cast Compactand the petite yet powerfulDoxy Go.However, I’m recommending the most uncompromising, mammoth model of the lot. Nothing about it is a novelty; this right here is a professional power tool. It’s mains-powered, so the formidable rumbling never stops; it’s ravishingly, ruinously relentless. Its lead is three metres, so it stretches to most places you want it to go. And it’s built to last, from solid metal: I owned the old version for more than a decade, and it was still impeccable when I levelled up to the latest model.The Die Cast is not subtle, but I’d argue that the push for sex toys to be “discreet” has roots in shame. Multiple women who’ve sought my advice for anorgasmia have called me, ecstatic, after my Doxy tip-off has given them their first-ever climax: something unabashed that works is better than something understated that doesn’t.It’s a shame that …at 918g and the size of a rounders bat, the Die Cast Max Plug-In is a heavy beast. People without strong wrists or with problems such as arthritis should check out theDoxy Original Plug-In, 651g, and explore wand-positioning cushions such as those by Liberator or Sportsheets.Speeds:eight power levelsVibe patterns:variable escalating pulse modePower:mains powered and supplied with plug adaptors for the UK, EU, US & AUWaterproof:noWarranty:one yearDoxyDie Cast Max Plug-In£160£160 at Ann SummersWhat we lovePunchy plug-in power that can take proper pressureWhat we don’t loveIt practically needs its own roof rack if you want to travel with itBest classy all-rounder:Lelo Smart Wand 2LeloSmart Wand 2from£159£159 at Sinful£179 at LeloWhat we loveChic, reliable and powerfulWhat we don’t loveHorn shape adds to its heftView image in fullscreen£159 at Sinful£179 at LeloLelo is the Idris Elba of the adult toy arena:chic, almost universally considered attractive, and a reliably fantastic performer.Why we love itThis ergonomic delight is easy to wield and functions excellently as amassage gunin addition to its racier applications. It’s elegant, intuitive to use and packs plenty of punch at the higher settings. It would have been my top pick were it not for the fact that I’m confident the Doxy could get an orgasm out of a cabbage.It’s a shame that …the large Lelo wand will intimidate some folks: for some reason its curved rhino-horn shape makes it seem even heftier than a straight wand. Luckily, there’s amedium size availabletoo.Speeds:10Vibe patterns:10Power:rechargeableRun time:four hours (but I suspect that’s only achievable for users who solely prefer the gentlest speed)Charge time:two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:one year, plus a 10-year quality guaranteeLeloSmart Wand 2from£159£159 at Sinful£179 at LeloWhat we loveChic, reliable and powerfulWhat we don’t loveHorn shape adds to its heftBest for long-distance lovers:Kiiroo ProWandKiirooProWandfrom£75£75 at Kiiroo£105.62 at SextoysWhat we loveCan be remotely app-controlled; 10-hour run timeWhat we don’t loveThe app could be simplerView image in fullscreen£75 at Kiiroo£105.62 at SextoysThe ProWand is a lightweight, velvety wand built to be comfortable for extended use – and boasting an impressive 10-hour-plus run time.Why we love itThe ProWand can be remotely controlled or connected to other compatible toys with theFeelConnect app, perfect for facilitating shared erotic experiences for lovers who live apart or frequently travel separately. I’ve worked with cybersecurity experts at Mozilla to investigate the hackability of internet-enabled sex toys, andthe company’s reportsays Kiiroo “do[es] a pretty good job protecting users’ privacy and security”.The glowing LED handle can be set to match the colour of lingerie and is dim enough to not illuminate that distracting pile of washing in the corner of your bedroom.It’s a shame that …the app takes a second to get the hang of, although overall the setup and navigation are much simpler than others I’ve tried.Speeds:fiveVibe patterns:sixPower:rechargeableRuntime:10+ hoursCharge time:four hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:one yearKiirooProWandfrom£75£75 at Kiiroo£105.62 at SextoysWhat we loveCan be remotely app-controlled; 10-hour run timeWhat we don’t loveThe app could be simplerBest budget wand:So Divine Wicked GameSo DivineWicked Gamefrom£54.99£59.99 at Superdrug£54.99 at AmazonWhat we loveTwo motors for internal or external stimulationWhat we don’t loveLess powerful than pricier wandsView image in fullscreen£59.99 at Superdrug£54.99 at AmazonSo Divine’s versatile value wand includes the option for vibrations to be emitted from each end of the toy.Why we love itThis flexibility is a very good thing. Turn on the domed head at the top for external body massage or the insertable shaft at the bottom to enjoy penetration and internal stimulation. Despite this toy having dual motors, you can’t run both ends at once – although only the most adventurous among us would need that.It’s a shame that …this toy doesn’t pack the power of pricier wands, and some prefer a material and design with more softness, flex and yield. However, it’s a great entry-level wand that gives you a chance to experiment with different stimulation styles and learn what you like before investing in a deluxe toy for three times the price.Speeds:threeVibe patterns:sevenPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:two hours and 30 minutesWaterproof:yesWarranty:two yearsSo DivineWicked Gamefrom£54.99£59.99 at Superdrug£54.99 at AmazonWhat we loveTwo motors for internal or external stimulationWhat we don’t loveLess powerful than pricier wandsHow I chose vibrators – and what you should considerView image in fullscreenThink about what materials and textures feel inviting to you.Photograph: Getty Images/Pcess609At least 20 toys were tested in each category, with 67 tested in total. In addition to his links to love and lust, Saint Valentine is also the patron saint of beekeeping, so he would feel quite at home amid the cacophony of buzzing that soundtracked the production of this article.I discounted any products not made from body-safe materials, such as porous jellies that can harbour bacteria and dirt, or plastics containing phthalates, which have been linked to cancer and hormonal interference. I considered things such as whether each device lived up to the claims made by its manufacturer; how easy it was to position and control; how fast it charged and how long the battery lasted, where relevant; and how attractive, adaptable, powerful and comfortable it was.What Ididn’tdo was automatically label a toy as a “holy grail” or an “almighty fail” if it didn’t happen to float my idiosyncratic boat, or provide what I personally need to reach orgasm, through no inherent fault of its own. Deciding upon the “best” vibrator is highly subjective, so I’ve tried to explain how different items might suit different folks.When making your own considerations, useful questions to ask include:Do I prefer gentle or potent vibrations (or both)? What styles of touch delight me, and do I want external or internal stimulation (or both)?What shape and size of toy will suit my body and my tastes?Do I want something simple, straightforward and intuitive, or experimental/multifunctional/tech-enabled?What materials and textures feel inviting to me?A note on volume: some reviews rate toys on how quiet they are, but I’ve NEVER met a vibe that’s as near-silent as it says it is. For that reason, I’ve only pointed out when a toy is notably loud enough to sound like you’ve rented it from a builders’ merchant.In almost all cases, you do have to put your hand in your pocket if you want the best. Strong motors, neat details and high-performance designs don’t tend to come cheap. I believe pleasure should be accessible to all, though, so there’s at least one budget option included in each category. It’ll have some compromises, but it should give you plenty of “Ooh!” for not much dough.Can vibrators decrease your sensitivity?Let me reassure you: using vibrators will not cause nerve damage to your genitals. However, if, over a prolonged period, youalwaysreach for a toy when masturbating – particularly if it’s a high-strength model like a mains-powered wand – you may inadvertently condition your body to become used to intense stimulation. Much like a curry fan who’s been mainlining vindaloo and is then served a masala, the comparatively gentle feelings provided by fingers or partners may begin to feel less spicy, and you may struggle to orgasm without the potent or pinpointed vibrations with which you’ve become familiar.A similar problem arises for people with penises who hold themselves very tightly and use rough motions during solo play. American sex educator Dan Savage nicknamed this “the death grip”, and it can cause erectile dysfunction and difficulties ejaculating via the relative tenderness of intercourse.Luckily, solutions are simple. First: chill out on your vibrator use, to give your body time to reappraise the delights of the delicate. You may want to try a period of abstinence, where you return to manual masturbation without grabbing a toy. Or if you’ve been cranking your toy’s power straight up to 11, try being a little less Spın̈al Tap and experimenting with softer speeds and patterns. Lubricant can help too, by cushioning sensitive tissues a little.If you find that sex without toys simply doesn’t feel as good, another option is to involve your toys in sex. Contrary to many people’s fears, vibrators can’t replace the profound intimacy and thrill of being with another human being, but they can vastlyenhanceshared experiences – they’re complementary co-pilots, not competitors.If you’re someone who feels threatened by toys, it may help to think of them as specialist equipment. You wouldn’t feel emasculated or belittled if you had to equip yourself with an axe to cut down a tree instead of just using your bare hands, right? Instead, it’s more impressive to learn to wield that equipment like a pro, whether you want to chop timber or set your partner’s night alight. Using the right apparatus the right way is the fastest route to successfully starting a fire. Ask your lover to show you how they like the toy to be positioned, and be eager to take on any feedback they give.What to do when your old toys finally dieIf all this toy talk has reminded you that you have enough bad vibes, shot bullets and dead rabbits gathering dust in your bedside cabinet to rival Watership Down, you’re not alone. Research conducted in 2025 by tech refurbishment specialists Back Market revealed that 15% of people keep old and broken sex toys stored ad infinitum because they’re embarrassed to throw them away. One in three surreptitiously chucks them in the household bin – even though anything with batteries, a plug or a charging port can be recycled. An unfortunate side-effect of increased sexual liberation and toy ownership is that worn-out erotic electricals are worsening the planet’s burgeoning e-waste problem, and valuable materials within them, including aluminium, gold, copper, lithium and steel, are being lost to landfill.If your ancient wand vibe is now more tragic than magic, head toRecycle Your Electricals, enter your postcode, then select Vibrator from the drop-down menu (yes, it’s a legitimate category). You’ll be given recycling instructions specific to your location; some councils will even collect your raunchy rubbish directly from your door. I’d wrap it in a bag, mind, for discretion. The binman doesn’t need to have the dirt onallyour filth.Alix Fox is an award-winning writer and broadcaster specialising in sexual wellbeing and culture, with 20 years of experience in receiving dick pics sent not to titillate, but because the worried texter wants an informed opinion on a weird lump/rash/wart. title: A vodkatini, a garibaldi and a shrub – your essential autumn cocktails – recipes | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Try a millionaire’s martini, a Campari that couldn’t be simpler and a booze-free blackberry fizz (plus an Aperol that doesn’t need a spritz)
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Try a millionaire’s martini, a Campari that couldn’t be simpler and a booze-free blackberry fizz (plus an Aperol that doesn’t need a spritz)
Content: What’s your poison? Six enterprising aperitifs to kick off cocktail hour.Photograph: Charlie Lee / The Guardian. Food styling: El KempView image in fullscreenWhat’s your poison? Six enterprising aperitifs to kick off cocktail hour.Photograph: Charlie Lee / The Guardian. Food styling: El KempCocktailsA vodkatini, a garibaldi and a shrub – your essential autumn cocktails – recipesTry a millionaire’s martini, a Campari that couldn’t be simpler and a booze-free blackberry fizz (plus an Aperol that doesn’t need a spritz)Mina HollandFri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBramble and ginger shrubView image in fullscreenI make a variation on this year-round. Bring on the autumn.2 tbsp shrub syrupGinger beer,to top1 spring of rosemary,to serveFor the shrub200g blackberries200g golden caster sugar1 grating each of nutmeg and black pepper½ tsp ground cinnamon100g vinegar(I use raw apple cider)To make the shrub, measure the berries and sugar into a sterilised jar, mashing them so they meld together. Add the spices and mix again. Put in the fridge for 24-48 hours.Strain the mixture; set aside the solids for baking or to top your morning porridge, and keep the syrup for your drink, putting it back into a sterilised jar. Add the vinegar, stir and put back in the fridge until you’re ready to drink.To a tumbler, add ice and two tablespoons of the syrup. Top with the ginger beer and rosemary to serve.Millionaire’s vodkatiniView image in fullscreenAn evening’s first drink is important to get right, and I often wring my hands over it. A vodka martini or a glass of fizz? My friends, the answer is both.Makes130ml vodka(from the freezer)15ml dry vermouth,or aromatised wine like Cocchi Americano3 drops Angostura bittersSparkling wine,to topLemon twistTo a cocktail shaker, add the vodka, vermouth, bitters, and a couple of cubes of ice. Stir gently for 20 seconds, then strain into a martini glass fresh out of the freezer. Top with sparkling wine, then briefly run the lemon twist around the glass rim before dropping it in. Serve.Mexican fizzView image in fullscreenI recently discovered Fever Tree’s Mexican lime soda – if you use this rather than sparkling water, you don’t need the maple syrup. Either way, this is something between a paloma and a margarita, and I can’t get enough of it.Makes160ml tequila blancoJuice of ½lime,plus a slice to serveTiny pinch of salt½ tsp maple syrup(optional)Mexican lime soda or sparkling water,to topTo a cocktail shaker, add the tequila, lime juice, salt and maple syrup, if using. Give it a quick shake.Put a handful of ice in a highball or large tumbler, and strain the content of the cocktail shaker over. Top with the lime soda, stir briefly and garnish with the lime slice on the glass rim.Aperol garibaldiView image in fullscreenA bittersweet drop to remind you of warmer days – but which I’ll happily put away year-round. Slips down dangerously easily.Makes1a2 large oranges45ml AperolHalve the oranges, then cut a half-moon slice from one of the halves and set aside, and squeeze the remaining oranges into your blender. Whizz for one minute, so the juice is frothy.To your glass (I like a stemmed old fashioned glass but a tumbler works just as well), add a few ice cubes and the Aperol, then pour the blended orange juice over. It will gradually mix, but you can give it a quick stir if you wish (I like to see the colour gradations of Aperol, juice, froth). Garnish with the half moon slice set across the diameter of the glass rim, and serve.Halve 2 large oranges, then cut a half-moon slice from one half and set aside. Squeeze the remaining orange juice into a blender and whizz for one minute, until frothy.To a stemmed old fashioned glass (a tumbler works just as well), add a few ice cubes and 45ml Aperol, then pour the blended orange juice over. It will gradually mix, but you can give it a quick stir if you wish. Garnish with the half moon slice set across the diameter of the glass rim, and serve.Campari shakeratoView image in fullscreenA single ingredient drink that can be scaled up or down according to your needs. For me, 60ml of Campari (two lidfuls from my shaker) is just right – and fits a mini martini glass perfectly.Makes1IceCampariAdd several ice cubes and your preferred volume of Campari to a cocktail shaker (you could also use a blender or Nutribullet). Holding it tightly with two hands, shake vigorously for as long as you have the energy – about 30 seconds. Strain into a freezer-chilled glass and serve.Mulled AJ garnished with a s’moreView image in fullscreenIf ‘the days drawing in’ was a drink, this would be it. For my children, the combination of warm, spiced AJ and – though I say so myself – a superior s’more is as good as it gets.Makes1 (or 2 small)250ml cloudy apple juice1 striporange peelJuice of½ lemon1 cinnamon stick3 cloves1 tsp soft dark brown sugar(optional)For the s’more1 marshmallow2 chocolate Leibnitz biscuitsPut the apple juice, orange peel, lemon juice, spices and sugar (if you are using it) in a small saucepan over the lowest heat. Leave to warm for 10-15 minutes, so the room smells delicious and you start to see faint steam rising from the pan. Do not let it boil.Meanwhile, put the marshmallow on a metal skewer and hold it just above an open flame, turning often, allowing it to bronze and char, if you like your s’mores like that (I do!). Put the toasted marshmallow on the chocolate side of a biscuit, then sandwich with the other. Decant the mulled AJ into a mug, and enjoy alongside the s’more.Explore more on these topicsCocktailsAutumn food and drinkFoodWineFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A warming, comforting, spiced drink that’s ideal for autumn, and pairs brilliantly with a slice of carrot cake
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A warming, comforting, spiced drink that’s ideal for autumn, and pairs brilliantly with a slice of carrot cake
Content: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenPalé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it – recipeA warming, comforting, spiced drink that’s ideal for autumn, and pairs brilliantly with a slice of carrot cakeBruce DorflingFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe move into autumn proper leads our taste buds to crave warmth and comfort in equal measure. And what could be more warming and comforting than a spiced vodka and citrus cocktail spiced with nut liqueur? Slice of carrot cake optional.Have your cake and drink itServes1For the vodka infusion (for 7-8 serves)Peel of1 unwaxed lemon, all white pith removed375ml good vodka– we useBelvedereFor the drink50ml lemon peel-infused vodka– see above and method15ml hazelnut liqueur– we useFrangelico15ml vanilla syrup –homemade or store-bought (Bristol Syrup Co make a good one)15mlfresh lemon juice15mlfresh orange juice15ml fresh carrot juice6 dashes foamer, or 1 egg white4 dashes aromatic bitters(we useAngostura aromatic), or 1 pinch ground cinnamon1 orange slice, to garnish (or 1 slice carrot cake, to accompany)The night before, infuse the vodka: put the lemon peel and vodka in a jar, seal and leave to steep overnight. Next day, strain the vodka into a clean jar or bottle, seal and store in a cupboard out of direct light, where it’ll keep almost indefinitely.To build the drink, measure all the liquids into a shaker filled with ice, shake hard, then double strain into a coupe. Garnish with an orange slice, or serve with carrot cake to nibble on alongside.Bruce Dorfling, bar manager,Palé Hall, Bala, Gwynedd, WalesExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodFruitVegetablesAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenHgelen Goh’s flourless walnut, date and espresso cake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotFoodHelen Goh’s recipe for flourless walnut, date and espresso cakeWith a deep, caramel richness and a bitter undertone, this cake is an excellent addition to your home baking rosterHelen GohFri 2 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s enough dark chocolate in this gluten-free cake to put it firmly in chocolate cake territory, but the hero flavour comes from the sweet, creamy nuttiness of walnuts, so it’s important to use very fresh ones, because stale walnuts can quickly turn bitter. The dates bring a deep, caramel richness, while the espresso pulls everything back from being overly sweet. Despite all that richness, the cake is wonderfully light in texture. Serve with creme fraiche and perhaps some poached pears, if you want to turn it into a full-blown dessert.Flourless walnut, date and espresso cakePrep10 minCook1 hr 30 min, plus coolingServes8-10150g unsalted butter,plus extra for greasing150g pitted dates120ml just-brewed espresso200g shelled walnuts1tbsp cocoa powder, plus extra for dusting1 tsp ground cinnamon¾ tsp baking powder½ tsp fine sea salt100g dark chocolate, broken into rough pieces5 large eggs, separated75g light brown sugar1 tsp vanilla extract75g caster sugarGrease a 20cm cake tin with a removable base, then line it with baking paper. Put the dates in a small bowl, pour over the hot espresso and leave to soften.Meanwhile, put the nuts in a food processor and process until finely ground, taking care not to overprocess or they will become oily. Tip into a medium bowl, add the cocoa powder, cinnamon, baking powder and salt, and stir to combine.Without washing the food processor, tip in the soaked date and coffee mix, then process to a smooth puree.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put the butter and chocolate in a heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of barely simmering water, making sure the base of the bowl doesn’t touch the water. Stir until melted and smooth, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.Meanwhile, put the egg yolks and brown sugar in the bowl of an electric mixer and beat on medium-high for about three minutes, until thick and pale. Turn down the speed to low, then gradually work in the melted chocolate and butter, followed by the date puree and vanilla. Fold in the walnut mix until combined, then scrape the batter into a large bowl.Thoroughly clean and dry the mixer bowl and whisk attachment. Whisk the egg whites until foamy, then gradually add the caster sugar and continue whisking until they form medium peaks. Fold one-third of the meringue into the batter to loosen it, then gently fold in the rest.Pour the batter into the lined tin, then bake for 55-60 minutes, until the edges are set but the centre still has a slight wobble – a skewer inserted into the centre should emerge with a few moist streaks, rather than be completely clean. Leave the cake to cool completely in its tin, then unclip and transfer to a serving plate. Dust with cocoa powder, then slice and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotCakeBakingDessertSnacksFruitNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Daniel Roseberry adds ‘aerodynamic‘ edge to Schiaparelli’s surrealist glamour at Paris show | Fashion | The Guardian
description: American in Paris showcases new simplicity with stretch cocktail frocks, but there’s still plenty of gold-foiled nipples and peekaboo fabrics to wow the frow
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: American in Paris showcases new simplicity with stretch cocktail frocks, but there’s still plenty of gold-foiled nipples and peekaboo fabrics to wow the frow
Content: A model walks the Schiaparelli spring/summer 2027 show during Paris fashion week.Photograph: Photo: Filippo Fior/SchiaparelliView image in fullscreenA model walks the Schiaparelli spring/summer 2027 show during Paris fashion week.Photograph: Photo: Filippo Fior/SchiaparelliFashionDaniel Roseberry adds ‘aerodynamic‘ edge to Schiaparelli’s surrealist glamour at Paris showAmerican in Paris showcases new simplicity with stretch cocktail frocks, but there’s still plenty of gold-foiled nipples and peekaboo fabrics to wow the frowJess Cartner-Morleyin ParisFri 2 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a world of mega brands, the house of Schiaparelli is small but perfectly formed. There are only 10 points of sale worldwide where Schiaparelli clothes can be bought. The size of the business has risen from $6m in 2020 to around $100m today, but Schiaparelli is still small fry compared with other names on thePariscatwalks.However, the Schiaparelli name punches above its weight. An exhibition at London’s V&A museum this year made a strong case for its founder, Elsa Schiaparelli, who collaborated with Salvador Dali and Jean Cocteau, as a creative force in the surrealism movement of the 1930s.View image in fullscreenKylie Jenner caused a stir with Schiaparelli’s hyper-realistic fake lion’s head.Photograph: Laurent VU/Sipa/Rex/ShutterstockKylie Jenner in a dress adorned with a fake lion’s head and Bella Hadid on the Cannes red carpet with an elaborate gold necklace covering her breasts have put the brand name all over TikTok. “It’s an amazing time at Schiap,” designer Daniel Roseberry said after his Paris show. “It’s a smaller house, but I feel like the voice is so big. It’s exclusive, but it’s real, because what we show on the catwalk is exactly what we sell.”Schiap – Elsa’s nickname has become a nickname for her house – is strong meat. In his haute couture collections, Roseberry has leaned into Schiaparelli’s visual signature of anatomical detail parlayed into glamour. A tight dress might have a padded spine, gloves embroidered with glossy red fingernails, a jacket buttoned with a row of tiny gold ears or noses.Roseberry is training for the New York City Marathon, and there was a sportiness and, by Schiap standards, a simplicity to the stretch cocktail frocks that opened the show. (“I’m in my aerodynamic era, I guess.”) Still plenty of gold-foiled nipples and peekaboo fabrics, however, and a finale of dinner jackets, snug and haughty with embroidery taken from the house archives.As an American in Paris, Roseberry was joined last year on the fashion week schedule by Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, both appointed to lead Loewe after Jonathan Anderson’s elevation to Dior.View image in fullscreenLoewe designers Jack McCollough, left, and Lazaro Hernandez after presenting their spring/summer 2027 collection on Friday.Photograph: Firas Al Toukhi/EPAThey have brought an American levity to the brand, bringing a more playful tone to the high-concept artiness and inside-joke wit with which Anderson turned a Spanish craft house into a fashion power player. The backwards baseball cap made perhaps its first Paris fashion week appearance in living memory.The distinctive silhouette of a basketball vest, with its longline hem, low scooped neck and piped hems, was the template for delicious slip dresses in sorbet colours, fringed at the edges with tiny beads in contrasting shades. Capri pants came with a kick at the knee, like bullfighter breeches. McCollough and Hernandez called it “the ease of American pragmatism, and nods to Spanish drama, ritual, history”.Explore more on these topicsFashionParisFashion industryFashion weeksDressesKylie JennerBella HadidnewsShareReuse this content
