title: I travelled all over the country on a €63 monthly rail pass: readers’ favourite holidays in Germany | Germany holidays | The Guardian
description: From cycling in Berlin and the Black Forest to world-class cocktail bars in Cologne and magical North Sea beaches, readers share their travel tips
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From cycling in Berlin and the Black Forest to world-class cocktail bars in Cologne and magical North Sea beaches, readers share their travel tips
Content: Covered porticoes in Münster.Photograph: travelview/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCovered porticoes in Münster.Photograph: travelview/Getty ImagesReaders' travel tipsGermany holidaysI travelled all over the country on a €63 monthly rail pass: readers’ favourite holidays in GermanyFrom cycling in Berlin and the Black Forest to world-class cocktail bars in Cologne and magical North Sea beaches, readers share their travel tipsTell us about a sunny autumn break– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 2 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google​Winning tip: History, buns and Italianate porticoes in MünsterIn an often overlooked corner of Germany, near the Dutch border, Münster is an absolute gem. Covered porticos will convince you you’re in northern Italy, gothic churches will remind you you’re in Mitteleuropa and the buns fromZeit für Brotwill insist you’re in heaven. Nature-lovers can take in theBotanical Gardensand relax by the Münstersche Aa river. Those of a historical bent can peek into the room where theTreaty of Westphalia was signedin 1648 and mull the report card of nation states in the nearly 400 years since. But really, it’s a great place just to drop-anchor and lose a few days.JeremyGermany’s highest railway bridge, near DüsseldorfView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Hackenberg-Photo-Cologne/AlamyIn the verdant countryside near Düsseldorf, the 129-year-old Müngsten Bridge, the country’s highest railway bridge, rises 107 metres above the River Wupper. The impressive iron and steel structure is billed as Germany’s answer to the Eiffel Tower (yes, really!) and if you’ve got a head for heights, you can don a harness and make the exhilarating climb to the highest point. You’ll be rewarded with incredible views across the valley, especially if you steel yourself (!) for the nerve-racking walk across the narrow beam that spans the top of the bridge. Eat your heart out, Sydney Harbour Bridge.BexProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.A wild North Sea island made for cyclingView image in fullscreenThe North Sea island of Sylt.Photograph: Westend61 /AlamySylt is more than a North Sea island to us. My German grandmother met my British army grandfather, and Sylt became my mother’s childhood island. It feels made for cycling, with peaceful paths winding between grassy dunes, sweeping beaches and little villages. Spend the day riding, watching the surfers and eating warm Nutella crepes by the sea, before settling into a traditional hoodedStrandkorb(hooded beach chair) to listen to the waves. Bike hire costs€8-€10 per day. It is wild, windswept and magical, somewhere our family history becomes real every time we return.FayTour the country for a month for €63View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Imago/AlamyGet theDeutschlandticket! An entire month of public transport for €63 – buses, trains, trams, ferries ... The only thing that isn’t included is faster long-distance trains, but you can figure out how to get from A to B using theDeutsche Bahnwebsite, which has a special “Deutschlandticket only” filter; the need to change trains means you’ll end up discovering places you wouldn’t otherwise visit. It’s worth it just for a week, or, if you do want to travel long distances quickly, just for inner-city transport. Use the German public transport app Mopla to buy one at any time.JosephCologne’s world-class cocktails barsView image in fullscreenCologne’s famous cathedral dominates the skyline and tops most travel itineraries. But having visited for a day on a previous trip, we returned for a city break with one thing in mind: cocktails. The mixology scene here is world-class. The jewel in the crown isSeiberts(pictured), which often and rightly features in lists of the world’s best bars, butLittle Link,WoodsandOna Morall contend and offer different vibes. While not sat at the bar, you’ll find excellent 20th-century art, street art and a lifesized Milka cow at the chocolate museum.JohnKite flying in a vast former airfield in BerlinView image in fullscreenTempelhofer Feld.Photograph: Nawintar Hengsrisuk/AlamyOn a warm autumn afternoon in Berlin, a friend and I rented classic Dutch bikes to explore the city. As the golden hour approached we discoveredTempelhofer Feld. Used as an airfield during a darker era, today it’s a vast recreational green space. Biking on the disused runway was enjoyably bizarre. Berliners and visitors alike were picnicking, kite flying, inline skating, lolling about on bales of hay, skateboarding, tightrope walking, birding … you name it. It is also an important site for rare flora and fauna and grazing animals.Sarahskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn ebike adventure through the Black ForestView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tanja Voigt/AlamyEbikesare the perfect way to explore the beauty and vastness of the Black Forest. Powering up gravel tracks that would be impossible on a push bike was so fun and a real hit with the teenager. Setting off from the astonishingly well preserved town of Gengenbach, we headed to the viewpoint atMoosturmobservation tower and theLothar Monument(pictured), where we were rewarded with a glorious 360-degree view of hills patterned with colour and wisps of cloud. On the way down it seemed churlish not to stop at theNaturfreundehausKornebenemountain hut and restaurant for possibly the best sausages of my life. A thoroughly deserved reward: ebiking counts as exercise, right?Alex500 years of architecture in GörlitzView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Albazil/AlamyGörlitz, near the Polish border, merited more than just the day trip I had planned from Dresden so I returned later in my holiday to explore its delights. It’s chock-a-block with charming, colourful buildings, making it beloved of German and international film-makers. Strolling through the cobbled streets of the old town is like leafing through a lavish picture book of 500 years of German architecture, from gothic through the renaissance to art nouveau – don’t missSt Peter’s Church. Eat hearty Silesian sausages at beer houses and if you feel like a swim head out by bus to Lake Berzdorf, with views of the mountains from the sandy beach – or even the middle of the lake where I ventured to.AprilTake the family car around a racing circuit in NürburgView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Xavier Bonilla/Getty ImagesWhen my son turned 16 we drove to Munich so he could buy his first beer legally. Breaking up the journey we stopped overnight near theNürburgringracetrack, to take the family estate car around theNordschleifecircuit. You turn up, pay €30-€35, and get in the queue. We were overtaken by everything apart from a coach full of Italian tourists and an ice cream van.TimA spectacle of water in KasselView image in fullscreenPhotograph: DPA /AlamyThe unexpected highlight of our German road trip was Kassel’s extraordinaryBergpark Wilhelmshöhe, a Unesco world heritage site. On water feature days, park below Wilhelmshöhe Palace (€8.50 per car, including bus travel for up to seven), ride to the Hercules monument, then follow the water downhill on foot. The free spectacle sends 750,000 litres tumbling without pumps through baroque cascades, waterfalls and a Roman-style ruined aqueduct, culminating in a soaring 52 metre fountain. Following the rushing water from one dramatic stage to the next was an adventure, and after the 2.3km descent, your car is waiting at the bottom.MaryView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsGermany holidaysReaders' travel tipsCity breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I’m allergic to the cold | Life and style | The Guardian
description: My condition is severe, so I have to a keep close watch on my body temperature and can’t eat chilled foods
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: My condition is severe, so I have to a keep close watch on my body temperature and can’t eat chilled foods
Content: ‘I didn’t realise how much it would change my life’: Shauna Castaner in California, where she lives.Photograph: Andri Tambunan/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I didn’t realise how much it would change my life’: Shauna Castaner in California, where she lives.Photograph: Andri Tambunan/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I’m allergic to the coldMy condition is severe, so I have to a keep close watch on my body temperature and can’t eat chilled foodsShauna CastanerFri 2 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 02.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2012, when I was 37, I started noticing that my fingers would get swollen and red whenever I held an iced drink. I thought it was strange, but I didn’t know what was going on. Then the same thing would happen when I handled food from the fridge. My instinct was to put my hands under hot water, but that made it worse.For a while, that’s all I experienced. I thought it was weird but not dangerous. I was busy with my three children, so didn’t worry.But then other areas of my body started to react. Once, I was eating ice-cream when the inside of my cheeks started swelling and my tongue felt weird. It was scary.In the spring of 2014, I went to the doctor. They referred me to an allergist for a test – they put an ice cube inside a metal container and stick it on your arm, cover it up and leave it for 10 minutes. When they take it off, they watch to see what happens as your body warms up. That is generally when the hives and swelling start.The allergist confirmed I hadcold urticaria, a rare condition that means you’re allergic to the cold, and that it was a severe allergy, meaning I could have an anaphylactic reaction. The doctor prescribed me some EpiPens and said I could take antihistamines, but that they didn’t always work.What I didn’t realise back then was just how much this would change my life. I joined a support group on Facebook. Reading other people’s stories made me nervous about what could happen to me. I thought: “What if it gets worse?”Cold urticaria affects people differently. Some have a genetic version and others, like me, develop it for no apparent reason. It’s an allergy to cold temperatures that can be triggered by the weather, but also temperatures inside buildings, and things like food and drink.double quotation markFrom mid-October to around April, it’s hard for me to leave my houseView image in fullscreenShauna Castaner at home.Photograph: Andri Tambunan/The GuardianI can’t eat or drink anything straight from the fridge or freezer. I’ve learned how to take the chill out of things without making them hot and gross. I microwave yoghurt for five seconds, and then another five if it still seems too cold.Over the years, I have worked out that my temperature threshold is about 73F (22.8C). There are variables: if it’s slightly colder but the sun is fully out I can comfortably be outside, but I would struggle if it’s warmer but windy. I have four weather apps and temperature gauges in every room of my house.I live in Sacramento, California. From mid-October to around April, it’s hard for me to leave my house. It doesn’t get freezing cold, but in the dead of winter I have to bundle myself up in layers.Summer is really hot, so we keep the air conditioning on in the house. I wear a cardigan, drink hot coffee and stay away from the vent. Showers are a huge issue: the longer I take, the hotter I get, which causes a bigger temperature difference between my body and the air. Quick temperature changes are a huge trigger. I always carry two EpiPens, hot coffee and a flask of whisky, because it warms you up.I also wear a medical bracelet that says I have cold-induced anaphylaxis. If I were ever unconscious and given IV fluids, they would need to be warmed before entering my body, otherwise I could die. That’s one of my biggest fears.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: I found my long-lost twin aged 49Read moreI don’t tell people about my allergy any more. They make stupid jokes, like: “I hate the cold. I’m allergic, too.” I want people to take it seriously.My condition has affected my life in a lot of ways. I had to give up my career as a photographer and am now a stay-at-home parent. It restricted my ability to do fun things outside with my children, which makes me sad.I wouldn’t wish this allergy on anyone. I often have dreams that it has disappeared and I’m eating ice-cream or walking along my favourite beach. Cold urticaria can get better or go away, but generally it’s progressive.I don’t hold out hope that it will go away, but I do appreciate time outside in a way that I didn’t before. For me, feeling the sun on my face on that first day when it’s warm enough to stand outside and take a deep breath feels life-changing every single time.As told to Isabelle AronDo you have an experience to share? title: While I dream of garden greenhouses, a coldframe will do me just fine | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: A hothouse in my garden may be just a fantasy, but I can still offer plenty of protection for tender plants
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: A hothouse in my garden may be just a fantasy, but I can still offer plenty of protection for tender plants
Content: Coldframes can defend plants against animals and birds as well as the early autumn chill.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyView image in fullscreenColdframes can defend plants against animals and birds as well as the early autumn chill.Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyGardening adviceWhile I dream of garden greenhouses, a coldframe will do me just fineA hothouse in my garden may be just a fantasy, but I can still offer plenty of protection for tender plantsAlice VincentFri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIthought I would have had a new coldframe by now, but the only new thing in the garden is a fox hole. It would be more polite of them to direct their exemplary digging skills towards where we’re excavating for new foundations, but so it goes.I’m writing this, then, in the hope that it will spur me on to order one. I like to think that, one day, in a fantasy life, I might be a greenhouse person. I’d fill it up with pelargonium cuttings and orange blossom and hold tiny little lunch parties for one. Or maybe have a clever walk-through one like Mary Keen’s – genius for making sure you go in there, what with it being on the path. But I think of glasshouse life in the same way I think of one day learning Italian. It’s a nice idea, but unlikely to happen.double quotation markA coldframe is not a mini greenhouse. I see it more as a designated hardy seedling hangout zoneColdframes, however, I can get on board with. A coldframe, crucially, is not a mini greenhouse, despite what it may look like. The clue is in the name: coldframes are cold – like many brunch deals, they are bottomless. Greenhouses, even small ones, are warmer as you can put heaters in them and they offer protection from the ground temperature.Coldframes are useful for protecting plants from the cooler edges of early autumnal days. I like to use them as a designated hardy seedling hangout zone. Helpful if you don’t have a greenhouse but arguably more so if you don’t have windowsills, or don’t want to fill your home with tiny pots of soil. Plonked outside in a sunny spot, your seedlings will benefit from all that direct sunlight, even on a grey day, while being protected from birds and cats and foxes and the worst of the chill.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI heard it through the grapevine: everything you need to know about growing grapesRead moreI like filling a coldframe with hardy annuals, in particular poppies (usually in 9cm pots, as they don’t love being pricked out or even having their roots messed around with at all) and cornflowers. But mostly it’s about the sweet peas – two seeds pushed into empty loo-roll tubes if you’re feeling organised, or root trainers if you’re not – and beginning a process that has the same growth period as a human foetus. By the spring equinox I usually have a couple of dozen strong-rooted, muscular plants to plant out, which will offer me plenty of flowers to huff at my desk come June.But you can also use your coldframe for pelargonium cuttings until it gets properly frosty outside – and now is a good time to take those too. Line it with bubble wrap for extra thermal protection.As for which to buy, a flatpack job with plastic panels is a good start (the fancy metal ones are beautiful, but as long as the lid hinges and stays work, you’re fine). And for the curious on a budget, don’t underestimate the effectiveness of an upturned big plastic tub.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: John Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisis | Economics | The Guardian
description: A new play about the art-loving Bloomsbury Group member speaks of the enduring battle of ideas with his free-market rival Friedrich Hayek
Author: Larry Elliott
Headline: A new play about the art-loving Bloomsbury Group member speaks of the enduring battle of ideas with his free-market rival Friedrich Hayek
Content: Keynes did not see growth as an end in itself but rather as a means to live the good life.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveView image in fullscreenKeynes did not see growth as an end in itself but rather as a means to live the good life.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveEconomicsJohn Maynard Keynes: the cultured economist who governments turn to in a crisisA new play about the art-loving Bloomsbury Group member speaks of the enduring battle of ideas with his free-market rival Friedrich HayekLarry ElliottFri 2 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sound of guns from the advancing German armies could be heard clearly byJohn Maynard Keynesas his train trundled across northern France in the spring of 1918. The evidence of the struggle on the western front was everywhere but Keynes, then a Treasury official, was not heading to Paris on war business; he was off to buy some art.Keynes made the risky trip to attend an auction of the studio of Edgar Degas, who had died the previous year. The man who would become the foremost economist of the 20th century returned to London with some impressionist treasures for the National Gallery, having successfully petitioned the chancellor of the exchequer to spend £20,000 at the sale.This story reveals much about Keynes. His skill in lobbying officialdom for funds at a time when the country was involved in a costly war. His love of art, which culminated in him being instrumental in setting up the Arts Council. His conviction that economics mattered less than the good things in life.View image in fullscreenKeynes (right) with the painter Duncan Grant.Photograph: World History Archive/AlamyAll of which makes the title of James Graham’s new play about Keynes,The Standard of Living, wholly appropriate. Keynes pored over statistics but was much more than a number cruncher. He had firm views about why the economy was malfunctioning in the 1920s and 1930s, but was just as interested in discussing philosophy with Bertrand Russell and Ludwig Wittgenstein. He believed a growing economy should provide the opportunity for more leisure time rather than the accumulation of monetary wealth. He revolutionised economics without having a revolutionary bone in his body.Born into a well-off academic family, Keynes went to Eton before studying maths at Cambridge. His circle of friends after university was the Bloomsbury Group, painters and writers who included Virginia Woolf, and two of his lovers, Lytton Strachey and Duncan Grant. This was a group that prided itself on being unconventional, on not accepting the status quo.Bloomsbury helped satisfy Keynes’s cultural needs but also helped shape his economic thinking. He did not see growth as an end in itself but rather as a means to live the good life or – as he put it – to live like the “lilies in the field”. In Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren he foresaw a time when the economic problem had been solved, when the working week would be considerably shorter and “when the accumulation of wealth was no longer of high social importance”.His willingness to challenge the orthodoxy was demonstrated in an early book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which correctly predicted that the punitive terms imposed by the treaty of Versailles in 1919 would result in a humiliated Germany remaining bitter and vengeful.To the surprise of his Bloomsbury friends, Keynes later fell in love with a Russian ballet dancer, Lydia Lopokova, and the couple married in 1925 when he was 42. While forthright and confident when expressing his opinions, Keynes was self-conscious about his appearance, considering himself repulsive. Others agreed. Virginia Woolf once described him as like “a gorged seal, double chin, ledge of red lip, little eyes, sensual, brutal, unimaginative”.View image in fullscreenKeynes and Lopokova.Photograph: Hulton Deutsch/Corbis/Getty ImagesOne of the central themes of the play is the battle of ideas between Keynes and the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek. The latter believed that left to their own devices, free markets provided the best economic outcomes and that over the long term crises would be resolved without the need for state intervention.Keynes took the opposite view, summed up by perhaps his most famous quote: “In the long run we are all dead. Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that when the storm is long past the ocean is flat again.”By this he meant that the economy had no natural tendency towards full employment. Rather, high unemployment could last indefinitely unless the government was prepared to step in and stimulate demand. This argument formed the centrepiece of his most famous book, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. The General Theory, as it is commonly known, challenged conventional economic thinking and had a profound influence on policymakers in the decades after the second world war, when it was seen as the responsibility of governments to manage demand to secure full employment.Keynes saw the many flaws in the capitalist system but was no Marxist. As an unashamed elitist, he saw it as his mission to save capitalism from itself, if only because he saw it as the best way to safeguard civilised values. “He is contemptuous of common men, especially when gathered together in herds,” the social reformer Beatrice Webb once observed. “He dislikes the human herd and has no desire to enlist the human herd on his side.”View image in fullscreenRory Kinnear as Keynes in The Standard of Living.Photograph: credit Manuel HarlanUnsurprisingly, the hard left have their suspicions about Keynes. As his biographer Robert Skidelsky wrote: “Marxists have long argued that Keynes’s ideas were taken up because they served the interests of the bourgeoisie in the 1930s and were dropped when they started to endanger capitalist profits in the 1970s.”It is certainly true that Keynes and his ideas fell out of fashion by the mid-1970s, a period when western economies were afflicted by rising inflation and weak growth at the same time. Postwar Keynesian economists were baffled by the appearance of high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, and the new right – spearheaded politically by Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan – emerged victorious from this era of “stagflation”. Inspired by Hayek’s ideas, it set about dismantling the postwar settlement based on full employment, state ownership, strong trade unions and generous welfare spending.Can a ballerina do a stomp? Natalia Osipova on making her fearsome, foul-mouthed acting debutRead moreThe 2008 global financial crisis saw the new right model come to grief. A belief that markets could never be wrong meant the dangers of excessive speculation were ignored and ultimately left the global banking system teetering on the point of collapse. For the first time since the 1930s there was a real risk of a full-scale depression and in those circumstances policymakers dusted down their copies of The General Theory in the search for a response.Keynes would have sensed a financial crisis was coming. He speculated on the financial markets, not always successfully. In 1920, he created what would be today called a heavily leveraged hedge fund using money provided by his Bloomsbury friends – taking bets on currency movements – only to see his syndicate’s capital wiped out when the pound unexpectedly fell.Even so, he was aware of the risks. “Speculators may do no harm as bubbles on a steady stream of enterprise,” he said. “But the position is serious when enterprise becomes the bubble on a whirlpool of speculation. When the capital development of a country becomes the byproduct of the activities of a casino, the job is likely to be ill done.”Today, Keynes and Hayek are still revered by their followers on the political left and right respectively. Yet, the past two decades have showed the enduring nature of Keynes’s insights, first in 2008 and then during the global pandemic of 2020.Faced with a crisis, belief in free markets goes out of the window as governments use every policy tool at their disposal to boost growth and prevent unemployment from rising. Or as the arch-critic of Keynes – the Nobel prize-winning economist Robert Lucas – put it in 2008: “I guess everyone is a Keynesian in a foxhole.”The Standard of Living is atTheatre Royal Haymarket, London, until 12 December.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsJohn Maynard KeynesTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Row erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skin | Global development | The Guardian
description: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ origins
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Artwork created in Tahrir Square for Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ origins
Content: The mural in Tahrir Square was designed by a volunteer youth group, Rasmet Basma, with the help of AI.Photograph: Rasmet BasmaView image in fullscreenThe mural in Tahrir Square was designed by a volunteer youth group, Rasmet Basma, with the help of AI.Photograph: Rasmet BasmaGlobal developmentRow erupts over Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun and Nefertiti with dark skinArtwork created in Tahrir Squarefor Chinese president’s state visit to Egypt is painted over amid allegations it revived Afrocentric claims about pharaohs’ originsSupported byAbout this contentHanaa Hammad in CairoFri 2 Oct 2026 04.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the eve of the Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.Depicting the PharaohTutankhamunand Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by a group of young volunteers, Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the 14th-century BCE pharaoh’s origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.View image in fullscreenA volunteer, Razan Mujahid, working on the mural.Photograph: Rasmet BasmaThe team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.View image in fullscreenThe mural has reignited a debate about the complexion of ancient Egyptians.Photograph: Rasmet BasmaThis is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, aNetflix documentaryprovoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedlygave an Afrocentric perspectiveof Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.Monica Hanna, a prominent Egyptologist and assistant professor of archaeology at the American University of Iraq–Baghdad, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.View image in fullscreenThe mural was repainted white just hours before President Xi landed in Egypt.Photograph: Hanaa Hammad“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.This article is published in collaboration withEgabThis article was amended on 2 October 2026 to clarify Monica Hanna’s academic title.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentEgyptAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaDisputed artStreet artRacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s son  | Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva | The Guardian
description: President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: President leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decades
Content: The Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a huge rally in the streets of Rio de Janeiro two days before the election.Photograph: António Lacerda/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, led a huge rally in the streets of Rio de Janeiro two days before the election.Photograph: António Lacerda/EPALuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazil’s Lula says only he can stop rise of fascism under Bolsonaro’s sonPresident leads huge rally in Rio before election on Sunday seen as most important for decadesTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 2 Oct 2026 17.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Brazilian president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has claimed he is the only thing standing in the way of far-right “fascists” reclaiming power, as he led a huge rally through the streets of Rio ahead of Sunday’s crunch election.Speaking on the eve of the demonstration, the 80-year-old leftwinger said he had decided to seek a historic fourth term because he believed only he could prevent the family of his rightwing rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, returning to government.“If it weren’t for me standing up to these fascists they’d easily win another election. I’m the one standing in their way,” Lulatold a popular podcast called Flow, before adding: “It’s either me, or it’s barbarism.”View image in fullscreenLula led a campaign march through central Rio de Janeiro, travelling from Candelária toward Cinelândia.Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockHours later, Lula flew to Rio, staging what his team called a “victory march” between two highly symbolic downtown locations that played an important role in Brazil’s fight for democracy during the 1964-1985 military dictatorship.“What’s at stake is not the victory of one man, it is the victory of an idea, it’s the victory of democracy,” Brazil’s president said after the parade set off from the Candelária church. The church is the location where more than a million people, including Lula, famously gathered in 1984 to demand direct presidential elections.Lula, who was among those who spoke at that historic demo when he was an up-and-coming politician in his 30s, added: “Either we consolidate democracy, or we will lose it.”From Candelária, a sea of red-clad Lula supporters marched a mile south towards Cinelândia, the scene of an equally well-known pro-democracy protest in 1968 called the March of the Hundred Thousand.View image in fullscreenLula, who is seeking re-election, used the the march to mobilise supporters two days before voters head to the polls on 4 October 2026.Photograph: Mariana Greif/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock“No gringo is going to lay a finger on Brazil’s things,” vowed Lula, in an indirect reference to claims Donald Trump’s administration is seeking to sway the vote in Bolsonaro’s favour with a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure.The decision to hold Friday’s rally between two such politically charged places spoke to how this year’s election has stirred up renewed fears over the future of Latin America’s biggest democracy.Election-eve polls suggest Lula holds only a slender lead over his adversary, whose father, the ex-presidentJair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a failed coup after Lula beat him in the 2022 election.View image in fullscreenTwo Lula supporters.Photograph: António Lacerda/EPAMany Brazilian democrats fear that if 45-year-old Bolsonaro wins this year’s election, he will move quickly to free his father and his fellow coup-plotters from jail – and then set about dismantling and co-opting the country’s democratic institutions, such as the supreme court.“This is the most important election of our lives – and we have to do everything we can to win,” said Marcelo Freixo, a politician from Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) who is running for a seat in congress.Freixo warned: “We spent 21 years living under a really harsh dictatorship. We fought so hard to attain our democratic institutions. And a victory for the Bolsonaro family – a family that always … openly defended the dictatorship and tried to stage a coup … would spell the end for our democratic process and institutions.”View image in fullscreenSupporters of the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, at Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years.Photograph: Pilar Olivares/ReutersValmir Aleixo, a 55-year-old history teacher who was one of thousands of people who joined Friday’s pro-Lula demo, said: “This is [a choice] between democracy and the savagery of far-right fascism. This is perhaps the most important election since the return of democracy in the 80s.”Noni Ostrower, 74, came to what was Rio’s largest leftwing protest in years carrying a homemade banner that read: “Democracy Is Valuable”.“I’m the daughter of two refugees from nazism. They came to Brazil from Germany because of this,” Ostrower said. “I was born here in Brazil … and today I have grandchildren and I absolutely do not want to see fascism return to Brazil – it would be a tragedy for the country. That’s why I’m here today.”During the campaign, Flávio Bolsonaro has vowed to pardon his 71-year-old father if elected, with some speculating Jair Bolsonaro could even become a minister. His brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, a radical former congressman with ties to Trump’s Maga movement, reputedly hopes to become foreign minister. Flávio Bolsonaro has announced plans to appoint five firmly conservative supreme court judges.Luiz Eduardo Soares, a prominent anthropologist and writer, said he feared what might happen if the Bolsonaro clan managed to reclaim power.“I think these elections could be the last ones in my life, for my generation … What was done over the course of 10 years in Hungary, [Bolsonaro] will do in two,” Soares predicted in reference to the European country’s transformation into an “electoral autocracy” under its former prime minister, Viktor Orbán.Diogo Nogueira, a famous samba singer who came to the rally wearing his trademark panama hat, said: “We need to win in the first round so we don’t allow this type of people to get back into government. If they ​do get back in, it won’t just be a problem for four years, but for 10 or 20.”Polls suggest the election is likely to go to a second round runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro on 25 October, with Lula expected to secure about 45% of votes on Sunday and Bolsonaro 40%, according to the Datafolha pollster. But at Friday’s rally Lula claimed he could pull off a shock first-round win by claiming more than 50% of the vote.In an online broadcast, Bolsonaro insisted his campaign would prevail. “Brazil is a few hours from deciding its future … for the next 30, 40, 50 years. It’s the end of an era. It’s the end of the Worker’s party era,” he claimed, asking undecided voters to back him to achieve that aim, even if they didn’t like him.Explore more on these topicsLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazilAmericasThe far rightActivismJair BolsonaronewsShareReuse this content

title: US Coast Guard says it intercepted ship carrying fuel to Cuba | Cuba | The Guardian
description: US says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continues
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continues
Content: US Coast Guard cutters escort the cargo ship, Grace, after intercepting it on 5 September.Photograph: U.S. Coast GuardView image in fullscreenUS Coast Guard cutters escort the cargo ship, Grace, after intercepting it on 5 September.Photograph: U.S. Coast GuardCubaUS Coast Guard says it intercepted ship carrying fuel to CubaUS says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continuesReuters in WashingtonFri 2 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fuel bound forCuba, as the ⁠Trump administration’s crippling ⁠oil embargo against ​the island nation continued.The vessel named Grace was stopped on 5 September in theCaribbeanSea between Cuba ⁠and Mexico while using tactics to evade authorities, the Coast Guard said. The New York Times reported that the ship ⁠was 91 metres (300ft) long.“Grace was transiting toCuba, carrying fuel, ​and was believed to be employing ‌tactics common amongst the ‌dark fleet,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.A Coast Guard team ‌boarded the ship and escorted it to Mexico, where a Mexican navy inspection team “confirmed the presence of large quantities of fuel in the vessel’s ballast tanks”. The vessel was also carrying several containers believed to contain illicit fuel, the statement said.US claims of Cuba’s ‘unique threat’ jar with reality of hunger and blackoutsRead moreThe Trump administration has openly stated ‌that its goal is to change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put the country ​under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.View image in fullscreenChildren walk in the dark in Havana, Cuba. The country is suffering blackouts amid Trump’s blockade.Photograph: Ramón Espinosa/APOil shipments from Cuba’s traditional suppliers, Venezuela and Mexico, ended abruptly after the US ousted the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. US Coast Guard ⁠cutters patrol the waters off Cuba, while sanctions and threats have dissuaded ​tankers from even ​setting sail.“The high seas ​are not a sanctuary for lawlessness,” Adm Kevin Lunday, the commandant ​of the Coast ‌Guard, said. “Dark fleet ​actors who employ ​deceptive tactics to engage in illicit activities will not evade justice.”The statement did not say how authorities knew the fuel was headed to Cuba or how much fuel Grace was carrying.Explore more on these topicsCubaUS foreign policyCaribbeanAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Speculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of position could become deciding factor in run-up to Sunday
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Speculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of position could become deciding factor in run-up to Sunday
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva holding an image of Our Lady of Aparecida. His rival Flávio Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat the patron saint ‘fake news’.Photograph: Jarbas Oliveira/EPAView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva holding an image of Our Lady of Aparecida. His rival Flávio Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat the patron saint ‘fake news’.Photograph: Jarbas Oliveira/EPABrazil‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of electionSpeculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of position could become deciding factor in run-up to SundayTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroFri 2 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 00.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA row of Biblical proportions has erupted in the run-up to Brazil’s presidential election, with the country’s patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, emerging as an unlikely kingmaker in the deadlocked race.Ahead of Sunday’s vote, the two frontrunners – the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro – are level in the polls.‘Viscerally dedicated to social issues’: behind Lula’s drive to win final term in Brazil’s crunch electionRead moreBut in recent days, speculation that Bolsonaro – son of the former presidentJair Bolsonaro– might strip the widely cherished patroness of her position have caused a nationwide outcry, leaving some to question if it could tip the knife-edge election in favour of Lula, who is Catholic.“It could sway things one way or the other,”said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has been tracking the unusual election row.It remains unclear precisely how the commotion began, but debate over the issue exploded last week when a remark by Bolsonaro, whose movement includes many evangelical Christians, went viral online. In a recent broadcast, the former senator said one of his first acts as president would be to “decree that Brazil belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ”.Some Catholics took that as a sign that the Protestant politician planned to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida, although only the Vatican – which declared her Brazil’s patroness in 1930 – has the authority to do so.View image in fullscreenBrazil’s rightwing senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal party during a campaign rally in São Paulo.Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty ImagesThose suspicions were reinforced by Bolsonaro’s reported links to JB Carvalho, an evangelical leader who has previously called for the patroness’s removal. In 2007, another Bolsonaro ally tried to introduce legislation to the same effect, although the bill was dropped.Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida “fake news”. He alleged the rumours were being spread by Lula supporters, as well as members of the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation. The conference rejected the charge.Lula’s leftwing movement has taken advantage of the furore, keenly aware it could hurt the far-right candidate’s chances in a country wherenearly 57% of the population is Catholic. With the result expected to be even tighter than the last one – when Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% – even a small number of votes could mean the difference between victory and defeat.Lula has appeared on the campaign trail holding statuettes of the Virgin Mary while his wife, Janja da Silva, has worn a pendant honouring Our Lady of Aparecida. “As long as I’m president, no one will disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida. No one. People need to learn to respect all religions,” Lula told a rally in the Amazon. Lula’s vice-president and running mate, a devout Catholic called Geraldo Alckmin, publisheda videodescribing how he had received messages from Catholics “worried about the direction of the country and the terrible news that has been circulating”. Alckmin assured voters he and Lula would preserve and protect “religious traditions, so sacred to Brazilian families”.The row speaks to the rivalry and tensions between Brazil’s once dominant Catholic church and the evangelical movement, which has grown rapidly since the 80s.Traumann said: “It touched a raw nerve, which is the growing power of the evangelicals. Evangelicals make up about 30% of the population, but their political power is much greater than 30% – and within Bolsonarismo it is even more significant”.Traumann believed that, irrespective of whether Bolsonaro really did intend to remove the patroness, the furore had tapped into “a genuine fear among Catholics of being pushed outside the system”. “I have no doubt that this is going to be important [in the election]. [Flávio Bolsonaro] knows it has landed badly,” he added.Luiz Antônio Simas, a historian and author of the bookSo Many Marys: Our Lady in Popular Culture, said the outcry “was a symptom of the popularity that Aparecida and the Virgin Mary in general have in the formation of our culture”.View image in fullscreenLula at a campaign rally in Belem, Brazil.Photograph: Marx Vasconcelos/Reuters“For Brazilian popular culture, Our Lady of Aparecida transcends altars … She is extremely powerful as a defining element of what we envision Brazilian popular culture to be,” Simas said, noting how Brazil’s “Black Madonna” was present in samba parades, football culture and Afro-Brazilian faiths.While the debate flared up on the eve of the election, Simas said Our Lady of Aparecida was a long-running point of tension between Catholics and evangelicals, who oppose the Catholic veneration of saints and images. He recalled a major outcry in 1995 when a neo-Pentecostal pastor kicked a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida on TV.Simas believed religious racism was at the heart of the outcry, given that Our Lady of Aparecida was a black representation of the Virgin Mary. “When all of this comes into contact with a turbulent political context, in a country experiencing the tensions of a highly contested pre-election scenario, all these controversies come to the surface,” Simas added.Explore more on these topicsBrazilAmericasJair BolsonaroReligionCatholicismEvangelical ChristianityChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayers | Australia news | The Guardian
description: Home affairs department orders all federal government agencies to conduct review of ‘legacy technology’ amid fallout from AI agent hacks
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Home affairs department orders all federal government agencies to conduct review of ‘legacy technology’ amid fallout from AI agent hacks
Content: Government agencies will need to fortify their cybersecurity defences to guard against future attacks.Photograph: quantic69/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGovernment agencies will need to fortify their cybersecurity defences to guard against future attacks.Photograph: quantic69/Getty ImagesAustralia newsOpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayersHome affairs department orders all federal government agencies to conduct review of ‘legacy technology’ amid fallout from AI agent hacksGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterFri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 20.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian government faces significant “tech debt” that could bring a big bill for taxpayers after theOpenAI Medicare breach, as government agencies will need to fortify their defences against future attacks by AI agents.This week, the home affairs department ordered all federal government agencies to conduct a “legacy technology stocktake” that requires a plan for each agency to “reduce legacy technology systems” to a level within the agency’s risk tolerance and appetite,the direction stated.OpenAI this weekrevealedan internal agent had gained non-public access to the Services Australia Medicare statistics portal during a training task seeking information on government spending on skin conditions in Victoria. The agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhileOpenAIhas apologised to Australia for the incident, it has served as a wake up call for the federal government, with the government-wide review now under way.The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, asked her department whether some of the A$160m funding allocated to the agency in the last budget for cyber upgrades can be accelerated.The statistics portal, Gallagher told reporters last month, is a “legacy system.”“It dates back decades.”Services Australia will be far from alone in managing legacy systems. They can – but not all do – present a security risk for businesses and government as they age and vendors cease providing new security updates.Prof Salil Kanhere, a University of New South Wales cybersecurity and AI expert said the age of the system alone does not tell an agency whether it needs replacing.“A 15-year-old system that is properly supported, patched and properly isolated would perhaps present less risk than even a newer system that might not be properly maintained,” he said.Those older systems with vulnerabilities are often known to human attackers, but AI agents persistent in looking for holes in a system may be able to discover them quicker.12:23Rogue AI hacks government system for first time - The LatestGartner, a technology analysis firm stated in a note to clients released after the Medicare hack that “technical debt, not a rogue AI agent attack” represented the greatest threat to legacy systems.“Agentic AI’s interactions with [government] resources will greatly increase,” the firm stated. “Underinvestment is no longer sustainable and agencies should urgently prioritise funding in light of AI-driven risks.”In the Australian government’s commonwealth cybersecurity posture in 2025 reportreleased in February this year, 59% of federal agencies and departments reported their ability to implement the “essential eight” measures to reduce cyber risk was being affected by use of legacy technologies.The essential eight includes requirements to patch applications and operating systems, using multi-factor authentication, and other security measures. Of those agencies being hindered by legacy tech, 34% blamed insufficient dedicated funding, while 18% said it was due to a lack of a viable replacement.Prof Yang Xiang, from Monash University’s department of software systems and cybersecurity, said the government stocktake was “very necessary” and there was urgency to needing to audit all government systems.“The agents bring significant changes in terms of the speed of getting into – hacking into – the system,” he said. “The cost to launch an attack is much reduced to launch an attack and with the help of agents, it is fairly easy for the hacker to launch a very large scale atack against any systems.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClearing the tech debt could prove costly for the federal government, but Xiang said agencies should identify priority systems for replacement. Kanhere said high-risk systems should take priority.“You do the high risk stuff first, I think it is absolutely needed, and then put the perimeter around [other systems],” he said. “It is possible to do it quite systematically once they have a good understanding of what needs to be done.”Some states have audited their legacy technology and have invested hundreds of millions to rectify the issues.AVictoria government cybersecurity auditof its IT servers found 25% of the operating systems used by servers were no longer supported by the vendor, with 48% in extended support.Ina South Australian audit report of legacy ICT systemspublished in June, of the ten agencies reviewed, nearly half of the 11,602 hardware devices or appliances were determined to be legacy devices. Almost one quarter of the operating systems and applications were also determined to be legacy.In one example, the Department for Child Protection’s case management system is now over 15 years old, and has limited vendor support.The SA government has allocated $325.6m over the past three budgets in part to address legacy technology.“Frontline workers spend significant time managing system limitations and maintaining records, reducing the time available to support vulnerable children and families.”A2025 Queensland government audit of IT systemsfound more than half of the 57 systems audited are at the end of life. Many of the systems identified by the government in 2012 as needing to be replaced were still in operation in 2025, including a patient administration system at Queensland Health, a forensic register at the Queensland Police Service, and a trust accounts system for young people in detention.The Queensland government in the 2025 budget allocated $1bn over four years for IT investment, including replacing or updating legacy systems.The Australian Cyber Security Centresaid in recent guidancethat the most effective way to mitigate risks associated with legacy IT is to replace it, and where it cannot be replaced, then legacy technology should potentially be segregated or isolated from the broader department network to restrict access to the rest of the department.Explore more on these topicsAustralia newsCybercrimeAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIComputingHackingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bruce Baird, former federal Liberal MP and NSW minister, dies aged 84 | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Baird, father of former NSW premier Mike Baird and journalist Julia Baird, helped win the Olympics for Sydney
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Baird, father of former NSW premier Mike Baird and journalist Julia Baird, helped win the Olympics for Sydney
Content: The former Liberal federal MP and NSW minister Bruce Baird has died aged 84.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe former Liberal federal MP and NSW minister Bruce Baird has died aged 84.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPNew South WalesBruce Baird, former federal Liberal MP and NSW minister, dies aged 84Baird, father of former NSW premier Mike Baird and journalist Julia Baird, helped win the Olympics for SydneyGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotFri 2 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 05.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBruce Baird, a former federal Liberal MP and deputy leader of the party’sNew South Walesbranch, has died aged 84.Baird, who also served as the NSW transport minister from 1988 to 1995, is the father of former state premier Mike Baird, the ABC journalist Julia Baird, and the marketing executive Steve Baird.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueAs a NSW minister, Baird was instrumental in lobbying for the 2000 Olympic Games to be based in Sydney. He then entered federal parliament as the member for Cook.Baird retired before the 2007 election, whenScott Morrisonwon the seat and went on to become prime minister.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereMorrison said Baird was “a giant, a mentor and a friend who celebrated and lived out his strong Christian faith, loved his family and served his country, his state and our community in the shire”.“His achievements are significant, most notably the transforming effect he had on our home city of Sydney as the minister for Sydney’s successful Olympic bid. But there are many more.”NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, said Baird was “driven by a strong sense of service, conviction, and compassion, earning the trust and respect of people regardless of their political affiliation”.“Above all, Bruce was a devoted husband to his late wife Judy, and a proud father and grandfather.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe political battle over Australian immigration is really a story of what kind of nation we want to be | Peter LewisRead moreIn a statement, a NSW Liberal spokesperson offered its “deepest condolences on behalf of all members to his family at this difficult time”.Baird was a passionate supporter of refugeesand advocated on their behalf throughout his career.While a Liberal MP, he opposed the Howard government’s mandatory detention of asylum seekers. After leaving office, he became a member of Kevin Rudd’s refugee resettlement advisory council.In 2010, Baird criticised the reopening of Curtin detention centre in Western Australia to house asylum seekers.“Don’t confuse treating people badly when they arrive with effective border control mechanisms, they are two different things,” he told the ABC.“If we rely on treating asylum seekers badly in this country then there is something about us that we need to have a hard look at. I don’t believe that is the Australian way.”Baird was also a regular feature of Manly’s Bold and Beautiful ocean swimming club. A member of the squad also confirmed his death on Friday.On Thursday, the club’s organiser, Peter Anthony, wrote to members describing Baird as a “wonderful friend to so many of us”.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesNew South Wales politicsLiberal partyAustralian politicsAustralian immigration and asylumScott MorrisonnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI disclose another hack on government department in Australia  | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday
Author: Henry Belot
Headline: Attack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until Thursday
Content: OpenAI has disclosed an attack on a NSW government department.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOpenAI has disclosed an attack on a NSW government department.Photograph: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpenAIOpenAI disclose another hack on government department in AustraliaAttack accessing historical data on bushfires occurred in June but not disclosed by the tech company until ThursdayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastHenry BelotFri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArtificial intelligence companyOpenAIhas disclosed another unauthorised hack on a government department in Australia.In June, an OpenAI agent hacked into aNew South Walesstate government department and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.The breach, which comes weeks after news ofa similar hack on a federal government department involving Medicare data, was not reported by the US based company until Thursday.The NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water is now working with the state’s cyber security agency to investigate the breach.The Australian Signals Directorate has also been informed of the hack on the NSW national parks and wildlife service.OpenAI told the NSW government that its agent had operated beyond its intended use and the statistics it obtained were not publicly available.The company first became aware of the breach on Tuesday and conducted a 48 hours review to determine its scope before informing the NSW premier’s office.“The results we reviewed do not show that the model retrieved any personal information,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.This latest breach has added to calls for tougher regulation of AI companies and for bolstered cyber security defences.“We simply cannot trust these companies. They have no respect for the sovereignty of our governments, of our way of life,” Greens MP Abigail Boyd said.Boyd said it was damning that the breach occurred in June but the government was not notified until this week.“We clearly cannot rely on these multinational big tech companies to comply with even the most minimal of social obligations such as notifying when, or even taking enough care to notice if, their products are hacking government systems,” Boyd said.On Wednesday, the department of home affairs on Wednesday told federal departments to examine their older software and ensure cyber security was up to date.The prime minister expressed his “extreme concern” about at an OpenAI agent hacking Australian Institute of Health and Welfare in June.The Victorian Department of Health and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research were also compromised by an OpenAI agent.An artificial intelligence agent is a system that autonomously solves problems, makes decisions, plans and performs complex tasks on behalf of another user or system, using all available tools.AAP contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsOpenAINew South WalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves | Oil | The Guardian
description: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Content: Emmanuel Macron said ministers had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks.Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron said ministers had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks.Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/ShutterstockOilG7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reservesLeaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US suppliesJoanna Partridge,Jillian AmbroseandMark SweneyFri 2 Oct 2026 14.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles afterDonald Trumpthreatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.The French President,Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unlessEuropetapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the currentG7chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.Trump said he was consideringa ban on diesel exportsafter the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.9:37Diesel export ban: will Trump push global energy prices even higher? - The LatestTrump said in a post on hisTruth Social platformthat Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September.The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to arecord high of £2 a litreon forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered thelargest release of government oil reservesin its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Explore more on these topicsOilG7Global economyInternational tradeEnergy industryEuropeCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement grows | Spain | The Guardian
description: Opposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Opposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-old
Content: Protesters near the Spanish parliament demand 'Fair rents NOW' after lawmakers rejected emergency housing measures on Friday.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/ReutersView image in fullscreenProtesters near the Spanish parliament demand 'Fair rents NOW' after lawmakers rejected emergency housing measures on Friday.Photograph: Alejandro Martinez Velez/ReutersSpainSpanish right wing votes down housing crisis plans as protest movement growsOpposition lawmakers join forces to defeat proposals made by Socialist-led coalition after eviction of 87-year-oldAshifa Kassamin MadridFri 2 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRightwing lawmakers in Spain have rejected emergency measures put forward to tackle the country’s housing crisis, pitting a fractured parliament against thewidespread protest movementthat has swelled in recent days.On Friday Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.As hundreds of protesters outside the parliament building in Madrid held up homemade signs bearing images of vultures, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building ​more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.Eviction of 87-year-old puts Spain’s deepening housing crisis in the spotlightRead moreNews of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, wasevicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.Tens of thousands of people heeded the call by housing campaigners to take to the streets, while encampments protesting against the housing crisis sprung up in cities acrossSpain.The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life intoSánchez’s beleaguered governmentand shifting attention away from the lingering impact ofrecent events in Ceuta.On Friday, asa pollsuggested that two-thirds of people in Spain supported the idea of government intervention in the housing market to limit prices, sources told the news site Eldiario.es that the Socialists were mullingwhether to bring forward next year’s elections, potentially to this November.After news broke that several rightwing parties were planning to vote against the proposed measures, Sánchez said the parliamentary vote would go ahead as planned. “You’re with the social majority or with speculators,” the Spanish prime minister said on social media, adding that the vote would reveal the “true colours” of the rightwing parties.View image in fullscreenA sprawling protest camp in Puerta del Sol, Madrid, where demonstrators are demanding affordable housing.Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockFollowing five hours of parliamentary debate on Friday, Sánchez made a last ditch appeal to lawmakers to back the measures. “What is behind these decrees is the desire to instil order and a sense of humanity in a market that – if we do not rein it in – will destroy our society,” he said. “Do the right thing, or history will judge you, and sooner than you think.”Across Spain, where rents have surged 80% within a decade and the cost of homes climbed by 63%, the issue of housing has long ranked as one of people’s biggest concerns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarlier this year, the Youth Council of Spain saidthe average rent in Spain had climbed to €1,176 ($1,323) a month– an amount equivalent to 98.7% of the average salary for under-30s.The figures help to explain why the protests that began with Abascal’s eviction have continued even after the investment firm that bought her apartment said it had struck a deal that would allow her to return to her home, with her rent returning to a level closer to that she had paid in the past.It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María RamírezRead moreThe government decrees presented in parliament on Friday were intended to quell some of this public uproar. As they were rejected, campaigners vowed to continue their push to improve access to housing.“They’re not going to stop us,” the Confederation of Tenants’ Unions said in a statement, as it called on people across the country to take to the streets this weekend. “In the face of a parliament that is out of touch, the answer is more organisation and mobilisation. The next step: a general strike.”Saturday will mark one week since a small group of protesters, intent on making their demands heard, set up 10 tents in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol plaza, a short walk from parliament. Since then,the encampment had swelled to more than 1,200 tents– a peaceful settlement in the heart of the capital with its own street names, a medical centre and even a co-working space.As news of the vote reached the camp on Friday, some said it was not what they had expected. “People here are disappointed,” said Marta García. “We had thought that at least one of the decrees would be approved.”Explore more on these topicsSpainHousingProtestPedro SánchezEuropeCommunitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge
Content: A woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA woman and child passing the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv city centre this week.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacksMayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridgePjotr Sauerin KyivFri 2 Oct 2026 10.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleValeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded.
