Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”View image in fullscreenSmoke rises after a Russian drone hit the Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv on Monday.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackling a blaze in the city centre.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAcross the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, asintensifying Russian attacksreshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plungeUkraineinto darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.View image in fullscreenRescue workers running to a shelter during an air threat.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian“The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor,Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in aninterviewwith the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the country,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.View image in fullscreenA volunteer medic crew on patrol in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUntil recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.‘We just have to adapt’: Kyiv residents prepare for a hard winter aheadRead moreKyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.View image in fullscreenA man with a tattoo reading ‘immortal’ standing near the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the stone age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeVitali KlitschkonewsShareReuse this content

title: Fires, fury and hundreds of arrests as France gripped by student protests | France | The Guardian
description: Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Government struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrations
Content: Firefighters tackling a blaze near the Lycée Berthelot high school in Aubervilliers near Paris on Friday. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersGovernment struggling to deal with worst crisis in months after being taken by surprise by massive demonstrationsByAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 2 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 08.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class.“We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”1:21Fires burn as French students protest against lack of investment in education – video“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers acrossFrance: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during theheatwaves in May and June.View image in fullscreenStudents protesting in Lyon on Friday.Photograph: Laurent Cipriani/AP“The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support.The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by thethousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schoolsacross the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week.Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.View image in fullscreenStudents kick back teargas canisters in Strasbourg.Photograph: Romeo Boetzle/AFP/Getty ImagesThe government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Léonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”.View image in fullscreenStudents gather outside the Lycée Voltaire in Paris.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersOutside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year.“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”View image in fullscreenHigh-school students face off with riot police in Montpellier.Photograph: Horcajuelo Guillaume/EPAOn Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.”Camille, 18, who said he wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”View image in fullscreenBins burning, with graffiti on one reading ‘fuck RN’, in Paris.Photograph: Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty ImagesFarther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special€1 mealsfor struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C-40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re doing nothing to remedy that.”Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Suicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attack | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Experts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisation
Content: Yaniv Hayoun, who was aboard the flydubai aircraft that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, is welcomed at the arrivals gate at Ben Gurion international airport in Israel on Wednesday.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APView image in fullscreenYaniv Hayoun, who was aboard the flydubai aircraft that made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, is welcomed at the arrivals gate at Ben Gurion international airport in Israel on Wednesday.Photograph: Tomer Appelbaum/APFlydubai plane incidentSuicide by plane or terrorism? Speculation over motive in flight 1073 attackExperts sceptical flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life and say key question is means of radicalisationJason BurkeInternational security correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”3:28How the stabbing incident unfolded on Israel-bound flydubai plane | DeconstructedMany of thedetails of what happenedon flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small grouprushed to the cockpitand overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”,Manes saidon eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.Flight mapIn a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been“fighting for my life”.The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by theUnited Arab Emirates(UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.1:18Flydubai pilot tells Indian prime minister Modi that he couldn’t ‘let anyone die’ – videoIn Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airportBenjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister,has claimedthe co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.Experts said there have been only a handful ofinstancesof suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.Flight altitude graphIn 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employersdeliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that thecrash of an AirIndia 787in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have beenfiercely disputed.Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”View image in fullscreenPeople disembark from a flydubai plane carrying Israeli passengers from the disrupted flight at Ben Gurion international airport near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APSecurity services have been warning of awave of radicalisationacross the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”There are now manyquestions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.View image in fullscreenA passenger with blood on his T-shirt onboard the flydubai plane.Photograph: Amit SegalThere are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plungeRead moreDubai international airport, theworld’s busiest airportfor international passenger traffic, has built some ofits appealon a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIsraelUnited Arab EmiratesAir transportMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attack | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
Author: William Christou
Headline: Smit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’
Content: 1:18Flydubai pilot tells Indian prime minister Modi that he couldn't 'let anyone die' – videoFlydubai plane incident‘I was fighting for my life’: Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls flydubai cockpit attackSmit Machchhar says in video call with Indian PM that he realised if he did not get up ‘passengers would lose their lives’William ChristouFri 2 Oct 2026 04.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Indian pilot who helped thwart anapparent attempt to crash a flydubai flightto Tel Aviv said his faith and his desire to save his passengers allowed him to make a “last push” to open the cockpit door as he fought for his life.Capt Smit Machchhar, who was recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, described to India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, how he helped save the plane and its more than 170 passengers.“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push,” Machchhar told Modi in a video call on Friday. “I was fighting for my life. At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”His Omani co-pilot apparently stabbed him and set the plane on a steep descent, with the aircraft plummeting about 17,000 feet in the span of a minute. While still being attacked, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers to enter, subdue the attacker and ultimately stabilise the plane.The full circumstances of the attack are still under investigation, but a relief crew on the flight helped land the plane safely in Tabouk, north-westSaudi Arabia. Saudi authorities arrested the co-pilot and have since interrogated him.Machchhar, a father of two, was seriously injured during the attack, but credited his 17 years of aviation experience with giving him the wherewithal to understand the gravity of the situation.Modi praised the captain for his actions, which he said helped prevent a “great tragedy.”“You have done such a great thing that people across the country and around the world are eager to see you and speak to you,” Modi told him. “You have truly made the whole country proud.”The motives and affiliation of the apparent attacker are still unknown, but Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said that an initial background investigation indicated he had undergone“Islamic radical indoctrination”.The attacker is to be sent back to theUnited Arab Emirates, where Emirati investigators will work to establish any links with terror organisations. Netanyahu said Israel would cooperate with the UAE on the investigation.Machchhar was hailed as a hero by world leaders, who said his actions had helped prevent a great disaster and save many lives.The pilot said that during the difficult moments he recited the Hanuman Chalisa, a devotional hymn dedicated to the Hindu deity Hanuman and traditionally recited as a prayer for strength and courage.“Lord Hanuman gave me courage,” Machchhar told Modi.He added that he felt proud of himself for the first time since the attack. “I am feeling very proud right now. I had not felt proud of myself until now,” he told Modi.“I am not thinking of it as a wound, I am thinking of it as a journey,” he said, while covered in bandages. “And it will take time, but I am very, very confident that I will recover.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentIndiaIsraelUnited Arab EmiratesSaudi ArabiaAir transportMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded  | Israel | The Guardian
description: In today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in real time
Author: Libby Brooks
Headline: In today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in real time
Content: Safely on the tarmac, the truth of what happened on flight 1073 is still emerging.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenSafely on the tarmac, the truth of what happened on flight 1073 is still emerging.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersFirst Edition newsletterIsraelFriday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfoldedIn today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in real timeLibby BrooksFri 2 Oct 2026 01.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGood morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers.This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more.This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world.So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines.Five big storiesUK politics| Ministers are working upsweeping plans for welfare changesincluding scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.Northern Ireland| Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute havebroken up without agreement, with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”.US news| Tennessee’s governor hassuspended all executionsin the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night.AI| When prompted, AI chat bots will edit imagesto remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.Europe news| Afast-growing protestby high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned.In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’View image in fullscreenAssaf Regavim filmed the first widely circulated video from inside the cabin.Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty ImagesInternational leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing inSaudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury.Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilothad previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a“terror attack”. Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with theUnited Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations.William Christou, a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.”‘The story changed moment to moment’William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots.“I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.”Back in the UK,Oliver Holmeswas looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation.Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.”Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing.Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story.“It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinatinghere on how we assessAI images.)‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.”The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that.This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead ofknife-edge Israeli elections, with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals.Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William.Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated. On Thursday, William tells me, the Israeli foreign ministry started briefing diplomats that the flydubai incident was an attempt to drive a further wedge between the UAE and Israel, a relationship already strained after leaks suggesting Netanyahu waspersonally alertedto the 7 October attacks by the UAE president a week before it took place, something the president has denounced as “an absolute lie”.‘These stories can be incredibly powerful’It’s a challenging time to report a story like this, saysTaz Ali, who led our live blog which covered the incident unfolding in real-time on Wednesday. “Readers are making connections with what’s happening in the Middle East in general, and you’re trying to answer their questions, first with very scant detail and later with a deluge of information, much of which is proved to be inaccurate.”Taz, who has a decade of experience in reporting on global events, knows the human drama of a potential hijacking immediately grabs reader’s attention. “Often those stories can be incredibly powerful, involve emergency landings, and sometimes they end in great tragedies”. And with the recent 25th anniversary of 9/11, the incident had an even deeper resonance. “Especially with the anniversary happening so recently, those memories would have been so raw in people’s minds when they came to this story.”What else we’ve been enjoyingView image in fullscreenBurlesque legend Blaze Starr reigns over Baltimore’s bawdy ‘block’ of strip-clubs and grindhouses.Photograph: unknownA new Taschen book of images from theNational Geographic’s archives charts a century of dramatic change. Andthis fantastic galleryshows a tantalising selection, from the burlesque clubs of Baltimore to a blimp crossing New York Harbour.Lucinda Everett, newsletters teamI lovedour pieceon whenbook clubsget dramatic, featuring werewolf smut, bad book choices, and infuriation when people don’tactually read the book.PoppyElle Hunt’s pieceabout the evolution and cultural significance ofhuman hairtackles many questions I never knew I needed answering. Case in point: what on earth is the purpose of pubic hair?LucindaGuardian contributor Katherine Rowland went to Chicago for the UnitedAstrologyConference and tellsa captivating storyabout the battle over who gets to interpret the stars and how they should do it.PoppyPhilip Oltermann’s interviewwith German artist and writer Philipp Ruch is a fascinating read. Ruch argues that “most of the theories we have to explain the rise of theNazisdon’t make sense – the data tells a far darker story”, one that could help us understand the rise of right-wing extremists today.Lucindaskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSportView image in fullscreenNeco Williams celebrates after putting Wales 2-1 up early in the second half.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersFootball| Wales ended their long wait for a Nations League win bybeating Norway2-1 in Cardiff, while Portugal maintained their perfect start with a4-2 victoryover Denmark in Copenhagen.Football| The United States is poised to hostthe first Women’s Club World Cupin January 2028, becoming the latest in a series of major Fifa tournaments staged in North America.Football| Andy Burnham’sintervention in the Manchester Citydebate has revived tensions between the Premier League and the prime minister.Something for the weekendOur critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right nowView image in fullscreenBang up to date … Blue Lights.Photograph: BBC/Two Cities TelevisionTVBlue Lights (BBC One) | ★★★★☆This Northern Ireland-set police drama has always been modern but never explicitly topical. Until now. Race riots, organised crime and institutional politics bring it bang up to date.Read Jack Seale’s full review.MusicMeshell Ndegeocello: Synonym | ★★★★☆In the jazz-soul singer’s ‘expression of queer liberation’, stars from Chaka Khan to Bill Callahan to Cynthia Erivo duet on equally varied songs from Cher to the Human League and beyond.Read Alexis Petridis’s full review.FilmKnife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie (in cinemas now)| ★★★★☆Alex Gibney’s documentary follows the celebrated author’s life up to and after the attack, but what shines through is Rushdie’s remarkable courage.Read Peter Bradshaw’s full review.ArtRenoir and Love (National Gallery, London, from tomorrow) | ★★★★★Grab your straw boater – and revel in the Impressionist’s light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes.Read Jonathan Jones’s full review.The front pagesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: GuardianTheGuardiansplashes with “Welfare changes may axe disability benefit for young”. TheTimesleads with “Emergency diesel talks after Trump ultimatum” and theTelegraphsays “Trump tells Europe to release diesel”. TheMailruns with “Labour frees first of 10 tidal waves of convicts”, whileThe i Paperhas “Burnham leaving the door open to snap general election in 2027”. TheSun, on Andy Burnham’s Manchester City comments, says “Own goal”. TheFinancial Timesgoes with “Global bond sell-off leaves US trapped in vicious loop”, and theMirrorleads on an interview with a survivor of the Manchester synagogue attack, saying “He stabbed me 3 times but I had to stop him”.The LatestPhotograph: The GuardianUS woman on death row survives two lethal injections in TennesseeA woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two rounds of lethal injections in Tennessee. Christa Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. A last-minute appeal to stop the lethal injection was overturned by the supreme court, but the state governor, Bill Lee, has suspended executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. Lucy Hough speaks to the attorney andanti-capital punishment campaigner Clive Stafford Smith.Cartoon of the day | Ben JenningsView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ben Jennings/The GuardianThe UpsideA bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all badView image in fullscreenBodhana Sivanandan at Harrow chess club. She has said she wants to become an outright grandmaster ‘as soon as possible’.Photograph: Jaimi Joy/ReutersEleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan has become theyoungest ever ‘woman grandmaster’at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board.Sivanandan, who lives in Harrow, was taught to play by her father when she was five. Within a year, she was beating him and by eight she had beaten the former British champion Peter Lee. If she reaches a rating of 2,500 in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever outright grandmaster.She fits her chess career around school, but takes everything in her stride. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework,” she says, “but I should be able to manage”. Her ultimate ambition, she says, is simply to be the best chess player in the world.Sign up herefor a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every SundayBored at work?And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.Quick crosswordCryptic crosswordWordiplyExplore more on these topicsIsraelFirst Edition newsletterUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuAir transportSaudi ArabianewslettersShareReuse this content

title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll | India | The Guardian
description: Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
Content: Supporters of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) protesting in Mumbai on Friday.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSupporters of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) protesting in Mumbai on Friday.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesIndiaIndia’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter rollThousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rightsHannah Ellis-Petersenin MumbaiFri 2 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are beingunfairly strippedof their vote.The movement, which calls itselfthe Cockroach Janta party (CJP)and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted intens of millions of peoplebeing deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.View image in fullscreenAbhijeet Dipke addresses supporters in Mumbai on Friday.Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty ImagesOpposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).Millions in India stripped of vote before critical state election, as government seeks to ‘purify’ electoral rollRead moreThe CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured intoresigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.View image in fullscreenSupporters of the All India Students Association demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar at a protest in Bengaluru.Photograph: Idrees Mohammed/AFP/Getty ImagesLast week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.View image in fullscreenA demonstrator holding a placard wears a mask depicting the face of Gyanesh Kumar.Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/ReutersThe election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared ​aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.No hope, no vote … how most of Delhi’s sex workers are being struck off electoral rollsRead moreAnger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try to stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election ​commission office in Delhi next week.Explore more on these topicsIndiaSouth and central AsiaProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community | UK news | The Guardian
description: Man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police say
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police say
Content: At the time of the arrests, police said they were doing everything they could to keep Manchester’s Jewish community and the wider public safe.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAt the time of the arrests, police said they were doing everything they could to keep Manchester’s Jewish community and the wider public safe.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUK newsTwo Iranian men charged over alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish communityMan, most likely in Iran, was in contact with men arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur, police sayVikram DoddandHannah Al-OthmanFri 2 Oct 2026 18.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo Iranian men have been charged in relation to an alleged terror plot targeting Manchester’s Jewish community.​Police say another man, most likely in Iran, was in contact with them as part of a plot to get a bomb to attack Jewish targets.They were arrested two Sundays ago in broad daylight in a Manchester street during the Jewish holiday period.Rahman Salehi, 34, from Salford, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, from Liverpool have been charged with preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.Police said the two men face charges that they gained materials and instructions to make a homemade bomb, identified possible targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack.Police said: “It is alleged that the two men were in contact with an overseas third-party who may be in Iran in relation to the plot.”The development, terrorism charges and detail given so far by British authorities marks an extraordinary chapter in British and Iranian relations.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Iran had a link to a weekend scare at RAF Fairford when five men were arrested close to the military base, along with three vans, one of which contained petrol in a barrel. Those men have now been bailed, having been arrested in the early hours of Sunday in the Gloucestershire countryside on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing a terrorist act.Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner and the senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism, said: “This week also brought into sharp focus some of the wider threats being projected into the UK from Iran.“While this [Manchester] incident and the investigation into the RAF Fairford incident are not connected in any way, I want to reassure the public that CTP, working with our national security partners, are using the full range of our capabilities to protect the UK from any hostile acts.”The alleged plot in Manchester, where the two arrests followed a joint counter-terrorism police and MI5 investigation, has significant potential ramifications on several fronts.A government statement, minutes after the police announced the charges, revealed one of those accused over the Manchester plot had been granted asylum status in the UK and the other had an asylum application pending.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said that both of the accused had come to Britain via small boats, one in 2020 and another in 2023, when the Conservatives were in power.Mahmood said Iran had shown hostile intent to the UK in a series of incidents.“The fact both suspects arrived by small boat several years ago is a reminder of the importance of our relentless work to tackle illegal migration into this country,” she said. “While numbers are down, I know there is more we must do.“We will be unrelenting in our efforts to protect our Jewish communities, root out antisemitism in this country, and maintain our border security.“It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime. They target our Jewish communities and try to silence their critics overseas, often through proxies and criminal networks to hide their involvement.“The prime minister has been clear there are strong indications of Iran’s involvement in the events near RAF Fairford. We are responding to these threats with new powers and record funding to disrupt hostile activity.This week marked the anniversary of an attack on the Heaton Park synagogue in Manchester, where two worshippers died, as well as the attacker who said he supported Islamic State and was shot dead by police.Jews in Britain have faced a dramatic increase in attacks since the 7 October attack on Israel by Hamas, which has ties to Iran. It led to an internationally condemned military response by Israel in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people.The Community Safety Trust, which offers security and advice to British Jews, said: “The charging of two men in connection with an alleged plot targeting the Manchester Jewish community will be deeply concerning to Jews across the UK.“These charges come exactly a year after the appalling terrorist attack at Heaton Park synagogue, and are a reminder of the ongoing terrorist threats facing British Jews.“We urge the Jewish community to remain calm and report any suspicious activity to police and CST.”In a statement, counter-terrorism police said the charges will allege the two men were “communicating with others using encrypted applications to acquire components to assemble a homemade explosive device”.Furthermore, the charges allege they obtained a document called “Steps for Making [a] Powder Chlorine and Car Brake Oil/Fluid Bomb”, obtained video instructions on how to make an improvised explosive device (IED), and got the “liquids, components and equipment” to make an IED.The charges also allege the men carried out internet research on targets, acquired “images, plans and maps of potential targets for attack” and carried out reconnaissance.Iran has faced attack by the US, with Britain allowing the RAF Fairford base to be used, which it said is for defensive operations by its Washington ally. Tehran’s embassy in London this week denied any involvement in the events at RAF Fairford.Evans said: “These are extremely serious charges and allegations, and have come about from a joint CTP investigation, working closely with our partners in the security services. This investigation has led to the disruption of what we believe to have been a plot targeting the Jewish community in Manchester.”The men were arrested on 20 September in ​Newton Street, in the Northern Quarter area of Manchester’s city centre, just before 3pm, hours before Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.Salehi and Ahmadyan are due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 3 October.Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and we remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendants in this case are active and they have the right to a fair trial.”As part of the investigation officers raided and searched properties on Epworth Street in Liverpool and Lancaster Road in Salford.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage | UK news | The Guardian
description: Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police
Content: Court artist sketch of Joshua Kerry at Westminster magistrates court in July.Photograph: Julia Quenzler/ReutersView image in fullscreenCourt artist sketch of Joshua Kerry at Westminster magistrates court in July.Photograph: Julia Quenzler/ReutersUK newsAnn Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel FarageJoshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say policeNadeem BadshahFri 2 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage.Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said.Vicki Evans, the head of counter-terrorism policing, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards.Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea.Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”In August, CTP reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.After its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: King Charles III to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of Britain’s colonial rule during Caribbean tour | Monarchy | The Guardian
description: Buckingham Palace say the king will not ‘shy away’ from Britain’s role in slavery when he visits Commonwealth nations later this month
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Buckingham Palace say the king will not ‘shy away’ from Britain’s role in slavery when he visits Commonwealth nations later this month
Content: The palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge ‘the wrongs of the past’ and would ‘renew his  commitment to that process’ during the trip.Photograph: Hannah McKay/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge ‘the wrongs of the past’ and would ‘renew his  commitment to that process’ during the trip.Photograph: Hannah McKay/AFP/Getty ImagesMonarchyKing Charles III to acknowledge ‘darkest days’ of Britain’s colonial rule during Caribbean tourBuckingham Palace say the king will not ‘shy away’ from Britain’s role in slavery when he visits Commonwealth nations later this monthAgence France-PresseFri 2 Oct 2026 15.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKing Charles III will acknowledge the “darkest days” of colonial rule and slavery while touring Caribbean countries on a visit beginning this month, a Buckingham Palace spokesperson said on Friday.The king will first visit the Bahamas and Guyana alone, followed by a trip with Queen Camilla toAntigua and Barbuda, where Charles will give a speech at a meeting of Commonwealth heads of government, the palace said.Charles, 77, who is still receiving treatment for cancer, will visit former colonies that are now independent from Britain and are members of the British Commonwealth.‘It’s inescapable’: will new revelations about enslavement force Britain to finally confront its past?Read moreHe remains head of state in the archipelago nations of theBahamasand Antigua and Barbuda, a role that is largely ceremonial.The palace spokesperson told reporters the king’s visit, from 27 October to 4 November, would not “shy away from the ‘darkest days of our past’, as His Majesty has described them”.Charles used the phrase in a speech in Barbados when he attended the ceremony in which it became a republic in 2021, removing his mother,Queen Elizabeth II, as head of state.He also said then that the “appalling atrocity of slavery” stains Britain’s history.The palace said Charles had worked to acknowledge “the wrongs of the past” and “right inequalities that endure”, and on this trip would “renew his personal, wholehearted and continuing commitment to that process”.The UK government reiterated last month its rejection of calls for the payment of slavery reparations after a Jamaican delegation filed a petition addressed to Charles on the issue.It called on the monarch to refer three questions on the legality of the transatlantic slave trade to theCaribbeanisland’s highest court of appeal based in London.Modern British royals have expressed remorse for the brutal slave trade thatenriched their ancestorsbut like the UK government have not issued an official apology for the slave trade.The palace said discussions about the colonial legacy and the slave trade were “important” but “primarily matters for governments to address”.On a 2022 Caribbean tour, Charles’s son Prince William and his wife, Catherine, were met with anti-monarchy protests and calls for slavery reparations. Charles’s younger brother, Prince Edward, later that year cancelled a visit to Grenada after pro-republican protests there.In Antigua and Barbuda, the royals will attend a parade to mark 45 years of independence.Guyana, the only English-speaking country in South America, is a republic and Charles will make a state visit on the 60th anniversary of its independence from Britain.The trip will feature plenty of meetings with local people and will focus on “the vibrant present and promising future of each country”, the palace said.The programme includes meetings with cricketing legends in Antigua and Barbuda, where the West Indies team is based, and meeting conservationists responsible for Guyana’s rainforest.Explore more on these topicsMonarchySlaveryColonialismCaribbeanKing Charles IIIQueen CamillaCommonwealth of NationsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palestine Action activists used whips and hammers to threaten guards at arms factory, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Five defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near Bristol
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Five defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near Bristol
Content: Prayers took place at lunchtime outside Woolwich crown court on 25 September.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPrayers took place at lunchtime outside Woolwich crown court on 25 September.Photograph: Martin Pope/Sopa Images/ShutterstockUK newsPalestine Action activists used whips and hammers to threaten guards at arms factory, court hearsFive defendants accused of being part of ‘black team’ tasked with overcoming security at Israel-linked firm Elbit near BristolHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentFri 2 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePalestine Action activists brandished whips, hammers and kebab skewers to intimidate security guards and keep them at bay during a break-in at an Israel-linked arms factory, a court has heard.Five defendants are accused by prosecutors of being part of a “black team”, wearing black jumpsuits, whose role was to overwhelm security guards, so that a “red team”, wearing red jumpsuits, could break into the Elbit systems factory in Filton, near Bristol, and smash up equipment including drones.Qesser Zuhrah, 21, Zahra Farooque, 26, Kamran Ahmed, 29, Heba Muraisi, 31, and Liam Mullany, 34, went on trial at Woolwich crown court on Friday charged with criminal damage and violent disorder over the raid during the early hours of 6 August 2024. They deny the charges.The prosecutor Deanna Heer KC told the jury that an alleged plan of the raid, discovered by police, said: “Shut Elbit Down. This is our primary objective as Palestine Action. We can do that by sticking together and ensuring its destruction with our brains and muscle.”Jurors were told that a security guard, Nigel Shaw, who had struck a member of the black team across the back of his legs with an umbrella, suffered a 4cm laceration to his head after being attacked.Heer said: “The role of the black team was to overwhelm the security guards so that the red team could break into the factory. They did so by threatening, intimidating and, if necessary, assaulting the guards, by throwing fireworks at them and brandishing weapons, such as whips and hammers and large kebab skewers.“When one of the black team was detained by a security guard, other members of the group attacked him, hitting him until he released their colleague, leaving the security guard with a laceration to his head.”She told the court the break-in was carefully planned and a prison van, driven by a member of the red team, crashed through the first perimeter fence surrounding Elbit’s factory at about 3.30am.The black team followed on foot shouting slogans including “Free Palestine” as the van was driven through a second perimeter fence at the site of the firm, whose parent company is based in Israel.Heer said: “The footage shows that the black team used or threatened violence against the security guards that night. It is clear, the prosecution submit, that Nigel Shaw was physically attacked and [was] caused injury but violence was also used or threatened by the black team before then when they threw fireworks or smoke grenades or cracked whips and brandished skewers in order to intimidate the security guards and keep them away.”She said the idea was for the red team to destroy “as much property as possible” before the police arrived and they used fire extinguishers filled with red paint to spray the walls and floor, crowbars and sledgehammers to smash apart computer equipment and drones and also damaged a disabled toilet.The court was told that the plan for the break-in described the black team, who had their faces covered, as “coverts” because the intention was “to get away without being caught”, unlike the red team who were labelled “overts”.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Guarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Guarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government says
Content: Andy Burnham delivers his conference speech, in which he set out plans for a national care service in England.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham delivers his conference speech, in which he set out plans for a national care service in England.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAndy BurnhamBurnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next electionGuarantee will remain until 2030 but MPs will vote on changes during this parliament, government saysRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 2 Oct 2026 12.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham will pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said.The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth.In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to avoid much larger pension increases in years when wages spike.Will pensioners be poorer as a result of Burnham scrapping the triple lock?Read moreIn his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee.However, guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, requiring MPs to vote on the changes.It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether to retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power.The guidance also shows that the government estimates that the adjustment to the triple lock would reduce state pension spending by £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s and by £50bn a year by 2050.However, the Resolution Foundation said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model.Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s.“Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings.“If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.”Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly.Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care changeswould be “electoral suicide”.However, YouGov has publishedpollingsuggesting voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.In his conference speech, Burnham confirmed he wouldend the pension triple lockand use the savings tofund a national care servicein England that would be free at the point of use.He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation.Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourPensionsState pensionsSocial carenewsShareReuse this content

title: Partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard found dead in Louisiana home | Louisiana | The Guardian
description: Kenan ‘Ken’ Urker, 34, who died of apparent drug overdose, was partner of woman convicted of murder of mother
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Kenan ‘Ken’ Urker, 34, who died of apparent drug overdose, was partner of woman convicted of murder of mother
Content: Gypsy Rose Blanchard and Ken Urker.Photograph: Ken Urker via InstagramView image in fullscreenGypsy Rose Blanchard and Ken Urker.Photograph: Ken Urker via InstagramLouisianaPartner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard found dead in Louisiana homeKenan ‘Ken’ Urker, 34, who died of apparent drug overdose, was partner of woman convicted of murder of motherMarina DunbarFri 2 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 18.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe on-and-off partner ofGypsy Rose Blanchard, who spent time in prison for her role in the murder of her abusive mother, was found dead inside his Louisiana home on his 34th birthday on Thursday in what authorities described as an apparent drug overdose.The sheriff’s office in Lafourche parish,Louisiana, confirmed Kenan “Ken” Urker – the father of Blanchard’s daughter – was discovered on Thursday after relatives asked police to conduct a welfare check at his residence.According to a sheriff’s office report on the case, Anita Blanchard said she and her husband – who is Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s half-brother – went to Urker’s home and saw him lying unconscious through an outside window.A man who was with the couple then entered the house through a window and found Urker unresponsive. The sheriff’s office report obtained by the Guardian states that Urker was not breathing and was “cold to the touch”.Authorities who arrived at the scene were “able to see Mr Urker from the living room area lying on his back in [a] bed”, the report said. Deputies reported that they then walked in the direction of the room where the bed was “and located paraphernalia (syringes and spoon) in the bathroom next to a brown powdery substance”.Authorities also found a syringe and a handgun on the nightstand beside the bed. Besides being cold to the touch, Urker “appeared to have been there for an extended period of time”.In an interview withPeoplepublished on Friday, the 32-year-old Gypsy Rose Blanchard said that she believed Urker died from an overdose – though she said she did not know whether it was deliberate.“I don’t know if it was intentional or not,” Blanchard said, adding that Urker “was not in a good state of mind lately”.In a statement published to her Instagram story on Friday, Blanchard said Urker “endured an unimaginable level of public scrutiny and relentless cyberbullying across social media platforms, including TikTok and Reddit”.“The cruelty directed toward him was something no human being should have to endure,” Blanchard wrote. “I believe the tremendous weight of that scrutiny and harassment had a profound impact on him, and I hope his passing serves as a reminder that there is a real person behind every screen, every headline, and every comment.”The sheriff’s office report on Urker’s death confirmed the case had been called in to the agency as an evident overdose.In a statement to the news media, Brennan Matherne, the Lafourche parish sheriff’s captain, said Urker’s death remained “under investigation” as of Friday. Matherne also said investigators as of Friday had not discovered “any signs of foul play”.Blanchard previously spent eight years in prison afterbeing convictedof second-degree murder in connection with the 2015 stabbing death of her mother, Clauddine “Dee Dee” Blanchard.Dee Dee Blanchard was found stabbed to death in her home in Springfield,Missouri, in June 2015. Gypsy Rose Blanchard had provided her then boyfriend, Nicholas Godejohn, with a knife and hid in a bathroom while he killed her mother.Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder. Godejohn, whom Blanchard met online, was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.Dee Dee Blanchard’s murder drew widespread attention after it was revealed that she had forced Gypsy Rose to pretend she was seriously ill and undergo medical procedures she did not need.Blanchard met Urker while serving her prison sentence, from which she was released in late December 2023. She said on theWe Need to Talkpodcast in June that Urker had contacted her after watchingMommy Dead and Dearest, a 2017 documentary about Gypsy Rose and Dee Dee.As Gypsy Rose put it, Urker sent her a “supportive letter, not on any kind of romantic level” and included his phone number. Urker proposed in October 2018. The pair later ended their engagement before reuniting in August 2019.They eventually split again and spent several years apart. During that time, Blanchard married Ryan Anderson. Anderson and Blanchard later separated, with her announcing the split four months after herreleasefrom prison.Blanchard and Urker rekindled their relationship in April 2024. Eight months later, they welcomed their daughter, Aurora Raina Urker.Ramon Antonio Vargas contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsLouisianaUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Federal judge halts Big Bend border wall construction in blow to Trump agenda | Texas | The Guardian
description: Plan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alike
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: Plan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alike
