Content: Crews install the first sections of a new border wall in the Big Bend region of west Texas, on Sept. 16, 2026.Photograph: Scott McWilliams/APView image in fullscreenCrews install the first sections of a new border wall in the Big Bend region of west Texas, on Sept. 16, 2026.Photograph: Scott McWilliams/APTexasFederal judge halts Big Bend border wall construction in blow to Trump agendaPlan to install barriers through popular national park sparked outrage from advocates and politicians alikeRoque PlanasFri 2 Oct 2026 19.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 19.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration fromexpanding the border walland other security infrastructure across the Big Bend region of west Texas, where contentious plans to build roads and vehicle barriers through a popular national park have led to furious backlash and public protests.US district judge Kathleen Cardone’s ruling after a Friday hearing in El Paso deals a major blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to expand the border wall through west Texas at breakneck pace, while riding roughshod over the objections of local business owners, landowners, public land advocates and politicians from both parties.A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for nowRead morePlans to mar Big Bend national park with new roads and 6-ft tall vehicle barriers have drawn the most national attention since the Trump administration started advancing the border wall construction earlier this year. Images of bulldozers plowing up ground for new roads at the park in August drew outrage, prompting Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, totemporarily haltconstruction. Constructionresumedin September.Friday’s ruling came after a hearing in a lawsuit filed by the Friends of the Ruidosa church, the Center for Biological Diversity and river guide Billy Miller seeking to overturn several Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waivers that suspended dozens of environmental and historical protection laws to speed construction.Cardone blocked the DHS waivers in her ruling, saying that the plaintiffs were likely to win and would suffer irreparable harm if construction moved forward. The ruling bars CBP from border security infrastructure construction or ground disturbance, unless it complies with the federal laws that DHS tried to suspend.“This is a historic victory for Big Bend and everyone who loves this wild corner ofTexas,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public land advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. “No administration has the right to destroy a crown-jewel national park for political theatre.”“But this fight is far from over,” he added. “We won’t rest until Big Bend’s environmental protections are fully restored and the illegal waiver that allowed so much destruction is gone for good.”CBP has already awarded five contracts for Big Bend totaling more than $6bn to expand what the agency calls the “smart wall” – a mix of 30-ft steel bollard fencing, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology.“We stand by our assessment and remain confident in our legal authorities to secure the border while preserving the unique landscape of the Big Bend region,” a CBP spokesperson wrote in an email in response to the ruling. “We are working with the Department of Justice on next steps.”The Republican-dominated Congress included a whopping $46.5bn for border wall construction in last year’s “big, beautiful” spending bill. That massive war chest led CBP to focus much of its efforts on the Big Bend region, which contains the longest unwalled stretch along the US-Mexico border.The plans have sparked furious responses from landowners and local political leaders, who say that unauthorized crossings are already rare there due to the region’s remoteness, the lack of nearby cities on the Mexican side and prominent cliffs that make it very difficult to cross through many stretches of the border there.Explore more on these topicsTexasTrump administrationUS immigrationNational parksUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: DoJ declines to reopen investigation into former Fed chair Jay Powell | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Kevin Warsh’s predecessor had been investigated over cost overruns related to central bank renovation project
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Kevin Warsh’s predecessor had been investigated over cost overruns related to central bank renovation project
Content: Jay Powell, the Fed chair, at a bank meeting in January.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersView image in fullscreenJay Powell, the Fed chair, at a bank meeting in January.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersFederal ReserveDoJ declines to reopen investigation into former Fed chair Jay PowellKevin Warsh’s predecessor had been investigated over cost overruns related to central bank renovation projectReutersFri 2 Oct 2026 18.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US ⁠justice department is not reopening a criminal investigation into former Federal Reserve chairJerome Powell⁠for cost overruns ⁠related ​to the central bank’s building renovation project, a department spokesperson said on Friday.Attorney generalTodd ⁠Blanche– in comments toBloomberg News, which first reported the development – said he has not ruled out ⁠continuing to look into the project’s oversight and potentially take ​action if evidence of ‌wrongdoing came to ‌light.The Fed’s inspector general on Wednesdaysaidit found ‌no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to the project cost overruns. But its conclusion there was lax oversight drew a fresh call for Powell’s resignation from Donald Trump, who across his two presidencies has been a vociferous critic of Powell.Powell has remained at ‌the Fed as a governor since stepping down as chair in May.His successor as Fed chair, Kevin ​Warsh said, on Thursday he would hire an independent auditor to “verify accuracy and compliance” for all of the project’s costs.Blanche told Bloomberg News that if the new review found any evidence ⁠of criminal wrongdoing, the justice department could investigate.At his final ​press conference ​as Fed chief in ​April, Powell said he would not leave the ​central bank’s board “until this ‌investigation is well and ​truly over, ​with transparency and finality”.A Fed spokesperson had no immediate comment on Blanche’s statements.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveJerome PowellUS politicsTrump administrationTodd BlancheUS economyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gains | US unemployment and employment data | The Guardian
description: Final jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Final jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%
Content: A man walks by a hiring sign posted outside a restaurant in Arlington, Virginia, on 3 June 2022.Photograph: Olivier Douliery/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man walks by a hiring sign posted outside a restaurant in Arlington, Virginia, on 3 June 2022.Photograph: Olivier Douliery/AFP/Getty ImagesUS unemployment and employment dataUS added just 29,000 jobs in September in sharp drop from last month’s gainsFinal jobs report before the midterm elections also shows the US unemployment rate rose slightly to 4.2%Gaya GuptaFri 2 Oct 2026 10.04 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 08.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS employers added just 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp drop from last month’s gains, and unemployment rose slightly to 4.2%, a sign of a cooling labor market in the final jobs report before the midterm election.The numbers were under half of economists’ expectations ofjust under 70,000 new jobs. Most job gains were concentrated in the healthcare industry, which added 17,000 new jobs, while the information, financial and professional industries saw losses, according to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.Earlier jobs figures were also revised down: Initial reports from July and August altogether dropped by 60,000. The labor market contracted by 10,000 jobs in July after revisions, while August saw 133,000 jobs added.Growth in average hourly earnings slumped to 3%, the lowest rate in over five years.The unemployment rate has remained relatively steady since last year, when it hit 4.5% in November. US jobless claims also inched lower for the fourth week in a row, the labor department said on Thursday.But a closer look at the data also reveals how not all Americans are experiencing the same labor market. Unemployment among Black Americans grew an entire percentage point to 7%, double the rate of white Americans.Though job growth slumped over the summer – the labor market unexpectedly contracted in July and figures in June and May were revised sharply down from initial reports – 162,000 jobs were added in August, the highest since March.A bar chart showing latest US jobs figuresJob openings and the number of hires have also remained little changed in August, according to the recent data from the labor department, as the “slow-hire, slow-fire” job market continues.Data from private employers released by the payroll firm, ADP, earlier this week had painted a much rosier picture of the labor market. It found that private sector hiring accelerated last month for the first time since May, carried by growth in the healthcare, education and hospitality industries, and private employers added 90,000 new jobs.The labor market has remained largely strong this year even as the US-Israel war on Iran has uppedinflation, especially energy prices. Last month, the Federal Reserveraised interest ratesfor the first time in three years, citing higher prices.At the time, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, emphasized the strength of the US labor market, which “is basically running consistent with full employment”, but he noted that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.Though the data still reflects an overall solid jobs market, the September release cools expectations for the USFederal Reserveto increase rates again in its final meeting before the 3 November midterms. Most central bank officials penciled in at least one more rate hike before the year’s end, which is now more likely to come at the Fed’s December conference.But higher prices continue to be the biggest economic pain point for Americans. Mortgage rates accelerated to their highest level in three years on Thursday from 7% to 7.28%, the largest weekly jump since 2022. The 10-year treasury yield, which underpins mortgages and other loans, also reacheda 24-year highas the recent global bond sell-off continued. Meanwhile, higher oil prices havecostAmericans an estimated $936 per household.Explore more on these topicsUS unemployment and employment dataEconomicsUS economyUS-Israel war on IranInflationUS interest ratesFederal ReservenewsShareReuse this content

title: G7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reserves | Oil | The Guardian
description: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies
Content: Emmanuel Macron said ministers had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks.Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron said ministers had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks.Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/Sipa/ShutterstockOilG7 to release up to 100m barrels of emergency oil and diesel reservesLeaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US suppliesJoanna Partridge,Jillian AmbroseandMark SweneyFri 2 Oct 2026 14.52 EDTFirst published on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles afterDonald Trumpthreatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.The French President,Emmanuel Macron, said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unlessEuropetapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the currentG7chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.Trump said he was consideringa ban on diesel exportsafter the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.9:37Diesel export ban: will Trump push global energy prices even higher? - The LatestTrump said in a post on hisTruth Social platformthat Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 a gallon (£1.18 a litre) for the first time in early September.The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to arecord high of £2 a litreon forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel after news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered thelargest release of government oil reservesin its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Explore more on these topicsOilG7Global economyInternational tradeEnergy industryEuropeCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: How best to punish City? Restitution over retribution, then hand club to the fans | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: There are no real precedents and emotions are still raw, but good can come from this mess if ownership models change
Author: Jonathan Liew
Headline: There are no real precedents and emotions are still raw, but good can come from this mess if ownership models change
Content: Often it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players?Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOften it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players?Composite: Getty ImagesManchester CityHow best to punish City? Restitution over retribution, then hand club to the fansJonathan LiewThere are no real precedents and emotions are still raw, but good can come from this mess if ownership models changeFri 2 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTShareA17-year transfer embargo. Replay the entire era with all the original players. Restore the 2009 squad and force them to mount a title challenge with Stephen Ireland, Martin Petrov and Richard Dunne. Force Ferran Soriano to drive a parade bus backwards through Manchester, once for every major trophy won. Ban the Poznan, or at least make City fans do it facing forwards.Yes, in the week since it emerged that Manchester City have beenfound guilty of all the financial chargeslaid against them by the Premier League, a great and cathartic silliness has begun to stalk the land. The Sainsbury’s account on Instagram posting a picture that reads “114 unexpected items in the bagging area”. The relentless trolling from Domino’s Pizza, which claims to have “irrefutable evidence that pineapple is the best pizza topping”.Manchester City verdict has big integrity implications, warns FA as club lodge appealRead moreThe City fan on BBC 5 Live arguing that the club’s defiance of unfair rules is part of a rich tradition of civil disobedience going back to the suffragettes and the Peterloo massacre, and therefore justified because “they’re trying to massacre Manchester City”. Liam Gallagher’s late-night diatribes on X, the most unhinged of which compares City to “Jesus prepared to die on the cross”. (The most popular reply, naturally, simply reads: “Sham Pain Supernova”.)And on some level it’s possible to see the ritualistic ridicule of City as the first downpayment on any punishment: a kind of collective healing, banter as therapy. Before the stripping of points and titles, the stripping of dignity. This is always how the British have dealt with anything, from an early general election to the death of a treasured celebrity. I heard my first Princess Diana joke within about 15 seconds of walking through the school gates the following Monday morning.Back in the real world of real consequences, the Abu Dhabi counteroffensive was beginning in earnest. While City launched their appeal,Etihad Airways was threatening to sue the Premier Leaguefor the “damaging implications” of the verdict and government officials from the United Arab Emirates were surreptitiously warning that the case could threaten diplomatic relations and billions of pounds of investment into the UK.Which sounds like a pretty hefty multi-pronged problem until you realise that these are all basically the same entity. Like one of those one-man stage shows you see at the Edinburgh fringe, where all the characters are played by a single guy scurrying around the stage frenetically putting on different costumes. UAE dignitaries? The leadership of Etihad Airways? The board of Manchester City? Goodness, your versatility astonishes us. That’s acting range for you.View image in fullscreenOne suggestion to start reversing the damage: force Manchester City fans to do the Poznan facing forwards.Photograph: Mike EgertonStill, all of this is a long-overdue reminder that when you allow state actors to control your football clubs, even the most minor footballing decisions become matters of diplomacy, geopolitics, peace and war. Witness the desperate contortions this week of Andy Burnham, who offered astiff-armed defence of City’s ownershipbeforebelatedly realisingthat appearing to side with English football’s most notorious cheats may just be the sort of thing that polls badly in certain swing postcodes.None of which, of course, gets us any closer to a workable solution. And of course you will have your own strong views over what should happen to City, assuming their trail of appeals and grievances is finally exhausted at some point. There are no real precedents here, and so there are no wrong answers. The emotions are still raw. Often it is said that victims should not dispense justice. But what happens when the victim is an entire sport, an entire generation of fans, clubs who lost their best players, broadcasters who as it turned out were pointing their cameras at a sham competition?These are almost philosophical questions, questions of justice and ethics and morality. Do you decide that the strict imperative is to punish or “cancel” the harm done, as Kant or Hegel might have argued? Do you agree with Durkheim that the point of punishment is not exemplary deterrence but the reinforcement of shared moral values, or with Bentham that the infliction of pain for its own sake simply prolongs the original sin, and that the emphasis should always be on averting future evil? And do any of these scenarios end with Victor Lindelöf lifting a Premier League trophy?View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham faced pressure this week after defending Manchester City’s owners.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA WireWhat follows here is little more than a personal prospectus, guided above all by two principles. Firstly that the relitigation of history – the messy and unsatisfactory business of reassigning trophies and medals – is an unserious solution for unserious people. Rewriting the past on the basis of a counterfactual is no more feasible than asking the shark to regurgitate, reassemble and reanimate the body of the surfer he has just crunched to pieces. It is one thing to tell the world that what we saw was not real. It is quite another to perpetrate the compound fiction that something entirely different happened instead.As Jamie Carragher put it so well on Sky Sports this week, winning is less about the silverware and the trinkets than the moments and the memories, the aura of victory and the hangovers the following morning, and those are gone for ever. Carved up, parcelled away. And of course City knew this at the time. The Touré goal, the 6-1 at Old Trafford, the Agüero goal, the Kompany goal: those moments are safe, banked, untouchable. “We know what we felt,” a lot of City fans have been saying in the last few days, and they’re right.The second principle is that any punishment should seek to inflict maximum punishment on City’s owners and as little as possible on City’s fans. The fans may have shared in the proceeds of cheating, may often have defended the owners in obnoxious and myopic ways, and perhaps it feels purgative and satisfying to throw them under the bus too. But ultimately they too are victims of a grand deception. They too were gaslit, lied to, told the dream was real life. In many ways the subterfuge is all the crueller because of how desperate they were to believe it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd so any redress that deprives one of the country’s biggest fanbases of their club, that forces them out of existence, that cuts the body off at the knees and forces it to beg for mercy at the very bottom of the food chain, is also doomed to failure. And let’s be real: this isn’t going to happen in practice. The commercial appeal of Manchester City uplifts the entire league. Broadcast and commercial contracts would need to be redrawn. Ultimately throwing them out of football altogether, kicking them down the stairs, would cost everyone at the top of English football a lot of money. And we know how much they hate that.But there is a recourse, albeit improbable and outlandish, that fulfils all the criteria of restitution, if not retribution. The new football regulator has the power to strip rogue owners of their position and force them to sell up. This sounds like a good punishment. But market intelligence suggests City are worth about £4bn now, compared with about £200m when the Abu Dhabi United Group took over in 2008. What kind of punishment enables the perpetrators to walk away with a 20-fold profit on their investment, much of which can be attributed to their cheating?No, City should not be sold; they should be taken back. Requisition. Nationalise. Give them some patriotic name such as the Great British Manchester Football Club. Return Phil Foden to the exchequer. Enzo Maresca, you are now an employee of the UK government. And while this sounds outlandish because itisoutlandish, there is a recent precedent here. Chelsea’s operations were briefly controlled by the government after sanctions were imposed on their owner Roman Abramovich and he agreed to offload the club. It was surreal, exceptional and only ever intended as a temporary measure.View image in fullscreenManchester city council owns the freehold to the Etihad Stadium.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAThere are plenty of levers that can be pulled here, if there is the political will to do so. Manchester city council owns the Etihad Stadium. A report by Tax Policy Associates has suggested that City may owe HMRC as much as £12m in unpaid tax over the Roberto Mancini contract. The cross-party Treasury committee has urged HMRC to scrutinise the findings of the Premier League case. Meanwhile, every week that City stay in their current ownership is a week in which money flows from fans and broadcasters and sponsors into the pockets of Abu Dhabi. No wonder City’s ruling regime has a vested interest in elongating this process as long as possible.Nobody bats an eyelid at the idea of the state owning a park or a motorway or a museum, or taking over a failing train company or steelworks or bank. In each case there is a recognition that the asset has a broader social value that requires a certain protection against market forces. And of course the longer-term ambition here is not to run Manchester City as an arm of the state, but eventually to give the club back to its people. To gradually assemble the governance structures that would allow fans a genuine voice in the running of their club and facilitate an eventual sale. And in the meantime to maintain one of the country’s most successful football clubs as a going concern, generating revenue that will allow it to pay back its debt to English football.None of this is going to happen. Abu Dhabi would rather hire the world’s 50 best lawyers to sue Burnham for the next 30 yearsbefore it allowed one of its prized assets to be given away for free. But also: is this not what we should want to happen? If any tangible good is to come from the sordid City case beyond memes and banter, perhaps it is a realisation that the ownership model of English football needs to be reimagined on a radical level. That a system built on the wholesale transfer of wealth from fans to owners is exploitation by any other name. That City are not the disease, but the symptom. And that the first rule of politics remains its most crucial: never waste a good crisis.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgages | US sports media | The Guardian
description: The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some headway
Author: Aaron Timms
Headline: The rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some headway
Content: Clay Travis has forged a lucrative career in media.Photograph: Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenClay Travis has forged a lucrative career in media.Photograph: Roger Wimmer/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesUS sports mediaClay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgagesThe rightwing media mogul has lost ground to the likes of Pat McAfee and Joe Rogan. He’s hoping his new venture can recapture some headwayAaron TimmsFri 2 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Maga media blowhard Clay Travisoffered$2m toColin Kaepernicklast week to appear on the daily talkshow he hosts with former CIA analyst Buck Sexton, it represented the culmination of a years-long obsession on the right with the onetime NFL star. In Travis’s telling of history, Kaepernick taking a knee during the 2016 NFL season was the event that catalyzed professional sports into the era of “woke” excess from which, he claims, it has been struggling to recover ever since.But more than simply confirming the right’s longstanding villainization of Kaepernick, Travis’s offer was also a smarmy bid for publicity for his new media venture, Sport & State. Sport & State, which launched in August, is Travis’s bid to get back to his roots as a media mogul who sold the wildly popular Outkick to Fox Sports for a rumored $100m, and reclaim some of the cultural territory lost to fellowsports brosand Magagitators like Pat McAfee, Joe Rogan, Tucker Carlson and Ben Shapiro. But if there’s one thing Sport & State won’t be doing, it’s engaging with anyone beyond the Magaverse. There has been no response from Kaepernick since Travis made his “offer” of $2m to charity in exchange for an interview, which suggests he understands that it was extended more in a spirit of trolling buffoonery than sincerity. No one associated with the left or progressive politics ever appears on Travis’s shows, for the simple reason that they are designed purely for the right to talk to itself. (Some would say the same could be said of the left, although the disregard for dissenting perspectives in the Magasphere seems way more extreme.) More than it heralds a renewal of Travis’s career or an injection of fresh energy into the Trumpist mediasphere, Sport & State is a case study in the stagnation that has taken hold on the right as Donald Trump stares down the barrel of defeat in November’s midterm elections.Will hordes of influencers, weed smokers and mid-point talkers bring down the US Open?Read moreHaving spent the better part of the past two months listening to the Clay Travis & Buck Sexton Show (which runs from noon to 3pm ET every weekday) and the Clay Travis Show (3-4pm), I can say with confidence that there are, in essence, only 11 topics a given day’s programming on Sport & State will cover: college football gambling picks; Trumpworld figures who are friends with Travis and Sexton; the wonderful job that these figures are doing in power (sometimes mixed with the preceding theme: “Our friend Kash, who is truly our friend, Clay and I are both buddies with him, he’s a good man,” Sexton affirmed on a recent episode); the low levels of testosterone apparently common among white males who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 (“white dudes for Kamala” is perhaps the gravest slur on the Clay Travis Show); trans women in professional sport (I haven’t calculated this precisely but at a guess I’d say this accounts for 20% to 50% of the discussion on any show that Travis hosts, even as the number of actual trans women competing in professional American sports remains exactly zero and there are probablyfewer than 10trans athletes in total in college sports); crime in America’s cities (in recent weeks the fixation has beenLindsay Clancy, but it’s liable to switch at any moment to Iryna Zarutska, Luigi Mangione, Charlie Kirk,Iryna Zarutska, or whatever murder happens to have taken place on that particular day in New York City); the problem with women (in summary: they are women); the fact that Travis and Sexton are both family men with wives and children; the fact that Travis has a law degree from Vanderbilt University; the fact that Travis studied law at Vanderbilt after he was rejected by Stanford (“I wanted to go to Stanford Law School, they didn’t want me, I went to Vanderbilt instead – I’ve now made a $10m donation to Vanderbilt Law School”); and the fact that Travis appeared on Fox News last night and will appear on Fox News again later today. Sprinkled throughout all of this are plugs for Hard Rock Bet (“Bet $5, get $100 in bonus bets”), which is the official gambling partner of Sport & State and holds equity in Travis’s upstart media concern, and companies such as Perfect 10 Mortgage, Crockett Coffee, XX-XY Athletics and Clay Travis Law, all of which – it should come as no surprise – Travis either outright owns or holds a stake in.The recursiveness and self-referentiality of the advertising and content on Sport & State are all part of the site’s commercial strategy, according to Travis’s lengthymission statement. The onshoring of all the advertising will, Travis claims, insulate his new venture from the vagaries of media’s traditional dependence on subscriptions and external advertisers. Gambling is the key revenue driver: Outkickbecamean affiliate of FanDuel after sports betting was legalized in 2018 and eventually made $350 for every new gambling account it helped set up, netting $2m in affiliate betting revenue on Super Bowl Sunday in 2021 alone, and Sport & State is set up to reap similar rewards through its partnership with Hard Rock Bet. But Travis’s expectation is that his home loan business, say, will also prosper as viewers stay online to hear his views on Ole Miss v LSU, Lane Kiffin or theapparent attempted hijackingof the Israel-bound passenger jet and what it means for the future of DEI in America.Inadvertently, perhaps, Travis’s sidequest companies offer a sense of what Sport & State’s ideal audience member looks like: a patriotic American male with a habit of deploying the phrase “perfect 10” unironically whose life revolves around mortgages, coffee, litigation, gambling and moaning about trans women. On the Crockett Coffeeblog, recent posts include “American Coffee Origins and Brewing Techniques”, “Discovering American Coffee’s Unique Flavors”, and “The Americano: A Complete History” (do I detect a theme here?); Travis sips throughout the day on Sport & State from a black spillproof coffee container, emphasizing his own commitment to the cause of caffeine and country.If there’s a persistent “Spider-Men pointing at each other” quality to the advertising on Sport & State, that extends to the content as well. Travis’s big idea is that in the age of AI and commodified writing, it’s better to go deep than big, that depth of audience commitment matters more than the old traffic era’s scale-focused contest for clicks. There may be some wisdom in the strategy, but that approach – drumming down and appeasing an already loyal base – seems to have become the media-obsessed Trump White House’s guiding political strategy too, a choice that risks self-sabotage as the midterms loom. Travis’s theory of media is second-term Trump’s theory of power: instead of growing the audience, the electorate, the constituency, the sole purpose of having attention is to give those listening more of the same. Discussion on Sport & State this week included a summary of Travis and Sexton’s Mondaymeetingwith Trump in the Oval Office. Their main point was to emphasize that “President Trump says he loves the show, says we’re doing a great job” and that various Trumpworld figures greeted them during their half-hour in front of the Resolute Desk. “We saw Karoline Leavitt, our very good friend”; “We also saw Susie Wiles – she said she is cancer-free now”; “We got a little quick high-five from Stephen Miller”.View image in fullscreenMany on the right saw Colin Kaepernick’s decision to kneel during the anthem as a pivot point in US sports and culture.Photograph: Marcio José Sánchez/APOver a chyron announcing THE VOICE OF SEAN HANNITY, the longtime Fox News host then called in to discuss: sports betting (what else?); the border collie he’s about to take delivery of at the conclusion of nine months of dog training (if this is what it takes to survive domestic cohabitation with Hannity as an animal, imagine how things must be for the humans in his house); Gavin Newsom and Kathy Hochul as the highest-taxing, and therefore worst, governors in America; and potential Democratic candidates for 2028 (Hannity thinks AOC will be the nominee, Travis thinks it will be Kamala Harris; they agreed to bet on the outcome, with the loser to buy the winner a steak dinner in a demonstration of red-blooded American masculinity). The segment concluded with Hannity, Sexton and Travis all saying “we had an awesome time” after five minutes of meandering conversation about nothing, and the welcome announcement that Travis would be on Hannity’s show on Fox the following day for more of the same. On the right, the Spider-Men are always pointing at each other, and they’re all the audience each other needs.Watching Sport & State’s live programming and reading its endless churn of tiresome posts about how sports and the world suck now because of Joe Biden and woke, it’s difficult to figure out what, exactly, the appeal of Travis as a right-wing media personality is. Rogan has the vague charisma of a lifelong stoner; McAfee has that dog in him, a kind of American mongrel who forever puts himself next to a gas pump or under the chassis of a hoisted car; Carlson has a habit of Mozart-laughing at his own jokes, which is at the very least engagingly bizarre; Shapiro … well, Shapiro doesn’t have much going for him, but he does talk quickly. Travis, by contrast, has neither a sense of personal style nor any real sense of humor; he’s a boring dad who drones on endlessly about mortgages and failed sports bets and his law degree. He also frequently looks exhausted on air, as does Sexton; together they form perhaps the puffiest-looking duo in American media. Who knows? Perhaps a pair of hungover-looking permadads sipping mournfully from their coffee canisters while they bemoan the latest poll numbers out of Ohio is exactly the new groove the right needs to salvage a listing presidency. But it seems unlikely.Travis claims he’s working “20 hours a day” to produce material for Sport & State, and perhaps it really does take that long to package up clips from the previous 24 hours’ appearances on the Sean Hannity Show and Jesse Watters Primetime and Titans on Tomorrow with Ben Shapiro, brew the Crockett Coffee and get it into the spillproof containers, go on air, play the clips, then restate their substance using different words 500 times in a row. But if this is the right’s idea of a bold new intervention in sports and media, it’s hard not to feel that as a cultural force, the Magaverse is now well and truly running on fumes.Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 49ers owner Jed York suspended, fined $500K after prostitution sting arrest | NFL | The Guardian
description: The NFL announced that York was suspended for six games and must pay a fine of $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The NFL announced that York was suspended for six games and must pay a fine of $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy
Content: Jed York was suspended six games and fined $500,000 by the NFL on Friday.Photograph: Kelley L Cox/APView image in fullscreenJed York was suspended six games and fined $500,000 by the NFL on Friday.Photograph: Kelley L Cox/APNFL49ers owner Jed York suspended, fined $500K after prostitution sting arrestNFL announces violation of personal conduct policyYork pleaded no contest after arrest at Ohio trailer parkAssociated PressFri 2 Oct 2026 14.26 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 15.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NFL suspended San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York for six games Friday afterhis arrestearlier this year in a prostitution sting in Ohio.The league announced that York also was fined $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy. York has not attended any games or league meetings so far this season and was credited with three games served. He is eligible to return on 20 October, following the team’s game the previous night against Washington. The NFL’s fall league meetings begin that day in New York.Fake wide receivers to undercover stings: did the 49ers have the wildest NFL preseason of all time?Read moreYork said in a statement released by the team that he accepts the punishment given by the league and apologized for his actions.“To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of theSan Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry,” he said. “This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one’s failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better. Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don’t take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead.”In August, York was arrested in a mobile home park by the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force after police said he was attempting to pay $160 for sex with a woman he believed to be a prostitute.York was booked into jail and was released after posting a $5,000 bond. York was initially charged with engaging in prostitution, but prosecutors amended that to disorderly conduct. He pleaded no contest to that charge and to possessing criminal tools for using his phone to respond to an undercover online prostitution advertisement.He was sentenced to one day in jail for both offenses to be served concurrently and was credited with one day served when he pleaded no contest. He also was fined $1,150. Police seized the $160 from York and that was later given to the human trafficking taskforce as part of the plea. York also completed an online course.He also owns stakes in the Premier League’sLeeds Unitedand Scotland’s Rangers through 49ers Enterprises.Explore more on these topicsNFLSan Francisco 49ersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tony Romo will not return to CBS Sports in wake of drunk driving arrest | US sports media | The Guardian
description: The former Dallas Cowboys star quarterback and the network mutually agreed to part ways after his July arrest for operating a vehicle under the influence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The former Dallas Cowboys star quarterback and the network mutually agreed to part ways after his July arrest for operating a vehicle under the influence
Content: Tony Romo will not return as an NFL analyst for CBS.Photograph: Michael Ainsworth/APView image in fullscreenTony Romo will not return as an NFL analyst for CBS.Photograph: Michael Ainsworth/APUS sports mediaTony Romo will not return to CBS Sports in wake of drunk driving arrestNFL analyst and network mutually agree to part waysEx-Dallas Cowboys star was on $180m contractGuardian sportFri 2 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTony Romo will not return as an NFL analyst for CBS Sports, the network announced Friday, afterhis July arrestfor operating a vehicle while under the influence.“CBS Sports and Tony Romo have mutually agreed to part ways,” the network said in a statement. “We thank Tony for his contributions over the past nine years and wish him the best moving forward.”The former Dallas Cowboys quarterback had been onindefinite leavefrom the network after his arrest during a traffic stop on 23 July in Wisconsin. According to the Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office report, Romo performed poorly on field sobriety tests before getting taken into custody, booked and released.The rise and fall of Tony Romo: what comes next for CBS’s $180m NFL analyst?Read moreHepleadedno contest to the charge on 1 September and was given a six-month driving ban. He was also ordered to have an interlock device placed on his vehicle, pay a fine of $834 and complete an alcohol assessment program.Romo said he will take time to consider his next steps.“I’m proud of what I accomplished at CBS Sports over the last nine years. I approached my role as a game analyst the way I’ve approached everything in my life – with a desire to win and be the best that I can be,” Romo said in a statement Friday. “I’m going to use this time to take a break, something I’ve never done before, and focus on my health and my family before moving on to my next opportunity. I am grateful for my time with CBS Sports and for the continued support of my family and friends, as well as theNFLcommunity and fans.”CBS saidJJ Wattwill continue to serve as the network’s lead NFL game analyst. When Romo was placed on leave before the start of this season, Watt was pulled up to fill in on the network’s top broadcasting team, alongside play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson.Romo, 46, had been the lead analyst for CBS’s NFL coverage since 2017 after making four Pro Bowl appearances during a playing career that ran from 2004 to 2016 and was spent entirely with Dallas. In 2020, he signed a then-record 10-year, $180m contract to be the network’s top analyst.After his no-contest plea last month, Romosaidhis ⁠football injuries indirectly led to an “over-reliance on alcohol” and vowed to “own my mistakes fully”.Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Victor Wembanyama said no to gambling money. In today’s NBA, that feels radical | Victor Wembanyama | The Guardian
description: As LeBron James and other NBA stars embrace the murk of betting and prediction markets, the Spurs’ 22-year-old cornerstone drew a refreshing line
Author: Owen Lewis
Headline: As LeBron James and other NBA stars embrace the murk of betting and prediction markets, the Spurs’ 22-year-old cornerstone drew a refreshing line
Content: Victor Wembanyama reacts during the Spurs’ Game 1 matchup against the Knicks in the 2026 NBA finals at Frost Bank Center.Photograph: Gregory Shamus/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVictor Wembanyama reacts during the Spurs’ Game 1 matchup against the Knicks in the 2026 NBA finals at Frost Bank Center.Photograph: Gregory Shamus/Getty ImagesVictor WembanyamaVictor Wembanyama said no to gambling money. In today’s NBA, that feels radicalAs LeBron James and other NBA stars wholeheartedly embrace the murk of betting and prediction markets, the San Antonio Spurs’ 22-year-old cornerstone has drawn a refreshing lineOwen LewisFri 2 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf the song fromLeBron James’s agonizing Polymarket adis as stuck in your head as mine thanks to the commercial playing during every YouTube video and HBO show (all I wanted to do was rewatch The Leftovers), let Victor Wembanyama be your antidote. At the Spurs’ practice on Thursday, San Antonio Express-News columnist Mike Fingerasked Wembanyamaif he would ever partner with a sports betting firm. It couldn’t have been easier for the 22-year-old to say yes. The NBA displays ads for both FanDuel and DraftKings, in addition to hawking betting odds on its broadcasts. Until the streaming service met its end a few months ago, plenty of NBA games streamed exclusively on FanDuel Sports Network. Then there are Wembanyama’s legendary peers: James is the new face of Polymarket; Kevin Durant reads FanDuel odds and invests in Kalshi;Giannis Antetokounmpois a Kalshi shareholder.“Absolutely not,” Wembanyamasaid instead. “I will never do that. Honestly, I think it’s very sad to see some players promote it. Everybody does whatever they want, but without me.”‘It’s sad seeing players promote it’: Wembanyama says he will never endorse gambling companiesRead moreStandards are so back. It shouldn’t feel miraculous that a star of Wembanyama’s stature is taking the position that players should not cash checks frompredatory companiesthat incentivize athletes to dabble in insider trading, but in 2026, we’ll take any anti-sellout ally we can find. This one may prove particularly valuable. Given his age and fame, Wembanyama should be around as a beacon to cut through the murk of betting for some time to come. How refreshing that, as rightwing terror reigns, the NBA’s best and biggest young star is a politically outspoken leftist.It’s not a stylish time to turn down buckets of money. Thanks to some combination of a disintegrating economy, a president and political party so craven and corrupt that scandal-worthy behavior often doesn’t register, and a significant overlap among the wealthy and the morally bankrupt, shame died a bloody death somewhere in the last decade. Most basketball podcasts keep themselves afloat with gambling companies’ life rings. No reputational damage seems to last. James’s Polymarket partnership was immediately and emphatically unpopular, but apparently not enough for anybody at thePhiladelphia 76ers’ media dayto ask him about it.So Wembanyama’s emphatic rejection of a sports betting partnership stands out. Had he simply said, “Sure, who knows what the future brings,” few would have batted an eye. But not only did he refuse the possibility, he also left behind a receipt.I will never do that.For Wembanyama, any eventual embrace of gambling will be met with fans’ usual criticism – and his own words echoed back at him.View image in fullscreenVictor Wembanyama poses for photos during the Spurs’ media day at the Victory Capital Performance Center in San Antonio.Photograph: Ronald Cortes/Getty ImagesWhat’s perhaps most refreshing about Wembanyama is – so far, at least; athletes tend to become more and more PR-friendly as they age – his willingness to ruffle feathers. Asked about the murders of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by ICE agents in January, Wembanyama said, “Yeah, PR has tried, but I’m not going to sit here and give some politically correct [answer]. Every day I wake up and see the news, and I’m horrified. I think it’s crazy that some people might make it seem like or sound like the murder of civilians is acceptable.” It’s similarly outrageous that the aggressive integration of sports betting and prediction markets into society has been successful. It’s not normal or ideal for professional sports leagues to be in bed with gambling firms, or for companies that allow people to trade money on every event imaginable to exist at all. A healthy NBA is one where the star poised to dominate the league for the next decade is willing to express sentiment along those lines out loud.There is one cynical way to look at Wembanyama’s response. He’s coming off a run of bad press on the court. After a brilliant playoff run through three rounds, he had adisastrousNBA finals. He threw a pass off a teammate’s back in the decisive moments of one game, missed two free throws towards the end of another (in which the Spursfailed to consolidate a 29-point leadinto victory). He showed flashes of violence in the playoffs, earning an ejection byelbowingNaz Reid in the neck, and at times succumbed to the same brand of foul-baiting he’d criticized in other players months earlier. As the Spurs crashed out, Wemby had never been less popular. Decrying the omnipresence of sports betting, which fans almost universally abhor, gets the Spurs’ big man back in their good graces. But it’s hard to say his swing in fortune is undeserved. Fun as it is to watch, what happens during a professional basketball game is rarely more than a metaphor for society. A clear appraisal of the real world is more representative of virtue.Explore more on these topicsVictor WembanyamaSan Antonio SpursSport bettingGamblingUS sportsPolymarketPrediction marketsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mercedes put team first as Russell and Antonelli face off on F1’s return to Sepang | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Championship leaders bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuit
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Championship leaders bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuit
Content: George Russell receives a fervent welcome from fans in Sepang.Photograph: Annice Lyn/ReutersView image in fullscreenGeorge Russell receives a fervent welcome from fans in Sepang.Photograph: Annice Lyn/ReutersFormula One 2026Mercedes put team first as Russell and Antonelli face off on F1’s return to SepangTitle rivals bring upgrades to first Grand Prix in Malaysia since 2017 on a demanding but well liked circuitGiles RichardsFri 2 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile the byzantine nomenclature of this weekend’s “Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia” will have Formula One’s statisticians muttering darkly under their breath for years to come, the import of the sport’s return to the Sepang circuit remains all too straightforward at the sharp end. Complicated only perhaps by a Red Bull resurgence and an enthused Max Verstappen, determined to make his mark on the championship run-in.The return to Malaysia for its first race since 2017 has been welcomed in F1. It is a much-liked circuit among drivers, albeit the high temperatures and humidity make for an enormous physical challenge.Lewis Hamilton backs Vasseur but believes Ferrari leadership structure could changeRead moreHowever, this is no long-term return to Sepang. It is back, as its torturously titled branding suggests, as a one-off replacement for the Bahrain GP, which wascancelled earlier this yearbecause of the war in the Middle East. The Bahrain GP it is then, right down to the Bahraini backing, a Bahrain GP trophy and Bahraini-themed activities at the circuit but the pole and the victory will most assuredly be earned in Sepang, leading to said statisticians deploying the asterisk on their keyboard.For the title protagonists, however, the name is moot. What matters is the race and both the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, and his rival and Mercedes teammate George Russell want to make a mark in Malaysia. Antonelli leads Russell by 66 points with eight rounds remaining. A handsome lead but he dropped 15 points to the British driver at the last round in Bakuwhere Russell showed the best form of his season, dominant across the weekend.Antonelli, who made a costly error in qualifying and finished fifth, declared it his “worst” weekend and vowed to re-establish the order in Malaysia, while Russell felt a confidence and ease with the car that he has not enjoyed all season. A platform, he felt, from which to build a late title tilt at Antonelli.The prospect of a comeback from Russell, applying pressure to his 20-year-old teammate who is in only his second season in F1, might put Mercedes too under pressure in managing them. A process of which they are all too aware, as the last time F1 was in Malaysia it was the first year after the Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg relationship at Mercedes had come apart with rancour. Nonetheless the team insist they will continue to allow their current drivers to race one another.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli arrives in Sepang having seen his title procession jolted at the last race.Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters“Does it [Russell finding form] change the dynamic? I think from the overarching philosopher’s standpoint, no,” said the team principal, Toto Wolff, this week. “Because we want to give both drivers equal opportunity and to go for a championship. But the team comes first. That has always been the Mercedes philosophy.”To that end they have brought a swathe of upgrades to Sepang, only their second major developments of the season, including adaptations to the floor, rear suspension and rear bodywork. They have been long-awaited but as ever with the first year of new regulations there is no guarantee they will simply bolt on and find lap time.Malaysia is the first test and fine-tuning will be required given it is something of a baptism of fire, with the circuit’s heat and its abrasive, high-degradation surface making for a far from normal run-out. Indeed, how the teams handle tyre degradation will probably define the race, a finely balanced test for the strategists of two or even potentially three pit stops.For Mercedes, in Friday’s practice sessions finding the right set-up and operating window to make the most of potential downforce gains was proving tricky, with Russell and Antonelli seventh and eighth in the second session.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey will probably find more pace come Saturday at which point they may have to deal with Verstappen and Red Bull, whose car has come on in leaps and bounds after their upgrade in Baku. Verstappen has yet to win this year and, while the title is gone, he is fiercely competitive and still determined to take the flag. The Red Bull was well balanced out of the blocks in Sepang, and Verstappen declared it “positive” and a “decent start”. Such guarded judgment is praise indeed, given how often this season Verstappen has had to wrestle with a recalcitrant car from the off.View image in fullscreenArvid Lindblad in action during the free practice session in Sepang.Photograph: Fazry Ismail/EPAHe was not quickest in second practice when Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc, also showing strong form, took the top spot from Verstappen’s Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar by a tenth. But the Dutchman, in fourth, did not set a time doing a qualifying simulation on soft tyres. Verstappen surely has more to come and will be hungrily eyeing a shot at a win that would make it two in a row separated by almost a decade since hetook the flag when it was last held in Malaysia in 2017.A point to prove then for the four-time champion but for Antonelli and Russell it is relative points that matter and perhaps most importantly in defining the championship, who asserts themself to the greatest effect in this one-off showdown in Malaysia.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: WNBA playoffs: A’ja Wilson pours in 36 as Aces oust bloodied Caitlin Clark and Fever | WNBA | The Guardian
description: A’ja Wilson scored 36 points as the defending champion Las Vegas Aces beat Caitlin Clark and the Indiana Fever 94-83 to advance
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: A’ja Wilson scored 36 points as the defending champion Las Vegas Aces beat Caitlin Clark and the Indiana Fever 94-83 to advance
Content: A’ja Wilson drives to the basket against Caitlin Clark during the first quarter of the Las Vegas Aces’ Game 3 playoff win over the Indiana Fever on Thursday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA’ja Wilson drives to the basket against Caitlin Clark during the first quarter of the Las Vegas Aces’ Game 3 playoff win over the Indiana Fever on Thursday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Ethan Miller/Getty ImagesWNBAWNBA playoffs: A’ja Wilson pours in 36 as Aces oust bloodied Caitlin Clark and FeverFour-time MVP adds 10 rebounds in 94-83 victoryClark finishes with 18 points in deciding Game 3Aces continue pursuit of fourth title in five yearsGuardian sportand agenciesFri 2 Oct 2026 00.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 00.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA’ja Wilson made sure her basketball spoke for itself Thursday night, as the four-time WNBA MVP scored 36 points to lead the defending championLas Vegas Acesto a 94-83 victory over the Indiana Fever in the deciding Game 3 of the first round.The third-seeded Aces, who have won three of the past four titles, moved on to play the winner of the Golden State-Dallas series, which will be decided Friday night in San Francisco.This is the second year in a row Las Vegas have ended the season forCaitlin Clarkand the Fever, who were seeded sixth. The teams met in the semifinals a year ago, with the Aces pulling out an overtime victory in the finale of the five-game series.Wilson bookended this series with sensational performances in Games 1 and 3, making sureher verbal confrontation with a Fever fanTuesday in Indianapolis wouldn’t be the enduring memory. The league did not punish Wilson, who opened the series with 38 points and 16 rebounds and followed up in this game by making 11 of 18 shots and grabbing 10 rebounds.Teammate Chelsea Gray added 23 points and Jackie Young scored 18.Clark scored 11 points in the first quarter but was held to seven the rest of the game. Kelsey Mitchell led Indiana with 23 points and Aliyah Boston had 19 points and 10 rebounds.Tensions ran high again Thursday, with both teams bringing the physical play expected when each season is on the line in a game that had the intensity of aWNBAfinals.Clark briefly left the court after taking an accidental elbow to the mouth from Loyd while the two contested a rebound with just over three minutes remaining. No foul was called on the play, which appeared to knock one of Clark’s teeth out and left her bleeding from the mouth with Las Vegas leading 82-77.The Indiana star returned before play resumed andshowed an official her bloody mouthwhile protesting the no-call. She remained in the game as the Aces pulled away in the closing minutes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCaitlin Clark reacts after being hurt during the second half of the Indiana Fever’s Game 3 playoff loss to the Las Vegas Aces on Thursday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Steve Marcus/APEarlier, Clark and Las Vegas’ Brianna Turner each picked up a technical foul just more than three minutes in The Fever were huddling on the court when Turner worked her way into the group, only to be shoved out by Clark.Early in the second quarter, Indiana coach Stephanie White was called for a technical while arguing that Turner brought down Lexie Hull, who instead picked up the foul.The Aces threatened to run away from Indiana in the third quarter, taking a 67-55 lead before going cold over the final 4:32 and making just one shot. The Fever twice cut their deficit to two points in the fourth to make Las Vegas sweat out the ending.Aces forward Stephanie Talbot, who started all but one game this season, did not play because of a leg injury and was replaced by Jewell Loyd, who scored 11 points. Talbot averaged 8.5 points and 3.5 rebounds in the first two games of the series.Explore more on these topicsWNBACaitlin ClarkLas Vegas AcesIndiana FeverShareReuse this content

title: Braves power past Phillies in Game 3 to book NLDS showdown with Dodgers | MLB | The Guardian
description: Michael Harris II, Ozzie Albies and Matt Olson homer as Atlanta beat Philadelphia 6-2 to win their NL Wild Card Series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Michael Harris II, Ozzie Albies and Matt Olson homer as Atlanta beat Philadelphia 6-2 to win their NL Wild Card Series
Content: Atlanta Braves second baseman Ozzie Albies celebrates his fourth-inning home run with Austin Riley during Game 3 of the National League wildcard series.Photograph: Mike Zarrilli/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAtlanta Braves second baseman Ozzie Albies celebrates his fourth-inning home run with Austin Riley during Game 3 of the National League wildcard series.Photograph: Mike Zarrilli/UPI/ShutterstockMLBBraves power past Phillies in Game 3 to book NLDS showdown with DodgersHarris hits three-run homer in decisive Game 3Kerr throws 3 1/3 scoreless innings for AtlantaBraves advance to face two-time champion DodgersAgenciesThu 1 Oct 2026 23.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Harris II hit a three-run homer in the first inning, Ray Kerr threw 3 1/3 scoreless innings and the Atlanta Braves beat thePhiladelphia Phillies6-2 on Thursday night in the decisive Game 3 of their National League wildcard series.Ozzie Albies hit a two-run homer in the fourth and Matt Olson added a solo shot in the seventh for the Braves, who advance to a best-of-five Division Series against the two-time defending World Series champion Los Angeles Dodgers.The Braves won a postseason series for the first time since winning the 2021 World Series and earned their first playoff series win against the Phillies. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.Phillies right-hander Aaron Nola was pulled after allowing three runs in 1 2/3 innings. Nola walked Ronald Acuña Jr and Matt Olson with one out in the first before giving up the homer to Harris, who hit into two double plays in Wednesday’s 4-3 loss in 10 innings, which forced Thursday night’s game.Kerr made his postseason debut in only his fourth career start. Braves manager Walt Weiss wanted a left-hander to face Phillies left-handed hitters Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper at least once.Kerr allowed only one hit – to Schwarber in the first – and one walk – to Schwarber in the fourth. Right-hander Grant Holmes followed Kerr and allowed one run in two innings to earn the win.Kerr left to a standing ovation from the sellout crowd and acknowledged the cheers by lifting his arm as he approached the dugout.Left-hander Chris Sale, the starter in Atlanta’s 5-3 win in Tuesday’s series opener, struck out Harper to end the eighth and closed out the win in the ninth by striking out Bryan De La Cruz and pinch-hitter Otto Kemp.Phillies right-hander Zack Wheeler, the winning pitcher in Sunday’s 7-3 victory over Tampa Bay that clinched the wildcard spot, walked Austin Riley in the fourth before giving up Albies’ homer to right field that gave Atlanta a 5-0 lead. Wheeler allowed two runs in four innings. Jonathan Bowlan, Philadelphia’s fourth pitcher, gave up Olson’s homer to center field.Kerr, 32, flourished in the postseason spotlight. He pitched in only nine games after being recalled by Atlanta on 16 August. He underwent Tommy John surgery in 2024 and didn’t pitch in 2025.Philadelphia’s 2022 World Series loss to Houston began a streak of five straight postseason appearances with progressively quicker exits – the NL Championship Series, two NLDS exits and now the wildcard loss.The game drew a sellout crowd of 41,731 after the Braves fell short of sellouts in the first two games of the series, with school and work conflicting with the 2.15pm first pitch for many fans. Afternoon starts also hurt attendance in other Wild Card Series games this week.The announced attendance at Truist Park was 30,127 on Tuesday and 37,150 on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsMLBBaseballUS sportsAtlanta BravesPhiladelphia PhilliesShareReuse this content

title: Why boxing is still a box-office smash hit even as the sport’s popularity wanes | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Fighters have always provided rich material for stories on stage and screen and the appeal to audiences has not wavered
Author: Emma John
Headline: Fighters have always provided rich material for stories on stage and screen and the appeal to audiences has not wavered
Content: Michael B Jordan and Sylvester Stallone have spent plenty of time in the ring and in front of the camera.Photograph: Barry Wetcher/Warner Bros/AllstarView image in fullscreenMichael B Jordan and Sylvester Stallone have spent plenty of time in the ring and in front of the camera.Photograph: Barry Wetcher/Warner Bros/AllstarBoxingWhy boxing is still a box-office smash hit even as the sport’s popularity wanesEmma JohnFighters have always provided rich material for stories on stage and screen and the appeal to audiences has not waveredFri 2 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 04.58 EDTShareThree of my greatest joys in life are watching sport, going to the theatre and playing violin. So it felt almost embarrassing to discover a classic play that combined all three, yet I’d never heard of it before. To be fair, Golden Boy has not been performed in the UK in more than 40 years and its curious premise may be one of the reasons.Written in 1937, it’s about a gifted young violinist in Depression-era America who also has a talent for boxing and is lured away from music by the pursuit of fame and money in the ring. In the current London production he is played by Josh O’Connor, who Knives Out fans have seen with his fists up as a boxer turned priest inWake Up Dead Man. O’Connor is no less convincing on stage than on film, attacking a heavy bag with the kind of power that does indeed make you worry for his precious hands. Nor is that ab definition entirely the work of a makeup artist.Quips, slights and a surprise twist: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury come face to faceRead moreA drama about a fatal choice between a future as struggling musician or stone-cold killer may seem unlikely, perhaps to the point of absurdity. It didn’t feel so in the room. For a start, playwright Clifford Odets, one of the foundational voices of American theatre, was reflecting a time when New York life was bleak, opportunities were few and boxing presented a mirage of escape from poverty. Equally, it was clear we were watching a kind of allegory. As our hero finds his feet inside the ropes, he is losing his more tender self and the chance of a quieter contentment.Boxing has always provided rich material for stories on stage and screen. There are more Hollywood movies about boxing than any other sport. Writers, directors and performers are endlessly drawn to it, despite the common belief, as held in Odets’s play, that an artistic nature is in opposition to physical violence. Perhaps part of the appeal is the way a fighter in the ring resembles the protagonist in a Greek tragedy, a human figure stripped down to its rawest state – facing destiny and learning the limits of autonomy. Perhaps it’s the performance potential of the choreographed ballet across the canvas as bodies duck, dodge, dance and explosively collide.Whatever the reason, it appears you can load a boxing narrative with any amount and variety of subtext, psychodrama or heavyweight (pun intended) themes. Thus it is possible to have an Odets play set in the grim exploitative fight-world of the 1930s that is an excoriating critique of capitalism and the dark dangers of the American Dream, but also to have Ron Howard’sCinderella Man. The 2005 film, in which Russell Crowe portrays the real-life James J Braddock during his title fight against Max Baer, manages to turn the exact same environment into a feelgood fairytale of muscular Christianity.View image in fullscreenRussell Crowe portrayed James J Braddock during his title fight against Max Baer in Cinderella Man.Photograph: Universal/Sportsphoto/AllstarIs it the fight game’s complex, even ambivalent, ethics that have kept dramatists coming back?Alfred Hitchcock, that master not just of suspense but of moral ambiguity, loved boxing: his only self-penned film, The Ring, came out 99 years ago this month. It is a silent black-and-white number, the kind where women wear cloche hats and circular eyeliner, and people’s limbs leap jankily about between frames. But it is still notable for its realistic fight scenes – the lead actor, Carl Brisson, had been a Danish and European champion – and for the director’s use of pioneering point-of-view camerawork to show a fighter sliding into a concussion.Hitchcock’s protagonist was a wannabe adulterer. In the 1940s, a slew of noirs found the boxing world an ideal backdrop for tales of vice and viciousness – Body and Soul, Champion, The Set-Up.Stanley Kubrick’s second feature-length film, Killer’s Kiss, belongs to the same genre and the tagline on the original poster wasn’t pulling any punches either – “Her Soft Mouth Was The Road to Sin-Smeared Violence!”Then there’s Martin Scorsese. HisRaging Bull, generally considered the acme of boxing movies, remains a brutal watch, portraying its real-life subject, Jake LaMotta, as an abusive and pathological antihero. Scorsese hadn’t wanted to make the film – it was his friend Robert De Niro who was fascinated by LaMotta’s self-destructive story and the physical transformation he would have to take on to tell it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRobert De Niro played Jake LaMotta, an abusive and pathological antihero in Raging Bull.Photograph: Maximum Film/AlamyThere, too, lies a huge part of boxing’s longevity in drama – the ultimate challenge it presents for actors. It is almost impossible to fake a boxer’s physique, especially on the unforgiving cinema screen: Daniel Day-Lewis, Jake Gyllenhaal, Will Smith and Hilary Swank, the big-names happily put themselves through months of training hell and daily sparring to prove their commitment to authenticity. Mark Wahlberg, a boxing nut, had a ring built in his home and honed his craft for five years before shootingThe Fighter. You have got to feel sorry for the guy that it was his co-star Christian Bale who ended up with the Oscar.Michael B Jordan, star of the Creed franchise, describes the process of making the films as like “therapy”, because he gets to immerse himself so completely in his role. “I like living like a fighter, training like a fighter,” he said. “I’ve broken my hand a few times doing this movie. Hands swollen. Like, I wanna feel it. I want to go home and ache.” Sylvester Stallone’s contribution to boxing, meanwhile, has earned him a place in its international hall of fame.If you want proof of how circular the relationship between the sport and its fictional depiction has become, look no further. Stallone’s 1976 script for Rocky was inspired by the bout between Chuck Wepner and Muhammad Ali the year before. In 2016, Liev Schreiber played Wepner in the arthouse biopicThe Bleeder. Next month, we will see the fight onscreen in Stallone’s own biopic,I Play Rocky. It is an extraordinary truth that as boxing’s own popularity has declined, its appeal to audiences at one remove has never wavered.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsBoxingSport filmscommentShareReuse this content

title: Manchester City’s England players are worried about their futures, admits Tuchel | England | The Guardian
description: England head coach Thomas Tuchel said the Manchester City players in his squad were concerned for their futures
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: England head coach Thomas Tuchel said the Manchester City players in his squad were concerned for their futures
Content: Thomas Tuchel said the Manchester City scandal was a big talking point in the England camp.Photograph: Antonio Bronić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel said the Manchester City scandal was a big talking point in the England camp.Photograph: Antonio Bronić/ReutersEnglandManchester City’s England players are worried about their futures, admits Tuchel‘It is of course a topic and we speak about it at dinner’Head coach has right-back dilemma for game in CroatiaJacob Steinbergin RijekaFri 2 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel has suggested Manchester City’s England contingent are worried about the clubbeing found guiltyof breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.Tuchel, who said he would be prepared to keep picking City players if they were relegated, revealed the case had been a major topic of conversation in theEnglandcamp before the Nations League game against Croatia. The head coach said there had been discussions during meals and delivered an honest response after being asked whether the situation had become a distraction.Pickford in spotlight against Croatia with England position under threat from TraffordRead more“If I say now it’s not then I can just speak for myself, which would be totally narrow-minded,” Tuchel said. “I think it is a distraction. It is. Let’s say it is a subject. If it’s a distraction, I don’t know.“It is of course a topic and we speak about it at dinner and at a table of eight or 12 people. We speak about it at breakfast. I know the Man City players get a lot of messages and phone calls and feedback about it.“Are they worried or concerned? I think that would be a very human reaction if you don’t know what’s going on for the club that you signed. They’re still young. They’re ambitious. They’re told they are totally innocent and don’t know what’s going on. It is a subject.“I am again not sure if it’s a distraction. I don’t see it when I see them in my meetings. I don’t see it how they behave with other teammates, and I don’t see it in training being a distraction. But it’s a topic. How can’t it be?”The Football Association blocked a subsequent question to Tuchel on whether the City case represented a danger to English football. City maintain their innocence and on Friday announced an appeal against the verdict.For Tuchel, the focus is on his squad. He selected three City players for this camp: Elliot Anderson, Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly, who has withdrawn injured.
