Interchangeable efforts I’ve tried in the past have suffered from insufficiently strong motors, so they haven’t been able to successfully transmit vibrations throughout each attachment, especially longer/larger ones. Love Not War is mounting an admirable battle against that challenge, however.It’s a shame that …at more than £50 a pop, amassing a collection of heads will cost you a pretty penny – although the brand will plant a tree for each one sold.Speeds:fourVibe patterns:sevenPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:two years, and Love Not War will repair toys to keep them alive for as long as possibleLove Not WarMayafrom£54.99£54.99 for base at SheSpot£54.99 for head at SheSpotWhat we loveRecycled aluminium build; interchangeable headsWhat we don’t loveAlternative heads are expensiveFor more, read19 self-care treats for the perfect pick-me-upBest soft and sensual option:Smile Makers the FirefighterSmile MakersThe Firefighterfrom£39.95£39.95 at Beauty Bay£49.95 at Victoria HealthWhat we loveFlickers gently but has a pointy end to do the jobWhat we don’t loveIts pink colour won’t be for everyoneView image in fullscreen£39.95 at Beauty Bay£49.95 at Victoria HealthBullets are often designed to treat the genitals like a game of darts: if the clitoris is the bullseye, they aim to hit it dead on. The Firefighter instead approaches stimulation more like a curling match: gently brushing, sweeping and edging towards a climax.Why we love itThe fluttering, flickering flame-shaped head will suit those who prefer a slow, delicate buildup before switching to the more traditional, targeted “pointy finger” part of the toy.It’s a shame that …it only comes in pink.The Surfer, another Smile Makers bullet, is a refreshingly unusual zesty orange.Speeds:fourVibe patterns:twoPower:rechargeableRun time:three hoursCharge time:two to two-and-a-half hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:two yearsSmile MakersThe Firefighterfrom£39.95£39.95 at Beauty Bay£49.95 at Victoria HealthWhat we loveFlickers gently but has a pointy end to do the jobWhat we don’t loveIts pink colour won’t be for everyoneBest budget bullet:The Rocks Off RO-90Rocks OffRO-90from£15.99£15.99 at Boots£17.99 at SinfulWhat we loveAffordable; wide range of shapes and coloursWhat we don’t loveOne-button controls are tediousView image in fullscreen£15.99 at Boots£17.99 at SinfulRocks Off makes a whole shooting range of cheap-and-cheerful battery-powered bullets. Take your pick of pointed, rounded, angled or lipstick-shaped tip; select a slick gloss, powdery matt or silicone finish; and choose from more colours than the fabric of Joseph’s dreamcoat, including one that changes from purple to pink in response to body heat.Why we love itIt’s a fair amount of bang for very few bucks. I singled out the RO-90 as my best budget buy because the AAA battery it takes is much easier to source than the N-size variety insidethe smaller RO-80 model. The slightly longer shaft makes it better suited to use for penetrative play, too, if that’s your bag.Hats off to Rocks Off as well for its collaboration with disability charity Enhance the UK to developa truly accessible toy range, Quest. A 5% share of sales from that collection goes back to the charity.It’s a shame that …single-button controls mean you have to cycle all the way through speeds/pulses to change them. I also question how the shiny metallic finishes might stand up to long-term cleaning.Speeds:threeVibe patterns:sevenPower:1 x AAA batteryRun time:three hours 30 minutesWaterproof:yesWarranty:two yearsRocks OffRO-90from£15.99£15.99 at Boots£17.99 at SinfulWhat we loveAffordable; wide range of shapes and coloursWhat we don’t loveOne-button controls are tediousThe best rabbit vibratorsAt a glanceBest rabbit vibrator overallJe JoueHera Flex£99 at Je JoueBest for temperature titillationLovehoneyGlow Bunny£51.99 at AmazonBest for air pulse stimulationWomanizerDuo 2£189 at WomanizerBest for an innovative shaftSatisfyerAir Pump Bunny 1£36.99 at AmazonBest sustainable rabbitNatural Love CompanySenna£99.95 at the Natural Love CompanyBest new animalSnail VibeCurve£109.99 at AmazonBest budget rabbitAnn SummersSelf Love Dual Simulation£55 at Ann SummersBest old-school throwback rabbitLovehoneyJessica Rabbit£34.98 at AmazonBest rabbit vibrator overall:Je Joue Hera FlexJe JoueHera Flexfrom£99£99 at Je Joue£115 at SuperdrugWhat we loveFlexible and poseable to fit every bodyWhat we don’t loveBig jump between lowest power levelsView image in fullscreen£99 at Je Joue£115 at SuperdrugThe Hera Flex is such a good problem-solver, it could probably win an algebra contest.Since everyone’s anatomy is different and distances between vaginas and clitorises vary, a frequent dilemma with rabbits is that once the shaft is inserted, the external stimulator doesn’t quite rest on the right spot. Many toys are too rigid to allow sufficient bending and angle adjustment to solve this issue.Why we love itThis Je Joue genius solves that: it’s as flexible as a yoga master, and both parts of it are poseable, allowing you to easily customise how it curves to fit your bits. Another irritating rabbit habit is that the “ears” intended to tickle either side of the clitoris can pinch, poke or catch against sensitive flesh, depending on how your body happens to be built. Here, the Hera is a hero once more, replacing the traditional bunny head with a plush, spongy, smooth “thumb”. If you’re someone with a more frilly clitoral hood or labia that gets painfully pulled by rabbit ears, this could be a real thumbs up. A quality, thoughtfully re-engineered rabbit reboot.It’s a shame that …there’s a bit of a jump between the first two power levels. A steadier climb would be preferable. The squishiness of the Hera Flex won’t suit folks who prefer firmer pressure on their hotspots, either. But as so often in the world of sex toys, that’s rather like saying, “people who prefer raspberries shouldn’t choose this banana”; it’s a question of taste, rather than a product being bad.Speeds:fiveVibe patterns:sevenPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:one hour and 30 minutesWarranty:one yearJe JoueHera Flexfrom£99£99 at Je Joue£115 at SuperdrugWhat we loveFlexible and poseable to fit every bodyWhat we don’t loveBig jump between lowest power levelsBest for temperature titillation:Lovehoney Glow BunnyLovehoneyGlow Bunnyfrom£51.99£79.99 at Lovehoney£51.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid rabbit with unique temperature play tipWhat we don’t lovePower levels won’t knock your socks offView image in fullscreen£79.99 at Lovehoney£51.99 at AmazonIf you just want to use this toy as an old-school rabbit, it’s a solid choice … but it also has new-fangled tricks up its sleeve.Why we love itThe temperature-play plate on the top of the shaft heats to 38C in less than two minutes, feeling almost like a warm tongue, and swiftly cools to 18C, giving a whole new meaning to “Netflix and chill”. I imagine the cold setting could be particularly enticing during sweltering summer nights, and it works nicely for nipple play, too.It’s a shame that …the power is perfectly acceptable, but not perfect for the power-hungry.Speeds:threeVibe patterns:fourPower:rechargeableRun time:one hourCharge time:three hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:100 daysLovehoneyGlow Bunnyfrom£51.99£79.99 at Lovehoney£51.99 at AmazonWhat we loveSolid rabbit with unique temperature play tipWhat we don’t lovePower levels won’t knock your socks offBest for air pulse stimulation:Womanizer Duo 2WomanizerDuo 2from£189£189 at Womanizer£189 at BootsWhat we loveDual-action air pulse tech; clever automatic modesWhat we don’t loveTakes more practice than similar, cheaper productsView image in fullscreen£189 at Womanizer£189 at BootsAdmittedly, this looks more like something Star Trek’s Captain Picard should be at the helm of than a conventional rabbit. Rather than stimulating the clitoris with vibrations, the Duo 2 uses pulses of air to create a throbbing, sucking effect. Womanizer was the first to introduce this technology to the adult market in 2014, when it represented one of the most groundbreaking innovations in years.Why we love itThe firm continues to be a pioneer. This toy boasts multiple proprietary features, including “Smart Silence”: it will only turn on when in contact with skin. This means the battery life is preserved,andyou don’t have to fumble to switch it off in a panic if your intimacy is interrupted.An Autopilot mode alternates between surprise pulse patterns and intensities to prevent masturbation from becoming predictable, while the Afterglow setting helps you gradually wind down post-climax, rather than simply switching off.It’s a shame that …the shape takes getting used to, and there are now more intuitive (and affordable) suction and vibration rabbit toys available. That said, I believe the Duo 2 is worth mastering due to its god-tier-level exclusive features.Speeds:14Vibe patterns:10Power:rechargeableRuntime:two hoursCharge time:two hoursWaterproof:yesWarranty:five yearsWomanizerDuo 2from£189£189 at Womanizer£189 at BootsWhat we loveDual-action air pulse tech; clever automatic modesWhat we don’t loveTakes more practice than similar, cheaper productsBest for an innovative shaft:Satisfyer Air Pump Bunny 1SatisfyerAir Pump Bunny 1from£36.99£49.99 at Sinful£36.99 at AmazonWhat we loveInflating shaft with a whopping warrantyWhat we don’t loveLoud inflating noises may have deflating effectsView image in fullscreen£49.99 at Sinful£36.99 at AmazonSatisfyer is known for two things. First, making excellent-quality, more affordable “dupes” of aspirational high-end sex toys – almost like an Aldi version of Lelo and co. Second, and in contrast to the first, rolling outvastmultitudes of its own novel inventions, including this Air Pump Bunny.Why we love itIt sports an inflatable shaft that can be enlarged by up to 15mm in diameter at the touch of a button, producing a “filling” sensation that some find mind-blowing. This could be just the ticket if your orgasm is intensified by the presence of a girthy internal toy, giving your vaginal muscles something to clench around as the waves of climax hit (more common than is discussed), especially if you need to build up to having something wide inside you. In addition to his links to love and lust, Saint Valentine is also the patron saint of beekeeping, so he would feel quite at home amid the cacophony of buzzing that soundtracked the production of this article.I discounted any products not made from body-safe materials, such as porous jellies that can harbour bacteria and dirt, or plastics containing phthalates, which have been linked to cancer and hormonal interference. I considered things such as whether each device lived up to the claims made by its manufacturer; how easy it was to position and control; how fast it charged and how long the battery lasted, where relevant; and how attractive, adaptable, powerful and comfortable it was.What Ididn’tdo was automatically label a toy as a “holy grail” or an “almighty fail” if it didn’t happen to float my idiosyncratic boat, or provide what I personally need to reach orgasm, through no inherent fault of its own. Deciding upon the “best” vibrator is highly subjective, so I’ve tried to explain how different items might suit different folks.When making your own considerations, useful questions to ask include:Do I prefer gentle or potent vibrations (or both)? What styles of touch delight me, and do I want external or internal stimulation (or both)?What shape and size of toy will suit my body and my tastes?Do I want something simple, straightforward and intuitive, or experimental/multifunctional/tech-enabled?What materials and textures feel inviting to me?A note on volume: some reviews rate toys on how quiet they are, but I’ve NEVER met a vibe that’s as near-silent as it says it is. For that reason, I’ve only pointed out when a toy is notably loud enough to sound like you’ve rented it from a builders’ merchant.In almost all cases, you do have to put your hand in your pocket if you want the best. Strong motors, neat details and high-performance designs don’t tend to come cheap. I believe pleasure should be accessible to all, though, so there’s at least one budget option included in each category. It’ll have some compromises, but it should give you plenty of “Ooh!” for not much dough.Can vibrators decrease your sensitivity?Let me reassure you: using vibrators will not cause nerve damage to your genitals. However, if, over a prolonged period, youalwaysreach for a toy when masturbating – particularly if it’s a high-strength model like a mains-powered wand – you may inadvertently condition your body to become used to intense stimulation. Much like a curry fan who’s been mainlining vindaloo and is then served a masala, the comparatively gentle feelings provided by fingers or partners may begin to feel less spicy, and you may struggle to orgasm without the potent or pinpointed vibrations with which you’ve become familiar.A similar problem arises for people with penises who hold themselves very tightly and use rough motions during solo play. American sex educator Dan Savage nicknamed this “the death grip”, and it can cause erectile dysfunction and difficulties ejaculating via the relative tenderness of intercourse.Luckily, solutions are simple. First: chill out on your vibrator use, to give your body time to reappraise the delights of the delicate. You may want to try a period of abstinence, where you return to manual masturbation without grabbing a toy. Or if you’ve been cranking your toy’s power straight up to 11, try being a little less Spın̈al Tap and experimenting with softer speeds and patterns. Lubricant can help too, by cushioning sensitive tissues a little.If you find that sex without toys simply doesn’t feel as good, another option is to involve your toys in sex. Contrary to many people’s fears, vibrators can’t replace the profound intimacy and thrill of being with another human being, but they can vastlyenhanceshared experiences – they’re complementary co-pilots, not competitors.If you’re someone who feels threatened by toys, it may help to think of them as specialist equipment. You wouldn’t feel emasculated or belittled if you had to equip yourself with an axe to cut down a tree instead of just using your bare hands, right? Instead, it’s more impressive to learn to wield that equipment like a pro, whether you want to chop timber or set your partner’s night alight. Using the right apparatus the right way is the fastest route to successfully starting a fire. Ask your lover to show you how they like the toy to be positioned, and be eager to take on any feedback they give.What to do when your old toys finally dieIf all this toy talk has reminded you that you have enough bad vibes, shot bullets and dead rabbits gathering dust in your bedside cabinet to rival Watership Down, you’re not alone. Research conducted in 2025 by tech refurbishment specialists Back Market revealed that 15% of people keep old and broken sex toys stored ad infinitum because they’re embarrassed to throw them away. One in three surreptitiously chucks them in the household bin – even though anything with batteries, a plug or a charging port can be recycled. An unfortunate side-effect of increased sexual liberation and toy ownership is that worn-out erotic electricals are worsening the planet’s burgeoning e-waste problem, and valuable materials within them, including aluminium, gold, copper, lithium and steel, are being lost to landfill.If your ancient wand vibe is now more tragic than magic, head toRecycle Your Electricals, enter your postcode, then select Vibrator from the drop-down menu (yes, it’s a legitimate category). You’ll be given recycling instructions specific to your location; some councils will even collect your raunchy rubbish directly from your door. I’d wrap it in a bag, mind, for discretion. The binman doesn’t need to have the dirt onallyour filth.Alix Fox is an award-winning writer and broadcaster specialising in sexual wellbeing and culture, with 20 years of experience in receiving dick pics sent not to titillate, but because the worried texter wants an informed opinion on a weird lump/rash/wart. She’s currently a PhD researcher at UCL’s Institute for Global Health, specialising in HIV prevention and care. Sherents a storage unit to house her collection of erotic apparatus. title: ‘If you can’t hold it, you don’t own it’: why media fans want to escape algorithms with CDs, DVDs and vinyl | Media | The Guardian
description: People describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choices
Author: Jane Clinton
Headline: People describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choices
Content: Some people have begun to buy secondhand CDs and DVDs from charity shops to wean themselves off subscription services.Photograph: Charday Penn/GettyView image in fullscreenSome people have begun to buy secondhand CDs and DVDs from charity shops to wean themselves off subscription services.Photograph: Charday Penn/GettyMedia‘If you can’t hold it, you don’t own it’: why media fans want to escape algorithms with CDs, DVDs and vinylPeople describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choicesJane ClintonFri 2 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor some, it is the security of knowing they have a physical copy of their favourite films and music, free from algorithms, interruptions and the vagaries of streaming. For others, it is the sound of needle on vinyl, the click of a cassette player and the ability to interact with a physical format.We asked people if they were moving back to CDs, DVDs, vinyl and older formats to escape algorithmically curated content. Here are some of their responses.‘I missed the physical connection with music’View image in fullscreenAsh says discovering new music for yourself requires more work and effort.Photograph: Dylan Odedra/Guardian CommunityAsh, 52, a university lecturer from Cornwall, says he initially embraced streaming but has since tempered that enthusiasm.“Algorithms make great suggestions, but it feels like you catch a lot of small fish (OK, bands),” he says. “Reading music magazines and artist recommendations and discovering new music for yourself requires more work and effort … it feels like catching the bigger fish.”Recently, he has returned to buying and listening to physical media. He says he has amassed more than 5,000 records and CDs from 1990 to 2009.“Technology and streaming felt liberating for a person who has a deep and wide music collection and a bad back. I stopped buying and streamed,” he says, but adds: “I spent more time making playlists than listening to music; I lost the ability to listen to a whole album and missed the physical connection with music.“I listen to records as an activity, but listen through tech more passively. It’s more like wallpaper than a work of art.”‘We scour flea markets and secondhand shops for shows and movies’CJ, 55, a compliance manager from Atlanta, says she decided to return to physical media when shows she liked began disappearing from streaming services.“HBO removed about 200 episodes of Sesame Street in 2022, so we realised any media we wanted to continue to watch or listen to could be gone, and we’d have no way to get it back,” she says. “As the saying goes, if you can’t hold it, you don’t own it, and we firmly agree with this.“There are so many shows that aren’t on streaming platforms that we want to rewatch. We scour flea markets and secondhand shops for shows and movies that are hard to find. We have also continued to buy CDs.“When access to media is so easy to cut off, it makes sense to return to owning what you can, so no one can take it away from you.”‘I wanted to support musicians’View image in fullscreenRuth’s CD collection has its own ‘walk-in closet’Photograph: Ruth/Guardian CommunitySpotify quickly “bored” Ruth, 67, a retired professor from Michigan, but there were other reasons behind her move to CDs and DVDs.“Most of all, I wanted to own my music and support the musicians, so I own 5,300 CDs; they have their own walk-in closet,” she says. “Owning my own books, music, and photos (no iCloud) has always seemed normal to me, and, increasingly, prudent.She adds: “No algorithm is as creative as a well-stocked human brain alive to its actual surroundings.”Ruth also rents physical film titles by mail from a store in Seattle. “We retired to a rural area with internet unreliable for streaming that wouldn’t sustain a movie without interruptions and buffering. We can stream music from the internet, although even then the connection will conk out every once in a while.”‘Now I don’t have to share my data with a company’This summer, Antonio, 40, began buying secondhand CDs from a charity shop in an attempt to get off music subscription services.“I have a ritual now,” says the software engineer, who lives in Reading. “Twice a month I buy between one and 10 CDs – depending on what is available.“I decided I didn’t want to rely on a subscription any more and have to deal with price rises, and now I don’t have to share my data – both personal information such as my name, bank account details, location, and my listening history – with a company.“Nowadays we hand over so much of our data (intentionally or unintentionally) to big corporations that, if I can reduce it in any way, I’m more than happy to do so.”‘Sometimes I’m ‘out of the loop’, but I prefer it’View image in fullscreenQuinn buys tapes from bands to support the artists.Photograph: Quinn/Guardian CommunityQuinn, 26, began collecting cassette tapes last year and “quickly fell in love with it”.He works nights and weekends, leaving him little time to go to concerts. “Buying tapes from bands gave me a way to engage with and support them, despite not being able to see their shows,” says Quinn, who works in food delivery and lives in Washington.“I really appreciate the format’s restrictions. There’s the routine of interacting with the tape and equipment to play it, the quirks that come with analogue tech and, of course, being able to share music with people by handing them a tape rather than a Spotify link.“My switch has definitely come with the desire to choose what I’m engaging with. Rather than having content presented to me, I’m seeking it out for myself, or finding it through friends, and that’s a huge part of being low-tech. Sometimes I’m ‘out of the loop’, but I prefer it.”‘I love the slowness of the setup to see the films’Tim’s young and adult children all enjoy watching films on older formats.“In Sweden many people have a summer house,” says the 61-year-old academic, who lives in Stockholm. “Ours, on the mainland, a 45-minute drive from Stockholm, located in the southern end of the Swedish archipelago, contains a video projector from around 2010, a DVD player, and the collection of DVDs watched by my big kids when they were small.“The biggest luxury for my small kids is when the cables are rigged, the choice of DVD made, and they sit through five minutes of ‘coming soon on Disney’ before we press play on Shrek or whatever the film is.”Tim says the “aged DVDs” often need a clean, as sticky fingers over the years have left their mark.“I love this middle stage between the digital and the analogue, and the slowness of the setup to see the films. Next step is to open the trunk containing my (younger) partner’s childhood VHS collection. We’ll see where that goes.”‘I feel less controlled’View image in fullscreenSophie says she feels less analysed watching DVDs and listening to CDs.Photograph: Sophie/Guardian CommunitySophie, 32, a librarian from Los Angeles, does stream music, but “mostly listens to CDS”. She also often watches DVDs from her own collection or checks them out from the library.She is “not a fan” of algorithms, something that informed her move to CDs and DVDs. “I enjoy watching DVDs and listening to CDs because nobody sees what I’m doing and they’re not analysing it. It feels less overwhelming to browse physical versions. I also feel less controlled.”Explore more on these topicsMediaMusic streamingTV streamingSpotifyDigital music and audioTelevisionInternetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely | Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya | The Guardian
description: Refugees from third countries are being sent to Equatorial Guinea, where they are often sent back to the very countries they fled
Author: Tutu Alicante
Headline: Refugees from third countries are being sent to Equatorial Guinea, where they are often sent back to the very countries they fled
Content: ‘Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them.’Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/APView image in fullscreen‘Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them.’Photograph: Monika Pronczuk/APOpinionTrump administrationTrump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomelyTutu Alicanteand Uzra ZeyaRefugees from third countries are being sent to Equatorial Guinea, where they are often sent back to the very countries they fledFri 2 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTShareFor nearly a year, the Hotel Bamy in Malabo,Equatorial Guinea, has been Adam’s prison. He is confined alone to a hotel room, under constant watch by the security officers and soldiers of a notoriously oppressive regime who control his movements. Not long ago, they barged into his room, handcuffed and beat him, and warned him not to tell anyone. There is no cell to point to, no charges or formal sentence, and nothing on paper to document his plight.Adam, 26, has chosen not to share his real name or even his country of origin out of fear for his safety. He fled indefinite, forced military conscription in his home country after enduring abuse during his military service.Adam sought safety in the United States. A US immigration judge heard his case, found that he would probably face persecution if forced to return to his country of origin, and issued a formal order shielding him from removal there. Then, in November 2025, the United States sent him to Equatorial Guinea, a country he had never set foot in and where torture reportedly occurs in every prison nationwide, according to the most recentstate department human rights report. Adam, and the other men onboard the flight, were told they were being transferred to another US detention facility. It was only midway through the 13 hour and 10 minute flight that they found out – while shackled – that they were headed toward Equatorial Guinea.None of this is happening in a vacuum. In November, the Trump administrationrepurposed $7.5mto pay the government of Equatorial Guinea to accept third country nationals from the United States, a275% foreign assistance increase and departure from longstanding US policyagainst direct provision of aid to a deeply corrupt and abusive regime. Congress appropriated these taxpayer funds for humanitarian assistance for refugees in dire need – money that is now used to detain, shackle and eventually send refugees back to the countries they fled. Since then, the US government has forcibly transferred at least 65 third country nationals to Equatorial Guinea. US immigration judges had granted protection to nearly all of these individuals due to the high risk of persecution or torture they face in their countries of origin. Yet one by one, Equatorial Guinea has been sending them back to harm in the very places from which they fled.Six people refused to get off ICE deportation plane – now they’re held in limbo in Equatorial GuineaRead moreIn the past few weeks, in retaliation for speaking out against the detention conditions and police violence, police in Equatorial Guineaviolently assaulted and arrestedtwo of the refugees, witnesses and lawyers say, including Ahmed Soliman, an Egyptian man from Arizona who has lived in the United States since he was three years old, and Samson Birhane. Today, they remain in police custody, detained incommunicado.This is part of an escalatingschemeby the Trump administration to send immigrants and refugees to countries around the world where they have no connection and often face grave harm. In Equatorial Guinea, it is also fueling the corruption and impunity our organizations have spent decades documenting and countering.Equatorial Guinea’s government and ruling family are, by any measure,among the most corrupt on earth. About a decade ago, the US justice department settled a civil forfeiture case against the country’s vice-president, Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, or “Teodorín”. He forfeited a $30m Malibu mansion, a Ferrari and Michael Jackson memorabilia.Some governments have rightly taken serious action to restrain Teodorín’s corruption, such as the sanctions the UK governmentimposedon him in 2021. Yet last September, the Trump administration did the opposite, and quietly paused corruption-related visa restrictions that had prevented Teodorín from traveling to the United States, clearing the way for him tomeet with Christopher Landau, the US deputy secretary of state, before the deal to accept non-Equatoguineans removed from the United States.In addition to these funds, the deal affords Teodorin something he has long sought: legitimacy and access in Washington DC.We are seeing that access to US policymakers deepening in real time.Last week, Teodorín was back in New York, meeting with Landau again, this time at the United Nations, where they celebrated what the government of Equatorial Guinea referred to as a positive evolution of the bilateral relationship. They discussed expanding cooperation beyond energy to banking, trade investment, security and diplomacy.Our organizations have worked for years to demand accountability for rampant corruption in Equatorial Guinea, and now, to fight for the refugees and torture victims being unlawfully sent there. After building the evidentiary dossier that led to UK sanctions, EG Justice is now challenging Equatorial Guinea’s participation in the US deportation scheme before the African Commission on People’s and Human Rights, while working with local attorneys to offer legal and humanitarian aid. In July, the African Commission on Human and People’s rightsissued an emergency ruling,ordering the government of Equatorial Guinea not to send people back to danger in their home country – a ruling that the government has ignored since, sending four people back to the very places from which they had sought, and received, protection.Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers sayRead moreHuman Rights First (HRF), for its part, together with partner organizations, successfully challenged the third-country deportation policy in federal court, but the US supreme court has since intervened to allow these rapid third-country deportations to resume while it rules on the case. HRF also leads theICE Flight Monitorplatform, uncovering in real time hidden deportation flights to Equatorial Guinea and beyond, whilepartnering with Refugees Internationalto shed light on proliferating and often opaque US third-country forced transfer agreements with 35 countries.Time is of the essence, as Adam has been sick with malaria and typhoid fever since November. His second asylum claim, filed with Equatoguinean authorities in January, remains in indefinite limbo. The judge in the case told local counsel that he does not have authority to hear it, as the vice-president is in charge of these cases. The habeas corpus petition his lawyer filed also remains unanswered. Guards tell him repeatedly to “go back to your country,” the very outcome a US judge already ruled would put him at high risk of persecution.There is a clearcut, fair, and humane path forward. We are pressing for coordinated Magnitsky-style sanctions against senior Equatoguinean officials, including Teodorín, in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the European Union simultaneously, building on the evidentiary dossier the UK relied on in 2021. In the United States, Congress must exercise fully its oversight authority to end misappropriation of migration and refugee resettlement funds to finance arbitrary detention and chain refoulement – and, in effect, to reward torturers.Adam and everyone held at Hotel Bamy should be released and given the chance to have their asylum claims heard in a country capable of hearing them, or returned to live safely in the United States. They deserve the protection that was promised to them and is enshrined in US and international law.Tutu Alicante is founder and executive director of EG JusticeUzra Zeya is president and CEO of Human Rights FirstExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionEquatorial GuineaUS immigrationMigrationAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: AI weapons systems are already here. Algorithms must not decide who lives and dies | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: Israel’s conduct in Gaza shows the danger of using AI in warfare. Humans must remain at the center of wartime decisions
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: Israel’s conduct in Gaza shows the danger of using AI in warfare. Humans must remain at the center of wartime decisions
Content: ‘When AI is used for targeting, it brings a similar feigned omniscience to killing.’Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAView image in fullscreen‘When AI is used for targeting, it brings a similar feigned omniscience to killing.’Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)AI weapons systems are already here. Algorithms must not decide who lives and diesKenneth RothIsrael’s conduct in Gaza shows the danger of using AI in warfare. Humans must remain at the center of wartime decisionsFri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.10 EDTShareAs tech leaderswarnabout the threats of artificial intelligence, most conjure up images of AI agents runningamok, such as hacking systems used to run our critical infrastructure, banks or even militaries. Yet one serious danger is mentioned less frequently – the threatposedby AI–empowered lethal weapons. Fully autonomous versions of these weapons are colloquially known askiller robots.Israel’s conduct in Gaza shows that, in an important respect, such AI weapon systems are already here. An algorithm has beendeciding who lives and who dies.For more than a decade, governments have been meeting in Geneva to stop the development of autonomous AI weapons. In early September,128governments met to approve areportthat could serve as the foundation for a binding treaty.But a collection of lawyers sent by Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin teamed up towater it down. Notably, they weakened a provision that requires humans to review military targets developed by AI before a strike.Fully autonomous weapons remain the focus; the use of AI to determine targets for conventional weapons is not. At risk is the longstanding quest to maintain a “human in the loop” – that is, meaningful or effective “human control” of AI-empowered weaponry.For many people, talk of killer robots conjures up images of Arnold Schwarzenegger’sThe Terminator. I have often thought about the problem in the context of the Tahrir Square uprising at the height of the Arab spring that led to the ouster of the Egyptian president Hosni Mubarak.These aren’t AI firms, they’re defense contractors. We can’t let them hide behind their models | Avner GvaryahuRead moreMubarak’s fate wassealedwhen the Egyptian army made clear it wouldrefuseto fire on Egyptian protesters. But killer robots would have had no such qualms. If Mubarak had been able to deploy them, he might have stayed in power.The negotiators in Geneva are not even addressing this problem. The Trump-Putin lawyers made sure that the agreed reportreferredonly to war, not repression.Today, amid the drone warfare in eastern Ukraine,RussianandUkrainiantroops are experimenting with fully autonomous weapons to overcome jamming of the signals used to control drones. We can expect these nascent deployments to expand.Yet the “killer robot” metaphor is deceptive. If we look at targeting decisions more expansively, AI has already taken over. In Gaza, the Israeli military is using AI to target Palestinians.Israel has longmonitoredphone communications in that territory. After the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, Israel used an AI system called “Lavender” to uncover patterns that it equated with the phone of a Hamas operative. People whose phones AI determined met these criteria could be killed.Because it was easier to target suspects at home, a separate automated system called “Where’s Daddy?” tracked them there, meaning that their families were often killed too. There was no pretense that Hamas was using its operatives’ homes for military purposes. It was simplyeasierfor the AI system to find suspected Hamas fighters where they slept. The families were the collateral damage.Theoretically, a human remained in the loop because an AI-picked target was routed through intelligence officers who approved it and sent it to others who launched the attack. In fact, this human role was nominal.In the past, Israeli targeting decisions weresubjectto significant review. But in Israel’s killing spree that followed the Hamas attack, the intense demand for targets took precedence over such review.Israeli intelligence officers who received the AI selections routinely passed them to the attackers without second guessing. As one officerdescribed: “I would invest 20 seconds for each target at this stage, and do dozens of them every day. I had zero added-value as a human, apart from being a stamp of approval. It saved a lot of time.”From computer to killing, the human judgment exercised wasperfunctory– a “rubber stamp”. In essence, an algorithmplayedGod.One Israeli officersuggestedthe practice might be justified because AI makes better decisions than humans do. It is dispassionate, while people’s judgment can be clouded, such as by the animosity toward all Palestinians that some Israelis felt after the Hamas attack.As one Israeli soldierexplained: “I have much more trust in a statistical mechanism than a soldier who lost a friend two days ago. Everyone there, including me, lost people on October 7. The machine did it coldly. And that made it easier.”Yet AI algorithms are inevitably affected by human input. How much evidence is required to identify someone as a Hamas fighter? What margin of error is tolerated?The answer to such questions depends on the judgment of the AIprogrammersand their commanders – ordinary Israelis who might have devalued Palestinian civilian life in the fury that followed the Hamas attack. Even the Israeli militaryconcededthat about 10% of the human targets slated for assassination were not members of the Hamas military wing at all.The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, epitomized the heedless attitude toward Palestinian civilians when hesaid: “It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It’s not true, this rhetoric about civilians were not aware, not involved – it’s absolutely not true. They could’ve risen up, fought against that evil regime.”That same contempt contributed to the Israeli military’s shocking willingness to tolerate civilian deaths. The Israeli militarypermittedananticipated20dead for the killing of a mere suspected low-level Hamas fighter.Forget ‘superintelligence’: error-prone AI nearly sparked world war three this month | Timnit Gebru and Emily M BenderRead moreUnder the rule of proportionality, international humanitarian lawprohibitsa wartime attack if it “may be expected to cause incidental loss of civilian life … which would be excessive in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated”. Although international law doesn’t specify the number of civilian casualties that are acceptable in a given situation, virtuallyno legal expertconsiders Israel’s shocking 20-to-one ratio to be lawful.These arewar crimes. They reflect an appalling devaluing of Palestinian civilian life.Evoking for me Hannah Arendt’s “banality of evil”, ordinary soldiers became complicit in extraordinary cruelty by trusting what they call the “system”. The essence of that system remained people – thegeneralswho ordered its creation, the military lawyers who excused the unjustifiable, the programmers who tweaked the algorithm, the intelligence officers who passed on the computer-generated targets, and the soldiers who launched the attack.But part of what made it easier to trust the system was the pseudo-scientific precision of AI. We are all familiar with the breezy, authoritative tone of today’s chatbots. When AI is used for targeting, it brings a similar feigned omniscience to killing.When inevitably flawed human beings make decisions, they can expect others to challenge them. But AI makes it easier for us to defer to its judgments. That deference risks magnifying the human biases that inevitably infect any AI system.As we seek to curb killer robots, we should also remain attentive to AI that can lull us into complacency about other targeting. The International Committee of the Red Crosscallsit “automation bias”.To have meaningful human control of AI, we need not just nominal endorsement of its decisions. We need intense questioning of its product, and accountability for commanders when junior officers fall short.Only that skepticism has any hope of ensuring that soldiers who deploy AI remember that real human beings are at the end of the kill chain they enable. Even in war, people should never be snuffed out by the mechanical application of an algorithm.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaComputingGazaIsrael-Gaza warcommentShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike survived her execution attempt. Tennessee must not try again | Austin Sarat | The Guardian
description: What happened to Pike was gruesome. No one deserves what she went through, not even those who commit horrible crimes
Author: Austin Sarat
Headline: What happened to Pike was gruesome. No one deserves what she went through, not even those who commit horrible crimes
Content: ‘Whatever fate awaits Christa Pike, one thing is clear. The state of Tennessee should not be allowed to try to execute her again.’Photograph: Joe Howell/Knoxville News-Sentinel/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Whatever fate awaits Christa Pike, one thing is clear. The state of Tennessee should not be allowed to try to execute her again.’Photograph: Joe Howell/Knoxville News-Sentinel/ReutersOpinionCapital punishmentChrista Pike survived her execution attempt. Tennessee must not try againAustin SaratWhat happened to Pike was gruesome. No one deserves what she went through, not even those who commit horrible crimesFri 2 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTShareBotched executionsare nothing new in US history. In the era when hangings were common, some condemned people were decapitated. Later, when the electric chair was in vogue, every now and again, someone would catch fire during an electrocution. And nitrogen hypoxia, the US’s newest execution method, hasalready proven notoriously unreliable.But, of all of the ways we have tried to execute people, lethal injection has the worst track record. More than 8% of all lethal injection executionshave been botched. Most of them resulted when those charged with carrying them out could not find a usable vein.Last night, we entered uncharted territory when Christa PikesurvivedTennessee’s effort to execute her with lethal doses of pentobarbital. It was the first time someone received a drug intended to kill them but did not die.The Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherent | EditorialRead moreRobin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center,toldthe New York Times: “This event is the worst we’ve seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era … There is no precedent.”Moreover, there is almost no precedent for what should happen next.Whatever fate awaits Christa Pike, one thing is clear. The state ofTennesseeshould not be allowed to try to execute her again.Beyond that, it is time to give up on the fantasy that this country will ever be able to find an execution technology that is safe, reliable and humane. We have not found one yet, and we never will.What happened to Pike was gruesome. No one deserves what she went through, not even those who commit horrible crimes.Pike was sent to death row for one such crime. The Tennesseandescribesher crime this way. “Pike lured Slemmer to a wooded area near the University of Tennessee’s Agricultural Campus with the promise of marijuana. With the help of … [her boyfriend], Pike tortured Slemmer before beating her to death with a chunk of asphalt. A pentagram was also carved into her body.”Pike was barely 18 years old at the time. She was herself the victim of violence and abuse throughout her life.As the date of her execution drew near, Pikeclaimedthat it should not go forward, because using lethal injection on her would be cruel. Little did she know what would be in store for her.As allowed by its execution protocol, state officials in Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to be enough to end her life. However, as NBCnotes, instead of killing her, it left her “snoring” and complaining about pain, as well as “kicking her feet so often that she knocked off the sheets laid on her”.After the Tennessee governor, Bill Lee, was contacted, he authorized the execution team to stand down, and Pike was taken to a hospital.This is not the first time that Lee has received a call about an execution gone awry. In May, he had also agreed to stop the execution of Tony Carruthers when officialscouldn’t find a vein for a backup IV.Lee granted him a one-year reprieve.Now he and his colleagues in Tennessee will have to decide what to do about Pike. So far, he has onlycalleda halt to the one other execution scheduled in the state this year and ordered a review of what happened during Pike’s execution.That is not enough.The last time someone survived when a method of execution that was supposed to kill them failed to do so was in 1946, when Louisianatried to put a man named Willie Francis to deathin the electric chair. Francis survived because the electric chair malfunctioned and the current wasn’t strong enough to kill him.He sued the state to prevent it from trying again. But to no avail. The United States supreme courtallowedLouisiana to put him in the electric chair again.The scourge of the death penalty hangs over America | Austin SaratRead moreWriting for the court, Justice Stanley Reed said: “Even the fact that petitioner has already been subjected to a current of electricity does not make his subsequent execution any more cruel in the constitutional sense than any other execution … The fact that an unforeseeable accident prevented the prompt consummation of the sentence cannot, it seems to us, add an element of cruelty to a subsequent execution.”Francis was executed soon after.Since then, many other executions have been botched, but few have lived to tell about them.Between 1946 and today, that hashappened only nine other times, including with Pike. Four of those execution survivors were killed by a second execution attempt, while others escaped that fate. Some died on death row.In another case, the state agreed not to try to execute the person a second time, and now three of them are still alive.Tennessee had its chance to execute Christa Pike. It shouldn’t get to try again.To do so would be a form of double jeopardy that is prohibited by the constitution. And it would be cruel.Justice Harold Burton, who dissented in the Francis case, got it right when he said that no one should be subject to a second execution. “The intent of the executioner,” Burton wrote, “cannot lessen the torture or excuse the result.” In his view, when the state seeks to execute someone, they have a duty “to make sure that there … [is] no failure”.It doesn’t get a do-over.In the end, this is not just a matter of what the law says. It is a matter of simple human decency.Austin Sarat, associate dean of the faculty and William Nelson Cromwell professor of jurisprudence and political science at Amherst College, is the author of Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death PenaltyExplore more on these topicsCapital punishmentOpinionTennesseeUS justice systemUS crimecommentShareReuse this content

title: A century after the weekend was invented, it has disappeared. Let’s reclaim leisure | Richard Morgan | The Guardian
description: Henry Ford’s 1926 policy held for decades before eroding into a 24/7 mindset. Here’s what we can do about it
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Henry Ford’s 1926 policy held for decades before eroding into a 24/7 mindset. Here’s what we can do about it
Content: ‘The weekend mindset is an invention overdue for radical reinvention.’Photograph: Diego Fiore/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The weekend mindset is an invention overdue for radical reinvention.’Photograph: Diego Fiore/AlamyOpinionUS work & careersA century after the weekend was invented, it has disappeared. Let’s reclaim leisureRichard MorganHenry Ford’s 1926 policy held for decades before eroding into a 24/7 mindset. Here’s what we can do about itFri 2 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTShareIt was a Saturday. In fact, the Saturday.Almost exactly a century ago, on 25 September 1926, Henry Ford instituted a policy of weekends for his workforce. Although various labor campaigns had existed for decades to try to carve out what we now call the weekend, this was the first widespread adoption.It caught on, buoyed by portraits of leisure gracing the covers of the Saturday Evening Post, drawn by an idealistic young artist from New York named Norman Rockwell. In 1929, Walt Disney leveraged Saturday matinees of his animated films to launch The Mickey Mouse Club. On Saturday 25 June 1938, President Franklin Roosevelt passed the Fair Labor Standards Act, formalizing the weekend as federal policy.Beyond workplace respite, the weekend began to form its own identity. In 1944, Frank Sinatra popularized Saturday as “the loneliest night of the week, because that’s the night my sweetie and I used to dance cheek-to-cheek”. And the 1948 lyrics to Tennessee Saturday Night blared: “Civilized people live there alright, but they all go native on a Saturday night.”My holiday was full of tantrums and hangry meltdowns. And it wasn’t the kids who were to blame | Emma BeddingtonRead moreThe postwar boom of suburban pleasures transformed weekends into an anchor of indulgence. Sábado Gigante in 1962. Saturday morning cartoons in 1963. The launch of TGIFriday’s as a singles bar in 1965. Super Bowl Sunday in 1967. And a banner year, 1969, saw the moon landing on a Sunday (for Americans, at least) followed by a weekend of Woodstock.Then, with a frenzy typical of the 1970s, a rapid-fire pop culture trifecta: Saturday Night Live in 1975, Saturday Night Fever in 1977, and Norma Jean Wright’s disco hit Saturday in 1978. All capped by the sloppy onslaught ofbrunch chaos.Weekend vibes seemed unstoppable.But it all began to come undone – not least thanks to an insidiousboast from Jerry Reynolds, a guard-forward on Louisiana State University’s basketball team, printed in Sports Illustrated in November 1983; he is credited with coining the term “24/7”, describing his jump shot as reliable “24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year”.The phrase “24/7” epitomized a new flattening of time accelerated by CNN, which launched its 24-hour news network on 1 June 1980 (a Sunday, whereas MTV launched a year later on a Saturday). In 1985, “24/7” was popularized by People and soon after by the all-hours creep of cyberspace, pitched simultaneously as an “information superhighway”, “global village” and “digital town square”. Of all the uncanny prescience in AT&T’s memorable “You Will” campaign from 1993, eeriest is its depiction of a 21st-century future where Saturdays and Sundays are indistinguishable from Wednesdays and Thursdays.Today, after 5,200 weekends since Ford’s first, try explaining the once-sacrosanct status of Saturdays and Sundays to a TikTok influencer, a personal trainer, a flight attendant, a local election canvasser, an Uber driver, or a blogger. In 2023,Pew foundthat married Americans had relatively unleisurely lives: 24.5 hours of leisure a week for those with children under 18 and 30.4 hours a week for those without. Divided over seven days, those tallies are grim to an extent insurmountable by even the most-bottomless mimosa.Thanks to the pandemic’s corporate encroachment of working from home and the atomized, optimized overcalculation of our schedules through digital calendars and presumptively social media, Saturdays now take up as much effort – planning, execution and stress – as any manic Monday. If a parent is only as happy as their least-happy child, a globalized worker is only as relaxed as their clients’ least-relaxed time zone. Nearly 20 years later, the 2009 concept of “Sunday scaries” now seems quaint; aren’t weekends scary enough?The weekend was once the week’s well-earned dessert but its ice-cream has long been melted by the burdensome breach of busyness. The slop we now have can perhaps be refrozen, but it will never again be the confection of yesteryear. We have endured too much fracturing flux. Our lives are too fluxed-up. Has 100 years of weekends worn out its welcome?Weekends were built in part to bolster church attendance, but a2024 Gallup surveyfound 56% of Americans attend religious services seldom or never. God can perform many miracles, but squeezing kindness and grace out of capitalism is not one of them.What we need is to abandon the weekend’s pretense of work-life boundary. That frontier has been hard-fought, sure, but so too has it been long breached. The battles have plainly favored labor over leisure. No more.The only way to fight workweek creep on the weekend is with weekend creep in the workweek. Not just casual Fridays or “Saint Monday” but full lunch hours, hard 5pm departures, and charging overtime for after-hours emails. Work “from home” from a park, from a spa, or from abroad. Bring pension thinking – the concept of employer gratitude for labor – to a 9-to-5 scale instead of a worklife that is, to quote the late Dolly Parton, “all taking and no giving”. We need to give our weekend warrior selves presence at Monday morning meetings.Like 61 million Americans, I am quite proudly, passionately, and perhaps foolishly a freelancer. It can often be a nightmare existence. Even by the US’s precarious standards, I live without a safety net. But I am free. My time is my own. I am writing this essay on vacation, splayed out in bed like a happy starfish, taking in the view of a moonlit seaside castle.Does your life feel out of control? Maybe you need some ‘pyt’ | Polly HudsonRead moreThe weekend mindset is an invention overdue for radical reinvention. In April, 69% of Americans had the audacity totell Gallup pollstersthat they had six or more hours of free time “on weekdays or weekends or both”. But I call [checks with editor] … malarkey. For a people who act like they invented freedom, Americans have a radiant knack for making excuses about what they can’t do. At the top of that list is “I can’t find the time.” In fairness, that’s true. Americans cannot find the time to live the lives they want. But that’s the best lesson learned from our construction of weekends: time is not found; it is made.Make time for yourself. For your loved ones. For your hobbies. For your ambitions. For your booty calls. For your bubble baths. For sushi. For tennis. For tattoos. For book club. For therapy. For karaoke. For leg day. For Lego. For mahjong. For your journal. For your marathon. For your second helping of cheesecake and your umpteenth viewing of The Golden Girls. For Final Fantasy Resonance or Grand Theft Auto VI – or both. For that trip to Japan. For that colonoscopy. For whatever you want whenever you want – because nobody, absolutely nobody, logs their achievements or fond memories in categorization by days of the week. We cannot list the top five Wednesdays of our lives.Weekends were built for factory labor, not Zoom meetings. The global rise of four-day workweeks show how arbitrary our current set-up is. Why not two-day workweeks if the work can still be done?Sabbaths began as days of rest. That antiquated thinking dangerously frames such rest in service of labor. I don’t know about you, dear reader, but I think God wants more for me than the life of a dishrag whose only peace is on the drying rack in between meals. For me, sabbaths are days of resistance – resistance training, to learn how to stretch and flex my mind and soul as much as my body. Try it. Make time for it. No Sunday Funday – or Taco Tuesday – is complete without it.Richard Morgan is a freelance writer in New York and the author of Born in Bedlam, a memoirExplore more on these topicsUS work & careersOpinionWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should think | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism works, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism works, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Zack Polanski with Hannah Spencer and Siân Berry at the Green party conference, Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenZack Polanski with Hannah Spencer and Siân Berry at the Green party conference, Brighton, 2 October 2026.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianOpinionGreen partyThe Green party’s anti-Zionism motion is yet another attempt to tell Jews how we should thinkJonathan FreedlandThe resolution shows little understanding of what Zionism is, who Jews are or how antisemitism worksFri 2 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareTomorrow I will be in synagogue to say Kaddish, the traditional mourner’s prayer,in memory of my fatherwho died eight years ago this week. If I were a member of the Green party, I would have reason to believe that that simple act could soon see me expelled as a racist.It sounds hyperbolic, butthe warning comesfrom Green party activists opposed to a resolution declaring that Zionism is racism, which will bedebated at the party conferencethis weekend. The motion, which if passed would instantly become party policy, holds that Zionism should be “treated as any other form of racism”. On that logic, given that the Greens do not admit members of self-described racist organisations, they could not tolerate members of self-described Zionist organisations – a category that includes almost every synagogue, or synagogue movement, in Britain and indeed the world. Which is why saying Kaddish could lead to expulsion.All this sounds arcane, but the Greens are no longer a fringe party. They beat Labour in a byelection in February, one of the events that catalysed the eventual removal of Keir Starmer. The Greens’ leader,Zack Polanski, hopes to win Starmer’s former seat of Holborn and St Pancras in next Thursday’s byelection. But the row over Zionism has cast a cloud over his campaign. If he loses the seat, many will conclude that the Green surge is over – which would relieve a significant electoral headache for Labour and Andy Burnham. So the stakes are high.The charitable reading is that this move originates in genuine, and widespread, horror at Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, followed by a series of unfortunate misunderstandings of what Zionism is, who Jews are and how antisemitism works.That, I repeat, is the charitable reading, but let’s go with it. It’s worth saying that if the proposers of this motion had simply wanted to express their revulsion at the catastrophic devastation of Gaza and those who executed it, they could have denounced Israel and the Israeli government. But their admitted purpose is to go much further – to attack Israel’s very existence and the movement that led to it: Zionism.As Polanski, who has been twisting in all directions on this subject, has tried to argue, Zionism means different things to different people. The great Israeli writer and peacenik Amos Oz used to describe it as a family name, an umbrella for a wide range of radically different worldviews. Before Israel’s founding in 1948, you’d have cultural Zionists slugging it out with religious Zionists, Marxist Zionists raging against rightwing militaristic Zionists, all of them wholly at odds with the dominant group: socialist Zionists. What they had in common was the simple belief that Jews had the right of self-determination in their ancestral homeland, the land they had for millennia calledEretz Yisrael, the Land of Israel, and which the rest of the world called Palestine.To this day, that’s essentially what it means to be a Zionist – that you believe in a Jewish national home in some portion of historic Palestine. There are rightwing Zionists who think it should be in all of that land; there are leftwing Zionists who think it should be broadly within the much smaller boundaries that existed before the 1967 war and alongside a Palestinian state. But both groups are Zionists. The racist minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is a Zionist, but so are many of the Jewish and Israeli anti-occupation activists who volunteer to act as a “protective presence”, putting their own bodies between settler extremists and Palestinian villagers in the West Bank. To brand everyone under that one umbrella as a racist shows a deep ignorance of what the word Zionism means and the sheer range of people who identify with it.It also reveals a wilful misunderstanding of Jews andJudaism. Social media has been full in recent days of supposedly progressive non-Jews telling Jews what Judaism is and what it is not – with an arrogance that, I suspect, they would find unacceptable iin a majority group addressing any other minority – and the same error recurs. Breezily, we are told that Zionism is merely a political ideology, wholly separate from Judaism, which means, happily, that one can denounce the former without expressing any animus towards the latter. If only it were so simple.Take that Kaddish prayer I’ll be saying. It refers to “Israel” three times. The Jews were calledAm Yisrael, the people of Israel, centuries before we were called Jews. What’s more, when I say the prayer, I will, following tradition, be facing east – towards Jerusalem. The prayer book in my hand will be full of references to Jerusalem and indeed to Zion, expressing in a hundred poetic ways a yearning to return. This is not some new, political thing. It’s what Jews have been saying and doing for millennia. Many, many centuries before Zionism was a political movement, it was a longing – the need to end a painful exile from the Land of Israel – enshrined in the very heart of Judaism.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy BurnhamRead moreWhich is one reason why, incidentally, the language of “settler colonialism”, repeated in the Green motion, fits Zionism so badly. When, say, the French settled in Algeria, they were not returning to the land where the French people were born, where French had been spoken two millennia earlier, and to which the dispersed and lethally persecuted French people had longed to return for 2,000 years. It’s also why, though of course there are plenty of anti-Zionist Jews, you will struggle to find a synagogue beyond the fringes of ultra-orthodoxy that does not identify in some way with Zionism – not, I stress, with this or that Israeli government or policy, but with the idea, the dream, of the Jews’ return to their ancient home. That dream became a matter of basic human survival after a history of bloody persecution reached its climax eight decades ago, in the murder of 6 million Jews by the Nazis and their collaborators across Europe. It’s that need for a refuge from antisemitism – a racism that claimed so many lives, for so long – that the advocates of Sunday’s motion would declare to be racism.A group of Jewish Greens tried to alert their comrades to these dangers, asking for an amendment that might allow Jews to go to synagogue, but they were rejected. When one committedly anti-Zionist Jew rose to speak at a party workshop last week, he wasshouted downwith cries of “Zionist”. Polanski, who is himself Jewish and has called for the motion to be amended, saysthere’s a simple solution: if Jews denounce Israel in the terms demanded, agreeing to condemn “the occupation … the apartheid … the genocide”, they should be left alone. But the resolution itself insists on more. For Jews to comply, they would have to deny all connection with their historic homeland. This has so often been a feature of antisemitism: century after century, Jews are told that if they only disavow this belief or that practice, if they only say these words, they will be admitted into polite society. Where once Jews were told to embrace Christ, now they are told to disavow the world’s only Jewish country. The specific demand has changed; but the impulse is the same.In each generation, those making such demands of Jews believe they are acting in a righteous cause. The Christian persecutors of the Inquisition were sure that they were honouring Jesus; today’s Greens are certain they are advancing the cause of anti-racism, even as they would hound and defame and shame a tiny minority. AnyGreen partymember voting for this motion should reflect on that history and consider the company they are joining. It will be full of people they despise – but they will fit right in.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
