title: AI threatens to destroy so much of our culture. Our greatest loss might be our ability to listen | Shirleene Robinson | The Guardian
description: Australians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019
Content: ‘Listening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing,’ writes Shirleene Robinson.Photograph: Dumitru Ochievschi/Alamy Stock VectorView image in fullscreen‘Listening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing,’ writes Shirleene Robinson.Photograph: Dumitru Ochievschi/Alamy Stock VectorOpinionLanguagesAI threatens to destroy so much of our culture. Our greatest loss might be our ability to listenShirleene RobinsonAustralians are conversing less every year, with a recent study showing we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 20.19 EDTShareWe talk a lot about losing our ability to write as a result of AI. I’m convinced our greatest loss might be our ability to listen. Listening to different views and entering into different worlds is integral to our humanity.But Australians are conversing less every year. While rapidly evolving AI tools and chatbots promise faster responses and so-called “empathetic” listening, a recentstudyshowed we lost an average of 338 spoken words each day between 2005 and 2019. That adds up to a staggering loss of 120,000 spoken words per person, compared with the year before.Hanson says Australia has a ‘language problem’ due to immigration. After arriving with little English, Marziyah is now a lawyer with a missionRead moreThis matters immensely. Language is culture. It tells us who we are.As an oral historian, I’ve spent much of my career studying the power of human speech and storytelling. Between 2018 and early 2024, I led a team at the National Library of Australia responsible for the largest oral history collection in the southern hemisphere, which began in 1957 and now consists of more than 58,000 hours of recording. More recently, I’ve immersed myself in listening to hundreds more hours of this collection, working on a new book and an accompanying podcast.The depth of the library’s collection, much of which is available online through Trove, is extraordinary. It holds accounts of First Nations Australians speaking about deep history and first-person memories reaching back into the 19th century.All up, I’ve now listened to thousands of Australians from different eras, places and backgrounds tell their stories in their own words.This has helped me understand exactly what we lose when we stop listening. When I listen to an oral history, I immerse myself in the life of someone I mostly likely will never meet. In a world where our social circles are reducing due to distance, remote work and increasing time online, the gift of hearing from someone different is precious.double quotation markI often hear Australian accents from the past or words no longer spoken, along with many professions described that no longer existDame Mary Gilmore, born in 1865, speaks of tallow candles and life before electricity. An Australian prime minister recalls being elected after their party spent 23 years in opposition. A mother who risked everything shares how she sought refuge here, crossing pirate-infested seas after the Vietnam war. A pioneer stationed in Antarctica reflects on challenges of distance. The next voice may be Dr Ella Stack, a Darwin doctor who survived Cyclone Tracy, stayed to help, recorded survivor memories, then ensured Darwin was rebuilt as mayor.I often hear Australian accents from the past or words no longer spoken, along with many professions described that no longer exist. As I listen, I’ve sometimes cried with laughter because of the ability of some people to share memories with humour.I’ve listened to people remembering times of great social disruption, such as the 1891 Queensland shearers’ strikes or the conscription debates of the first world war. I’ve been deeply moved by the courage of First Nations Australians who shared testimonies of being part of the Stolen Generations.Everything Australians put online could be scraped for AI under proposed new rules. How will you be affected?Read moreListening to other people from diverse backgrounds and perspectives who may not hold the same views as us can improve our mental and physical wellbeing, foster the exchange of information, grow understanding and spark new ideas. It is also deeply linked to building empathy.Empathy is the richest gift listening offers. That will be our greatest loss if we speak and hear less. By engaging with experiences of others without requiring instant gratification and artificial agreement, we enter into other’s lives. We grow to be patient and appreciate difference. We learn we can disagree but in ways not unnecessarily destructive.Mostly we learn that, although a century or more of time may separate us as well as our diverse backgrounds and experiences, we can still connect through moments of shared humanity and experiences of love, loss, change, challenge, joy and resilience. These voices from the past can resonate as powerfully as ever in our present.Dr Shirleene Robinson is an oral historian and visiting fellow at the University of Technology Sydney’s school of communication and social sciences. She editedThe Memory Tapes: Voices from the Oral History Collection of the National Library of Australiaand hosted the accompanyingpodcastExplore more on these topicsLanguagesOpinionHistorySocial historyIndigenous AustraliansAI (artificial intelligence)commentShareReuse this content

title: There is a way to look after people, the planet – and Britain’s growth. It’s what we call the ‘wellbeing economy’ | Jamie Driscoll | The Guardian
description: Imagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happen, says Green party politician Jamie Driscoll
Author: Jamie Driscoll
Headline: Imagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happen, says Green party politician Jamie Driscoll
Content: A wind farm off the coast of Great Yarmouth.Photograph: NJphoto/AlamyView image in fullscreenA wind farm off the coast of Great Yarmouth.Photograph: NJphoto/AlamyOpinionEconomicsThere is a way to look after people, the planet – and Britain’s growth. It’s what we call the ‘wellbeing economy’Jamie DriscollImagine the UK with a 20-year investment plan, with green homes and fast transport. We already have the tools to make it happenFri 2 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTShareYou’ve just left school. What’s your future?I know a physics graduate making flat whites; a 30-year-old living in his childhood bedroom who feels like a failure; a lad in Blyth who turned down a job 15 miles away because there’s no bus, and for young people his age car insurance is almost £2,000 a year. Britain’s young people are our greatest resource, and we are failing them because capital markets won’t allocate investment where it is needed. Saying “hope”in a conference speechsounds warm. But people need a plan.The first priority of any government is the security of its people. Financial markets are sending price signals thatAI boomsand share buybacks are more important than clean energy or warm homes. We fund aircraft carriers and artillery shells. But wind turbines and council houses are part of our national security, too. Imagine a country with a 20-year investment plan, with retrofitted homes and fast transport connections that leave nowhere behind. That’s a future filled with the potential of proud work for young people.But four words run Britain: “We can’t afford it.” Governments call this mindset “prudence”. My response to it isHostage Nation, my plan to fix Britain. This is a report that lays out how to source the finance, shows what we need to build – and tracks why it would make us more prosperous and resilient. I joined the Green party to achieve this vision. As we approach the party conference, I hope this will become official Green policy that we’ll fight the next election on.Nine sets of fiscal rules have been broken and abandoned since the financial crash. Andy Haldane, a former chief economist of the Bank of England,said current fiscal ruleswere “far from optimal; in fact I’d go as far as to say silly”. TheInstitute for Fiscal Studies saidin 2024 that changing policy based on fiscal headroom projections was “almost literally mad”. What if we’re not really hostages to the bond market? What if politicians have got Stockholm syndrome instead?Bond markets are just complex betting shops. That’s their business model: guess the future, and price accordingly. That price changes when the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates or thestrait of Hormuzcloses. Why do we let bookies decide whether we build railway lines? Give a country nothing to build and struggling people will find someone to blame.Businesses want customers more than they want tax cuts or light-touch regulation. I once asked the chief executive of a global engineering firm if he would invest in green hydrogen. “I’m not investing half a billion in a plant and staff unless I can sell it for 20 years,” he said. No government gave that signal.Provide demand, and supply chains will organise themselves. When I was mayor of the North of Tyne combined authority, I moved our adult training providers from one-year to rolling three-year contracts. Employment training places rose from 22,000 to 35,000 a year on the same real-terms budget. That’s what certainty brings.Markets are great at providing barber shops and burger vans, but markets don’t build reservoirs. The only organisation that can guarantee orders for infrastructure 20 years from now is the state. Public ownership is a must for public planning. We’re not short of need:100,000 council homes a year; fully renewable energy with a storage grid; clean transport; insulating every home; buses and trains that run as one network and are cheaper and more convenient than cars; regenerated high streets with sports centres and warm youth clubs. What George Monbiot callspublic luxury.We can fund it with off-market finance. The government savings bank National Savings and Investments (originally the Post Office Savings Bank) has been goingfor more than 160 years, and 24 million of us use it. The government could offer savers national infrastructure Isas – a fair, safe return for investment in public works. The gilt market carries on; this is a separate channel insulated from tariff antics and international conflicts. No hedge fund has ever shorted a premium bond.We invest£70bn a yearin cash Isas. Our pension pools hold more than £2tn, yetless than 5% is invested in British firms. There is tax relief on both. If you want to speculate on Silicon Valley, that’s your right. But tax subsidies should be reserved for savings that build Britain.As for infrastructure, the state can outcompete private capital. For a business, wages are an expense. For a country, wages lower the welfare bill. The state collects40p in every pound back in tax. Money flows through high streets and pays business rates. A2014 pilot in Sunderlandshowed that a £5,000 investment in insulation and energy-efficient boilers for people with COPD lowered bills and reduced hospital admissions by 25% and GP appointments by 60%. Combine retrofit and clean energy at cost andenergy bills fall by 67%. It turns out the cheapest way to heat a home is also the quickest way to decarbonise a country.This is what awellbeing economy looks like. In the North of Tyne we judged projects on mental health, environmental impact and community wealth before a penny was released.What about inflation? Train the workers, build the supply chains, then release the money. This creates real capacity and builds assets on the public balance sheet. We have the powers. We don’t need new treaties or quangos. We need to wake up the state machinery we already have.In 1946 Britain was so poor we started rationing bread. The national debt was two-and-a-half times the size of the economy. That generation built the NHS. Then anaverageof 126,000 council homes every year for 35 years. Eight prime ministers and two parties kept building. Today our relative debt is under half that. We have machines they could only dream of. They weren’t richer than us. They were braver.I don’t have a crystal ball, but I’ll wager the upcoming budget will tinker around the edges of these issues. Voters already know the Greens care, and with a plan to really fix Britain – and fund it – support will keep growing. Hostage Nation is backed by 134 endnotes that are there to be checked. We can start this plan tomorrow. Values win sympathy, but answers win seats.Jamie Driscoll is a Green party councillor on Newcastle city council and former North of Tyne mayorExplore more on these topicsEconomicsOpinionEconomic growth (GDP)commentShareReuse this content

title: Should we refuse to give the Bayeux tapestry back to France? Of course not! So why are we keeping the Parthenon marbles? | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: It is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to Greece, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: It is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to Greece, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: The Parthenon marbles in the British Museum on 11 May 2023.Photograph: Matt Dunham/APView image in fullscreenThe Parthenon marbles in the British Museum on 11 May 2023.Photograph: Matt Dunham/APOpinionParthenon marblesShould we refuse to give the Bayeux tapestry back to France? Of course not! So why are we keeping the Parthenon marbles?Simon JenkinsIt is simply wrong for the British Museum to hoard what doesn’t belong to Britain. Let the squabbling end and the sculptures be returned to GreeceFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTShareFor the Bayeux tapestry to return to Francewould be a scandal. It is British, probably made in Canterbury by British women, and displays one of the greatest events in British history. The tapestry certainly does not belong in Normandy. It is right that it is now on British soil in the British Museum. Its display is so brief that the herd of visitors desperate to catch a glimpse of the medieval artwork must be jostled to keep moving, as if watching Shakespeare’s Henry V on fast-forward. So let’s keep it. Everybody knows possession is nine-tenths of the law. We can call it a long-term loan.I am joking, of course. This is largely what I assume the British Museum is worriedmight happen if it lent the precious Elgin, or Parthenon, marbles to Athens. In the Guardian last month, the Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, argued that the status of the Bayeux tapestry is parallel to that of the Parthenon marbles. “Both were conceived as single works, intended to be seen and understood as a whole,”he wrote, arguing it was time for the marbles to be reunited.The British Museum director, Nicholas Cullinan, even appeared to agree. He remarked that the Bayeux tapestry loan offered a “glimmer of possibility” of a deal on theParthenon marbles, which were acquired by the British Museum in 1816.Cullinan’s predecessors have long come across as jingoistic hoarders, as if the museum were a lasting memorial to the British empire.In the 1980s, the then director, Sir David Wilson, had an infamous clash with Greece’s then culture minister, Melina Mercouri, who had travelled to London to appeal for the sculptures return. “I want my marbles back,” she demanded to Wilson in front of TV cameras.The debate has since swirled back and forth. But it is as unedifying as watching grownups argue over a bag of sweets. Insofar as the public cares,a majority of Britonsthink the marbles should go back to Greece.There was a refreshing breakthrough in 2022after George Osborne became the museum’s chairand boldly opened negotiations with Athens. He even held a public debate on the matter. The objective was certainly confused. Was it a discreet exchange of some classical artefacts, or was it to be the final reuniting of the Parthenon pediments in the new Athens museum? The latter clearly made sense, both artistically and because of the significance of the Parthenon to Greek national identity.Since then, the prospect of apossible returnof the marbles has been bedevilled by politics and diplomacy. The Greek government rejects any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum’s “ownership”. But such de-acquisitioning would only be possible if the law were changed. Boris Johnson, once an ardent supporter of the marbles’ return,reversed his position when in office. For his part, Rishi Sunak refused to change the law and clearly wanted the marbles to stay in Britain.Cut to Andy Burnham, who we may have expected to adopt a different stance. During his brief stint as culture secretary between 2008 and 2009, Burnham was reportedly a champion of the marbles’ return. In 2002,he even sponsored a private member’s billon facilitating their transfer back to Greece. His advocacy is longstanding. As recently as 2023, Burnham, then mayor of Greater Manchester, declared: “Send them back, no strings attached. And let’s use culture to change how Britain is seen around the world.”But Burnham has done a Johnson and Sunak and let it be known hehas reversed his position. Elgin’s ghost seems to spook the Downing Street rafters.The bottom line is there is no agreement on the nature of what a loan could look like. And to make matters worse, the British Museum is lending two minor Parthenon fragments to an exhibition of Greek sculpture opening in November in Frankfurt’s Liebieghaus museum. This has so infuriated Athens that it hasreportedly refused to lendnine fragments of the Parthenon marbles to the exhibition, as if proximity to the British ones would be contaminating. Talks are reportedly back to stalemate. This is desperately sad. I have followed this debate since first visiting the Parthenon with its then surveyor in the 1970s. The temple and its carvings must rank among the founding compositions of western culture.Bringing their sculptural integrity back to life and on the site of its creation should so clearly be the ambition of every historian and archaeologist worth their salt. For museum leaders to go about hoarding, empire-building, nit-picking and point-scoring is frankly pathetic. Modern national museums are outrageous in how they amass collections and then sometimes prevent others from seeing them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen I was chair of the National Trust, we tried to persuade the Tate Gallery and others to lend us paintings from their basements that never saw the light of day. The answer was almost always: “No, they are ours, not yours!” We thought they belonged to the public.As for leaders such as Johnson and Burnham, they demand a course of action in opposition yet lack the guts to do it in power. This has gone on long enough. Greece should drop its obsession with formal “ownership”. London should dispatch its 17 pediment sculptures on indefinite loan to Athens. Then, together, all ofEuropecan rejoice.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsParthenon marblesOpinionBritish MuseumGreeceDisputed artMuseumsEuropeHeritagecommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s true: this is my final column. You have exactly 24 hours to complain before my inbox self-destructs | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: Yes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: Yes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyOpinionThe GuardianIt’s true: this is my final column. You have exactly 24 hours to complain before my inbox self-destructsMarina HydeYes, after 25 years I’m signing off, and I’ve cherished every moment – especially storming the French embassy with a (toy) AK-47Fri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareJournalism 101 – a course I have yet to complete – dictates that if you have something salient to say you should get there fast. So right now, I should mention that this is my last ever column for the Guardian. I’ll level with you: I spent a long time wondering how to write it. At first, I thought it should be about all the things I’ve learned, purely because that would be a hell of a lot shorter than a column about all the things I keep failing to learn, no matter how many times I make the mistakes. For example: if you’ve got a good joke, you’d best put it in the intro. (Why is there literally no joke in this intro?)Or: remember that people love the piss-taking until it strays into the arena of something they like, when it suddenly becomes wholly unacceptable. Take the time I wrote: “Arguing on the internet is like playing real tennis:even if you win, you’re still a twat”. This prompted an immediate missive from a member of the Cambridge University real tennis club, which appeared on the letters page under the headline “Real tennis has been served badly by this unfair slur” and began: “Like many Guardian readers, I have thoroughly enjoyed and always look forward to reading Marina Hyde’s witty and caustic commentaries on the world about us. However …” Incidentally, I told this story at one book tour event, and then at the signing afterwards, a lovely young lady came up to get a book dedicated to her father, Jeremy. And of course, she said: “I should probably mention, he’s the guy who wrote in from the Cambridge University real tennis club.” Truly, the circle of life. To Jeremy, and the many other Jeremies who have written in over the years, let me just say: we all know the real twats are rackets players.In the end, though, this could only be largely a column of thanks. I’ve ended up covering so many things over my time at the Guardian – from World Cups to Olympic Games to just the 47 general elections – but for the past few years, my permanent berth has been here in the Opinion section. And I want to pay tribute to all the people on this hallowed desk. I have tried to be the easiest columnist to deal with … like that means anything. Columnists are very possibly the worst demographic in journalism. And as you know, that really DOES mean something. As I say, I’ve tried to keep my interventions in the editorial process very limited, but I do have to accept I have basically said three things to the Opinion desk, on repeat. 1. “So what if it’s in bad taste?” (I stand by that one.) 2. “It’s not offensive – what you’ve done is confuse the subject of the joke with the object of the joke.” (I mean … that genuinely is so obnoxious. I can only apologise.) And 3. the extremely timeworn: “why have you put a headline on this that makes me look like a – ”. And then I have to use a word that even in the Guardian you’re only allowed to use if it’s in reported speech.The amazing editors and subeditors have borne all of that with good humour and equanimity. I don’t know what they’ve said after we’ve put down the phone to each other, but God knows they’d have been entitled to it.I think we can all live without my retrospective, but I will say my time at the Guardian began in lively fashion, working on the Diary column. Quite soon after starting, we were given a one-offOsama bin Laden puppetby the Spitting Image creators, which I was dispatched to get photographed on the steps of the French embassy in London. (But why?) The only problem was that the latex Osama was carrying a toy AK-47, and just as I’d propped him against the door of the embassy to get the picture, it swung open and I was pulled inside by French security. Things escalated fast. In the end, the incident was attended by 10 police squad cars and five police motorcycles, and Knightsbridge was brought to a total standstill.Again: why? Why did we do this? Genuinely the reasons for it are lost in the mists of time for me. Like so many stunts pulled by what we used to call newspapers, it made absolute sense in the context of the news cycle in which it happened, and makes absolutely no sense once ripped from those temporal moorings. But over two decades on, I would obviously like to thank the various police forces on the scene – French, Met, and diplomatic – for deciding not to press charges, which would, I sense, have made the rest of my so-called career rather tricky.Over time, that old Fleet Street wild west gave way to the digital wild west in which we live now – a place of no less remarkable incident. One of the bizarre things that came with the advent of social media was seeing which famous people reposted your columns. Probably my favourite was when I wrote one about a new ITV show whereRob Lowe played a police chief in Brexit Britain. (I know – how did it not get a second season?) In the course of this column, I happened to digress all the way back to that time in 1988 when Rob was campaigning for Michael Dukakis at the Democratic national convention, on the eve of which he ended up making a sex tape in his convention hotel in Georgia with two girls, one of whom was 16. And then I mentioned that at my school, we were all totally thrilled and excited when that story came out, because it meant that Rob Lowe was definitely open to sex with 16-year-old girls. (cf “so what if it’s in bad taste?”)Imagine the lift on my eyebrow when Rob Lowe only went andreposted this column, particularly bearing in mind that for the past few years his timeline had consisted of incredibly wholesome content about dropping his children off at university and so on. Did it indicate that he still had a bit of the animal left in him (my preferred reading, as I don’t think you ever truly kill it off) or had he simply not read through to the relevant bit? We will, I think, never really know – and I always enjoyed such mysteries.While we let that one settle, it feels like a great moment to begin my lengthy thanks to the Guardian’s legal department, with whom it may not surprise you to learn I have shared many, many intense moments over the years. There was a point not so long ago when someone on the Opinion desk relayed to me that someone in the legal department had said: “really the best person at legalling Marina’s column is Marina”. First: no. But second: this honestly might be the greatest compliment I ever got. It’s like the old proverb goes: legal a woman’s column and you feed her for a day. Teach a woman to legal her own column and you feed her for a lifetime. I want to thank legal for all the incredibly nutritious masterclasses.And, speaking directly to the department, I am very much hoping we don’t get a complaint on this last column, although that would in some ways be amusingly on-brand. Looking back over what I’ve typed so far … I feel likeRob Loweis the most obvious vulnerability? Alas, my Guardian email address will no longer work, so – hate to say it – you guys will be on your own with this one should it materialise. What we had was simply too special to be exported over to my new inbox. (This regretful bounce-back also applies to any rackets players who may now be seeking to get in touch.)skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFinally, then: that email address, and what it has meant to me. Many people don’t believe this, but in all the 25 years I have worked for the Guardian, I never had a private email address. Thus I have been in a constant – constant! – dialogue with Guardian readers who write in about my columns. Long before all the amazing digital metrics that we now have on where and how deeply our work is read, I had multiple daily emails from Guardian readers with subject headlines like “thank you”, “screw you” and – occasionally – “shame on you”. They ran the full gauntlet from adoring to bracing to skin-flaying. I would honestly not have had it any other way.If you write opinion on the news, ultimately you are in the audience business, and to have an ongoing back-and-forth with the one you’re serving has been as much of a privilege as it has been endlessly enlightening and stimulating. So how could I not save the most important people in this column to last? Thank you so much, dear readers – and I hope to see you down the trail. In the meantime, my very best wishes to you and yours. It has, I promise you, been an absolute honour.Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnistShe’s been making sense of the madness for the last 25 years: celebrate the end of an era with Marina Hyde’s final column collection, What a Time to Be Alive! title: For too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Ed Miliband and Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference, Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenEd Miliband and Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference, Liverpool, 27 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAOpinionAndy BurnhamFor too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that?Andy BeckettThe PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changesFri 2 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.01 EDTShareHow much can aLabourgovernment change the country? According to many voters, journalists and politicians, including plenty in the party itself, the answer to that stubbornly recurring question has always been: not that much. Labour governments can’t restructure the economy, radically redistribute wealth, truly empower the disadvantaged or adopt a genuinely ethical foreign policy without upsetting too many powerful interests, from the British rich to the US government to global financial markets.This endlessly repeated conventional wisdom – internalised by some on the left as well as centrists and the right – has haunted many Labour governments, from the first, tentative ones in the 1920s to Keir Starmer’s diligent but failed administration a century later. Yet conventional wisdom can be wrong, especially in volatile periods such as the current one, when precedent may count for little.At last year’s Labour conference, Andy Burnham was widely derided for what was seen as a half-launched and clumsyleadership coup attempt. Much of the media and Starmer’s cabinet reckoned his chances of being prime minister were gone for good. Yet, at this week’s unusually packed and perhaps unwisely optimistic gathering, Burnham’s can-do presence was almost as dominant as Tony Blair’s in his early leadership years: a constant point of reference, from the main hall to the merch stands to leftwing fringe events.Moreover, Burnham appears to want to use his personal dominance – which may well be briefer than Blair’s, given Labour’s more fragile position in a more fragmented politics – to open up an array of huge issues that his party has long been advised to keep closed. Electoral reform, social care, public intervention in failing privatised utilities, the pension triple lock, evenrejoining the EU: announcements about exploring or pursuing all these punctuated hisconference speech, in a sequence of softly voiced political shocks.“Change will be difficult,” he acknowledged. But he insisted: “More of the same isn’t good enough.” At an excited fringe event the night before, his ally Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who in that job and his previous one as energy secretary has pioneered Labour’s unexpected recent interest in confronting difficult problems and dangerous interests, summed up the party’s defiant new mood. “All politics is a risk. Progressive politics is a particular risk,” he said with relish. Burnham might have similar charisma and communication skills to Blair in the 1990s, but New Labour ministers did not dare say such provocative things.Defenders of that now remote-seeming political culture would argue that avoiding head-on clashes was one of the reasons Blair was twice re-elected. But Burnham, who served in the Blair government at a formative age, does also have a strong conciliatory impulse, such as his frequently stated keenness to cooperate with other parties. However, as with his reluctance to criticise them by name – his conference speech was almost completely free of the usual party-political attacks – this apparent absence of aggression is in one sense the opposite: a determined attempt to break with the ultra-partisan politics of the post-Brexit decade that has excited many journalists but increasingly exhausted and alienated the public.Burnham might come across as a nice bloke but he is ruthless, wrongfooting opponents and renderingtheir tactics obsolete, as his supposedly formidable Labour enemies such as Morgan McSweeney learned this year. Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage’s perpetual outrage and tribalism suddenly seem rigid and unreasonable next toBurnham’s talk of hopeand national togetherness, and his disarming admission this week that all politicians must do better, that “this country isn’t where any of us would want it to be”.Labour’s modest but persistent rise in the polls suggests that sufficient voters have had enough of the old high-argument, low-achievement politics to make Labour the leading party again for a period, perhaps up to the next general election and even beyond, when many of his ambitious reforms are actually meant to take place. Of course, proposing, let alone implementing, major changes to the status quo such as loosening the triple lock will also make many voters absolutely furious (even if that policy initiallyappears popular), and provide regular targets for Labour’s enemies in Westminster and the media. Yet, with the electorate more divided than ever, and the bar for re-election probably set as low as winning over less than a third of voters, being controversial or unpopular matters less for a government than before – provided it holds its nerve and pleases a large enough core of supporters. Burnham’s sweeping attacks on Labour bogeymen such as the privatised utilities seem likely to achieve that. Meanwhile, his cross-party overtures and support for electoral reform may well lure voters and politicians from the Lib Dems and Greens.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRightwing economic myths could derail Burnham’s project – to destroy them, look to Keynes | Larry ElliottRead moreLike Pedro Sánchez in Spain, another centre-left premier of similar age who has managed to stay in power for eight years, Burnham is a paradoxical politician: both frank and evasive; opposed to populism and good at populist gestures; prepared to echo the left’s critique of capitalism but also pro-business; a self-styled lone saviour who is able to work in coalitions. Photogenic and politically agile – you could say shameless – Sánchez and Burnham seem better suited to today’s world of flux, short attention spans and deep discontent than the previous generation of stiff social democrats such as Starmer. Perhaps the modern centre-left is finally working out how to govern and reshape the societies that its more popular 1990s predecessor never sufficiently reformed.For too long, it has been the right that expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. If Burnham’s barely begun administration is to become a significant one – perhaps like that of Harold Wilson, another slippery, charming Labour leader with Merseyside connections – it will need to enact big reforms as well as talk promisingly about them.Sixty years ago, Wilson won an election landslide, and commemorative items competed with the cult of Burnham on the merch stands at conference in Liverpool. “Wilson’s greatest hits”, said the cover of a souvenir record, “Featuring Creation of the Open University, Equal Pay Act, Abolished Capital Punishment, Race Relations Act, Abortion Act, Decriminalised Homosexuality”. Wilson’s premiership was often unpopular and struggled economically, but it lastingly changed Britain by resolving some contentious social questions. Burnham may have to settle for doing the same.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionLabourPensionsElectoral reformSocial carecommentShareReuse this content

title: I went curtain shopping during a Kyiv air raid. And not because I’m ‘resilient’ | Diana Berg | The Guardian
description: We can’t count on tomorrow so it would be rational to own less. Yet we make our homes nicer, just to anchor ourselves in the here and now, says Ukrainian artist Diana Berg
Author: Diana Berg
Headline: We can’t count on tomorrow so it would be rational to own less. Yet we make our homes nicer, just to anchor ourselves in the here and now, says Ukrainian artist Diana Berg
Content: Ihor Malchevsky, a deputy department head at Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv, escapes from the building after it was hit by a Russian drone strike on Monday.Photograph: Thomas Peter/ReutersView image in fullscreenIhor Malchevsky, a deputy department head at Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv, escapes from the building after it was hit by a Russian drone strike on Monday.Photograph: Thomas Peter/ReutersOpinionUkraineI went curtain shopping during a Kyiv air raid. And not because I’m ‘resilient’Diana BergWe can’t count on tomorrow so it would be rational to own less. Yet we make our homes nicer, just to anchor ourselves in the here and nowFri 2 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 04.59 EDTShareIwas standing in front of a locked basement door in a buildingin our neighbourhood, laughing, as Ukrainian air defence shot down drones directly above me. I had run into the first residential building I could reach, and I even took a photo of the locked door – a shelter, and the shelter locked – because I wanted to remember it. I was on my way to buy curtains.I hadn’t checked whether there was an alert before I left home. I had simply set out for the shop, 20 minutes away through our residential district, on foot. But somewhere along the way, things started exploding in the sky above me – and I was suddenly walking through a city under attack because I had decided that my windows needed new curtains. What the fuck was I laughing at? I should have been terrified, and I was. It was just that I still wanted the curtains, and the absurdity was hilarious.The curtain shop was closed because of the raid – this international chain, it turns out,shuts when the sirens go off, unlike many Ukrainian-owned stores. So I came back the next day and bought them. They are better than the old ones and cover the windows properly. Only after I had hung them did I realise that they also let me see less of the war from my sofa: theflashes of air defence, the smoke, whatever was happening outside. I had not made the war any safer. I had only made it slightly harder to see.I had been away from Kyiv for a month and while I was gone, the rhythm of the war, which I have lived with for years, had changed: attacksnow came by day, alerts could swallow half of it, and explosions, drones and smoke had become part of the daytime soundscape in a way that felt new even to me. My response, apparently, was to buy curtains.In January 2022, back in Mariupol, when everyone around us was waiting forRussiato invade, my husband bought an expensive coffee machine. I thought it was ridiculous. He told me he was tired of living in fear and anticipation, that he wanted to live here and now, and that if the machine survived only a couple of weeks he didn’t care. Since the full-scale invasion, he has bought a television, an electronic piano, a huge monitor for my laptop, a washing machine and a dryer – every year something large that could be smashed in a second.View image in fullscreenDiana Berg outside a locked shelter door during an air raid in Kyiv.Photograph: Diana BergWe don’t do the big things. Our flooring still needs repairing, and the flat we have lived in since we fled Mariupol in 2022 needs renovation. We don’t invest in it because spending serious money, time and energy on a place a missile could destroy tomorrow feels slightly insane. There is a strange logic in this, a logic that isn’t really there when I look at it closely. But the small things keep sneaking in.I left all my books in Mariupol. When we fled, they were not exactly high on the evacuation priority list, and later they were lost when our rented flat was destroyed in theairstrike on the Drama Theatre. I started buying books again in Kyiv, one at a time, and somehow I now have a bookcase full of them. We got plants. We got cats – four now, two from Mariupol and two adopted during the full-scale war. One of them can barely see, barely hear and limps after an accident; we chose him in 2023, apparently deciding that what our lives really needed was another vulnerable creature to worry about.The rational wartime strategy would be to own less, need less, attach yourself to less. We have left home twice, both times with only what we could carry, so nobody needs to explain to us what attachment costs.It isn’t that we don’t know what can happen. Last week a building belonging to my husband’s workplace was hit. He was in a different one, but he could have been there, and I don’t know how to convey that fear. I keep my Instagram mostly to cats, standup, sport, beauty and interiors, because I don’t want to spend every waking hour looking at war – but the news gets through even those filters.In my feed I saw a post from a soldier at the front, showing footage from the site of that building: the car park, the burnt-out cars, and the news that his wife, who had worked with my husband, had been killed there. There were photographs of the two of them walking into the new house they had bought and planned to renovate, the walls still bare, the new car they had bought 10 days earlier – and then that same car, gutted in the car park along with everything around it. She had been inside. It was one and the same strike. What is there to say?During an attack, we have our own little scale of urgency. Ballistic missile: bathroom. Now. Cruise missile: you can finish your coffee. Drones take the longest, so you can usually carry on. For now.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn fact, I am writing this column from the bathroom, the safest place in the flat. There is an air-raid alert and I can hear air defence outside; the four cats are with me. On Telegram, people post live videos from all over Kyiv, often before anything appears in the official news, and as I write this,Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv is on fire. One person has been killed. People are climbing out of upper-floor windows on to fire ladders. I am sitting in the bathtub, watching it live on my phone and writing about curtains.During another alert that lasted through the afternoon and into the night, we visited friends for a Sunday barbecue. We sat outside while something was burning or being intercepted somewhere above us; meanwhile, someone turned meat on the grill and my friend’s mum told me about the new flowers in her garden. At some point I had the very clear thought that, theoretically, something could fall straight on to my plate. Then I looked back at the flowers.This is what I find difficult about the word “resilience”, so often used about people living in war zones. It sounds like a virtue, something noble you develop when tested – but it feels much less noble than that. The curtains hide a little of the war from me. I feel guilty for shutting my eyes to the horror outside, but in reality it’s more like refusing to allow the war to make every decision.So the curtains are hanging now. They make the room warmer and they cover the windows better. The photo of the locked door is still on my phone. Next: I need to paint the walls in the bathroom. I’ve already chosen the colour.Diana Berg is a Ukrainian artist, writer and cultural manager from Mariupol, and the founder of Platform TU, an independent cultural initiative now operating in exile after Russia’s full-scale invasionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsUkraineOpinionKyivRussiaEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: We don’t need to panic about AI. We need to hold its creators accountable when things go wrong | John Quiggin | The Guardian
description: If a chatbot prompt like ‘find Australian medicine statistics’ results in a website breach, the responsibility does not lie with a piece of code
Author: John Quiggin
Headline: If a chatbot prompt like ‘find Australian medicine statistics’ results in a website breach, the responsibility does not lie with a piece of code
Content: Forcing corporations to bear liability for damage caused will slow the rush to produce increasingly powerful AI models, writes John Quiggin.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenForcing corporations to bear liability for damage caused will slow the rush to produce increasingly powerful AI models, writes John Quiggin.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)We don’t need to panic about AI. We need to hold its creators accountable when things go wrongJohn QuigginIf a chatbot prompt like ‘find Australian medicine statistics’ results in a website breach, the responsibility does not lie with a piece of codeThu 1 Oct 2026 21.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 02.40 EDTShareThe recent panic about abreach of Medicare computer securityby an “AI agent” contrasts sharply with other recent cases such as the Telstra and Optus outages that left many Australiansunable to reach Triple Zero. In those cases, no one blamed the computers involved. The mistakes were clearly sheeted home to the corporations that operated them.This wasn’t always the case. When the term “artificial intelligence” was coined some 70 years ago, the first mainframe computers(absurdly primitive by modern standards)were viewed with the same awe and concern as the AI agents of the present day. There were even “algorithms” (though the term wasn’t used in that way at the time) that were supposed to pick ideal dating matches.Failures were inevitable, and blame-shifting became routine. “The computer made a mistake” was the 1960s equivalent of “your email must have gone to junk”. Gradually, however, we realised that the problem was not with the computer but with incorrect information fed into it or badly written programs invoked as a result.As AI models go rogue, do you still trust OpenAI and Anthropic to stop them? I don’t and neither should you | Chris Stokel-WalkerRead moreWe need to make a similar adjustment when we discuss AI “agents”. If someone enters a prompt like “find Australian medicine statistics” into a program like ChatGPT or Claude, and the result is a breach of Medicare’s site, the responsibility does not lie with a piece of code. Either the human who entered the prompt or the corporation producing the code made a mistake, and they should be held liable for the resulting damages. If it’s impossible to work out who is at fault, liability should be joint and several – that is, both are liable for the full amount of the same loss, and the cost can be allocated between them.Fixing the problems of agentic software won’t be easy. The frequency with which early computer programs malfunctioned made “debugging” (a term predating its use in computing) an essential part of information technology. Bugs might be found in the operating system, the program itself or the information fed into it. In one case,the problem was a literal bug: a moth that got caught in the relays. But with enough determination the source of the problem could usually be found and fixed.Traditional debugging is much more difficult with agentic programs. It may be possible, after the fact, to work out what the program has done. But it’s impossible to inspect the hundreds of billions of parameters in a large agentic model and work out why the agent did it.In this context, the idea of constraining the program with “guardrails” or “harnesses” is naive in the extreme. The whole point of telling a computer program to perform a task is to get around obstacles to that task. And with no understanding of the internal workings, external constraints will be treated as obstacles.In most cases, the only solution will be to abandon many of the capacities that are supposed to make agents useful, such as the ability to log in to sites using passwords or to make payments on the user’s behalf.This will be a huge wrench for corporations that have grown up with the Silicon Valley ethics of “move fast and break things” and “ask for forgiveness, not permission”. They are far more comfortable talking about “hallucinations” and “rogue agents” than about their own responsibility for programs that produce massive errors and real-world damage.But once AI corporations are made to bear the financial consequences of their reckless negligence, a different kind of calculus will come into play. Instead of thinking,“what cool thing can we make this program do”, the first question will be,“what could go wrong if we let it run”.Anika Wells named on Time100 list as one of ‘world’s most influential rising stars’ after social media banRead moreForcing corporations to bear liability for damage caused by their actions will, in all probability, drastically slow the “hyperscaling” rush to produce more and increasingly powerful agentic software. That’s a good thing for the environment as well as the economy.And none of this will preclude the many benign uses of “AI” software, including massively improved internet search, document summarisation and translation, and software coding. These uses come with the adjustment problems that always arise with new technology, eliminating some jobs while creating others, and so on. But there is no reason to fear that they will accidentally cause a nuclear holocaust or even drain our bank accounts.John Quiggin is a professor at the University of Queensland’s School of EconomicsExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinioncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversary | Movies | The Guardian
description: Ahead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made now
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Ahead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made now
Content: ‘It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden’ … Pete Postlethwhaite in Brassed Off.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden’ … Pete Postlethwhaite in Brassed Off.Photograph: AJ Pics/AlamyMovies‘I thought Brassed Off might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley’: the director of Andy Burnham’s favourite film on its 30 year anniversaryAhead of a live performance in the Royal Albert Hall, the writer Mark Herman explains why he’s not surprised it’s one of the new Prime Minister’s favourites and a why film like this wouldn’t get made nowRobyn VinterFri 2 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is one of the prime minister’s all-time favourite films and has endured in the hearts of the British public since it was released in 1996. Ostensibly a story about a small town colliery band’s journey to the finals of Britain’s biggest brass band competition at theRoyal Albert Hall, Brassed Off is unashamedly political.“I think the people who went expecting a political film got the bonus of a bit of a comedy,” says its writer, Mark Herman, three decades on. “And the people who went expecting comedy got the bonus of the political message. I think anybody who went got a sort of bonus they might not have expected.“On the face of it, a brass band film is not an easy pitch but word of mouth really rolled and suddenly it went on and on in places for months,” he recalls. “I thought it might be popular within a 10 mile radius of Barnsley for about two weeks,” laughs Herman. “So yeah, it’s amazing.”Set in the fictional industrial South Yorkshire town of Grimley a decade after mineworkers brought themselves to destitution trying to save their livelihoods, it captures the hopelessness felt by former miners who struggled to keep themselves out of the dole queue during the slow and painful destruction of the mining industry by the Tory government.StarringPete Postlethwaite, Tara Fitzgerald and Ewan McGregor, it follows the Grimley Colliery Band as they await a judgment from British Coal as to whether their pit will be closed. A resounding success, Brassed Off went on to be number 85 in the BFI’s list of Top 100 British Films and spawned a popular stage play. To add to the plaudits, Andy Burnham recently named it as one of his four favourite films.“How do I feel about that? It’s good!” says Herman. “It’s very flattering, but I’d have been more surprised if he’d have chosen Notting Hill.”On its 30th anniversary, fiction and real life are set to collide when Grimethorpe Colliery Band – the group that inspired the film – heads to the real-life Royal Albert Hall to perform the music alongside a special screening.The film’s success at the time was “surprising and very rewarding” but the enduring appeal, Herman believes, is because, “It’s not about a brass band in Grimley, it’s about the universal subject of being downtrodden.“It’s really interesting hearing teens and 20-year-olds talking about the film, because it’s such an old film for them, but it really hits them. They get the message everybody got 30 years ago, because it’s still relevant and still plays.” But these films are a dying breed and Herman admits he is “fairly pessimistic” about the current state of the British film industry. “I feel like films like Brassed Off wouldn’t be made [now].”View image in fullscreen‘It’s still relevant and still plays’ … Ewan McGregor, Tara Fitzgerald and Pete Postlethwaite.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/Alamy“I’ve spent the last 10 years trying to get films similar to Brassed Off off the ground but can’t,” he says. “It seems to be blockbusters or micro-budget at the moment and there’s no space for mid-budget British films like those, films like I want to make.“The studios are not as brave as they were,” he adds. “They’d stick their neck out, in what I call the old days. It was quite a risky film to make, Brassed Off, but now they seem to only want to put money behind dead certs.”His favourite films of the last year wereI Swear, the biography of a man with severe Tourette syndrome, andThe Ballad of Wallis Island, an offbeat comedy drama written by and starring the comedians Tim Key and Tom Basden.His path – from childhood in the East Yorkshire seaside town of Bridlington, to studying graphic design at Leeds Polytechnic (now Leeds Beckett University) and the National Film and Television School – would still open doors for youngsters in the industry, he thinks. But it is not an easy industry to break into, and now, in his early 70s, he thinks the advice he got when he was young – advice he took for a short while – to move to London, probably still stands.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve spent the last 10 years trying to get films similar to Brassed Off off the ground’ … Mark Herman.Photograph: Gary Calton/the Guardian“If I’d have [stayed in] London and networked I’d have probably done more films, but maybe not ones I care about as much,” he says.Instead he wrote a powerful script, unashamed to spell out in no uncertain terms how the Conservative government destroyed communities and ruined lives, the effects of which continue. Higher mortality rates from suicide, alcohol and drugs developed – and persist to this day – in former pit towns and the shadow of Margaret Thatcher still lingers like an oil stain in these communities.In a climactic scene in the Royal Albert Hall, Postlethwaite’s character, Danny, the band’s conductor, gives a memorable speech – later immortalised in the protest song Tubthumping by Chumbawamba – shouting: “I thought that music mattered. But does it bollocks. Not compared to how people matter.”During filming, Birmingham town hall was substituted for the London venue, which was too expensive and “didn’t look anything like the Albert Hall”, Herman jokes.Brassed Off Live will be a “strange experience … when our fake Albert Hall is on screen and you’re sitting in the Albert Hall. It’s a thrill. Thirty years ago would we ever imagine being in the Albert Hall still watching it? It’s amazing.”Brassed Off Live is at theRoyal Albert Hall, London, on Friday 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmAndy BurnhamRoyal Albert HallComedy filmsPete PostlethwaiteDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy  | Television | The Guardian
description: He won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David Brent
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: He won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David Brent
Content: ‘I feel so lucky, it’s insane’ … Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesView image in fullscreen‘I feel so lucky, it’s insane’ … Lenny Rush as Val in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesTelevisionInterviewFangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedyZoe WilliamsHe won a Bafta while only a teen, and now he’s the lead in a creepy sitcom adapted by Alan Partridge’s writers. Ahead of The Reluctant Vampire, he talks mates, mums who write him letters – and his love of David BrentFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly when absolutely badgered willLenny Rushadmit that the title role of The Reluctant Vampire, Val, was written for him: “Shane Allen, the executive producer, loved the books when he was young, and he was the exec onAm I Being Unreasonable?. So yes, the scripts were written with me in mind. I’m so happy they were so good. I’d have felt awful if they said ‘We’ve written this for you’ and …” he trails off, pulling a face of exquisite pained courtesy.Rush likens the show to The Naked Gun and Airplane!, and it has the writing team behind Alan Partridge, so can conjure awkwardness out of thin air. But it also taps into a comic tradition that goes even further back: a delight in the ridiculous, people talking to bats and gargoyles, invisible women interjecting by surprise, a surrealism whose comedy comes from the audacity of acting it with such commitment. “In my opinion,” says Rush, “sometimes things are labelled as a family show but they’re aimed at kids. I really do get the feeling that The Reluctant Vampire is for everyone.”The Reluctant Vampire was written in the 80s by Eric Morecambe, in a surprising digression into children’s fiction from the comedy giant. It’s about the young scion of a bloodsucking household who doesn’t have any skills: his teeth aren’t pointy, he hates the taste of blood, and it transpires that he’s not a vampire at all but a rogue human. In the hands ofNeil and Rob Gibbons, it’s like watching the essence of British comic sensibility – slapstick shot through with genuine pathos.View image in fullscreenRush with Sian Clifford as Valeeta, Gabriel Nagy as Vernon and Tom Davis as Victor in The Reluctant Vampire.Photograph: James Pardon/BBC/Buffola Pictures“You’ve gotTom Davisplaying a vampire, this big character, with these big movements and this big voice, that can’t not attract a younger audience,” says Rush, “but the lines are genuinely funny.”The show opens with Davis in full vampire regalia, ready to strike an elderly victim in her bed, only for Rush to derail it all by rushing in saying he needs a wee.Still only 17, Rush has been a fixture on TV for many years, starting aged seven in CBeebies documentary series Our Family. Then, aged eight inApple Tree Houseon CBeebies he played Eli, a young rascal on an estate of well-intentioned young rascals. If you have children this age, you’ll feel like you’ve known him for ever, and if you are watching thelatest season of Slow Horses, you’ll know him as the foul-mouthed, ancient-beyond-his-years kid whose steel trap of a mind effortlessly vanquishes the spies.But his breakthrough role was in Am I Being Unreasonable?, for which he won a Bafta at 14 for best male performance in a comedy – and he was nominated again for the same award this year. That role, Ollie, along with his magisterial Bafta acceptance speech, sealed his reputation as a guy who has hacked your mainframe, and could effortlessly make you laugh at any time.View image in fullscreenRush with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/AppleYou can see in Rush’s performance as Val how much he’s gorged on Mr Bean, Alan Partridge, Monty Python. “I probably watched some things I shouldn’t have when I was younger,” he says. Never mind the age-appropriateness, how he found the time is anyone’s guess, since he has spent so long watching the British version of The Office that he knows it episode by episode, and has been working – as well as going to school – since he was seven. David Brent has always been his inspiration, and he delivers the kindest reading of that character I’ve ever heard. “You think: ‘What an idiot.’ Then you think: ‘What a not very nice man.’ Then you get to the end of series two, and there’s a really big element of pity. He’s just a man! Trying to find his way! He just wants to be part of the gang. It’s actually a tragedy.”The opening episode of The Reluctant Vampire makes a lot of his stature, his parents measuring him and wondering if he’ll ever be tall enough to be a vampire. Rush, who has a form of dwarfism known as spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, never went into acting for his condition to be a “talking point. I never thought I could be an inspiration for disabled people or young people.” The impact of his visibility on the world around him came as a complete surprise. “When Am I Being Unreasonable? came out, I started to get messages from mums, saying: ‘My little boy’s got a disability or a form of dwarfism, he’s struggling a bit at the moment at school. But he’s seeing you on telly and it’s giving him confidence.’ It’s so mad that I can be doing what I love and making people feel like that. I’m so pleased that that’s how people have seen it.”Actually, though, the unvampiric vampire is a metaphor for belonging that is universal to teenagehood. “Going to school, trying to fit in, trying to impress, failing miserably. I think that’s why it’s so relatable. Even though it’s about vampires. Or you could see it as someone trying to find their place in society: ‘Am I doing this right? Am I good enough?’ It shouldn’t be so awkward, but it is.”View image in fullscreen‘I say I’m working with Gary Oldman and my mates don’t even look up’, say Rush.Photograph: BBC/Boffola PicturesHe’s not bringing a lot of his own experience of school to the travails of Val, incidentally – he never stopped attending, but was always off filming something and must have been artlessly cool. Which also made his parents very focused on his attendance. “My mum took school really seriously – not even necessarily, to be honest, the education side; she just found it very important for me to be seeing my mates. So I’d be on the PlayStation, and go: ‘I’m working with Gary Oldman,’ and they wouldn’t even look up from the game. You can get swept away really easily, on set. You have assistant directors coming into your dressing room, asking what you want for lunch, it’s quite insane. You have to have the right people around you.”After Am I Being Unreasonable?, Rush got two episodes of Doctor Who, even if he wasn’t exactly a devotee. “I’ve not told Russell T Davies this, but I never watched Doctor Who. I knew what it was! I knew it was an honour to get asked. I knew it was a real moment in your career, especially to get cast young – I think Andrew Garfield was in it at a young age.” He played Morris Gibbons, a 13-year-old genius and adviser in the science unit, a really smart move after the role of Ollie, in which he’s also a genius but of a more cunning, domestic kind.Am I Being Unreasonable? sometimes seemed to hang off his every expression – the plot of that show was absolutely wild, full of the worst parenting in the world, elaborately revealed secrets, dead pets. Rush’s command of the mood was what tethered it to earth. “Ollie was the breakthrough part, and after that I saw myself as an actor. But when I’d look online, before and after, people would say ‘He’s a great comic actor’ or ‘He’s a great young comic’. And I’m really thankful for that, but I never saw myself as a comedian or a comic actor. And as much as I love comedy, I don’t want that to stick as my thing.” His mum asked him recently whether he’d ever try standup. “It’s a bit of an annoying thing about British culture, and quite sad in my opinion, that it’s easy to get pigeonholed, and if I ever did try standup, it would take me further away from the Slow Horses kind of work.”His next role is Dobby in the Harry Potter series that’s been beset by controversy – not just about whether actors can be in it without tacitly endorsing JK Rowling’s views, but also bizarre racist death threats to cast members. Rush hasn’t started yet, definitely hasn’t had any death threats, and is tight-lipped, saying only: “It’s pretty incredible – I feel so lucky, it’s insane.” It’s casting against type, this house elf, because Dobby’s not the effortless manipulator of all he surveys: his emotional top note is craven gratitude and anxious helpfulness. Maybe Val is a useful bridging role, because as a not-really-vampire, Rush ventures into new territories of panic and pitfall.The Reluctant Vampire has palpable ensemble chemistry, between Rush, Sian Clifford as his mother, Davis as his dad,Asim Chaudhryas a Lurch-like character. Newcomer Gabriel Nagy is a great foil as his brother, a functioning, evil vampire. “I never felt like anyone was learning from me,” he says. “I felt like I was learning from them. I never felt like number one on the call sheet, having to keep everyone in high spirits. I remember Tom telling me, it sounds obvious but it was so true and so clever – if you’re doing a comedy, you want to make people laugh at home, so your goal in that scene is to make your co-star laugh. Try and get them to break.” They’re all pros, of course, so no sign of anyone corpsing; but like every classic comedy since TV began, you can feel that they’re smiling on the inside.The Reluctant Vampire is on BBC One on Sunday4 Octoberat 6.40pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV comedyDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom? | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’
Content: Familiar face … the Skanderbeg Tower is designed to echo a bust of Albania’s national hero.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/AlamyView image in fullscreenFamiliar face … the Skanderbeg Tower is designed to echo a bust of Albania’s national hero.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/AlamyArchitecture‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom?Sixty top architecture firms from around the world have mooted 500 eye-catching projects across Albania, sparking fury and protests. Now they’re being celebrated in an 800-page tome that some are calling ‘a smoking gun’Oliver WainwrightFri 2 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast autumn, I was sitting with a prominent architect in New York, when their phone wouldn’t stop buzzing. They finally checked the messages and chuckled. “Oh, the AlbanianArchitectureArmy chat is blowing up again,” they said. “It looks like Edi has some new projects for us.”Edi was Edi Rama, the prime minister of Albania since 2013, who has been presiding over the rapid transformation of the former communist country with a fleet of glamorous building projects. There are twisting towers in Tirana, along withprize-winning public spaces, striking coastal resorts, and many more dazzling visions on the way – all now brought together in a hefty new book,The Albanian Files.double quotation markCritics see the 800-page book as a 2.2kg dossier of evidenceThe country’s makeover, it turns out, is partly coordinated via a WhatsApp group (“Albanian ArchArmy” for short) which includes some of the most famous architects in the world. It is a forum where achievements are shared, new projects celebrated, and the great prime minister-patron showered with praise for his bravery and boldness. The New York architect describes the situation in the manner of a superhero movie: Rama sends out the signal and the world’s starchitects rally to the rescue with their daring designs. Look hard enough and you might even see theAlbanian double-headed eagleprojected into the night sky.View image in fullscreenHub … Saranda port development plan by XDGA, shown in The Albanian Files.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller PublishersThe WhatsApp chat might be confidential, but The Albanian Files is the next best thing. It is a remarkable document, in ways that are both intended and not. In his foreword, Rama describes the book as “a precious behind-the-scenes record” of a process that is “liftingAlbaniain a way that nobody saw coming”. It is an eye-opening directory of dreams, in which 60 international practices (and not a single Albanian one) lay out their plans for over 500 projects up and down the country.To Rama’s critics, however, the book is an 800-page, 2.2kg dossier of evidence. They point to theopacity of decision-making, thedestruction of heritage, theforced evictions, thetrampling of protected landscapes, and therole of Albania’s construction industry in laundering money for organised crime. The publication is full of first-hand testimonies by architects documenting their experiences, andone opposition MP has called it the “smoking gun”– although there is no suggestion that the architects have been involved in any wrongdoing. Rama is right that nobody saw it coming: most of the projects in the book’s pages are news to the local population, which has reacted with fury.“Starchitects go home!” read one placardat a noisy protest in June, outside a venue in Tirana, where many of the architects in the book were gathered for an exclusive event to celebrate their work and launch the publication. “Where is the public?” read another. Tickets for the architecture festival, titledLandscapes of Abundance, cost up to €200, in a country where the median monthly wage is €700. It came at a charged moment, just a few weeks after huge national protests were ignited by the multibillion dollar plans todevelop Zvërnec nature reserve and the nearby island of Sazan into a luxury resort, backed by the Trump family.Dubbed theflamingo revolution, in reference to the fragile habitats critics say will be trampled by the project, the protests have now continued for over 120 days, with ever-louder calls for Rama’s resignation. Architecture has found itself unexpectedly in the firing line.View image in fullscreenAnger … Albanians protest at development of coastal nature reserve in June this year.Photograph: Armando Babani/Getty Images“It feels like living in an autocratic kingdom,” saysLorin Kadiu, director of Citizens.al, an investigative news platform that has been tracking construction projects in Albania since 2018. “Not just the lack of transparency, but the fact that we must all be subjected to the aesthetic tastes of one person. The whole country must be painted the way he wants.”Rama, who trained as a painter, first rose to prominence as the mayor of Tirana in the 2000s, when he made international headlines with his programme of painting thedreary soviet blocks a rainbow of jaunty colours. The cheap and cheerful makeover worked, and Rama was hailed for his maverick artistic approach.But, now, many of his former supporters feel like his architectural ambitions have gone too far.An open letter, handed out at the protests, denounced the “art-washing of bulldozer politics,” and asked the assembled architects if they enjoy “the freedom to do here what would be forbidden, challenged, or otherwise made impossible in your own countries?” Of the architects contacted by the Guardian, only one responded, to say they do not do anything in Albania that they would not be allowed to do in another place. They added that “the freedom in Albania is certainly alluring and as such the personal responsibility is greater”.As Rama writes pointedly in his foreword to The Albanian Files, the architects are attracted to work in Albania by the “freedom from ‘no’ in all its forms”. The pages are studded with visions for virgin coastlines, verdant forests, and pristine dunes and lagoons. In Gjipe, a bay that many consider the last virgin beach in southern Albania, Dutch firm MVRDV hasproposed a mirrored glass hotel that would span the gorge, “like a jewel on the coastline”.It comes hot on the heels of their apartment towerin Tirana shaped like the head of Skanderbeg, Albania’s national hero (which also bears a striking resemblance to Rama). In the protected dune area of Rana e Hedhun, the venerable Portuguese architectÁlvaro Siza has masterplanned a hillside development with a cable car and a tower-block on the beach.A few pages later, Swiss maestro Valerio Olgiati proposes a cluster of concrete towersrising from the sand, peppered with defensive windows. It looks as if he might be preparing to fend off an invasion from the sea.The coastal glow-up continues with the Florentine luxury yacht designerLuca Dini(studio mission: “to astonish even the most discerning”). He presents an illustrated voyage through his 17 projects, including the Life Marina Complex, spanning seven kilometres of virgin coastline near Saranda, and the Atara resort, with a golden “crown” that hovers above the cliffs like another military lookout post. It almost reaches parody when his comic-style illustrations conclude with an image of a super-yacht hurtling above a skyline, with the designer himself declaiming from the deck: “[we] create spaces that harmonise with the environment.”View image in fullscreenComic-style illustrations … Luca Dini’s section in The Albanian Files.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller PublishersThe book’s editor, Anneke Abhelakh, asked the architects to submit their own texts, and they are striking in their honesty. At times it reads like a hot-mic transcript. “Because there are not many rules and my clients care very little for the context,” writes Berlin-based architect Sam Chermayeff, “we are forced to think through our own values.” He recounts the “truly wild” experience of working in Albania, including how he was called, out of the blue, by one of Rama’s associates, and soon asked to designtwo towers in Tirana, totalling 45,000sq m – quite something for a designer better known for experimental kitchens.“Of course I agreed,” he adds, “not really understanding what was happening.” Contacted for comment, Chermayeff responded: “I do ask Albanian clients the same questions that I ask of clients in any country and am equally assured,” adding that “as in Germany or the US, I really do not know more than what I am told,” and that he does not work in or near protected areas. “I do not do anything,” he added, “I would not do at another place.”Austrian architect Chris Precht describes how he was approached on Instagram by Rama himself, “asking if I would be interested in working in Albania”.
