He now has 29 projects to his name, including a €4m “Garden of Eden”, built in the courtyard of the prime minister’s own office.“It is an unimaginable reality,” says a campaign group of Albanian architects and urban planners,Arkitektët Shqiparë, which has created an online database of all of the projects – published in Albanian, unlike the book. “A narrow group of foreign architects is contacted directly by the prime minister’s office and receives projects without a competitive procedure.”View image in fullscreenBeside the seaside … Olgiati’s proposal for concrete towers on the beach in Lezha.Photograph: Oliver Wainwright/Lars Müller PublishersThe foreign architects describe it differently. “Rama never appoints the architects himself,” one member of the ArchArmy group tells me. “But he makes introductions to developers. And it is understood that, if they choose one of his architects, they [the developers] will get permission to build what they want.”Rama has consistently denied the allegations. In a furious interview with CNN in June, he denounced the claims of corruption as “fake news”. He has long maintained that the wider protests have beenstoked by the US president’s enemies, including Iran. “If it were not Jared Kushner,” he said, “nobody would give a shit about flamingos, about Albania, about nothing. It’s the whole hate against Trump that creates all this scrutiny.”Contacted by the Guardian, the prime minister’s office did not respond to requests for comment in detail but called the allegations “hearsays” and “bitter assessments”. During a speech this week to launch the competition for a new tower,Rama insistedthe competition juries are “mostly architects, urbanists and academics who are entirely free,” that “the Albanian side is in the minority” and that there is “never any orientation or influence” on the jury. He added that today Albania “is the largest open ‘university’ in architecture,” as young Albanian architects have the opportunity “to meet, to follow, to work concretely with masters”.The book’s subtitle is Freedom and Architecture, and there is an air of carte blanche to many of the designs. “Working as an architect in Albania is liberating,” writes the Belgian Xaveer De Geyter, alongside his proposal for a colossal trio of M-shaped towers for the port of Saranda, “provoking a degree of freedom that sometimes leaves us in a cold sweat.” Spanish studio Arquitectura-G praises Albania’s permitting process as “significantly faster and less restrictive” than elsewhere, driven by “a clear vision coming from the prime minister.” Portugal’s Manuel Aires Mateus concurs: “There are times when things have to be top-down.”The palpable thrill of building on virgin terrain is also evident. Japanese doyen Kengo Kuma describes the exhilaration of flying over Albania in a helicopter. “I found it very exciting,” he writes, “as most of the nature is untouched.” In Asia, he adds, “it is very difficult to find a project in such ‘virgin land’”. The Berlin-based Indian architect, Anupama Kundoo, talks of the opportunity to create, “free from the baggage” ofEuropeand other “developed countries”.Kundoo is working on a masterplan for a “laboratory settlement” of 50,000 people in the protectedDivjakë-Karavasta national park. Such a project has only been made possible by a controversial 2024 law, which allows the construction of five-star resorts in protected areas, from which the Trump-backed plan in Zvërnec also benefits.There is no suggestion that any of the architects named in this article are breaking any laws.“The developers are in a hurry,” says Kadiu. “There is a sprint to build as much as possible before these laws are repealed.” Pressure is growing. Albania has entered the concluding phase of its EU accession negotiations, but these lax regulations remain an obstacle. Both the 2024 law, and 2015 legislation that gives preferential treatment to “strategic investors”, were criticised byan EU report last yearas being in conflict with its standards.A European Parliament resolution in June this year “expressed serious concerns” and called for an “immediate moratorium on new permitting procedures, construction works and development interventions” within protected areas. Rama continues to defend both laws as pragmatic, modernising policies that balance environmental conservation with high-value economic development.Beyond fears for the environment, and the opaque permitting and procurement processes, another burning question remains: how can one of the poorest countries in Europe afford to build these extravagant schemes? There has been an astronomical rise in property prices, but no comparable increase in wages or bank mortgages being issued, leading critics to suspect that dark money is involved.The Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime identifies Albania’s real estate and tourism sectors as major sites of money-laundering, noting that the construction sector is “heavily infiltrated by illicit funds”. Its 2020 report estimated that€1.6bn of “dirty money” had been laundered through Albanian real estatein the previous three years.As I reported in 2022, leaked wiretaps revealed Italian mafia figures discussing how Tirana’s high-rise boom was a prime opportunity for laundering their cash, with construction prices of roughly €500 per sq m paling in comparison to the listing prices of up to €4,000 per sq m.Albania’s own Special Prosecution Office against Corruption and Organized Crime, SPAK, is making progress. InJune, it seized €150m of assets, including apartments, villas and commercial properties, tied to an alleged cocaine trafficking network. The same month, Pëllumb Gjoka, once named a “strategic investor” by the Albanian government with approval to build a €52m resort on the coast,was sent to prison for ordering mob hits.View image in fullscreen‘It’s a classic example of what happens when you think you’re the benevolent leader’ … Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama.Photograph: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesResearch by Citizens.al shows that several projects in The Albanian Files are linked to ongoing SPAK investigations (none of the architects named in this article are implicated), alleging criminal capital has been funnelled throughshell companies, construction contracts and property transactions. Over 40% of the projects in the book don’t even mention who the client is, leading many to ask: why the opacity?One former member of the ArchArmy is rueful about the way things have turned out. “Like the others, I joined with a real conviction that this could be a positive change for the country,” they tell me. “Rama knew Albania was going to develop very quickly, and he didn’t want to fuck it up. It’s better to have some good architects involved to make sure it turns out halfway decent, rather than people building generic apartments along the coast without any control.” The architect says they backed out after being part of a competition jury that “didn’t feel democratic” and the fact that issues around land ownership “always felt very vague”.They add: “Rama still very much believes that he’s doing the right thing for the country. It’s a classic example of what happens when you think you’re the benevolent leader, but you stay in power too long.”This sentiment is echoed in one of the most revealing contributions to the book. Reinier de Graaf, of Dutch firm OMA, writes an open letter to Rama – intended as a parody, but the humour is moot. “Given Albania’s enduring status as an enlightened architectural patron,” he writes, “our profession would benefit greatly if the country never had another election again, and if you … would just continue as president for life – maybe even king.”He adds: “In a world of autocracies, may we have one benevolent autocrat with taste?”Explore more on these topicsArchitectureAlbaniaOrganised crimeEuropeConstruction industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral review – Beethoven explodes into bright bursts of gorgeous dance | Dance | The Guardian
description: Spinning off from the classic symphony with composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner, Tanowitz’s dancers find fresh thinking space
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: Spinning off from the classic symphony with composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner, Tanowitz’s dancers find fresh thinking space
Content: Every angle planed to the exact degree … Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEvery angle planed to the exact degree … Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewPam Tanowitz: Pastoral review – Beethoven explodes into bright bursts of gorgeous danceBarbican, LondonSpinning off from the classic symphony with composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner, Tanowitz’s dancers find fresh thinking spaceLyndsey WinshipFri 2 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePam Tanowitz’s work is the antidote to the trend in dance for dark and shadowy stages, buckets of theatrical haze, claustrophobic soundscapes and gloopy movement. This stage is so bright and clean, like a sharp palate cleanser, and full of white space – literally, and in a more figurative manner. Tanowitz’s dance can be eccentric, odd even, but it’s also seriously thought-through and specific, every choice utterly distinct and deliberate, every angle planed to the exact degree.This UK premiere of Pastoral is a collaboration between New York choreographer Tanowitz, Pulitzer prize-winning composer Caroline Shaw and artist Sarah Crowner. Inspired by Beethoven’s Pastoral Symphony and the idea of the pastoral in art, Shaw pulls apart and deconstructs the Beethoven, with three live musicians (on various reed instruments) and excerpts of orchestral recordings that emerge like echoes or memories, plus real-world sounds of the street, the skies and the city.Tanowitz likes a bit of deconstruction too, taking apart or adding to phrases and motifs, with flashes of wit and eccentricity. Her style, simplistically speaking, nods to Merce Cunningham’s mid-century abstraction, with flattened lines and pleasing symmetry. Crowner’s work also harks back to the 1950s and 60s (to geometric abstraction and so-called hard-edge painting). She’s designed a floor-to-ceiling curtain and a vast canvas, with pale pink slices cutting through deep greens. They divide the space, creating “rooms” amid otherwise white walls. Reid Bartelme’s costumes have the dancers in ombre chiffon, an offbeat spectrum through coral-pink-red-lilac-chartreuse. The colours hum, on the edge of concord and discord.View image in fullscreenThe colours hum … Pam Tanowitz: Pastoral at the Barbican, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianThere’s something refreshing and challenging in the sparseness of the score, the dance and the stage, with all its thinking space. There’s zero fuss, even when the dancers have to execute fiendishly tricky balances. When Anson Zwingelberg suddenly dances a gorgeous phrase, like an exquisite miniature, it appears and evaporates with no fanfare.In the same way Beethoven’s music will unexpectedly slide into view, images and associations make fleeting impressions. When the dancers gather against the green, for example, as if picnicking in a 19th-century painting. Or when the pastoral idyll is interrupted by an angry red square canvas and the sound of a bird call like a siren – a threat against nature, perhaps. It’s a dance full of curiosity, and curiosities; a tangy conversation between three distinctive artists.At theBarbican, London, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDancePam TanowitzBarbicanLudwig van BeethovenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The singer’s hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old self
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: The singer’s hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old self
Content: Teen spirit … Hayley Kiyoko.Photograph: Grace ScuittoView image in fullscreenTeen spirit … Hayley Kiyoko.Photograph: Grace ScuittoMoviesInterview‘It’s radical to release a film called Girls Like Girls in this climate’: hitmaker turned director Hayley Kiyoko on sexuality, safety and becoming ‘Lesbian Jesus’Lucy KnightThe singer’s hit 2015 single Girls Like Girls was her breakthrough moment and also the first time she felt confident in her sexuality. Now she has directed a film based on the song – a love letter to her 17-year-old selfFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlot of Hayley Kiyoko’s teenage summers were spent waiting, bored and pining, as she sat at the computer willing her crush to message her back on AOL instant messenger. Like Coley, the 17-year-old protagonist of Girls Like Girls, the film the pop star has co-written and directed, Kiyoko fell hard for a girl who “put me through my own heartbreak and haunted me for a long time”, she says.Although the 35-year-old singer became known by fans as “lesbian Jesus” following the release of her breakthrough single Girls Like Girls in 2015 (the film is an extended version of the story first told in the song’s music video), feeling comfortable in her sexuality didn’t actually come until after its release. Her gay identity was, at the time, the topic she was “the most scared of writing about”, and the song’s confident refrain “Girls like girls like boys do, nothing new” came from wanting to “manifest feeling confident”.View image in fullscreenPool cute … Maya da Costa and Myra Molloy in Girls Like Girls.Photograph: Dan Power/Focus Features“Once I released Girls Like Girls, not only the song but the music video, and saw that so many people in the world felt the way I felt, and that I could still be loved for who I was, that was a big indicator of allowing myself to feel that type of love,” she says. After directing the music video, in which two teenage girls, one of whom has a boyfriend, develop romantic feelings for one another, Kiyoko became “very fixated on being able to tell this story on a feature film level”.It took just over a decade to make that happen, with a “pivot” to a different form in between, via the publication of Girls Like Girls the YA romance novel in 2023, which helped to get the film greenlit. The film is “definitely a love letter to my younger 16-, 17-year-old self who desperately was seeking that kind of love,” Kiyoko tells me via Zoom, dialling in from Bangkok where she has been celebrating the film’s Thailand release. The sun is shining on her and her eyes are bright as she excitedly tells me about meeting her Thai fans for the first time.double quotation markWe watch movies to dream and to see representation that maybe we lack in our livesThe Bangkok screening was “super-special” because one of the film’s stars, Myra Molloy, who plays Coley’s love interest Sonya, is from Bangkok, Kiyoko says. The Canadian actor who plays Coley, Maya da Costa, has Vietnamese heritage: it was important to Kiyoko to create not just a queer love story, but one that reflected her Asian heritage, too. Growing up in Los Angeles, “I never was able to buy a ticket at a cinema and see myself reflected back to me in my own experience as a queer person, as a mixed-race Asian person,” she says (Kiyoko is of Japanese descent on her mother’s side). “I never believed that my stories really mattered, because I never got to see them.”Born Hayley Kiyoko Alcroft, the singer grew up close to the limelight. Her father, Jamie Alcroft, is an actor and comedian, while her mother is the figure skater and Emmy award-winning choreographer Sarah Kawahara. Kiyoko herself has been performing since she was five, initially as an actor in commercials and later Disney Channel and Nickelodeon shows. She started learning the drums at six years old and wrote her first song at eight. In her late teens, she was part of the all-girl band the Stunners, which supported Justin Bieber in 2010 but broke up a year later without having released an album.View image in fullscreenLike the clappers … Hayley Kiyoko on the set of Girls Like Girls.Photograph: Dan Power/Focus FeaturesKiyoko’s solo career took off after she released Girls Like Girls as a single, which happened to be just days before same-sex marriage was legalised by the US federal government in June 2015. Back then it felt like an appropriate anthem for a time full of hope and steps forward for the LGBTQ+ community. Now, however, the picture is less positive: there has been a major increase in the number of anti-LGBTQ+ policies across the US in recent years, with the American Civil Liberties Uniontracking more than 500 anti-LGBTQ+ billsbeing considered so far in 2026 alone.Kiyoko describes the current political climate as “heartbreaking”, and though she is keen to make clear that she is “not the spokesperson for what’s going on in the world”, she says: “It’s not safe for our community, and we are continually fighting for pride events and pride festivals to continue to be funded.” Reflecting on the video for her 2016 song One Bad Night, in which she highlighted the violence transgender women experience, she says she would go about making it differently, were she to make it now.View image in fullscreenDaddy daze … Zach Braff as Coley’s father in Girls Like Girls.Photograph: Focus FeaturesShe stands by it being “really important” to spotlight trans people’s stories, but now thinks it’s more important, rather than focusing on the violence queer people experience, to “create art that is more queer joy and showing us in spaces where we are thriving … How radical is it that right now in this awful political climate, we get to release a movie called Girls Like Girls in cinemas and to remind the world that our stories and our love matters and that we will never go anywhere?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe queer couple at the heart of the Girls Like Girls film do face adversity, with Sonya describing her relationship with Coley as “wrong” at one point, but for the most part it’s an intentionally positive portrayal of self-discovery. In particular, Coley is unequivocally accepted by her father, without fanfare. Kiyoko, who has spoken previously about how her parentsinitially dismissed her sexuality as “a phase”, says “everyone has their own journey with their family dynamics”, but says it felt important to show an accepting father figure in the film. “We go to watch movies to dream and to fantasise and to see representation that maybe we lack in our lives.”Kiyoko says “it’s been really healing” to promote Girls Like Girls right after getting engaged earlier this summer, “celebrating this traumatic moment of my teens” while also being able to show her fans that she now has “a partner who makes me feel so seen and loved”. The singer’s fiancee, Becca Tilley, is a former contestant on the dating show The Bachelor. The pair met in 2018 when the reality TV star was trying to set Kiyoko up with her younger sister, but Tilley’s sister “bailed, and she ended up going instead”, Kiyoko says. “We’ve been together ever since.” Wedding plans are on hold as “I’ve been in Girls Like Girls universe”, she says, but she hopes that soon “we’ll be able to get into that”.Certainly, Kiyoko’s career seems to be in full flow right now: she will be headlining the 35th iteration of the famed lesbian music festival The Dinah, which she is “very excited” about, particularly at a time when lesbian spaces are not “very accessible or available to people”. After that, she hopes to continue developing herself as a film-maker, and wants to take on more film and TV directing jobs. Music “will always support my storytelling”, she says, but she has “no idea” if she will continue to release new albums and go on tour.While Kiyoko rides the high of her first feature film finding global audiences, where is her own personal Sonya, the girl who broke her teenage heart, now? She doesn’t know, “but I’m grateful for the trauma because it led to my directorial debut”, she says with a grin. “I really do feel like I finally found my home, which is directing,” she says. “And I hope to continue to do that for ever.”Girls Like Girls is in cinemas2 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio | Music | The Guardian
description: When a rarity blew up on TikTok, the solitary ambient artist had fraudsters trying to steal her royalties. It reinforced her DIY mentality – until reforming her band Helen reminded her of the beauty of collaboration
Author: Jenn Pelly
Headline: When a rarity blew up on TikTok, the solitary ambient artist had fraudsters trying to steal her royalties. It reinforced her DIY mentality – until reforming her band Helen reminded her of the beauty of collaboration
Content: ‘I get to show a side of myself that doesn’t always show through, which is that I like having having fun’ … Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.Photograph: Colin SmithView image in fullscreen‘I get to show a side of myself that doesn’t always show through, which is that I like having having fun’ … Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.Photograph: Colin SmithMusicInterview‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trioJenn PellyWhen a rarity blew up on TikTok, the solitary ambient artist had fraudsters trying to steal her royalties. It reinforced her DIY mentality – until reforming her band Helen reminded her of the beauty of collaborationFri 2 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn mid-September, I watched as Liz Harris soundchecked to 1,500 empty seats at midtown Manhattan’s historic Town Hall theatre. Soon each plush red chair would be filled for the second of two sold-out nights, but this ornate seclusion felt oddly perfect. It is fair to infer that most of her concertgoers generally listen to the uncanny experimental music she makes as Grouper alone, just as she creates it.Harris started Grouper in 2005 in the DIY noise warehouses of Oakland, California. At 46, she now lives farther north, in coastal Astoria, Oregon, where she creates densely tessellated visual art and spare, lucid albums that have made her a titan of modern ambient music. Painfully beautiful and often inscrutable, hers is a sonic language all its own, creatingthickets of sound using little more than guitar or piano, voice and space; her angelic and alien songs have influenced artists as disparate asPhoebe BridgersandMk.gee, and been sampled by Lil B and 100 Gecs. It is intensely solitary work, often characterised as sad but full of profound relief. “Like a bloodletting,” Harris offers.Harris reflects on its origins in the abstract drone of her 2005 debut Way Their Crept. “I thought there was some really dark part of me, and I was trying to understand it and incorporate it,” she says now. She is uneasy being the face of her music and generally keeps herself at arm’s length from the industry. “I’ve always been backing away from that,” she says, preferring to remind herself before shows “that we’re all in the room together”.View image in fullscreenHelen … l-r Jed Bindeman, Scott Simmons, Liz Harris.Photograph: Colin SmithWhen Harris and I meet at her Williamsburg hotel prior to the show, she’s wearing a T-shirt that says “Birth Ends in Death”, merch from her friend and occasional collaborator, the ambient musician Jefre Cantu-Ledesma. In addition to these milestone Grouper shows – coming five years after her last album, Shade – we’re speaking in light of the second record by Helen, the dream-pop trio in which she sings and plays guitar alongside drummer Jed Bindeman, who runs Portland shop Little Axe Records, and bassist Scott Simmons, also of lo-fi bandthe Lavender Flu. Their new album, Linda’s Head, like their 2015 debut The Original Faces, evokes scrappy Flying Nun indie-pop remade in their own stark Pacific Northwest image. But there’s a striking clarity and weight to the new one. If Grouper is the sound of a woman singing to herself, on Linda’s Head, she sings out.Helen’s appeal, for Harris, is in part its collectivity. “I get to relax more in Helen,” she says. “It feels as if I get to show a side of myself that I’ve always had, but that doesn’t get to show through Grouper, which is that I like having fun and I like my friends. I’m not just in the corner crying,” she says with a hearty laugh. Helen has a “bright energy”, she says, but, as with Grouper, a darkness gently haunts the music and Harris’s beguiling layered harmonies. The band’s name references Washington’s Mount St Helen, the site of a deadly volcanic eruption shortly before Harris was born in 1980, and it also alludes to a childhood spectre. “When I was a total loner social reject in junior high, I was trying to talk to ghosts all the time,” says Harris. “I thought I was talking to a ghost named Helen that lived in my house.”The songs consider what Harris calls “ecstatic nihilism” in a brutal world. “We’re all going through this time where things are really fucked up – it’s the war on Gaza and straight-up fascism in this country,” she says of the US. “There’s this urge to escape, but at the same time, a very pressing urge to be present and have community.” She hears both on Linda’s Head, and says the collaborative process of making the music lifted her spirits during a time when she was navigating medical difficulties. “Jed would be like, ‘Come on, let’s practise,’ and I’d drag my feet there. I’d always leave thinking, ‘Thank God I did that.’ It was really restorative.”In conversation, Harris is gracious and direct – she sounds as comfortable discussing her art, process and many tattoos as she does politics and music-industry corruption – which may surprise those who know her through her often cryptic music. Touring and performing like this is daunting for her, but she’s enjoying it. She says she’s been feeling more “integrated” lately, which she hears in Helen.A pair of songs on Linda’s Head, Dead Shark and Dead Shark II (alternate versions of the same tune), are disarmingly vibrant for Harris, despite their morbid origins. They were inspired by an actual shark Harris saw one day at the coast when she was feeling especially low. She observed its large, lifeless body floating by. “It distracted me from my own shit, and took me out of my headspace, this poor creature,” she says. “The song is about connecting and the process of feeling bad and going out into nature and letting it change you.”Helen: Dead Shark II – videoThe macabre titles recall Harris’s 2008 breakthrough, Dragging a Dead Deer Up a Hill, when she pivoted from abstract noise to acoustic, subtle art songs. That earlier title derived from a core childhood memory: Harris encountered a dead deer in the woods with a friend who dared her to hoist it up a hill. It incited a realisation about her agency in the world, and later inspired a title about the process of unburdening yourself of the past.When she was two years old, Harris’s parents were among the many seeking structure after the chaos of post-hippy late-60s San Francisco. The family moved from nearby Bolinas, where her father built houses with back-to-the-lander Lloyd Kahn, to a Fourth Way commune in Sonoma County. They joined a spiritual group – called the Group – where kids defiantly referred to the initiated as “groupers”. Harris still has friends from then: “There was a grouper at the show last night.”View image in fullscreen‘I’m pretty happy at the place I’ve landed’ … Liz HarrisPhotograph: Kait De AngelisThe adults enacted the Group’s dogma on to children who were shuffled between households. Theoretically, they followed the teachings of famed mystic Gurdjieff. Harris was told that they wererealpeople, but most of the world was asleep. “It was so confusing, and actually just instilled terror in me,” she says. “It made me terrified of other people, but also terrified of, how do I make sure that I stay real? I can’t become one of thesleepers.” I ask if this affected 2008’s Heavy Water/I’d Rather Be Sleeping, still her signature song, but she says that was about a depressive period and retreating into her “very active dream world”.Making music in her 20s was a way to begin processing it all. “I would still call it a cult,” she says of the Group, “and what happened was exploitative. But it’s not holding my focus in the way that it used to. There were enlightening things and shitty things – all of it led to where I’m at now. I still have my existential crises, but I’m pretty happy at the place I’ve landed.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHarris helps to maintain that balance by avoiding the music industry, but during the pandemic, she became caught in the undertow of a uniquely modern phenomenon when her 2008 rarity Poison Tree went viral. Harris wrote the gothic hymn in her mid-20s after relocating to Portland and feeling intensely isolated. “I went dark with it:I’ve never been able to connect with people. There’s something wrong with me, and people can see it,” she recalls. “I was having self-punishing thoughts and then trying to process it and turn it into something more expansive or rational-minded.”The song’s unlikely TikTok moment means “there’s this younger generation of really sweet, rad, open-minded kids” newly discovering Grouper, says Harris. She delights in recounting how her friends’ teenage children are now independently getting into her work.This current Grouper tour has been Harris’s first time “out in the world” since the song “fluffed up, or whatever you want to call it”, she says. “I hate saying ‘gone viral’.” She was late to learning about Poison Tree’s second life; she pays little attention to stats and doesn’t know how to look them up. When Brian Foote, general manager of her label Kranky, first told her that Poison Tree had accrued 20m plays (it now has more than 300m on the world’s biggest music streamer) she told him, “‘Well, that’s weird because I haven’t even put that on digital.’ He was like, ‘Yeah, that’s why I’m telling you.’”The song had been fraudulently registered and uploaded by someone else and had already earned around six figures. Fortunately, since that person used the same distribution platform as Harris, she and Foote were able to shut down the scammer and get back what she was owed.‘A sacred kind of sound’: inside a solar-powered journey to preserve the music of church organsRead moreAs an independent artist, Harris has learned first-hand that an elevated digital profile comes with a range of new concerns – like fake remixes and songs posted with the same titles as hers by bad actors trying to skim whatever royalties they can. “You have to spend all this stupid energy whack-a-mole-ing” these infringing tracks, she says. “I have learned that people think [streaming] platforms are a lot more regulated than they are. It is not regulated. I think it’s rational that I have a fear of immersing myself more into the music industry.”As Harris’s self-contained world expands – her label YellowElectric, her zine Presence, plus the gallery, Anita, she occasionally runs from her studio – her independence feels heroic. She carries a sweatshirt repping Portland punk legends Dead Moon to our interview, a fitting nod to her regional DIY forebears. Those ideals feel of a piece with Helen’s graceful, threadbare sound, too. “I’ve always adamantly wanted to be a balanced person,” she says. “In my 30s, I toured too much and got burnt out. I thought, ‘I want to have other things I’m doing. I don’t want to get stuck in a corner.’ In some ways, that still happens, but I’m intentional about having a full life.”On her current tour, she channels older material through this light. The first song of her set is Invisible, a downcast and tactile acoustic ballad from 2008. The incantatory lyrics – “I’ve become invisible” – seem to temper an innate shyness with the texture of a devotional. When she sings it now, glowing and a cappella, it becomes a “ritual chant” to ground herself.“It feels more like singing about a special quality, or a superpower,” she says. “I can turn myself invisible – like a person who’s here but isn’t. That could be really dark. Or it could be that I have the power to retreat as I need.”Linda’s Head is released via Kranky on 2 October. Grouper tours Europe and the UK from 29 October, including sets at Club 2 Club festival, Turin (1 November) and Le Guess Who? festival, Utrecht (7 November)Explore more on these topicsMusicExperimental musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: How Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’ | Thrillers | The Guardian
description: In the film-maker’s Houston-set film, Ali stars as a devout Muslim who moonlights as a vicious hitman
Author: Radheyan Simonpillai
Headline: In the film-maker’s Houston-set film, Ali stars as a devout Muslim who moonlights as a vicious hitman
Content: Bassam Tariq at Toronto Film Festival, September 2026.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbView image in fullscreenBassam Tariq at Toronto Film Festival, September 2026.Photograph: Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images for IMDbThrillersInterviewHow Bassam Tariq pivoted from stalled Blade reboot to new Mahershala Ali thriller: ‘I’m happier I made this movie’Radheyan SimonpillaiIn the film-maker’s Houston-set film, Ali stars as a devout Muslim who moonlights as a vicious hitmanFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 09.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMahershala Aliis swinging around a blade inYour Mother Your Mother Your Mother. That’s not a nod to Ali’s previousattachmentto Marvel’s Blade. It’s of a piece with Ali’s character, Latif, a devout Muslim who also happens to be a contract killer, though he fashions himself a righteous killer. Latif justifies his violence as divine retribution, dispensing victims he believes to have offended God. His sword, according to writer and director Bassam Tariq, is a part of Latif’s code, a negotiation with his faith.“You are forced to strike with intention when you use a sword,” Tariq says, speaking in a recent interview in Toronto.Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review – Mahershala Ali is a grieving hitman in soulful thrillerRead moreThe film-maker seems equally purposeful in our conversation as we dive deep into his pulpy samurai-coded neo-western. In Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, he grapples with grief, spirituality, violence and the culture in America writ large. The movie is a visceral and stylish genre thriller – think Steven Soderbergh’s The Limey by way of Nicolas Winding Refn’s Drive. It’s also a textured portrait of Houston, navigating the city’s cultural tapestry, but also the hostility and tension between its siloed faiths and ideologies. That’s the conflict playing out between Ali’s Latif, who’s struggling to raise three kids on his own, andJon Cho’s Pastor Hwan, a militant evangelical Christian posting fire-and-brimstone sermons online while waging a heavily armed and indiscriminately brutal religious crusade.“It feels a little different in Texas right now,” Tariq says. He describes a palpable contrast between what he refers to as the “Mamdaniera” in New York, where he lives, and Houston, where he grew up. “Something that I found particularly in Texas, where I started writing [this] is, whether they’re religious or not, people are connected to the third spaces that are religious. All the social services are cut. So, if you’re going to go hang out or play basketball, it’ll probably be at a mosque or a church. You end up being a part of those communities. At the same time, you can start building dogmatic ideas, [like,] ‘We’re better than other people’. The nature of it has been really politicized. I think it’s a dark moment right now.”Mahershala Ali on Marvel’s collapsed Blade reboot: ‘If they wanted to do it, we would’ve done it’Read moreYour Mother Your Mother Your Mother fearlessly cuts through that tension while capturing what makes those communities so vibrant and inspiring, and searching for a sense of hope in its heartfelt and intimate interrogation of faith and fatherhood. Those themes were especially important to he and Ali, Tariq says.“We connected on these things while we were on this [other] movie together,” says Tariq, referring to Marvel’s Blade. “You might have heard of it.”He’s being cheeky. The fallout from the aborted Blade reboot, which Tariq was set to direct, has become an intricate part of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother’s lore. Ali was attached for several years to star as Marvel’s vampire-slayer, once played byWesley Snipes. He only recentlyconfirmedthat the long-delayed reboot is simply not happening.“We were very close to shooting when the pencils went down,” says Tariq, describing the moment before he departed Blade in 2022. “Even though we had no script, which is why it shut down.”View image in fullscreenMahershala Ali in Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosTariq says they had their action sequences all planned out, following a year and a half of prep that included extensive fight training and choreography for Ali. That was Marvel’s process at the time: the action comes first, allowing time for VFX and set design, and the rest comes after.“It was like Bollywood, dude,” he says today. “You have dance scenes. Figure out all the choreography. And then we’ll figure out what the story is later … Now [Marvel’s] not moving forward until they have a great script.“I’m not trying to throw any shade on the writers,” Tariq adds, adding that they had big shoes to fill given that theearlier Bladein his mind was a near-perfect movie. “They worked really hard on it. It’s just a very tough thing to crack.”Tariq says he’s more than at peace with how everything turned out. He’s actually a squirrelly mix of nerves and excitement when I speak to him, the evening before Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother premieres at the Toronto film festival, his whispery voice barely containing that mix of emotion. He’s taking a moment for this interview before settling back in with his family, including two kids aged 12 and nine.They’re in town for the occasion. They’ve been along for the whole ride, from the writing process in Houston to production in Atlanta, observing onset, during ADR and the sound mix. “I’m trying to just keep everyone close,” he says, before tying that ethos to the story of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which is ultimately about a father’s wayward journey back to his kids. “You live the movie that you make.”View image in fullscreenAli, Tariq and Jahleel Kamara on the set of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.Photograph: Jaclyn Martinez/Amazon MGM StudiosThe seeds for the film were planted after Tariq’s own harrowing experience following the birth of his first child in 2014, when his wife had an infection that sent her to the emergency room. “My son was only breastfed at the time,” says Tariq. “So I had to go around New York City trying to find breast milk for my son. I couldn’t find it anywhere.”He poured that frantic search into the earliest iteration of Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, which opens with Ali’s Latif scouring for breast milk after his wife passes, while having the same crisis of faith that Tariq experienced.“I remember that frustration,” says Tariq. “I felt like that anger towards divinity. And then, of course, my son was fine. I realized all he really needed at that moment was just for me be present as a father. To have that miraculous moment when you hear your kid wanting you, that’s something that I think about. I’ve been trying to contemplate: how do I put that in a story that’s propulsive and exciting?”You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead morePart of the solution came from working on Blade, where Tariq connected and collaborated with Ali, and mapped out those elaborate fight scenes, which would have been abandoned after Marvel pulled the plug. Instead, Tariq and Ali were able to salvage what they prepared for the superhero movie, and bring it all over to their more intimate film about a father discovering that his kids are his superpower.“I’m a lot happier that I made this movie,” says Tariq, comparing working within the Marvel machine versus having the freedom to really explore and express himself on Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.“As you know, with all these things, there are these massive systems, and they have so many stakeholders to please. It’s just the nature of these things where they have to gross a certain [amount], and they have to look a certain way. There’s a glossiness. And that’s fine. I think some people have thrived in it and made some incredible films. For where I am right now, this feels like the right space. My mind and heart feel very much at ease.”Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is out now in the US, in Australia on 9 October and in the UK on 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsThrillersAction and adventure filmsMahershala AlifeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive’: how Ross McElwee made a film about unimaginable loss, grief and guilt | Movies | The Guardian
description: When his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary project
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: When his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary project
Content: Adrian as a boy in Venice, as seen in Remake.Photograph: Giant Squid FilmsView image in fullscreenAdrian as a boy in Venice, as seen in Remake.Photograph: Giant Squid FilmsMoviesInterview‘I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive’: how Ross McElwee made a film about unimaginable loss, grief and guiltXan BrooksWhen his son died aged 27, the director could barely bring himself to watch his old clips of the boy. When at last he did, it was the genesis of an extraordinary projectFri 2 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoss McElwee is the film-maker who spun home movies into art, framing himself and his friends and his son Adrian. The director used to film Adrian for a few minutes each month. He tracked the kid from infancy to adulthood, trying to catch the significant turns of his life. When tragedy struck it back-shadowed the footage. Maybe every home movie is a ghost story at heart.It feels crass to compliment McElwee on his latest documentary, Remake, because it isn’t the picture he’d ever have chosen to make. It is instead a grief-struck tour-de-force: a magnificent film about film-making and its real-world repercussions. McElwee filmed Adrian because he loved him, but now fears he might have hurt him. So he sifts through the material in search of clues, addressing his son as though he’s still in the room. “I look at the footage to convince myself that you were alive,” he says. “But also to convince myself that you’re gone.”The plan, he explains, was for a completely different film. A Hollywood producer wanted to shoot a fictionalised version of his 1986 documentarySherman’s March. McElwee decided to follow the process – to make a new documentary about adapting an old documentary. That might be funny, he thought. But events overtook him. Adrian’s mental health was deteriorating. He became addicted to opioids. He died from a fentanyl overdose at the age of 27, in the bathroom of McElwee’s Boston home.“Everything immediately ground to a halt,” the director recalls. “My son was gone. I was devastated. And compared to everything I was facing, the film seemed banal and frivolous.” He took a year to regroup and plotted a new course.A more traditional film-maker would have junked the original idea. McElwee has audaciously chosen to preserve it, so that the remake plays as a kind of absurd counterbeat to the anguish of Adrian’s death. The film would have been too depressing otherwise, he says. “And in a sense I’m remaking my life by picking up the camera again. I’m reconstructing the life of my son from the scraps and pieces that had ended up being filmed.”Adrian, we learn, was gung-ho for a Hollywood version of Sherman’s March. Remake shows him discussing the project at length. He feels that his dad should be making more mainstream movies. He says, “Why not just do some big blockbuster hit?”View image in fullscreenCharleen Swansea at McDonald’s, as seen in Sherman’s March.Photograph: Little Field FilmsAfter seeing Remake, I rewatch Sherman’s March. It’s a joyous, insightful, free-ranging affair; a film that delights in taking the road less travelled. McElwee is ostensibly making a civil war documentary, but he keeps being set up with various “nice southern girls”. In one scene, Charleen Swansea – his voluble former English teacher – demands that he turn off his camera before a big date. “This isn’t art,” she roars. “This is life!”The success of Sherman’s March made Swansea a cult celebrity. A poll of American critics named her “the greatest documentary character of all time”. But when McElwee revisits Swansea for Remake, he finds she is now in the grip of dementia. She has no memory of the movie, or of teaching him English. “Things just disappear,” she says with a frown.View image in fullscreen‘There is a possibility that I was in denial’ … Ross McElwee.Photograph: Boston Globe/Getty ImagesPeople disappear, that’s the tragic logic of life. Except that on the screen, in the footage, Adrian still feels alive, which is both a comfort and a torment. McElwee dips back through the archive to show him as a gorgeous, earnest little kid, netting crayfish on the rocks (“I just love the deep surprise of the ocean,” he says). Now here he is again as a tense, watchful teenager, raising his hand to block the camera lens. “There was no evidence for me that my films were a problem for him,” McElwee tells me. “Overall I would say that they were more a plus than a minus.” All the same, he can’t help but wonder.Might the issue be one of divided loyalties? McElwee has a set of responsibilities as a parent and a set of responsibilities as an artist. But maybe these are always going to be at loggerheads.McElwee nods. “Yeah, they’re antithetical. And when it works, the antithesis is what gives a film its creative friction. Because it never resolves itself. It’s always part of the problem. You have the camera, which means you have the power and other people don’t. And that’s the big responsibility. You can’t push your subject to say what you want them to say. You have to keep that in mind when you shoot and you edit.”View image in fullscreen‘They recognise what it means to you’ … Victoria Mapplebeck and her son, Jim.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianIf McElwee has a British counterpart, it might be the film-maker Victoria Mapplebeck. OnMotherboard, her fabulous 2024 documentary, Mapplebeck condensed two decades of life as a working single mother alongside her phlegmatic son, Jim.After speaking with McElwee, I call Mapplebeck. She says she relates to Remake and the ethical issues it raises. It’s about the compulsion to film and its effect on a family; the granting of consent and how that is understood by both parties.‘Mum, I can’t think straight any more’: the mother who filmed her son’s entire childhoodRead more“Watching it,” she says, “I felt both ashamed and moved. Because the thing with both Jim and Adrian is that at times they do provide consent [to film] because they recognise what it means to you. I think Jim definitely got more from the process than Adrian did. It was a useful way to get us talking. But fundamentally I needed to do it more than Jim did.”In his 2011 film Photographic Memory, McElwee painted Adrian as a troubled but basically resilient young man. The pair promoted the picture at the Venice film festival. Adrian posted pictures of speedboats, gondolas and wild parties. It should have been a triumphant moment. But McElwee now worries that his film got Adrian wrong and that the subsequent fuss turned his head and caused problems.“Did I give him a false impression of who he was? That he was more or less invincible and could therefore keep doing drugs?” He doesn’t know; he fears the worst. “For a child to see himself in a movie that his father has made and to then travel with him to festivals – often that would be wonderful for both father and son. But then all these other things arose from that. So there is a possibility that it had a corrosive effect on him and that I was somehow in denial about that. It was only later – after he got into trouble and then after he died – that I began to see the film in a different light.”View image in fullscreenAdrian in Remake.Photograph: Giant Squid FilmsI’m glad McElwee has made space for his unquiet old work. It speaks to Remake’s themes of representation and memory, and suggests that a film is never truly finished. The Sherman’s March remake, for instance, is initially billed as a comedy feature from the director of Paul Blart: Mall Cop. We then see it redrafted as a dramatic miniseries and a TV sitcom before it’s finally rolled out as a verbatim live opera. McElwee wonders what his son would have made of all that.What, for that matter, would he have thought of Remake? That’s the unanswerable question; the director can’t say. “I’d like to think that he came out the other side sober, and that he would think it had honoured him and was honest, and also that I was admitting the mistakes I’d made. But I’ll never know for sure.”Another thought strikes him. “It’s also possible that he’d say, ‘Yeah, this is good but you need to get a proper Hollywood deal.’ He was relentless about that. He liked my films, but I could tell they were never quite up to snuff in terms of the interest they generated and the money they made. He saw them as interesting exercises but a waste of time when I could have been doing something else.”McElwee is 79 and slowing down. Ideally, he’d like to make one last documentary – something light, warm and funny. But something is missing: the old itch, the compulsion. “I’ve been to family reunions in North Carolina,” he says. “Also, I had a nephew who got married. Each time I thought, ‘Gosh, I should be filming this.’ And I just can’t do it. This whole past year. I want to take a break and let life be life without me trying to turn it into art.”It reminds him of what Charleen said in Sherman’s March: “This isn’t art, this is life.” That’s four decades ago now. McElwee almost smiles. “I’m a slow learner,” he says.Remake is out nowIn the UK, the charityMindis available on 0300 123 3393. title: ‘You could have an amazing time for £30,000’: UK castles cash in on Traitors-style events | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: From stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit show
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: From stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit show
Content: Duns Castle estate in Berwickshire, Scotland, plays host to murder mystery events.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyView image in fullscreenDuns Castle estate in Berwickshire, Scotland, plays host to murder mystery events.Photograph: Maciej Olszewski/AlamyThe Traitors‘You could have an amazing time for £30,000’: UK castles cash in on Traitors-style eventsFrom stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit showPatrick GreenfieldFri 2 Oct 2026 08.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Thursday night, the singer-songwriter James Blunt, Love Island host Maya Jama and mathematician Hannah Fry were among the 21 Celebrity Traitors returning to UK screens for another round of deceit and detective work. Famously, contestants do not stay at Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands during filming, and the venue is not a hotel, so fans cannot book their own overnight stays without hiring the entire Ross-shire estate. But that has not stopped people from trying to recreate their own versions.Theshow’s surging popularityhas been accompanied by a bonanza in Traitors-style events across the UK. From stag and hen dos to castle conspiracy weekends, event companies now host year-round imitations for fans looking to recreate the drama of the candle-lit roundtable. The show is also proving to be a boom for the owners of Britain’s crumbling castles – with wealthy fans even hiring them out for their own private events.The Celebrity Traitors: episode one – as it happenedRead more“We see a huge spike in people searching for Traitors-style experiences on our pages every time it comes back on TV,” said Roger Masterson, founder of Celtic Castles, which specialises in castle stays and rentals. “We’ve got castle hotels that put together Traitors packages. A 15-bedroom castle might sleep 30, so they’ll bring in couples and organise the faithfuls and traitors over the weekend. They build a story around it and play the game. There are huge varieties with how it’s done.”View image in fullscreenThe dining room at Duns Castle.Photograph: groupaccomodation.com/PACompanies organising team bonding exercises are by far the most common customers. GOTO Events, which runs tailored Traitors-style experiences, offers packages from five people to 1,000, complete with their own version of the missions that contestants play to build up the prize pot and a Claudia Winkleman-style host. A GOTO spokesperson said these had become the most popular experience they offer.“Ever since the show launched, it’s just not died down. We keep thinking things will slow down and they haven’t,” the spokesperson said.“Everyone pretty much takes it as a bit of fun because you know that someone is lying. In one of my first events, the big boss was one of the betrayers and got called out in the first round. It was funny. Everyone loves calling out their boss.”But a Traitors-style experience often does not come cheap. Daylong events are a few hundred pounds, while those looking for the full castle experience pay much more. Rothes Glen castle in the Scottish Highlands is offering a three-night package from £4,388 a room for two guests for a castle conspiracy weekend in August next year. A private event will set you back even more: hiring a luxury castle for the weekend can set you back tens of thousands of pounds – and that’s before the cost of organising the game, says Masterson.View image in fullscreenGuests stay in luxury at Dalhousie Castle, near Edinburgh.Photograph: Dalhousie Castle/PA“If you were looking at an exclusive-use property, let’s say for 30 people, they might charge £10,000 a night on a bed and breakfast basis. So, a two night stay would be 20 – then add another 10 for the event. You could have an amazing time for £30,000 for the whole weekend,” he says.The boom is also helping fund repairs to Britain’s crumbling castles, he says. “I’ve been with owners and I ask them why they’re moving into the hospitality market. And they say: ‘Well, we need £100,000 to replace the roof’.”Since the first episode on Thursday, Traitors mania is set to take over the country once again, running until Friday 30 October. Celebrities will compete for up to £100,000 for their chosen charities.“We are expecting another surge [with the new series]. We are ready to go,” said GOTO.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsScotlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Stories shortlisted for 4thWrite prize offer ‘a whole world in a few pages’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The six stories on the shortlist for the 10th year of the writing award run by 4th Estate and the Guardian and open to unpublished writers of colour are ‘affecting in new and surprising ways’, said judge and author Gurnaik Johal
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The six stories on the shortlist for the 10th year of the writing award run by 4th Estate and the Guardian and open to unpublished writers of colour are ‘affecting in new and surprising ways’, said judge and author Gurnaik Johal
Content: Shortlisted writers (left to right, top to bottom) … Svetlana Chigozie Onye, Clementine Wolodarsky, Ope Adedeji, Darren Chan, Meher Iqbal, and Diya Nair.View image in fullscreenShortlisted writers (left to right, top to bottom) … Svetlana Chigozie Onye, Clementine Wolodarsky, Ope Adedeji, Darren Chan, Meher Iqbal, and Diya Nair.BooksStories shortlisted for 4thWrite prize offer ‘a whole world in a few pages’The six stories on the shortlist for the 10th year of the writing award run by 4th Estate and the Guardian and open to unpublished writers of colour are ‘affecting in new and surprising ways’, said judge and author Gurnaik JohalEmma LoffhagenFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe shortlist for the 10th year of the 4thWrite prize – the short story competition for unpublished writers of colour run by the publisher 4th Estate in association with the Guardian – has been revealed.The six shortlisted stories were “affecting in new and surprising ways”, said judge Gurnaik Johal, who was shortlisted for the prize in 2018.Clementine Wolodarsky was shortlisted for I Only Mug Girls, which judge and author Sanam Mahloudji described as “a fun and absurd ride of a story about an unlikely friendship between a lying misfit who works at the corporate office of Gail’s and the lonely divorcee she meets on the train”.Darren Chan made the shortlist for Love Bite, described as “a really impressive and affecting story … sharp and funny and shot through with darkness” by judge and novelist Kamila Shamsie.Ope Adedeji was selected for Omugwo, which tells the story of a woman convinced her newborn granddaughter is the reincarnation of her sister. The story is a “moving exploration of grief and mother-daughter relationships”, said judge and Guardian books commissioning editor Ella Creamer.Meher Iqbal appears on the list for Darkroom, which Mahloudji praised as “a sensitive and sensorially rich coming-of-age story about a young teenage friendship” that “captures the isolation and regret of jealousy with beauty and depth”.Diya Nair was chosen for Minty Fresh, which “depicts an office relationship in such a compelling and life-like way”, said Mahloudji. The story has “a subtle humour and details that feel true to life in their complexities and contradictions”.Completing this year’s list is Svetlana Chigozie Onye with London 2060, which follows a water rationing officer in a drought-ravaged future London as he navigates a secret relationship and personal tragedy.“The 4thWrite shortlist is a reminder of what short fiction can do: give us a whole world in a few pages and leave us thinking long after the ending,” said judge Chanté Joseph. “It was a joy to read such distinct voices and discuss them with the other judges.”The winner of the prize will receive £1,000, a one-day publishing workshop at 4th Estate and publication of their story on the Guardian website.This is the 10th year of the prize, which is open to writers aged 18 and over living in the UK or Ireland.Last year’s winnerwas Piyumi Kapugeekiyana for The Original Is Not Here. Other past winners include Yan F Zhang forFleeting Marrowin 2024 and Tian Yi forThe Good Sonin 2023.A number of previous longlisted and shortlisted writers have gone on to publish books: Bolu Babalola, author of Love in Colour and Honey & Spice; Guy Gunaratne, author of Mister, Mister and In Our Mad and Furious City; Kasim Ali, author of Good Intentions and Who Will Remain; Gurnaik Johal, author of We Move and Saraswati; and Kit Fan, author of Diamond Hill and Goodbye Chinatown.Along with Mahloudji, Joseph, Shamsie, Johal and Creamer, this year’s judging panel includes agent Emma Paterson of Aitken Alexander Associates and 4th Estate publishing director Kishani Widyaratna.Explore more on these topicsBooks4thWrite short story prizeAwards and prizesShort storiesPublishingnewsShareReuse this content
