title: TV tonight: Sienna Miller’s slick and seriously nasty divorce drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Dominic West co-stars as the scheming tech-mogul husband in War on Sky Atlantic. Plus: Sly Stallone and Catherine Zeta-Jones join Graham Norton on the sofa. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Dominic West co-stars as the scheming tech-mogul husband in War on Sky Atlantic. Plus: Sly Stallone and Catherine Zeta-Jones join Graham Norton on the sofa. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Playing dirty … Sienna Miller as Carla and Dominic West as Morgan in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreenPlaying dirty … Sienna Miller as Carla and Dominic West as Morgan in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Sienna Miller’s slick and seriously nasty divorce dramaDominic West co-stars as the scheming tech-mogul husband in War on Sky Atlantic. Plus: Sly Stallone and Catherine Zeta-Jones join Graham Norton on the sofa. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Jack SealeandSimon WardellFri 2 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWar9pm, Sky Atlantic“If they play dirty,” says Nina Sosanya’s lawyer, Beatrice Ubosi, “we will be total and utter filth.” Let’s hope that’s a promise – this slick, stylish divorce drama could get seriously nasty. Sienna Miller’s film star Carla has her beady eyes on the fortune of tech slimeball Morgan (Dominic West). But as befits an extremely rich man, he has a very expensive and ruthless legal team. Expect fireworks.Phil HarrisonPlay for Today: Village Idiot9pm, Channel 5View image in fullscreenDefiant … Barbara (Phyllis Logan) fends off the developers in Play for Today: Village Idiot.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/© Vertigo Production. 2026/Photographer: Valeria LuongoWhen a high-speed rail project threatens her cottage, pensioner Barbara (Phyllis Logan) defiantly chains herself to the porch. Can her grandson Peter (Max Harwood) – now a nervy liaison officer for the corporate baddies – resolve the situation? Unlike its HS2 inspiration, the results are cheap and cheerful.Graeme VirtueThe Walking Dead: Dead City9pm, Sky OneThe zombie drama turns into something like a particularly fraught episode of ER, but not because of the undead: two rival gangs flood the hospital, with wounds they have inflicted on each other. It’s a delicate ethical dilemma for Maggie and co: can they just let them die?Jack SealeHave I Got News for You9.30pm, BBC OneIt’s series 72 of the bulletproof satirical quiz and, from the rise of Andy Burnham to the bin-defeating triumph of Nigel Farage, Paul Merton and Ian Hislop have plenty to get their teeth into. They are joined by Gyles Brandreth with Richard Ayoade in the hosting chair.PHLive From the Lycett Arms10pm, Channel 4Thirst rodeo: an unashamedly boozy knees-up in a London East End pub has turned out to be an effective delivery mechanism for Joe Lycett’s chaotic, raunchy energy. After variable efforts from previous guest bar managers Sara Cox, Lenny Henry and Mel Giedroyc, how will his celebrity supervisor fare this week?GVThe Graham Norton Show10.40pm, BBC OneAnother big-name lineup for Graham as the sofa is graced by Trump-friendly Hollywood lunk Sylvester Stallone. He’ll be joined by Catherine Zeta-Jones, 50 Cent and Andrew Garfield, touting his lead role in Paul Greengrass’s film about the peasants’ revolt, The Uprising. Probably best to stay off the politics, Graham …PHFilm choiceTeenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Jane Schoenbrun, 2026),MubiView image in fullscreenPsychosexual blowout … Gillian Anderson as Billy and Hannah Einbinder as Kris in Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.Photograph: © MUBIIn her previous two movies, indie director Jane Schoenbrun explored the uncanny spaces we inhabit between the internet, TV and our daily lives. For her latest dark and delirious drama, she delves into movies and their unsettling hold on us. Hacks’ Hannah Einbinder plays Kris, an up-and-coming queer film-maker hired to reboot Camp Miasma, a “problematic” Friday the 13th-style slasher horror franchise. For research, she visits the original’s reclusive star, Billy (Gillian Anderson), who, bizarrely, lives in the film’s abandoned summer camp location. As the women get closer, reality and Camp Miasma’s grisly fiction start to blur in a giddy, psychosexual blowout.Simon WardellThe Last First: Winter K2(Amir Bar-Lev, 2026),Apple TV“No tents. No food. I think some people will die this night.” It’s a chilling start to Amir Bar-Lev’s sobering, cautionary documentary about the 2021 race to be the first to climb the world’s second-highest peak, which resulted in five deaths. The copious interviews and footage (every team seemingly had a camera crew) focus mainly on the Icelandic/Pakistani trio of John Snorri Sigurjónsson and Ali and Sajid Sadpara. They got to base camp first but were soon joined by “rock star” Nepali-British climber Nims Purja and, fatefully, a large commercial expedition of mostly amateurs.SWExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best recent poetry – review roundup | Poetry | The Guardian
description: Have It by John Cooper Clarke; The Dodo Stories by Mary Mulholland; Red River Valley by Ian McMillan; Some Sacred Harbour by Roger Robinson; Otherwhere by Carolyn Forché
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Have It by John Cooper Clarke; The Dodo Stories by Mary Mulholland; Red River Valley by Ian McMillan; Some Sacred Harbour by Roger Robinson; Otherwhere by Carolyn Forché
Content:
John Cooper Clarke.Photograph: Ki Price/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Cooper Clarke.Photograph: Ki Price/Getty ImagesPoetry roundupPoetryReviewThe best recent poetry – review roundupHave It by John Cooper Clarke; The Dodo Stories by Mary Mulholland; Red River Valley by Ian McMillan;  Some Sacred Harbour by Roger Robinson; Otherwhere by Carolyn ForchéJennifer Lee TsaiFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenHave Itby John Cooper Clarke(Picador, £16.99)The latest collection from the original “people’s poet” displays his characteristic swagger, delivered with a distinctively northern humour. Merging blistering social satire and brash wit, Cooper Clarke irreverently tackles themes from the ridiculous to the sublime, including the malaise of contemporary urban life, the erosion of nature and the environment, money and the prospect of a cashless society, death and ageing, fascism, bachelorhood, popular culture and the NHS. His punk rock values caustically underpin the collection: “Me and my shrinking crowd / Each under our own personal cloud”; “We wish you no serious harm/ However, everybody sucks but us”. There’s heavy use of doggerel and jokes as he stridently proclaims his passion for writing. “It’s a meaningless job but someone’s got to do it / Thank God it’s me”. Overall, Cooper Clarke’s consummate performance skills in playing to the crowd demand applause as he advocates for the “blood royal of the working class”.The Dodo Stories by Mary Mullholland (Nine Arches, £11.99)Mulholland’s compelling debut collection explores complex questions of inheritance, migration and colonialism. “i go to the old country we’re from, / long to belong, to be like that fennel-lapping lizard in funchal”. She delves into personal and public archives, memory, dreams and the unconscious to uncover her family histories, stretching back to her great grandparents and the silenced stories of Portuguese indenture to the Caribbean. Her descriptions of wildlife and landscapes are skilfully rendered: “the three-night flower smells of pineapple and banana, scarab beetles hurry to the feast and stay like lovers”; “purpleheart, greenheart, spiny fiddleheart, and palms that walk by themselves, shift-shape”. At the heart of this richly evocative book is a moving tribute to her “exotic morpho mother”, the eponymous Dodo, and a desire for healing from the effects of intergenerational trauma. “May she receive this / benediction, an invocation to wish her well”.View image in fullscreenRed River Valley by Ian McMillan(Carcanet, £12.99)McMillan’s latest is inspired by his family life, living in a village near Barnsley as a poet and broadcaster in the community. These clear, accessible poems blend the surreal with the quotidian, as in the opening, Sudden Memory of My Dad Wearing Shorts, which reimagines his father singing his favourite song, “Red River Valley”. There is a madcap, maverick energy to the book, which explores encounters with people and familiar places such as the barber’s, a cricket club, a train station, the motorway, a bookshop. McMillan often engages in wry commentary to reflect on societal inequalities  and austerity in Britain. Overall, his compassionate outlook finds solace and the possibility of transformation in the everyday, where “It’s moments like this when all the stars align. / Evening games in winter; a touch of the sublime”.View image in fullscreenSome Sacred Harbour: New and Selected Poemsby Roger Robinson (Bloomsbury, £12.99)A testament to a lifetime’s work from the prize-winning poet, educator, performer and musician. The title piece is an artistic manifesto on survival and the vital importance of creativity in society. Robinson elucidates this philosophy as “creating a platform where sacred stories – the moments that define a life and its joys, traumatic hurts and recoveries – could be told. Something about bringing the margins to the centre”. These exquisitely crafted and dextrously lyrical poems centre around Black Atlantic and Black British identity, grief, migration, racial tragedies and injustices, family, music. Robinson emphasises a shared communal consciousness, “praise for these moments of quick recognition, / miracles of synchronicity and signalled kinship”. Sonically resonant and often biblically charged, the collection illuminates the breadth and depth of human experience, where “the shoots of spring always bring hope / and a chance for renewal”.View image in fullscreenOtherwhere: New & Selected Poems 1976–2026
by Carolyn ForchéOtherwhere: New and Selected Poems, 1976-2026by Carolyn Forché(Bloodaxe, £14.99)A landmark retrospective spanning five collections across five decades, this impressive volume opens with an eloquent preface, Older Than Glass, Younger Than Music, which delineates Forché’s poetics. What is remarkable about her work is a visionary ability to merge poems of personal intimacy with geopolitical realities, distinguishing her as a “poet of witness”. War, displacement and genocide are juxtaposed with elegiac meditations: “The word forwindis, in another language, the word forsoul”. The collection includes a new sequence entitled If There is Ink, addressing contemporary global crises. The title poem focuses on the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine and questions the limits of language: “if there is something to write that would raise the cities/ from the ruins the apartment blocks hospitals schools/ that would put the cities back as they were/ I would give everything to fill this pen with it”.Explore more on these topicsPoetryPoetry roundupreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Horror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comedies | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Obsession is a terrifying, violent nightmare of lovestruck madness – but the Globes’ rigid awards categories have forced it into an absurd choice
Author: Tom Beasley
Headline: Obsession is a terrifying, violent nightmare of lovestruck madness – but the Globes’ rigid awards categories have forced it into an absurd choice
Content: Musical or comedy? Obsession.Photograph: Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenMusical or comedy? Obsession.Photograph: Toronto film festivalHorror filmsHorror films like Obsession are shut out of the Golden Globes – unless they pretend to be comediesTom BeasleyObsession is a terrifying, violent nightmare of lovestruck madness – but the Globes’ rigid awards categories have forced it into an absurd choiceFri 2 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 05.55 EDTShareWhat do this year’s wish-gone-wrong taleObsession, gross-out transformation bloodbathThe Substance, and Jordan Peele’s generational masterpieceGet Outhave in common? Well, they’re all modern horror success stories, with critics and at the box office, and they broke free of genre snobbery to become awards-season contenders.They’re also toe-tapping laugh riots. At least that’s what theGolden Globeswould have you believe.The Globes present a conundrum for horror. Its major categories are split into either “drama” or “musical or comedy” and it’s fair to say neither of those is an obvious home for throat-ripping gorefests or white-knuckle ghost-train rides. So if you’re managing an awards push for a hotly tipped horror, what road do you take? The answer, often, is titters and tap-dancing.That’s what has happened with Obsession. Perthe Hollywood Reporter, Focus Features will submit it for consideration in the musical or comedy categories. This is despite the fact the movie is a pitch-dark story about what happens when a lonely man Bear (Michael Johnston) uses a magical trinket to force female pal Nikki (Inde Navarrette) to fall devotedly in love with him. The consequences are stark, with a descent into madness that includes Navarrette delivering some of the most terrifying facial expressions since Gordon Brown attempted to smile. The closest thing Obsession has to a knock-knock joke is when someone is graphically bludgeoned to death with a brick. Not exactly a zinger worthy of the Apollo.But it’s easy to see how this impulse towards category chicanery arises. Traditionally, the drama category is where the big-hitters duke it out. This year, it’s likely to be a straight fight between Christopher Nolan’s exceptional take onThe Odysseyand the Spanish LGBTQ+ epicLa Bola Negra. That’s not to mention Dune: Part Three, which could ride a Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King-style wave if Denis Villeneuve can bring Frank Herbert’s books to a satisfying conclusion.While the musical or comedy category looks uncommonly formidable this year – with Martin McDonagh’s fast-talkingWild Horse Nineset to battle Olivia Wilde’s summer hitThe Inviteand the small matter of the Michael Jackson biopic – it’s less intimidating than a straight fight with Nolan’s Homeric juggernaut.As horror doesn’t fit neatly, it’s able to tactically pick its battles. In actuality, though, this makes it very difficult for horror to ever emerge victorious. Most horror fits more suitably into the drama category. The Exorcist won as a drama back in 1974, despite the fact it would go on to lose to The Sting at theOscars, but even The Silence of the Lambs – the last film to complete a clean sweep of the Academy’s Big Five – struggled at the Globes, having been pitched as a drama. The only one of its Oscars it replicated at the Globes was for Jodie Foster.Horror hasn’t fared too much better in the musical or comedy category. Tim Burton’s gothic bloodbathSweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Streetdid win in 2008, but that one genuinely had some Sondheim warbling amid the slashed throats.It’s a sticky wicket for horror movies at the Globes. They are seldom seen as “worthy” enough to compete as dramas, but they feel like too much of a square peg in a round hole to be considered as viable musical/comedy winners. They’re essentially pushed aside like a lonely kid on Halloween with eyeholes cut into a bedsheet, desperate for someone to trick or treat with.You may well argue that the Golden Globes don’t matter. The ceremony has often been dismissed as more obsessed with A-list stars than celebrating cinematic excellence and the whole thing almost went the way of the dodo in 2021 amid controversy around the lack of diversity in its voting body. So while it’s true that the Globes aren’t the be-all and end-all when it comes to awards season, they set the tone for the months to come. They’re often the first major awards to be handed out, giving momentum to winners and stalling the campaigns of those who lose out. And given the uphill struggle involved in getting horror even nominated at the Oscars, this sort of early-season momentum can be pivotal.There’s one case, though, that the Obsession team might be looking at. Navarrette’s remarkable central performance is believed to be the movie’s best chance at scooping a statuette and there’s a recent precedent that may go in her favour. While The Substance’s status as a “musical or comedy” might have cost it a chance at the top prize, it did enable Demi Moore to win for best actress. And while a topsy-turvy race in that category would ultimately hand the Oscar to Anora’s Mikey Madison, Moore’s victory was a big moment for horror that Navarrette will hope to repeat.Still, awards season remains an inhospitable place for horror movies. Obsession is a true breakout hit, cementing a new star in Navarrette and minting a directorial hot prospect in Curry Barker. But none of that will help it when it comes to the Golden Globes. Presumably, they should have put in a musical number.Explore more on these topicsHorror filmsGolden GlobesAwards and prizesGolden Globes 2026Film criticismOscarscommentShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: His hyperactive stylistic shifts and high-speed rhythms have a delirious, head-spinning beauty of their own
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: His hyperactive stylistic shifts and high-speed rhythms have a delirious, head-spinning beauty of their own
Content: Hallucinatory … Chidi Obialo AKA Heavensouls.Photograph: AUTHKS/PRView image in fullscreenHallucinatory … Chidi Obialo AKA Heavensouls.Photograph: AUTHKS/PRAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the beautiful, breakneck chaos of Heavensouls and the week’s best new tracksHis hyperactive stylistic shifts and high-speed rhythms have a delirious, head-spinning beauty of their ownLaura SnapesandBen Beaumont-ThomasFri 2 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromBiafra, Nigeria/Texas, USARecommended if you likeLos Thuthanaka, Jpegmafia, DJ Sabrina the Teenage DJUp nextAlbum Cantu of the Sower released via NTS Recordings on 7 OctoberMany listeners might find blown-out noise, hyperactive stylistic shifts and breakneck rhythms a hellish prospect, and fair enough. But for a certain stripe of sensory freak, such swarming intensity can tip over into a state of heady relaxation. The ultra-prolific Heavensouls’ latest project scratches that itch: the six songs on Cantu of the Sower glitter like rich seams of rare crystal, billowing from arcade glitter to compression-straining bass, sprite-like playfulness to warm, rushing brass. Languid trumpet lines float around trash-compactor crunch; sugary breakbeats reach tweaky maximalist peaks. I don’t know about you, but I could bathe in it.This isn’t shitpost music, fidgeting for its own sake. Cantu … glows with wonder at its own abundance, and the found-sound snippets of chatter ground its sense of an observant musician full of love for his fellow man. A sample of civil rights activist Stokely Carmichael makes 20-year-old Chidi Obialo’s mindset explicit: “I want my liberation more than I want anything else.” You hear it as Fela Kuti-worthy hand percussion is swept away by a hallucinatory, howling tide of guitar.Obialo was raised in Nigeria and moved to the US age seven. As a teenager, he started putting out wildly varied, collagist music, aiming to create a “rabbit hole” for listeners to get lost in. If you are of the shitpost sensibility, there’s the Sidepeices, his funny, glitchy duo with Atlanta’s Stickerbush. (Not for nothing is Obialo wearing a Captain Beefheart shirt above.) But then this year’s Westside Trapped, his gorgeously heavy love letter to Nigeria, is more approachable, in keeping with Sault’s luxuriant spirituals. Already 15 releases in to a brief career, Obialo’s talent for delirious, head-spinning beauty is clear, whichever way he chooses to express it.Laura SnapesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenDizzy dance .. Mei Semones.Photograph: Saeka ShimadaMei Semones – HowlUndeterred by unrequited love, the Japanese-American jazz-popper swears she’d “rather chase ’til I die and so / I’ll never have to learn to be still” – borne out in her gorgeous, dizzy dance of bossa nova guitar and strings.LSAngèle – Love Triangle (ft Caroline Polachek and SebastiAn)A malevolent electroclash beat by SebastiAn builds the drama in this menage-à-trois tale, where two of pop’s best bilingually vie with each other to see who walks away with their heart intact.BBTRomy Mars – The RageMars uses a gorgeously drowsy, wordy slow jam to taunt an ex. “Now you’re in film school studying movies / When they talk about my family do you lose sleep?” That’s mum Sofia Coppola and grandpa Francis Ford, FYI.LSMadra Salach – Ribbon FactoryTaut, insistent and wracked with pain, this is a gothic nightmare from an Irish folk band who keep turning up the volume on their word of mouth with every impassioned live performance.BBTBlackhaine – ConsumerAfter reworking rage rap under dull moorland cloud – and doing devastating choreo with Playboi Carti – the north-west rapper and dancer has announced his debut album with this symphonic, slowly syncopated stunner.BBTRyley Walker – CarrierThe Illinois guitarist signs to label du jour AD93 for a teeth-gritted turn to distortion that brings to mind fellow travellerWilliam Tyler’s Time Indefiniteand Sunn O)))’s glistening noise.LSHodge – Moments of JoyFull of body-high synth melodies and bird-call detailing, this track taken from the Bristolian producer’s new album, Big Splash, will have you mulling a last-minute dash to Ibiza’s closing parties.BBTSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistHip-hopExperimental musicElectronic musicfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Greg Freeman: All Set the Bone review – ambitious alt-country double album spreads its talents a touch thin | Music | The Guardian
description: The Maryland singer-songwriter’s third album has an impressive sense of scale compared to last year’s breakout Burnover, but is less immediately appealing
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: The Maryland singer-songwriter’s third album has an impressive sense of scale compared to last year’s breakout Burnover, but is less immediately appealing
Content: Lyrical anxieties … Greg Freeman.Photograph: Nat CambellView image in fullscreenLyrical anxieties … Greg Freeman.Photograph: Nat CambellMusicReviewGreg Freeman: All Set the Bone review – ambitious alt-country double album spreads its talents a touch thin(Transgressive)The Maryland singer-songwriter’s third album has an impressive sense of scale compared to last year’s breakout Burnover, but is less immediately appealingShaad D'SouzaFri 2 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreg Freeman’s third album All Set the Bone feels, at its best and most nervy, like an off-brand pressure cooker: too hot, bursting at its seams, rattling with kinetic energy. The Maryland-born singer-songwriter has a voice that often sounds like it’s straining at its limits, and although he is ostensibly part of agrowing indierock revivalthat’s been taking hold over the past few years – a cosy perennial – there’s nothing particularly comfortable about the songs on this double album. On Marooned, frantic stabs of guitar and drums create queasy unease; opener Cahokia muddles up the catharsis of a great American road song, descending into proggy bedlam. And his lyrics most often drum up anxieties big and small: “Who do you look to when you’re all on your own?” he asks on Culture. “When all your heroes lost their microphones?”View image in fullscreenGreg Freeman: All Set the Bone albumFreeman broke out with last year’sBurnover, a set of taut story-songs that were at turns witty, delirious and devastating. Freeman’s secret was in his ability to weld that literary streak to loud, bolshy, riff-heavy music that wouldn’t sound out of place on mainstream rock radio. All Set the Bone is several orders more ambitious in its scale, and its songwriting, which is more imagistic and diffuse. The result is an impressive record but one that’s less immediately appealing. Freeman wrote it while travelling through the US and reckoning with “a lot of change in my personal sense of … everything”, and you can hear that searching quality in the final product. All Set the Bone contains fewer fireworks than Burnover, but Freeman still has plenty of spark.Explore more on these topicsMusicIndiealbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Geneva Lewis: Barber, Zorn, Glass album review – virtuosity and warmth | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The young New Zealand violinist has chosen an all-American programme for her label debut, and impresses with works by Barber, Zorn and Glass
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The young New Zealand violinist has chosen an all-American programme for her label debut, and impresses with works by Barber, Zorn and Glass
Content: Warm … Geneva Lewis.Photograph: Julien Mignot/Courtesy of Julien MignotView image in fullscreenWarm … Geneva Lewis.Photograph: Julien Mignot/Courtesy of Julien MignotClassical musicReviewGeneva Lewis: Barber, Zorn, Glass album review – virtuosity and warmthLewis/BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra/New(Delos)The young New Zealand violinist has chosen an all-American programme for her label debut, and impresses with works by Barber, Zorn and GlassClive PagetFri 2 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 10.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAformer BBC New Generation Artist, violinist Geneva Lewis has chosen an all-American programme for her Delos recording debut. She’s accompanied with palpable empathy by fellow New Zealander Gemma New conducting the BBC Scottish Symphony Orchestra.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Geneva Lewis: Barber, Zorn, Glass.Photograph: Julien MignotSamuel Barber’s concerto receives an airy, poetic reading with Lewis and New embracing the music’s lyrical pastoralism while pointing up the opening movement’s scotch snap. The ongoing Celtic motif is seized upon by the orchestra and pays off in a moto perpetuo conclusion that feels second cousin to a highland fling. Lewis’s tone is warm and full of feeling, aching in the allegro and andante, feisty and folkish in the finale.John Zorn’s Partita for the Firebird is a modernist take on a baroque suite (including a catchy courante that channels a hoedown) with subtle allusions to Stravinsky’s ballet. Lewis’s virtuosity is on full display with laser-focused double stopping and filigree pianissimos at the very top of the instrument.Philip Glass’s Violin Concerto No 1, written in memory of his father, was his first major work for standard symphony orchestra. Slightly viscous orchestral textures and resonant engineering make it harder for the soloist to make a mark, but New leads an exhilarating account and Lewis’s silvery tone is especially haunting in the pensive slow movement.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Ravishing Renoir, cool Britannia and mighty Aphrodite – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Swoon at immaculate impressionism, ’ave it large with 90s Brit art and fashion and head to the beach with Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Swoon at immaculate impressionism, ’ave it large with 90s Brit art and fashion and head to the beach with Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse
Content: Joyful and sumptuous … Dance at Bougival by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1883.Photograph: © Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Picture FundView image in fullscreenJoyful and sumptuous … Dance at Bougival by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, 1883.Photograph: © Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Picture FundArt Weekly newsletterArt and designRavishing Renoir, cool Britannia and mighty Aphrodite – the week in artSwoon at immaculate impressionism, ’ave it large with 90s Brit art and fashion and head to the beach with Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 2 Oct 2026 07.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 07.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekRenoir and LoveJoyful and sumptuous, yet realist and raw, Renoir’s impressionist paintings glow in this immaculate exhibition.National Gallery, London, from 3 October until 31 JanuaryAlso showingThe 90s: Art and FashionThe fin de siecle decade gets a fresh look that puts fashion alongside art to take us back to when Britannia thought it was cool.Tate Britain, London, from 8 October until 14 FebruaryAphrodite: The Making of a GoddessThe ancient god of love and desire, often known by her Latin name Venus, returns on her shell in the art of Botticelli, Michelangelo Pistoletto and more.Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, from 8 October until 11 AprilMike Nelson: Double Negative (The Clown)Another soul-harrowing installation by the sculptor of urban labyrinths.Modern Art Oxford, from 3 October until 11 AprilPainting the French RivieraThere are masterpieces here by Cézanne, Picasso and Matisse, but it’s a weary slog and the beach is miles away.Royal Academy, London, until 31 JanuaryImage of the weekView image in fullscreenDavid Hockney, Dog Painting 17, 1995.Photograph: David Hockney/Christie’s Images Ltd. 2026How much is that doggy in the window? Well, if it’s a rare painting of Hockney’s adored dachshund Stanley, you’re looking at an estimated £1.5m-£2.5m. The painting will be sold at auction on 14 October during the Frieze art fair, but anyone cansee it for free at Christie’s in London from Thursday.What we learnedSome art seems better when it’s brokenBalraj Khanna paints biomorphic blobs, candy-coloured galaxies and cosmic spectacleCeleb set designer Es Devlin’s studio has a lot going onA row has erupted over a Cairo mural depicting Tutankhamun with dark skinA Van Gogh is up for grabs, alongside a Cézanne and a Monet as an ‘almost mythical’ private collection goes on saleskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMasterpiece of the weekFête Galante by Jean-Baptiste Pater, probably about 1721-5View image in fullscreenPhotograph: © The National Gallery, LondonPeople are picnicking on the grass, in a woody parkland that’s given extra mystery by classical sculptures and urns, even though a view through the trees reveals ordinary rural buildings rather than a great house. This is the ambiguous pleasure-world of the fête galante, a genre of painting invented by Pater’s teacher Antoine Watteau, in which lovers dance and talk and sometimes go off together into the woods, in an enigmatic, timeless and softly brushed fantasy realm. Pater is nothing like as poetic as Watteau, but still, you get the idea in this typical example of his work: women in silk dresses that catch the light and men in archaic, Renaissance-style costumes have escaped the cares of the city and the everyday to gather and celebrate love in this clearing under the gentle, feathery trees. Renoir revives this suggestive yet delicate genre in the much more material and solid setting of 19th-century Paris in his impressionist paintings.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in touchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsPierre-Auguste RenoirNational GalleryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A warming, comforting, spiced drink that’s ideal for autumn, and pairs brilliantly with a slice of carrot cake
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A warming, comforting, spiced drink that’s ideal for autumn, and pairs brilliantly with a slice of carrot cake
Content: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenPalé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Palé Hall’s Have your cake and drink it – recipeA warming, comforting, spiced drink that’s ideal for autumn, and pairs brilliantly with a slice of carrot cakeBruce DorflingFri 2 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe move into autumn proper leads our taste buds to crave warmth and comfort in equal measure. And what could be more warming and comforting than a spiced vodka and citrus cocktail spiced with nut liqueur? Slice of carrot cake optional.Have your cake and drink itServes1For the vodka infusion (for 7-8 serves)Peel of1 unwaxed lemon, all white pith removed375ml good vodka– we useBelvedereFor the drink50ml lemon peel-infused vodka– see above and method15ml hazelnut liqueur– we useFrangelico15ml vanilla syrup –homemade or store-bought (Bristol Syrup Co make a good one)15mlfresh lemon juice15mlfresh orange juice15ml fresh carrot juice6 dashes foamer, or 1 egg white4 dashes aromatic bitters(we useAngostura aromatic), or 1 pinch ground cinnamon1 orange slice, to garnish (or 1 slice carrot cake, to accompany)The night before, infuse the vodka: put the lemon peel and vodka in a jar, seal and leave to steep overnight. Next day, strain the vodka into a clean jar or bottle, seal and store in a cupboard out of direct light, where it’ll keep almost indefinitely.To build the drink, measure all the liquids into a shaker filled with ice, shake hard, then double strain into a coupe. Garnish with an orange slice, or serve with carrot cake to nibble on alongside.Bruce Dorfling, bar manager,Palé Hall, Bala, Gwynedd, WalesExplore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodFruitVegetablesAutumn food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for flourless walnut, date and espresso cake | Food | The Guardian
description: With a deep, caramel richness and a bitter undertone, this cake is an excellent addition to your home baking roster
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: With a deep, caramel richness and a bitter undertone, this cake is an excellent addition to your home baking roster
Content: Hgelen Goh’s flourless walnut, date and espresso cake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.View image in fullscreenHgelen Goh’s flourless walnut, date and espresso cake.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Isobel Clarke. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Francis Quinn.The sweet spotFoodHelen Goh’s recipe for flourless walnut, date and espresso cakeWith a deep, caramel richness and a bitter undertone, this cake is an excellent addition to your home baking rosterHelen GohFri 2 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s enough dark chocolate in this gluten-free cake to put it firmly in chocolate cake territory, but the hero flavour comes from the sweet, creamy nuttiness of walnuts, so it’s important to use very fresh ones, because stale walnuts can quickly turn bitter. The dates bring a deep, caramel richness, while the espresso pulls everything back from being overly sweet. Despite all that richness, the cake is wonderfully light in texture. Serve with creme fraiche and perhaps some poached pears, if you want to turn it into a full-blown dessert.Flourless walnut, date and espresso cakePrep10 minCook1 hr 30 min, plus coolingServes8-10150g unsalted butter,plus extra for greasing150g pitted dates120ml just-brewed espresso200g shelled walnuts1tbsp cocoa powder, plus extra for dusting1 tsp ground cinnamon¾ tsp baking powder½ tsp fine sea salt100g dark chocolate, broken into rough pieces5 large eggs, separated75g light brown sugar1 tsp vanilla extract75g caster sugarGrease a 20cm cake tin with a removable base, then line it with baking paper. Put the dates in a small bowl, pour over the hot espresso and leave to soften.Meanwhile, put the nuts in a food processor and process until finely ground, taking care not to overprocess or they will become oily. Tip into a medium bowl, add the cocoa powder, cinnamon, baking powder and salt, and stir to combine.Without washing the food processor, tip in the soaked date and coffee mix, then process to a smooth puree.Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put the butter and chocolate in a heatproof bowl set over a saucepan of barely simmering water, making sure the base of the bowl doesn’t touch the water. Stir until melted and smooth, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.Meanwhile, put the egg yolks and brown sugar in the bowl of an electric mixer and beat on medium-high for about three minutes, until thick and pale. Turn down the speed to low, then gradually work in the melted chocolate and butter, followed by the date puree and vanilla. Fold in the walnut mix until combined, then scrape the batter into a large bowl.Thoroughly clean and dry the mixer bowl and whisk attachment. Whisk the egg whites until foamy, then gradually add the caster sugar and continue whisking until they form medium peaks. Fold one-third of the meringue into the batter to loosen it, then gently fold in the rest.Pour the batter into the lined tin, then bake for 55-60 minutes, until the edges are set but the centre still has a slight wobble – a skewer inserted into the centre should emerge with a few moist streaks, rather than be completely clean. Leave the cake to cool completely in its tin, then unclip and transfer to a serving plate. Dust with cocoa powder, then slice and serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotCakeBakingDessertSnacksFruitNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: A vodkatini, a garibaldi and a shrub – your essential autumn cocktails – recipes | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: Try a millionaire’s martini, a Campari that couldn’t be simpler and a booze-free blackberry fizz (plus an Aperol that doesn’t need a spritz)
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Try a millionaire’s martini, a Campari that couldn’t be simpler and a booze-free blackberry fizz (plus an Aperol that doesn’t need a spritz)
Content: What’s your poison? Six enterprising aperitifs to kick off cocktail hour.Photograph: Charlie Lee / The Guardian. Food styling: El KempView image in fullscreenWhat’s your poison? Six enterprising aperitifs to kick off cocktail hour.Photograph: Charlie Lee / The Guardian. Food styling: El KempCocktailsA vodkatini, a garibaldi and a shrub – your essential autumn cocktails – recipesTry a millionaire’s martini, a Campari that couldn’t be simpler and a booze-free blackberry fizz (plus an Aperol that doesn’t need a spritz)Mina HollandFri 2 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBramble and ginger shrubView image in fullscreenI make a variation on this year-round. Bring on the autumn.2 tbsp shrub syrupGinger beer,to top1 spring of rosemary,to serveFor the shrub200g blackberries200g golden caster sugar1 grating each of nutmeg and black pepper½ tsp ground cinnamon100g vinegar(I use raw apple cider)To make the shrub, measure the berries and sugar into a sterilised jar, mashing them so they meld together. Add the spices and mix again. Put in the fridge for 24-48 hours.Strain the mixture; set aside the solids for baking or to top your morning porridge, and keep the syrup for your drink, putting it back into a sterilised jar. Add the vinegar, stir and put back in the fridge until you’re ready to drink.To a tumbler, add ice and two tablespoons of the syrup. Top with the ginger beer and rosemary to serve.Millionaire’s vodkatiniView image in fullscreenAn evening’s first drink is important to get right, and I often wring my hands over it. A vodka martini or a glass of fizz? My friends, the answer is both.Makes130ml vodka(from the freezer)15ml dry vermouth,or aromatised wine like Cocchi Americano3 drops Angostura bittersSparkling wine,to topLemon twistTo a cocktail shaker, add the vodka, vermouth, bitters, and a couple of cubes of ice. Stir gently for 20 seconds, then strain into a martini glass fresh out of the freezer. Top with sparkling wine, then briefly run the lemon twist around the glass rim before dropping it in. Serve.Mexican fizzView image in fullscreenI recently discovered Fever Tree’s Mexican lime soda – if you use this rather than sparkling water, you don’t need the maple syrup. Either way, this is something between a paloma and a margarita, and I can’t get enough of it.Makes160ml tequila blancoJuice of ½lime,plus a slice to serveTiny pinch of salt½ tsp maple syrup(optional)Mexican lime soda or sparkling water,to topTo a cocktail shaker, add the tequila, lime juice, salt and maple syrup, if using. Give it a quick shake.Put a handful of ice in a highball or large tumbler, and strain the content of the cocktail shaker over. Top with the lime soda, stir briefly and garnish with the lime slice on the glass rim.Aperol garibaldiView image in fullscreenA bittersweet drop to remind you of warmer days – but which I’ll happily put away year-round. Slips down dangerously easily.Makes1a2 large oranges45ml AperolHalve the oranges, then cut a half-moon slice from one of the halves and set aside, and squeeze the remaining oranges into your blender. Whizz for one minute, so the juice is frothy.To your glass (I like a stemmed old fashioned glass but a tumbler works just as well), add a few ice cubes and the Aperol, then pour the blended orange juice over. It will gradually mix, but you can give it a quick stir if you wish (I like to see the colour gradations of Aperol, juice, froth). Garnish with the half moon slice set across the diameter of the glass rim, and serve.Halve 2 large oranges, then cut a half-moon slice from one half and set aside. Squeeze the remaining orange juice into a blender and whizz for one minute, until frothy.To a stemmed old fashioned glass (a tumbler works just as well), add a few ice cubes and 45ml Aperol, then pour the blended orange juice over. It will gradually mix, but you can give it a quick stir if you wish. Garnish with the half moon slice set across the diameter of the glass rim, and serve.Campari shakeratoView image in fullscreenA single ingredient drink that can be scaled up or down according to your needs. For me, 60ml of Campari (two lidfuls from my shaker) is just right – and fits a mini martini glass perfectly.Makes1IceCampariAdd several ice cubes and your preferred volume of Campari to a cocktail shaker (you could also use a blender or Nutribullet). Holding it tightly with two hands, shake vigorously for as long as you have the energy – about 30 seconds. Strain into a freezer-chilled glass and serve.Mulled AJ garnished with a s’moreView image in fullscreenIf ‘the days drawing in’ was a drink, this would be it. For my children, the combination of warm, spiced AJ and – though I say so myself – a superior s’more is as good as it gets.Makes1 (or 2 small)250ml cloudy apple juice1 striporange peelJuice of½ lemon1 cinnamon stick3 cloves1 tsp soft dark brown sugar(optional)For the s’more1 marshmallow2 chocolate Leibnitz biscuitsPut the apple juice, orange peel, lemon juice, spices and sugar (if you are using it) in a small saucepan over the lowest heat. Leave to warm for 10-15 minutes, so the room smells delicious and you start to see faint steam rising from the pan. Do not let it boil.Meanwhile, put the marshmallow on a metal skewer and hold it just above an open flame, turning often, allowing it to bronze and char, if you like your s’mores like that (I do!). Put the toasted marshmallow on the chocolate side of a biscuit, then sandwich with the other. Decant the mulled AJ into a mug, and enjoy alongside the s’more.Explore more on these topicsCocktailsAutumn food and drinkFoodWineFruitrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The simple secrets behind great ramen | Japanese food and drink | The Guardian
description: It’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hit
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hit
Content: Top secret: at its simplest, a great ramen is a balance of only five elements.Photograph: Charlie Lee/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha HawkinsView image in fullscreenTop secret: at its simplest, a great ramen is a balance of only five elements.Photograph: Charlie Lee/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha HawkinsJapanese food and drinkThe simple secrets behind great ramenYou need five things: broth, flavour-giving tare, noodles, fat and toppings. And it’s the toppings that make it really special. Here are five versions, from a Toyko classic to a new Cardiff cult hitWatch our guide to the UK’s best ramen renegades inFeed with Jimi FamurewaJames ChantFri 2 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt its simplest, ramen is the balance of five elements: broth, tare (secret seasoning sauce), noodles, fat and toppings. If you understand that, this seemingly cryptic and complex corner of Japanese food culture opens right up. The first four take time, but if you pick up a shop-bought stock and some decent noodles, I won’t tell anyone. But the toppings are where the real payoff is: the fastest way to turn a midweek nothing into something worth showing off.A universal noteSpring onions should be used to top every bowl (finely diced white onion will work as a backup). Where there’s a broth, aim for 300ml, and where dashi is mentioned, instant is fine – unless you’re vegan, in which case steep 20g each of kombu and dried shiitake in one litre of cold water overnight, and keep the mushrooms for the soboro. Noodle portions are 130g unless stated otherwise, and any specialist items should be available online or at your local Asian supermarket.None of these toppings belong to one bowl, so swap them about – and they’re all good beyond ramen: chashu in a cheese toastie, say, soboro on rice, or ajitama in a caesar salad. The tares are multiuse, too: the tantanmen tare is great in scrambled eggs; the miso tare on corn on the cob, and the shio tare will improve pretty much anything.Tokyo shoyuView image in fullscreenRamen’s platonic ideal, and one piece of pork gives you the topping, tare and fat.Broth50:50 chicken stock and dashiTare3-4 tbsp chashu braising liquidFat1 tbsp, skimmed from chilled braising liquidNoodlesmedium classicToppingspork belly chashu, shop-bought menma (seasoned bamboo), ajitamaFor thechashu(serves 6-8)Roll and tie 500g pork belly and brown it all over in a pan. Deglaze the pan with 150ml sake, add 300ml each of shoyu, mirin and water, 30g demerara sugar, six sliced garlic cloves and a sliced 4cm piece of ginger, and simmer gently, turning, for two hours,. Cool in the liquid to room temperature, then chill overnight. Cut into 1cm-thick slices and torch or pan-fry to serve.TantanmenView image in fullscreenSichuan dan dan noodles, but make it ramen. Sesame, spice, and a soboro that works like a ragu.Broth50:50 kombu-shiitake dashi and unsweetened soy milkTare2 tbsp tahini, 1½ tbsp shoyu, 2 tsp black vinegar, 1 tsp sugar, a pinch each of MSG and ground Sichuan pepperFat1 tbsp rayu chilli oilNoodlesmedium classicToppingsspicy mince soboro, pak choiSpicy mince soboro(serves 6-7)Soften a small diced onion and 2cm piece grated ginger in oil for five minutes. Add five grated garlic cloves followed by 500g fatty pork mince – although any mince works, but vegan mince will need more water - and fry until it’s in grains, not lumps. Add three tablespoons of doubanjiang (chilli bean sauce), one and a half tablespoons each of shoyu and mirin, plus a splash of water. Cook for 15 minutes until glossy.Hakata tonkotsuView image in fullscreenJapan’s most famous ramen export. Thin, straight noodles in a creamy pork bone broth, eaten fast by design.BrothtonkotsuTare30ml shio (30g salt, 10g sugar and 10g MSG dissolved in 70ml sake, 20ml mirin and 110ml water – makes 230ml/about 7 bowls)Fat1 tsp sesame oilNoodlesthin, straightToppingsajitama, pork belly chashu, shop-bought kikurage (wood-ear fungus), beni-shogaAjitama(serves 6)Warm 100ml water, dissolve 10g brown sugar in it, then add 100ml each shoyu and mirin and chill. Pierce six fridge-cold large eggs at the wide end and boil for seven minutes, stirring for the first 30 seconds to centre the yolks. Plunge into iced water, peel, and submerge in the cold marinade for 12-72 hours.Chippy Lane mazesobaView image in fullscreenA late-night Cardiff cult classic – chicken, curry sauce and chips – our version of nagoya mazesoba. Sauce in the bowl, hot noodles on top, toss hard.Brothnone – rules are meant for breakingTare100ml shop-bought Japanese curry roux, made thick and saltyFat1 tbsp each butter and chicken fat (from the thighs)Noodlesthick (200g)Toppingsshio koji chicken, crispy onions, beni-shoga, and grated cheese, if you’re feeling cheekyShiokoji chickenthighs(serves 4-5)Coat 500g skinless and boneless chicken thighs in 50g shio koji, 20g mirin, half a tablespoon of shoyu and one teaspoon each of grated ginger and garlic. Leave up to three hours. Add 100ml water, cover and cook over a low heat for 45 minutes. Uncover and reduce until it crisps. Shred the meat and toss through the glaze.Sapporo yasai misoView image in fullscreenUsually built on pork broth and lard for Hokkaido winters, this version is plant-based, but stands up.Brothkombu-shiitake dashiTare60g a bowl – 100g each white and red miso with 2 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp each mirin and shoyu, 1 tsp each grated raw garlic and gingerFat2 tbsp vegetable oil, fried with grated garlic and gingerNoodlesthick, wavy, yellowToppingsstir-fried cabbage and beansprouts, sweetcorn, toasted sesame seeds, and butter, if you’re not veganStir-fried cabbage and beansprouts(serves 4)Get a wok very hot with a little neutral oil. Add 200g shredded cabbage and 150g beansprouts, and toss hard for two minutes – you want char, not steam. Season with a tablespoon of shoyu, a teaspoon of sesame oil and a pinch each of salt, sugar and shichimi togarashi.James Chant is the owner of Matsudai Ramen in Cardiff.Watch him make ramenin Feed with Jimi FamurewaExplore more on these topicsJapanese food and drinkNoodlesFoodMain courserecipesShareReuse this content
